chapters.title: Childhood Growth Hormone Deficiency and Hypopituitarism
chapters.summary: Severe neonatal presentation includes recurrent hypoglycemia, prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and micropenis with cryptorchidism in males. Childhood presentation features progressive deceleration of linear growth velocity (<25th percentile or <4-5 cm/year), delayed bone age, truncal adiposity, midfacial hypoplasia with frontal bossing, and a high-pitched voice.

chapters.title: Growth Hormone Insensitivity
chapters.summary: Patients exhibit extreme short stature (height SDS -4 to -10), severe midfacial hypoplasia with prominent forehead and depressed nasal bridge ('doll-like' facies), blue sclerae, high-pitched voice, sparse hair, small hands and feet (acromicria), micropenis in males, delayed dentition, marked truncal adiposity, and recurrent fasting hypoglycemia in infancy.

chapters.title: Normal Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature
chapters.summary: Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) describes children whose height is >2.25 SD below the population mean (<1.2th percentile) with normal birth weight/length, normal body proportions, no evidence of systemic, endocrine, nutritional, or chromosomal abnormalities, and normal growth hormone sufficiency. Normal variants include Familial Short Stature (FSS) and Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP).

chapters.title: Growth Hormone Treatment of the Short Child Born Small for Gestational Age
chapters.summary: Small for Gestational Age (SGA) is defined as birth weight and/or length ≥2 standard deviations below the mean for gestational age and sex (<2.3rd percentile). Approximately 85-90% of SGA infants demonstrate spontaneous catch-up growth within the first 2 years of life (extended to 4 years in preterm infants). The 10-15% who fail to catch up remain at substantial risk for persistent short adult stature and adult metabolic disease.

chapters.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Prader–Willi Syndrome
chapters.summary: Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS) is a complex neurogenetic disorder resulting from loss of expression of paternal genes in the 15q11.2-q13 imprinted region, caused by paternal deletion (65-75%), maternal uniparental disomy 15 (20-30%), or imprinting defects (1-3%). Pathophysiology is characterized by hypothalamic dysfunction producing severe neonatal hypotonia, infantile feeding failure, followed by insatiable hyperphagia, morbid obesity, hypogonadism, and growth hormone deficiency.

chapters.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Turner Syndrome, Noonan Syndrome, and SHOX Gene Mutations
chapters.summary: TS features growth failure, gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries), webbed neck (pterygium colli), low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, lymphedema, and left-sided congenital cardiac defects (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation). NS features short stature, pectus excavatum/carinatum, hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, bleeding diathesis, and right-sided cardiac defects (pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). SHOX deficiency features mesomelia, Madelung wrist deformity, and muscular hypertrophy.

chapters.title: Management of Adults with Childhood-Onset Growth Hormone Deficiency
chapters.summary: The transition period spans late adolescence to early adulthood (from completion of linear growth through age 25), during which peak bone mass, skeletal muscle mass, cardiac maturation, and adult lipid/body composition profiles are established. Growth hormone plays a vital metabolic role in somatic maturation beyond linear elongation.

chapters.title: Skeletal Dysplasias
chapters.summary: Features include severe rhizomelic limb shortening (proximal segments shortest), macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, trident hand configuration, thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, and foramen magnum stenosis. Radiographs show narrowed interpedicular distances in the lumbar spine, square iliac wings, horizontal acetabular roofs, and metaphyseal flare.

chapters.title: Growth Hormone Excess and Other Conditions of Overgrowth
chapters.summary: Pituitary gigantism presents with massive linear growth acceleration crossing percentiles upwards, coarse facial features, prognathism, macrodactyly, excessive perspiration, arthralgias, and visual field defects or cranial neuropathies from tumor mass effect. In genetic overgrowth, Sotos syndrome features macrocephaly, pointed chin, and learning disabilities (NSD1); Marfan syndrome features arachnodactyly, pectus deformities, and ectopia lentis (FBN1).

chapters.title: Adrenal Insufficiency
chapters.summary: Chronic manifestations include progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, generalized hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, vermilion border, scars, gingiva; primary AI only due to POMC/ACTH elevation), postural dizziness, salt craving, and hypoglycemia. Acute adrenal crisis presents with refractory hypotension, vascular collapse, shock, vomiting, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (primary AI), and neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

chapters.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
chapters.summary: Classic salt-wasting (SW) CAH presents at 1-3 weeks of life with life-threatening salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, shock) and prenatal virilization in 46,XX females (clitoromegaly, labial fusion, urogenital sinus; Prader stages I-V). Classic simple-virilizing (SV) CAH retains sufficient aldosterone synthesis (~1-2%) to prevent salt crisis but causes prenatal virilization in females and rapid post-natal somatic growth with premature epiphyseal fusion in both sexes. Non-classic (NC) CAH presents in childhood or adolescence with premature pubarche, hirsutism, severe acne, and menstrual irregularities.

chapters.title: Cushing Syndrome in Childhood
chapters.summary: The cardinal clinical hallmark of pediatric Cushing syndrome is the combination of progressive excessive weight gain crossing percentiles upwards alongside concurrent severe deceleration or cessation of linear growth (crossing height percentiles downward). Other signs include facial plethoric mooning, dorsal fat pad ('buffalo hump'), violaceous dermal striae (>1 cm wide), hirsutism, hypertension, osteopenia, and emotional lability.

chapters.title: Mineralocorticoid Disorders and Endocrine Hypertension
chapters.summary: Aldosterone, synthesized in the adrenal zona glomerulosa by aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), binds the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the renal collecting duct principal cells. MR activation upregulates the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, promoting sodium and water reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. Renin, stimulated by hypovolemia and renal hypoperfusion, drives angiotensin II-mediated aldosterone synthesis.

chapters.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism
chapters.summary: Because maternal thyroxine (T4) crosses the placenta in modest amounts (~30-50% of fetal levels at delivery), >95% of affected newborns appear clinically normal at birth. Clinical signs emerge subtly over weeks and include prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (>2 weeks), wide posterior fontanel (>0.5 cm), umbilical hernia, macroglossia, abdominal distension, hypothermia, hoarse cry, cold/mottled skin, and delayed passage of meconium. Newborn screening (NBS) utilizing primary TSH or primary T4 with reflex TSH detects infants before neurocognitive injury occurs.

chapters.title: Autoimmune Thyroid Disease
chapters.summary: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause of acquired hypothyroidism and sporadic goiter in children and adolescents, displaying a 4:1 to 7:1 female predominance with peak incidence in early adolescence. Clinical manifestations include painless, non-tender, firm goiter (with a pebbly or lobulated surface), linear growth deceleration with progressive weight gain (declining height velocity with increasing BMI), fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and delayed puberty. Severe juvenile primary hypothyroidism can occasionally present paradoxically with pseudoprecocious puberty (Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome: breast development and vaginal bleeding in girls, testicular enlargement without virilization in boys) mediated by TSH cross-activation of FSH receptors.

chapters.title: Non-thyroidal Illness Syndrome
chapters.summary: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS), formerly known as euthyroid sick syndrome, encompasses alterations in circulating thyroid hormone and TSH concentrations that occur in patients with acute or chronic non-thyroidal systemic illnesses (sepsis, severe trauma, cardiopulmonary bypass, starvation/anorexia, ketoacidosis, burns, and critical illness) in the absence of intrinsic hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid gland pathology. NTIS represents an evolutionary conserved adaptive metabolic response that downregulates basal metabolic rate and cellular energy expenditure to conserve protein and substrates during catabolic stress.

chapters.title: Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH) and Resistance to TSH (RTSH)
chapters.summary: Clinical presentation in RTH-beta is highly variable due to differential tissue distribution of TR-beta versus TR-alpha. Most patients are clinically euthyroid because elevated circulating thyroid hormones compensate for impaired receptor sensitivity. However, tissues where TR-alpha predominates—notably cardiac myocytes—are exposed to high circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, resulting in resting sinus tachycardia, palpitations, and systolic hypertension. Other frequent findings include diffuse goiter (due to persistent TSH stimulation), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; 40-60%), sensorineural hearing loss, learning disabilities, and mild short stature with delayed bone age.

chapters.title: Thyroid Neoplasia
chapters.summary: Thyroid nodules (TN) occur in approximately 1-2% of children and adolescents, which is significantly less frequent than in adults (where prevalence is 20-50%). However, the risk of malignancy in a pediatric thyroid nodule is substantially higher: approximately 22-26% of solitary nodules in children are malignant, compared to only 5-10% in adults. Any thyroid nodule discovered clinically or incidentally on imaging in a pediatric patient warrants systematic, dedicated diagnostic investigation.

chapters.title: Abnormalities in Calcium Homeostasis
chapters.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
chapters.summary: Extracellular ionized calcium (iCa) is maintained within a narrow physiological range (1.15-1.32 mmol/L; total serum calcium 8.8-10.2 mg/dL in older children, higher in neonates) by the integrated feedback loop between parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), and the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR). The CaSR, a G-protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid cells and renal thick ascending limb tubules, detects minute shifts in iCa. Hypocalcemia relieves CaSR tonic inhibition, triggering rapid PTH exocytosis; PTH stimulates renal tubular calcium reabsorption, osteoclastic calcium resorption, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) synthesis of calcitriol, which enhances enterocyte calcium absorption.

chapters.title: Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis
chapters.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
chapters.summary: XLH manifests after weight-bearing begins in toddlers with progressive lower-extremity bowing (genu varum/valgum), waddling gait, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, cranial synostosis, severe dental abscesses (due to defective dentin mineralization), and marked disproportionate short stature. Traditional therapy with oral phosphate salts (20-40 mg/kg/day divided 4-5 times daily) plus calcitriol (20-30 ng/kg/day) required cumbersome dosing and frequently caused nephrocalcinosis and tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Burosumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody directed against intact FGF23, administered subcutaneously at 0.8-2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks, directly restores renal phosphate reabsorption, heals rickets, accelerates growth, and eliminates nephrocalcinosis risk.

chapters.title: Rickets: The Skeletal Disorders of Impaired Calcium or Phosphate Availability
chapters.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
chapters.summary: Clinical signs vary by developmental age. In neonates and young infants: craniotabes (soft, ping-pong ball-like compressibility of parietal/occipital bones), delayed closure of the anterior fontanel (>2 years), frontal bossing, delayed tooth eruption with enamel hypoplasia, and hypocalcemic tetany/stridor. In older infants: enlargement of costochondral junctions ('rachitic rosary'), Harrison groove (depression along the lower chest border at the diaphragmatic insertion), and widening of wrists and ankles. Once weight-bearing begins: progressive varus (bowleg) or valgus (knock-knee) lower-extremity deformities, waddling gait, hypotonia, motor developmental delay, and pathognomonic greenstick fractures.

chapters.title: Pseudohypoparathyroidism
chapters.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
chapters.summary: Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) and related disorders are caused by molecular and epigenetic defects at the complex GNAS locus on chromosome 20q13.3, which encodes the alpha-subunit of the stimulatory G-protein (Gs-alpha). Gs-alpha couples G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to adenylyl cyclase, generating intracellular cyclic AMP. GNAS undergoes tissue-specific parent-of-origin genomic imprinting: in most tissues, Gs-alpha is expressed biallelically; however, in renal proximal tubules, thyroid thyrotropes, pituitary somatotropes, and gonads, Gs-alpha is expressed predominantly or exclusively from the maternal allele, while the paternal allele is silenced.

chapters.title: The Management of Osteoporosis in Children
chapters.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
chapters.summary: According to the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents requires: (1) The presence of one or more low-trauma / fragility vertebral compression fractures, regardless of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density; OR (2) A clinically significant fracture history defined as >=2 long-bone fractures by age 10 years, or >=3 long-bone fractures by age 19 years, COMBINED with a low bone mineral content (BMC) or areal bone mineral density (aBMD) DXA Z-score <= -2.0, adjusted for age, sex, and height/growth status. A low DXA Z-score alone does not constitute osteoporosis in children.

chapters.title: Delayed Puberty Onset and Hypogonadism
chapters.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
chapters.summary: Delayed puberty is clinically defined as the failure to initiate secondary sexual development by >=2 to 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean: in girls, the absence of breast bud development (Tanner stage 2 thelarche) by age 13.0 years, or failure to achieve menarche within 3 years of thelarche or by age 15.0 years (primary amenorrhea); in boys, the absence of testicular enlargement (testicular volume <4 mL or long axis <2.5 cm) by age 14.0 years. Arrested puberty is defined as the failure to complete pubertal progression over a 4-to-5-year span.

chapters.title: Precocious Puberty
chapters.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
chapters.summary: Precocious puberty is traditionally defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.0 years in girls (thelarche or pubarche) or before age 9.0 years in boys (testicular enlargement >=4 mL). Precocious puberty is categorized pathophysiologically into: (1) Central Precocious Puberty (CPP; GnRH-dependent), driven by premature hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis activation; (2) Peripheral Precocious Puberty (PPP; GnRH-independent), resulting from autonomous gonadal or adrenal sex steroid production independent of pituitary gonadotropins; and (3) Benign pubertal variants (premature thelarche, premature adrenarche).

chapters.title: Management of Infants Born with Disorders/Differences of Sex Development
chapters.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
chapters.summary: Disorders or Differences of Sex Development (DSD) are congenital conditions in which the development of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical. The 2006 Chicago Consensus classification categorizes DSD based on karyotype: (1) 46,XX DSD (disorders of gonadal development [ovotesticular DSD] or androgen excess [congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aromatase deficiency, maternal androgen exposure]); (2) 46,XY DSD (disorders of testicular development [complete/partial gonadal dysgenesis: SRY, SOX9, NR5A1/SF1, WT1] or disorders of androgen synthesis/action [androgen insensitivity syndrome, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, 17-beta-HSD-3 deficiency]); and (3) Sex chromosome DSD (45,X Turner, 47,XXY Klinefelter, 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis, 46,XX/46,XY chimerism).

chapters.title: Menstrual Disorders and Hyperandrogenism in Adolescence
chapters.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
chapters.summary: Menarche is a late pubertal milestone, typically occurring 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche (average age 12.5 years, Tanner stage 4). In the first 2-3 post-menarchal years, physiological immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis leads to frequent anovulatory cycles. However, normal menstrual parameters in adolescents are defined as: cycle length between 21 and 45 days; bleeding duration <=7 days; requiring <=3-6 pads or tampons per day without soaking; and cycle regularity establishing within 24-36 months. Any cycle length <21 days or >45 days (or >90 days at any time) represents abnormal uterine bleeding requiring clinical investigation.

chapters.title: Hyperprolactinemia
chapters.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
chapters.summary: The clinical presentation of hyperprolactinemia varies by sex and tumor size. Pediatric macroprolactinomas are more common in males and adolescent boys, who frequently present with mass effect symptoms: persistent headaches, visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopsia from optic chiasm compression), growth deceleration, delayed puberty, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (hyperprolactinemia directly suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility). In adolescent girls, microprolactinomas are more frequent, presenting with primary or secondary amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea (present in 30-50%), and mild hirsutism.

chapters.title: Hypoglycemia
chapters.summary: Hypoglycemia in infants and children is defined clinically by Whipple's triad: (1) Symptoms and neuroglycopenic signs consistent with low blood glucose; (2) Concomitantly documented subnormal plasma glucose concentration (<50-55 mg/dL [2.8-3.1 mmol/L]; <60 mg/dL in neonates with suspected congenital hyperinsulinism); and (3) Rapid relief of clinical symptoms upon glucose administration. In neonates, transitional physiological glucose nadirs occur in the first 24-48 hours of life, after which plasma glucose must be maintained >60 mg/dL in infants and >70 mg/dL in older children to prevent irreversible neurocognitive injury.

chapters.title: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents
chapters.summary: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells within the islets of Langerhans, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility is strongly linked to human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II alleles on chromosome 6p21, specifically HLA-DR3-DQ2 and HLA-DR4-DQ8 haplotypes. Progressive lymphocytic insulitis is driven by autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Circulating islet autoantibodies serve as essential diagnostic markers: glutamic acid decarboxylase-65 (GAD65), insulinoma-associated protein-2 (IA-2), insulin autoantibodies (IAA; prominent in young children), and zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). The presence of >=2 persistent autoantibodies marks preclinical stage 1/2 T1D.

chapters.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Youth
chapters.summary: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) in youth has emerged as a major public health challenge, driven by the global epidemic of pediatric obesity. Unlike adult T2D, youth-onset T2D is characterized by a significantly more aggressive disease biology: accelerated decline in pancreatic beta-cell function (loss of 20-35% of beta-cell capacity per year, ~4 times faster than in adults), early development of insulin dependence, and rapid accrual of microvascular and macrovascular complications. It disproportionately affects adolescents aged 10-19 years during pubertal insulin resistance peaks, with strong predilection for racial and ethnic minorities (Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian/Pacific Islander youth).

chapters.title: Disorders of Lipid Metabolism
chapters.summary: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recommend a two-tiered screening strategy for pediatric dyslipidemia: (1) Universal lipid screening for all children once between ages 9 and 11 years, and once between ages 17 and 21 years (using non-fasting non-HDL cholesterol or a fasting lipid profile); and (2) Targeted screening starting at age 2 years (fasting lipid profile) for children with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease (men <55 years, women <65 years) or parent with total cholesterol >=240 mg/dL, or children with high-risk personal conditions (type 1/2 diabetes, hypertension, BMI >=95th percentile, CKD, post-cardiac transplant, Kawasaki disease with aneurysms).

chapters.title: Endocrinologic Sequelae of Anorexia Nervosa and Obesity
chapters.summary: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a serious psychiatric disorder characterized by pathological restriction of energy intake, distorted body image, and intense fear of weight gain, resulting in severe state of chronic undernutrition and negative energy balance. The endocrine alterations in AN represent an evolutionary conserved adaptive survival mechanism designed to downregulate metabolic rate, shut down non-essential reproductive and skeletal functions, and mobilize energy substrates to preserve vital cerebral and cardiac homeostasis.

chapters.title: Diabetes Insipidus: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance
chapters.summary: In 2022, an international endocrine consensus updated the nomenclature of diabetes insipidus to eliminate confusion with diabetes mellitus: 'central diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D), and 'nephrogenic diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R). Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is synthesized by hypothalamic magnocellular neurons in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported down the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary. In response to hyperosmolality (>280-285 mOsm/kg) or hypovolemia, AVP binds basolateral V2 receptors (AVPR2) on renal collecting duct principal cells, triggering cAMP-mediated exocytic insertion of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels to concentrate urine.

chapters.title: Autoimmune Endocrine Disorders
chapters.summary: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes (APS) are classified into three major inherited forms: (1) APS-1 (APECED: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy), an autosomal recessive monogenic disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3; (2) APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome), a polygenic, HLA-DR3/DR4-associated complex disorder characterized by the mandatory presence of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes; and (3) IPEX syndrome (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked), a fatal infantile disorder caused by FOXP3 mutations.

chapters.title: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia and Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma in the Paediatric Population
chapters.summary: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes menin, a nuclear scaffold protein regulating gene transcription, cell cycle progression, and genome integrity. Following Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele leads to tumor development in classic endocrine target organs ('the 3 Ps'): parathyroid glands (>95% penetrance), enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tissues (pNETs; 30-70%), and the anterior pituitary gland (30-40%).

chapters.title: McCune-Albright Syndrome
chapters.summary: The classic clinical triad of MAS comprises: (1) Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (FD) of bone; (2) Café-au-lait skin hyperpigmentation; and (3) Hyperfunctioning autonomous endocrinopathies. Because the mutation occurs postzygotically during embryogenesis, the clinical phenotype is remarkably heterogeneous, depending entirely on the timing of the mutation and the anatomical distribution and percentage of mutated cells within tissue mosaics. Diagnosis is established clinically by the presence of >=2 classic triad features (or 1 classic feature plus confirmed GNAS mutation in tissue).

chapters.title: Management of Acute and Late Endocrine Effects of Childhood Cancer Treatment
chapters.summary: The hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) axis is highly vulnerable to cranial radiation therapy (CRT) used for brain tumors, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and leukemia prophylaxis. Radiation damage progresses in a dose- and time-dependent hierarchical vulnerability: Growth Hormone (GH) deficiency is the earliest and most sensitive defect, occurring at low-to-moderate doses (>=18-24 Gy) in >80-90% of exposed children within 2-5 years. Gonadotropin (LH/FSH) deficiency occurs at >=30-40 Gy; notably, low-dose cranial radiation (18-24 Gy) can paradoxically trigger central precocious puberty by damaging inhibitory cortical pathways. TSH deficiency and ACTH deficiency occur at higher doses (>=40-50 Gy), often presenting insidiously 5 to 15+ years after completion of cancer therapy.

chapters.title: Care of Transgender and Gender Diverse Youth
chapters.summary: Medical care for transgender and gender diverse (TGD) youth is guided by evidence-based consensus guidelines from the Endocrine Society and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH Standards of Care, Version 8). TGD identities are recognized as healthy expressions of human diversity. For prepubertal children (Tanner stage 1), care is strictly non-medical, focusing on social transition (clothing, name, hair, pronouns) and family counseling; medical or endocrine interventions are strictly contraindicated prior to the biological onset of puberty.

chapters.title: Management of Endocrine Emergencies
chapters.summary: Pediatric endocrine emergencies are acute, life-threatening derangements of hormone excess, hormone deficiency, or metabolic fuel dysregulation requiring rapid clinical recognition and physiological stabilization. The major entities encompass: (1) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); (2) Acute adrenal crisis; (3) Thyroid storm and severe thyrotoxicosis; (4) Severe acute hypocalcemia and hypercalcemic crisis; and (5) Severe symptomatic neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

chapters.title: The Endocrine Response to Critical Illness
chapters.summary: The endocrine response to severe critical illness (septic shock, polytrauma, major burns, cardiopulmonary bypass) follows an evolutionary conserved biphasic pattern: (1) Acute phase (first hours to days): marked hyperactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system, driving massive cortisol and catecholamine surges to maintain blood pressure and substrate delivery, alongside selective central down-regulation of anabolic pathways (suppression of TSH, low T3/T4 [NTIS], and hypogonadotropism) to conserve energy; (2) Chronic phase (prolonged critical illness >1-2 weeks): characterized by central neuroendocrine exhaustion, persistent hypopituitarism (suppressed pulsatile secretion of ACTH, TSH, GH, and gonadotropins), profound lean tissue catabolism, and immune dysfunction.

atlas.title: Childhood Growth Hormone Deficiency and Hypopituitarism
atlas.summary: Severe neonatal presentation includes recurrent hypoglycemia, prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and micropenis with cryptorchidism in males. Childhood presentation features progressive deceleration of linear growth velocity (<25th percentile or <4-5 cm/year), delayed bone age, truncal adiposity, midfacial hypoplasia with frontal bossing, and a high-pitched voice.

etiology.text: Etiologies include developmental gene defects (HESX1, PROP1, POU1F1, LHX3, LHX4, OTX2, SOX2, SOX3), GHRH receptor mutations, and acquired lesions including craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, histiocytosis, trauma, and cranial irradiation.

epidemiology.text: Congenital isolated growth hormone deficiency occurs with an incidence of approximately 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000 live births. Acquired causes represent a significant proportion of pediatric endocrinopathy in cancer survivors who received cranial radiotherapy.

diagnostics.text: Diagnostic evaluation integrates auxology, bone age radiography, serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3, two pharmacological GH stimulation tests demonstrating peak GH <7-10 mcg/L, and high-resolution pituitary MRI.

atlas.title: Growth Hormone Insensitivity
atlas.summary: Patients exhibit extreme short stature (height SDS -4 to -10), severe midfacial hypoplasia with prominent forehead and depressed nasal bridge ('doll-like' facies), blue sclerae, high-pitched voice, sparse hair, small hands and feet (acromicria), micropenis in males, delayed dentition, marked truncal adiposity, and recurrent fasting hypoglycemia in infancy.

etiology.text: Etiologies include homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in GHR, STAT5B, PTPN11, IGF1, IGFALS, IGF1R, and PAPP-A2, producing insensitivity to growth hormone or impaired IGF-I generation.

epidemiology.text: Autosomal recessive GHI is rare globally but occurs with high prevalence in consanguineous populations and in specific genetic isolates, notably in southern Ecuador (E180splice GHR mutation) and Mediterranean regions.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by normal to elevated GH with severely low IGF-I/IGFBP-3, low or absent serum GHBP (in extracellular GHR defects), lack of IGF-I response to exogenous rhGH in an IGF-I generation test, and targeted genetic sequencing.

atlas.title: Normal Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature
atlas.summary: Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) describes children whose height is >2.25 SD below the population mean (<1.2th percentile) with normal birth weight/length, normal body proportions, no evidence of systemic, endocrine, nutritional, or chromosomal abnormalities, and normal growth hormone sufficiency. Normal variants include Familial Short Stature (FSS) and Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP).

etiology.text: Idiopathic short stature encompasses heterogeneous non-pathological variations in growth without identifiable systemic, endocrine, or nutritional defects, including polygenic familial short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

epidemiology.text: By statistical definition, children with heights more than 2 SD below the mean comprise 2.3% of the pediatric population, the majority of whom have non-pathological short stature.

diagnostics.text: Evaluation requires serial height velocity measurement, midparental target height calculation, bone age radiography, basic metabolic/celiac screening, and exclusion of Turner syndrome in females.

atlas.title: Growth Hormone Treatment of the Short Child Born Small for Gestational Age
atlas.summary: Small for Gestational Age (SGA) is defined as birth weight and/or length ≥2 standard deviations below the mean for gestational age and sex (<2.3rd percentile). Approximately 85-90% of SGA infants demonstrate spontaneous catch-up growth within the first 2 years of life (extended to 4 years in preterm infants). The 10-15% who fail to catch up remain at substantial risk for persistent short adult stature and adult metabolic disease.

etiology.text: SGA results from heterogeneous maternal, placental, or fetal mechanisms leading to intrauterine growth restriction, including maternal vascular disorders, placental insufficiency, and fetal epigenetic anomalies (e.g., 11p15 loss of methylation in Silver-Russell syndrome).

epidemiology.text: SGA affects 2.3% of newborns by definition. Of these, 10% to 15% fail to exhibit spontaneous catch-up growth by age 2 years, accounting for roughly 20% of all adults with short stature.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires accurate gestational age determination, verified birth records (weight/length < -2 SDS), serial auxology documenting failure of catch-up growth, and exclusion of dysmorphic syndromes and systemic disorders.

atlas.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Prader–Willi Syndrome
atlas.summary: Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS) is a complex neurogenetic disorder resulting from loss of expression of paternal genes in the 15q11.2-q13 imprinted region, caused by paternal deletion (65-75%), maternal uniparental disomy 15 (20-30%), or imprinting defects (1-3%). Pathophysiology is characterized by hypothalamic dysfunction producing severe neonatal hypotonia, infantile feeding failure, followed by insatiable hyperphagia, morbid obesity, hypogonadism, and growth hormone deficiency.

etiology.text: PWS is caused by absent expression of paternal active genes in the 15q11.2-q13 chromosomal domain, resulting from paternal microdeletion (65-75%), maternal uniparental disomy (20-30%), or imprinting center defects (1-3%).

epidemiology.text: Estimated prevalence is 1 in 15,000 to 1 in 25,000 live births, affecting males and females equally across all racial and ethnic groups.

diagnostics.text: DNA methylation analysis of the SNRPN locus on 15q11-q13 detects >99% of PWS cases by demonstrating maternal-only methylation, followed by FISH or MS-MLPA to differentiate deletion from UPD or imprinting defect.

atlas.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Turner Syndrome, Noonan Syndrome, and SHOX Gene Mutations
atlas.summary: TS features growth failure, gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries), webbed neck (pterygium colli), low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, lymphedema, and left-sided congenital cardiac defects (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation). NS features short stature, pectus excavatum/carinatum, hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, bleeding diathesis, and right-sided cardiac defects (pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). SHOX deficiency features mesomelia, Madelung wrist deformity, and muscular hypertrophy.

etiology.text: Turner syndrome is caused by complete or partial loss of the second sex chromosome. Noonan syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in RAS-MAPK genes (PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS). SHOX deficiency is caused by microdeletions or point mutations in the pseudoautosomal SHOX locus.

epidemiology.text: Turner syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 2,500 live female births. Noonan syndrome affects 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 2,500 live births of both sexes. SHOX deficiency accounts for 2-15% of children classified with idiopathic short stature.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype or microarray for Turner syndrome, targeted multi-gene NGS panel for Noonan syndrome, and MLPA or sequencing of the SHOX gene on Xp22.33/Yp11.32.

atlas.title: Management of Adults with Childhood-Onset Growth Hormone Deficiency
atlas.summary: The transition period spans late adolescence to early adulthood (from completion of linear growth through age 25), during which peak bone mass, skeletal muscle mass, cardiac maturation, and adult lipid/body composition profiles are established. Growth hormone plays a vital metabolic role in somatic maturation beyond linear elongation.

etiology.text: Childhood-onset GHD persistent into adulthood arises from congenital pituitary developmental defects (PROP1, POU1F1), congenital CNS malformations, or acquired insults such as craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, histiocytosis, surgery, and radiotherapy.

epidemiology.text: While up to 80% of children with isolated idiopathic GHD re-test as growth hormone sufficient in adulthood, virtually 100% of those with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies or severe structural lesions have permanent GHD.

diagnostics.text: Diagnostic evaluation requires re-testing after epiphyseal fusion and ≥1-3 months off somatropin using ITT (peak GH <5.0 mcg/L transition, <3.0 mcg/L adult), glucagon test, or macimorelin, unless the patient has ≥3 other pituitary deficiencies and IGF-I <-2.0 SDS.

atlas.title: Skeletal Dysplasias
atlas.summary: Features include severe rhizomelic limb shortening (proximal segments shortest), macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, trident hand configuration, thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, and foramen magnum stenosis. Radiographs show narrowed interpedicular distances in the lumbar spine, square iliac wings, horizontal acetabular roofs, and metaphyseal flare.

etiology.text: Skeletal dysplasias are heterogeneous monogenic disorders affecting bone and cartilage formation, most frequently caused by mutations in FGFR3 (achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia), COL2A1, COL1A1/COL1A2 (osteogenesis imperfecta), and SHOX.

epidemiology.text: Collectively, skeletal dysplasias occur in approximately 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 5,000 live births, with achondroplasia being the most common non-lethal form (1 in 15,000 to 1 in 40,000).

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis integrates clinical auxology, skeletal radiographic survey (skull, spine, pelvis, long bones, hands), and targeted or exome-based genetic sequencing.

atlas.title: Growth Hormone Excess and Other Conditions of Overgrowth
atlas.summary: Pituitary gigantism presents with massive linear growth acceleration crossing percentiles upwards, coarse facial features, prognathism, macrodactyly, excessive perspiration, arthralgias, and visual field defects or cranial neuropathies from tumor mass effect. In genetic overgrowth, Sotos syndrome features macrocephaly, pointed chin, and learning disabilities (NSD1); Marfan syndrome features arachnodactyly, pectus deformities, and ectopia lentis (FBN1).

etiology.text: Etiologies include pituitary somatotroph adenomas, syndromic gigantism (X-LAG / GPR101, McCune-Albright, Carney complex, MEN1, AIP mutations), and primary genetic overgrowth syndromes (Sotos, Marfan, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Weaver).

epidemiology.text: Pituitary gigantism is extremely rare in pediatric practice, with an annual incidence of roughly 1 per million population. Primary genetic overgrowth syndromes occur more frequently.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires demonstrating failure to suppress serum GH to <1.0 mcg/L during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), elevated IGF-I/IGFBP-3, contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI, and genetic panel testing.

atlas.title: Adrenal Insufficiency
atlas.summary: Chronic manifestations include progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, generalized hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, vermilion border, scars, gingiva; primary AI only due to POMC/ACTH elevation), postural dizziness, salt craving, and hypoglycemia. Acute adrenal crisis presents with refractory hypotension, vascular collapse, shock, vomiting, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (primary AI), and neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

etiology.text: Etiologies include congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2), autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease, APS-1, APS-2), X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1), congenital adrenal hypoplasia (DAX1/NR0B1), Triple A syndrome (AAAS), bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, and exogenous steroid withdrawal.

epidemiology.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 individuals, with congenital adrenal hyperplasia being the most frequent genetic etiology in children and autoimmune adrenalitis predominant in adolescents.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by morning cortisol (<3-5 mcg/dL) and elevated ACTH (>100 pg/mL in primary AI), failure of cortisol to rise to ≥18 mcg/dL on a standard cosyntropin stimulation test, elevated plasma renin activity, and targeted autoantibody or genetic testing.

atlas.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
atlas.summary: Classic salt-wasting (SW) CAH presents at 1-3 weeks of life with life-threatening salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, shock) and prenatal virilization in 46,XX females (clitoromegaly, labial fusion, urogenital sinus; Prader stages I-V). Classic simple-virilizing (SV) CAH retains sufficient aldosterone synthesis (~1-2%) to prevent salt crisis but causes prenatal virilization in females and rapid post-natal somatic growth with premature epiphyseal fusion in both sexes. Non-classic (NC) CAH presents in childhood or adolescence with premature pubarche, hirsutism, severe acne, and menstrual irregularities.

etiology.text: Autosomal recessive enzymatic block in adrenal steroidogenesis, caused by CYP21A2 mutations (21-hydroxylase deficiency, >95%), CYP11B1 (11-beta-hydroxylase), HSD3B2 (3-beta-HSD), CYP17A1 (17-hydroxylase), StAR (lipoid CAH), or POR (oxidoreductase).

epidemiology.text: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency occurs in approximately 1 in 14,000 to 1 in 18,000 live births globally (higher in Yupik Inuits, 1:280). Non-classic CAH is one of the most common autosomal recessive disorders, affecting 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 individuals depending on ethnicity.

diagnostics.text: Universal newborn screening via blood spot 17-OHP immunoassay and LC-MS/MS; confirmation by serum 17-OHP, 21-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, plasma renin activity, and comprehensive CYP21A2 gene deletion/sequencing analysis.

atlas.title: Cushing Syndrome in Childhood
atlas.summary: The cardinal clinical hallmark of pediatric Cushing syndrome is the combination of progressive excessive weight gain crossing percentiles upwards alongside concurrent severe deceleration or cessation of linear growth (crossing height percentiles downward). Other signs include facial plethoric mooning, dorsal fat pad ('buffalo hump'), violaceous dermal striae (>1 cm wide), hirsutism, hypertension, osteopenia, and emotional lability.

etiology.text: Etiologies include ACTH-dependent Cushing disease (pituitary corticotroph adenoma, >75% of older children), ectopic ACTH secretion, and ACTH-independent adrenal pathology (adrenocortical adenoma/carcinoma, PPNAD in Carney complex [PRKAR1A], and McCune-Albright syndrome [GNAS]).

epidemiology.text: Endogenous Cushing syndrome is rare in pediatrics, with an incidence of approximately 2 to 5 per million per year. Adrenal tumors predominate in early childhood (<5 years), while pituitary microadenomas predominate in adolescents.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires demonstrating hypercortisolemia using 24-hour UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, or overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, followed by plasma ACTH measurement, high-dose dexamethasone suppression, pituitary dynamic MRI, and BIPSS.

atlas.title: Mineralocorticoid Disorders and Endocrine Hypertension
atlas.summary: Aldosterone, synthesized in the adrenal zona glomerulosa by aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), binds the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the renal collecting duct principal cells. MR activation upregulates the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, promoting sodium and water reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. Renin, stimulated by hypovolemia and renal hypoperfusion, drives angiotensin II-mediated aldosterone synthesis.

etiology.text: Mineralocorticoid disorders encompass primary aldosterone excess (Conn adenoma, bilateral hyperplasia), monogenic low-renin hypertension (GRA / CYP11B1-CYP11B2 chimera, AME / HSD11B2, Liddle syndrome / ENaC), and mineralocorticoid resistance (PHA1 / MR or ENaC; PHA3 / UTI and uropathy).

epidemiology.text: Endocrine causes account for approximately 5% to 10% of pediatric secondary hypertension, with monogenic forms carrying high risk of premature cerebrovascular complications if unrecognized.

diagnostics.text: Screening uses paired PAC/PRA ratio, serum electrolytes (hypokalemia), urinary free cortisol/cortisone ratio (AME), and targeted genetic testing for CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimera, SCNN1B/SCNN1G, and HSD11B2.

atlas.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism
atlas.summary: Because maternal thyroxine (T4) crosses the placenta in modest amounts (~30-50% of fetal levels at delivery), >95% of affected newborns appear clinically normal at birth. Clinical signs emerge subtly over weeks and include prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (>2 weeks), wide posterior fontanel (>0.5 cm), umbilical hernia, macroglossia, abdominal distension, hypothermia, hoarse cry, cold/mottled skin, and delayed passage of meconium. Newborn screening (NBS) utilizing primary TSH or primary T4 with reflex TSH detects infants before neurocognitive injury occurs.
atlas.etiology: Primary congenital hypothyroidism is caused by thyroid dysgenesis (80-85%: ectopia ~60%, athyreosis ~30%, hypoplasia ~10%) or thyroid dyshormonogenesis (10-15%: TPO, SLC5A5, SLC26A4, TG, DUOX2, IYD). Central CH occurs in 1:25,000 live births (TSHB, TRHR, PROP1, POU1F1, HESX1).
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence is ~1 in 2000 to 1 in 3000 live births, with a female-to-male ratio of 2:1 in thyroid dysgenesis. Higher prevalence occurs in Hispanic and Native American populations; lower in Black infants.
atlas.diagnostics: Venous TSH and free T4 confirmatory assay; 99mTc pertechnetate or 123I scintigraphy; neck ultrasound; knee radiographs for osseous maturation (distal femoral epiphysis).

atlas.title: Autoimmune Thyroid Disease
atlas.summary: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause of acquired hypothyroidism and sporadic goiter in children and adolescents, displaying a 4:1 to 7:1 female predominance with peak incidence in early adolescence. Clinical manifestations include painless, non-tender, firm goiter (with a pebbly or lobulated surface), linear growth deceleration with progressive weight gain (declining height velocity with increasing BMI), fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and delayed puberty. Severe juvenile primary hypothyroidism can occasionally present paradoxically with pseudoprecocious puberty (Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome: breast development and vaginal bleeding in girls, testicular enlargement without virilization in boys) mediated by TSH cross-activation of FSH receptors.
atlas.etiology: AITD includes Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune lymphocytic destruction; anti-TPO, anti-TG) and Graves' disease (autoimmune stimulation of TSHR via TSI/TRAb). Linked to HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22, and syndromes including Turner, Down, Klinefelter, T1D, and APS.
atlas.epidemiology: Hashimoto thyroiditis affects 1-3% of children, 4:1 to 7:1 female predominance. Graves' disease affects ~1 in 10,000 children, peak in adolescence (80% females).
atlas.diagnostics: TSH, free T4, total T3; anti-TPO, anti-TG, TSI/TRAb antibodies; thyroid ultrasound (heterogeneous hypoechogenicity, increased vascularity ['thyroid inferno'] on Doppler).

atlas.title: Non-thyroidal Illness Syndrome
atlas.summary: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS), formerly known as euthyroid sick syndrome, encompasses alterations in circulating thyroid hormone and TSH concentrations that occur in patients with acute or chronic non-thyroidal systemic illnesses (sepsis, severe trauma, cardiopulmonary bypass, starvation/anorexia, ketoacidosis, burns, and critical illness) in the absence of intrinsic hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid gland pathology. NTIS represents an evolutionary conserved adaptive metabolic response that downregulates basal metabolic rate and cellular energy expenditure to conserve protein and substrates during catabolic stress.
atlas.etiology: Adaptive neuroendocrine response to acute or chronic severe illness (sepsis, burns, trauma, cardiac surgery, starvation). Driven by proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha), endogenous/exogenous glucocorticoids, and dopamine.
atlas.epidemiology: Present in 40-70% of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) patients; prevalence and depth correlate with APACHE/PRISM illness severity scores.
atlas.diagnostics: Low free T3, elevated reverse T3 (rT3); in severe stages, low free T4 and suppressed TSH. Transient rebound hyperthyrotropinemia (TSH 5-15 mIU/L) occurs during recovery.

atlas.title: Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH) and Resistance to TSH (RTSH)
atlas.summary: Clinical presentation in RTH-beta is highly variable due to differential tissue distribution of TR-beta versus TR-alpha. Most patients are clinically euthyroid because elevated circulating thyroid hormones compensate for impaired receptor sensitivity. However, tissues where TR-alpha predominates—notably cardiac myocytes—are exposed to high circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, resulting in resting sinus tachycardia, palpitations, and systolic hypertension. Other frequent findings include diffuse goiter (due to persistent TSH stimulation), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; 40-60%), sensorineural hearing loss, learning disabilities, and mild short stature with delayed bone age.
atlas.etiology: RTH-beta: Autosomal dominant dominant-negative mutations in THRB (3p24). RTH-alpha: Mutations in THRA (17q21). Allan-Herndon-Dudley: X-linked mutations in SLC16A2 (MCT8). Resistance to TSH (RTSH): Inactivating TSHR mutations.
atlas.epidemiology: RTH-beta prevalence is ~1 in 40,000 live births; equal gender distribution. RTH-alpha and AHDS are rare orphan disorders.
atlas.diagnostics: Free T4, free T3, TSH, reverse T3; glycoprotein alpha-subunit/TSH ratio; TRH stimulation testing; pituitary MRI; THRB/THRA/SLC16A2 genetic sequencing.

atlas.title: Thyroid Neoplasia
atlas.summary: Thyroid nodules (TN) occur in approximately 1-2% of children and adolescents, which is significantly less frequent than in adults (where prevalence is 20-50%). However, the risk of malignancy in a pediatric thyroid nodule is substantially higher: approximately 22-26% of solitary nodules in children are malignant, compared to only 5-10% in adults. Any thyroid nodule discovered clinically or incidentally on imaging in a pediatric patient warrants systematic, dedicated diagnostic investigation.
atlas.etiology: Differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PTC 80-90%, FTC 5-10%); medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC 2-5% in MEN2). Genetic drivers: RET/PTC fusions, NTRK/ALK fusions, BRAF V600E, DICER1, RET point mutations (M918T, C634).
atlas.epidemiology: Thyroid nodules occur in 1-2% of children, but have a 22-26% malignancy rate. PTC has a female predominance (3:1 in adolescents). Excellent prognosis (>98% 30-year survival).
atlas.diagnostics: TSH, neck ultrasound (cervical lymph nodes); ultrasound-guided FNA with Bethesda reporting; RET/NTRK molecular panels; postop serum thyroglobulin (Tg) and anti-Tg antibodies; neck US.

atlas.title: Abnormalities in Calcium Homeostasis
atlas.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
atlas.summary: Extracellular ionized calcium (iCa) is maintained within a narrow physiological range (1.15-1.32 mmol/L; total serum calcium 8.8-10.2 mg/dL in older children, higher in neonates) by the integrated feedback loop between parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), and the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR). The CaSR, a G-protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid cells and renal thick ascending limb tubules, detects minute shifts in iCa. Hypocalcemia relieves CaSR tonic inhibition, triggering rapid PTH exocytosis; PTH stimulates renal tubular calcium reabsorption, osteoclastic calcium resorption, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) synthesis of calcitriol, which enhances enterocyte calcium absorption.
atlas.etiology: Hypocalcemia: Early/late neonatal; hypoparathyroidism (DiGeorge/22q11.2, CaSR activating mutations, APS-1); pseudohypoparathyroidism; vitamin D deficiency. Hypercalcemia: FHH (heterozygous CaSR), NSHPT (homozygous CaSR), primary hyperparathyroidism, Williams syndrome (7q11.23), subcutaneous fat necrosis, immobilization.
atlas.epidemiology: DiGeorge syndrome occurs in 1:4000 live births. FHH prevalence is ~1:78,000. Primary hyperparathyroidism is rare in children (1-2 per 100,000).
atlas.diagnostics: Ionized and total calcium, phosphate, magnesium, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; spot urine Ca/Cr and 24-hr urine calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR); renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis; ECG (QTc interval).

atlas.title: Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis
atlas.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
atlas.summary: XLH manifests after weight-bearing begins in toddlers with progressive lower-extremity bowing (genu varum/valgum), waddling gait, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, cranial synostosis, severe dental abscesses (due to defective dentin mineralization), and marked disproportionate short stature. Traditional therapy with oral phosphate salts (20-40 mg/kg/day divided 4-5 times daily) plus calcitriol (20-30 ng/kg/day) required cumbersome dosing and frequently caused nephrocalcinosis and tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Burosumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody directed against intact FGF23, administered subcutaneously at 0.8-2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks, directly restores renal phosphate reabsorption, heals rickets, accelerates growth, and eliminates nephrocalcinosis risk.
atlas.etiology: FGF23-dependent: XLH (PHEX, Xp22.1, X-linked dominant); ADHR (FGF23 R176/R179); ARHR (DMP1, ENPP1); TIO (phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors). FGF23-independent: HHRH (SLC34A3), Fanconi syndrome. Hyperphosphatemia: HFTC (FGF23, GALNT3, KL mutations).
atlas.epidemiology: XLH incidence is ~1 in 20,000 live births; most common form of heritable rickets. ADHR, ARHR, HHRH, and HFTC are rare orphan diseases.
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum phosphate, calcium, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TRP) and TmP/GFR; intact serum FGF23; 24-hr urine calcium; renal ultrasound; PHEX/SLC34A3 genetic panel.

atlas.title: Rickets: The Skeletal Disorders of Impaired Calcium or Phosphate Availability
atlas.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
atlas.summary: Clinical signs vary by developmental age. In neonates and young infants: craniotabes (soft, ping-pong ball-like compressibility of parietal/occipital bones), delayed closure of the anterior fontanel (>2 years), frontal bossing, delayed tooth eruption with enamel hypoplasia, and hypocalcemic tetany/stridor. In older infants: enlargement of costochondral junctions ('rachitic rosary'), Harrison groove (depression along the lower chest border at the diaphragmatic insertion), and widening of wrists and ankles. Once weight-bearing begins: progressive varus (bowleg) or valgus (knock-knee) lower-extremity deformities, waddling gait, hypotonia, motor developmental delay, and pathognomonic greenstick fractures.
atlas.etiology: Calcipenic: Nutritional vitamin D/calcium deficiency; malabsorption (celiac, cystic fibrosis); VDDR1A (CYP27B1), VDDR1B (CYP2R1), VDDR2A (VDR with alopecia). Phosphopenic: XLH (PHEX), ADHR (FGF23), ARHR, HHRH (SLC34A3), Fanconi.
atlas.epidemiology: Nutritional rickets remains prevalent globally in exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation, dark-skinned infants in high latitudes, and restricted diets.
atlas.diagnostics: Serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; wrist/knee plain radiographs (widening, cupping, fraying); urine Ca/Cr and TmP/GFR.

atlas.title: Pseudohypoparathyroidism
atlas.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
atlas.summary: Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) and related disorders are caused by molecular and epigenetic defects at the complex GNAS locus on chromosome 20q13.3, which encodes the alpha-subunit of the stimulatory G-protein (Gs-alpha). Gs-alpha couples G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to adenylyl cyclase, generating intracellular cyclic AMP. GNAS undergoes tissue-specific parent-of-origin genomic imprinting: in most tissues, Gs-alpha is expressed biallelically; however, in renal proximal tubules, thyroid thyrotropes, pituitary somatotropes, and gonads, Gs-alpha is expressed predominantly or exclusively from the maternal allele, while the paternal allele is silenced.
atlas.etiology: GNAS locus (20q13.3) encoding Gs-alpha; tissue-specific maternal imprinting in renal proximal tubules, thyroid, pituitary, and gonads. PHP-1A: maternal coding mutations. PPHP: paternal coding mutations. PHP-1B: maternal methylation defects at DMRs. POH: paternal GNAS null mutations.
atlas.epidemiology: PHP prevalence is estimated at 0.3-1.1 per 100,000 live births; equal gender distribution.
atlas.diagnostics: Serum calcium, phosphate, intact PTH, TSH, free T4, IGF-1, LH/FSH; hand radiographs (short 4th/5th metacarpals); GNAS genetic and epigenetic methylation analysis.

atlas.title: The Management of Osteoporosis in Children
atlas.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders
atlas.summary: According to the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents requires: (1) The presence of one or more low-trauma / fragility vertebral compression fractures, regardless of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density; OR (2) A clinically significant fracture history defined as >=2 long-bone fractures by age 10 years, or >=3 long-bone fractures by age 19 years, COMBINED with a low bone mineral content (BMC) or areal bone mineral density (aBMD) DXA Z-score <= -2.0, adjusted for age, sex, and height/growth status. A low DXA Z-score alone does not constitute osteoporosis in children.
atlas.etiology: Primary: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (COL1A1, COL1A2, CRTAP, LEPRE1, PPIB, WNT1, LRP5, PLS3); idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis. Secondary: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure, immobilization/neuromuscular (cerebral palsy, DMD), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, IBD, hypogonadism.
atlas.epidemiology: Osteogenesis imperfecta affects ~1 in 15,000 to 20,000 births. Secondary osteoporosis affects up to 30-50% of children on long-term systemic glucocorticoids.
atlas.diagnostics: Lateral thoracolumbar spine radiographs / DXA VFA (modified Genant scale); DXA lumbar spine and total body less head (TBLH) Z-scores adjusted for height/age; serum 25-OH-D, calcium, phosphate, PTH; urine Ca/Cr; COL1A1/COL1A2 genetic sequencing.

atlas.title: Delayed Puberty Onset and Hypogonadism
atlas.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
atlas.summary: Delayed puberty is clinically defined as the failure to initiate secondary sexual development by >=2 to 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean: in girls, the absence of breast bud development (Tanner stage 2 thelarche) by age 13.0 years, or failure to achieve menarche within 3 years of thelarche or by age 15.0 years (primary amenorrhea); in boys, the absence of testicular enlargement (testicular volume <4 mL or long axis <2.5 cm) by age 14.0 years. Arrested puberty is defined as the failure to complete pubertal progression over a 4-to-5-year span.
atlas.etiology: Hypergonadotropic (primary): Turner (45,X), Klinefelter (47,XXY), 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis, anorchia, radiation/chemotherapy. Hypogonadotropic (central): CDGP (>60% in boys), Kallmann syndrome (ANOS1/KAL1, FGFR1, PROKR2), normosmic CHH, chronic illness, anorexia.
atlas.epidemiology: CDGP is the most common etiology of delayed puberty in boys (65%) and girls (30%). Turner syndrome affects 1:2000 live female births; Klinefelter affects 1:600 male births.
atlas.diagnostics: Bone age radiograph; basal and GnRH-stimulated LH/FSH; early morning total testosterone (LC-MS/MS) or estradiol; pelvic ultrasound; karyotype; smell test (UPSIT) and olfactory MRI.

atlas.title: Precocious Puberty
atlas.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
atlas.summary: Precocious puberty is traditionally defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.0 years in girls (thelarche or pubarche) or before age 9.0 years in boys (testicular enlargement >=4 mL). Precocious puberty is categorized pathophysiologically into: (1) Central Precocious Puberty (CPP; GnRH-dependent), driven by premature hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis activation; (2) Peripheral Precocious Puberty (PPP; GnRH-independent), resulting from autonomous gonadal or adrenal sex steroid production independent of pituitary gonadotropins; and (3) Benign pubertal variants (premature thelarche, premature adrenarche).
atlas.etiology: Central (GnRH-dependent): Idiopathic (>85% in girls); CNS lesions (40-75% in boys: hypothalamic hamartoma, optic glioma/NF1, hydrocephalus, radiation); Genetic (MKRN3 [paternal transmission], DLK1, KISS1). Peripheral (GnRH-independent): CAH (CYP21A2), testotoxicosis (LHCGR), McCune-Albright (GNAS), Leydig/granulosa tumors.
atlas.epidemiology: Precocious puberty affects ~1 in 5000 to 1 in 10,000 children; 5:1 to 10:1 female predominance for central precocious puberty.
atlas.diagnostics: Bone age radiograph; basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH (peak LH >5.0 IU/L confirms CPP); estradiol, total testosterone, 17-OHP, DHEAS; pelvic ultrasound (uterine length >3.5 cm, ovarian volume >1-2 mL); brain MRI with thin hypothalamic cuts.

atlas.title: Management of Infants Born with Disorders/Differences of Sex Development
atlas.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
atlas.summary: Disorders or Differences of Sex Development (DSD) are congenital conditions in which the development of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical. The 2006 Chicago Consensus classification categorizes DSD based on karyotype: (1) 46,XX DSD (disorders of gonadal development [ovotesticular DSD] or androgen excess [congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aromatase deficiency, maternal androgen exposure]); (2) 46,XY DSD (disorders of testicular development [complete/partial gonadal dysgenesis: SRY, SOX9, NR5A1/SF1, WT1] or disorders of androgen synthesis/action [androgen insensitivity syndrome, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, 17-beta-HSD-3 deficiency]); and (3) Sex chromosome DSD (45,X Turner, 47,XXY Klinefelter, 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis, 46,XX/46,XY chimerism).
atlas.etiology: 46,XX DSD: CAH (CYP21A2 >90%), aromatase deficiency (CYP19A1), ovotesticular DSD. 46,XY DSD: Testicular dysgenesis (SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1); androgen resistance (AR / CAIS/PAIS); 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (SRD5A2); 17-beta-HSD-3. Sex Chromosome DSD: 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis.
atlas.epidemiology: Atypical genitalia at birth occurs in ~1 in 4500 to 1 in 5000 births. 21-hydroxylase CAH affects ~1 in 14,000 to 18,000 live births.
atlas.diagnostics: Urgent pelvic ultrasound (Müllerian structures); karyotype / SRY FISH; 17-OHP, electrolytes, testosterone, DHT, androstenedione, AMH; hCG stimulation test; gonadal biopsy/laparoscopy.

atlas.title: Menstrual Disorders and Hyperandrogenism in Adolescence
atlas.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
atlas.summary: Menarche is a late pubertal milestone, typically occurring 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche (average age 12.5 years, Tanner stage 4). In the first 2-3 post-menarchal years, physiological immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis leads to frequent anovulatory cycles. However, normal menstrual parameters in adolescents are defined as: cycle length between 21 and 45 days; bleeding duration <=7 days; requiring <=3-6 pads or tampons per day without soaking; and cycle regularity establishing within 24-36 months. Any cycle length <21 days or >45 days (or >90 days at any time) represents abnormal uterine bleeding requiring clinical investigation.
atlas.etiology: Amenorrhea: Outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen), gonadal dysgenesis (Turner), FHA (exercise, anorexia), hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease. Hyperandrogenism: PCOS, NCAH (CYP21A2), Cushing syndrome, androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumors.
atlas.epidemiology: PCOS affects 6-10% of adolescent girls; leading cause of anovulatory infertility and adolescent hirsutism.
atlas.diagnostics: Urine beta-hCG; total/free testosterone (LC-MS/MS), DHEAS, androstenedione; 17-OHP (morning follicular); TSH, prolactin, LH, FSH; transabdominal pelvic ultrasound; fasting lipid panel and 2-hr OGTT.

atlas.title: Hyperprolactinemia
atlas.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
atlas.summary: The clinical presentation of hyperprolactinemia varies by sex and tumor size. Pediatric macroprolactinomas are more common in males and adolescent boys, who frequently present with mass effect symptoms: persistent headaches, visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopsia from optic chiasm compression), growth deceleration, delayed puberty, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (hyperprolactinemia directly suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility). In adolescent girls, microprolactinomas are more frequent, presenting with primary or secondary amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea (present in 30-50%), and mild hirsutism.
atlas.etiology: Prolactinoma (microprolactinoma <10 mm, macroprolactinoma >=10 mm); Stalk compression (craniopharyngioma, germinoma); Drugs (D2 antagonists: risperidone, haloperidol, metoclopramide); Severe primary hypothyroidism (TRH stimulation); Macroprolactinemia (prolactin-IgG).
atlas.epidemiology: Prolactinomas represent ~50% of all pediatric pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. Microadenomas predominate in adolescent females (amenorrhea/galactorrhea); macroadenomas predominate in males (mass effect).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum prolactin (repeat to confirm); 1:100 dilution to exclude hook effect; PEG precipitation for macroprolactin; TSH, free T4, IGF-1, cortisol; visual field perimetry; high-resolution sellar MRI with contrast.

atlas.title: Hypoglycemia
atlas.summary: Hypoglycemia in infants and children is defined clinically by Whipple's triad: (1) Symptoms and neuroglycopenic signs consistent with low blood glucose; (2) Concomitantly documented subnormal plasma glucose concentration (<50-55 mg/dL [2.8-3.1 mmol/L]; <60 mg/dL in neonates with suspected congenital hyperinsulinism); and (3) Rapid relief of clinical symptoms upon glucose administration. In neonates, transitional physiological glucose nadirs occur in the first 24-48 hours of life, after which plasma glucose must be maintained >60 mg/dL in infants and >70 mg/dL in older children to prevent irreversible neurocognitive injury.
atlas.etiology: Hyperinsulinism: CHI (ABCC8, KCNJ11, GLUD1, GCK, HADH, HNF4A); insulinoma; Beckwith-Wiedemann (11p15); infant of diabetic mother. FAOD: MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD, CPT. Ketotic: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia; hypopituitarism (GH, ACTH). GSD: GSD-I (G6Pase), GSD-III.
atlas.epidemiology: CHI incidence is 1:30,000 to 1:50,000 live births (up to 1:2500 in founder populations). MCAD affects ~1 in 15,000 births.
atlas.diagnostics: Critical sample at glucose <50 mg/dL (insulin, C-peptide, BOHB, FFA, cortisol, GH, acylcarnitine, lactate, total/free carnitine); glucagon challenge test; 18F-DOPA PET/CT; genetic testing panel.

atlas.title: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents
atlas.summary: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells within the islets of Langerhans, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility is strongly linked to human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II alleles on chromosome 6p21, specifically HLA-DR3-DQ2 and HLA-DR4-DQ8 haplotypes. Progressive lymphocytic insulitis is driven by autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Circulating islet autoantibodies serve as essential diagnostic markers: glutamic acid decarboxylase-65 (GAD65), insulinoma-associated protein-2 (IA-2), insulin autoantibodies (IAA; prominent in young children), and zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). The presence of >=2 persistent autoantibodies marks preclinical stage 1/2 T1D.
atlas.etiology: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells mediated by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell insulitis; HLA-DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 susceptibility. Biomarkers: GAD65, IA-2, IAA, ZnT8 autoantibodies.
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence is rising globally by 2-3% per year; peak incidence occurs in two age cohorts: 4-6 years and 10-14 years (early puberty).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting glucose >=126 mg/dL, 2-hr OGTT >=200 mg/dL, HbA1c >=6.5%, or random glucose >=200 mg/dL with symptoms; islet autoantibody panel; DKA evaluation (venous blood gas, BOHB, electrolytes, BUN/Cr); CGM metrics.

atlas.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Youth
atlas.summary: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) in youth has emerged as a major public health challenge, driven by the global epidemic of pediatric obesity. Unlike adult T2D, youth-onset T2D is characterized by a significantly more aggressive disease biology: accelerated decline in pancreatic beta-cell function (loss of 20-35% of beta-cell capacity per year, ~4 times faster than in adults), early development of insulin dependence, and rapid accrual of microvascular and macrovascular complications. It disproportionately affects adolescents aged 10-19 years during pubertal insulin resistance peaks, with strong predilection for racial and ethnic minorities (Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian/Pacific Islander youth).
atlas.etiology: Insulin resistance coupled with rapid beta-cell failure; driven by visceral adiposity, pubertal hormones, genetics (TCF7L2), and ethnicity. Autoantibody negative (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 negative).
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence has risen markedly over the past two decades; peak age 12-16 years; female-to-male ratio ~1.5:1; high prevalence in Black, Hispanic, Native American, and South Asian youth.
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting glucose, 2-hr OGTT, HbA1c; islet autoantibody panel (exclude T1D); baseline urine microalbumin/Cr, lipid profile, ALT/AST, dilated eye exam; in HHS: effective osmolality, BUN/Cr.

atlas.title: Disorders of Lipid Metabolism
atlas.summary: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recommend a two-tiered screening strategy for pediatric dyslipidemia: (1) Universal lipid screening for all children once between ages 9 and 11 years, and once between ages 17 and 21 years (using non-fasting non-HDL cholesterol or a fasting lipid profile); and (2) Targeted screening starting at age 2 years (fasting lipid profile) for children with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease (men <55 years, women <65 years) or parent with total cholesterol >=240 mg/dL, or children with high-risk personal conditions (type 1/2 diabetes, hypertension, BMI >=95th percentile, CKD, post-cardiac transplant, Kawasaki disease with aneurysms).
atlas.etiology: Primary: HeFH / HoFH (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9); FCS (LPL, APOC2, GPIHBP1); familial combined hyperlipidemia. Secondary: Obesity-associated insulin resistance (hypertriglyceridemia + low HDL), nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, CKD, diabetes.
atlas.epidemiology: HeFH prevalence is 1:250; most common monogenic cardiovascular disorder. Obesity-associated dyslipidemia affects >20-30% of obese adolescents.
atlas.diagnostics: Universal screening at 9-11 yr and 17-21 yr; fasting lipid panel (total chol, TG, HDL-C, direct LDL-C, non-HDL-C); liver enzymes (ALT/AST), TSH, urinalysis; LDLR/APOB/PCSK9 genetic sequencing.

atlas.title: Endocrinologic Sequelae of Anorexia Nervosa and Obesity
atlas.summary: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a serious psychiatric disorder characterized by pathological restriction of energy intake, distorted body image, and intense fear of weight gain, resulting in severe state of chronic undernutrition and negative energy balance. The endocrine alterations in AN represent an evolutionary conserved adaptive survival mechanism designed to downregulate metabolic rate, shut down non-essential reproductive and skeletal functions, and mobilize energy substrates to preserve vital cerebral and cardiac homeostasis.
atlas.etiology: Anorexia Nervosa: Psychiatric starvation; adaptive neuroendocrine down-regulation (low T3, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, high GH/low IGF-1, hypercortisolemia). Obesity: Adiposity, insulin resistance, hyperleptinemia, blunted GH peaks (pseudo-GH deficiency), low SHBG.
atlas.epidemiology: Anorexia nervosa affects 0.5-1.0% of adolescent females (10:1 female predominance). Pediatric obesity affects ~20% of children in developed nations.
atlas.diagnostics: AN: LH, FSH, estradiol, total/free T3, rT3, TSH, GH, IGF-1, 24-hr urinary free cortisol; DXA bone mineral density; ECG (QTc, bradycardia). Obesity: Fasting lipid panel, ALT/AST (MAFLD), fasting glucose/HbA1c or OGTT, total/free testosterone, SHBG.

atlas.title: Diabetes Insipidus: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance
atlas.summary: In 2022, an international endocrine consensus updated the nomenclature of diabetes insipidus to eliminate confusion with diabetes mellitus: 'central diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D), and 'nephrogenic diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R). Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is synthesized by hypothalamic magnocellular neurons in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported down the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary. In response to hyperosmolality (>280-285 mOsm/kg) or hypovolemia, AVP binds basolateral V2 receptors (AVPR2) on renal collecting duct principal cells, triggering cAMP-mediated exocytic insertion of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels to concentrate urine.
atlas.etiology: AVP-D: Craniopharyngioma, germinoma, LCH, pituitary surgery (triphasic response), septo-optic dysplasia, AVP mutations, Wolfram syndrome (WFS1). AVP-R: X-linked AVPR2 mutations (>90%), AQP2 mutations, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia.
atlas.epidemiology: AVP-D prevalence is 1:25,000; equal sex distribution. Congenital AVP-R is rare (1:100,000 live male births).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality; plasma copeptin (basal >21.4 pmol/L confirms AVP-R; stimulated <4.9 confirms AVP-D); water deprivation test with DDAVP challenge; high-resolution sellar MRI.

atlas.title: Autoimmune Endocrine Disorders
atlas.summary: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes (APS) are classified into three major inherited forms: (1) APS-1 (APECED: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy), an autosomal recessive monogenic disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3; (2) APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome), a polygenic, HLA-DR3/DR4-associated complex disorder characterized by the mandatory presence of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes; and (3) IPEX syndrome (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked), a fatal infantile disorder caused by FOXP3 mutations.
atlas.etiology: APS-1: Autosomal recessive AIRE mutations (21q22.3); failure of thymic central tolerance. APS-2: Polygenic; HLA-DR3/DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22. IPEX: X-linked recessive FOXP3 mutations (Xp11.23); regulatory T cell deficiency.
atlas.epidemiology: APS-1 prevalence is 1:100,000 (higher in Finns, Sardinians, Iranian Jews). APS-2 prevalence is ~1:20,000 (female predominance 3:1). IPEX is a very rare infantile lethal disorder.
atlas.diagnostics: APS-1: Anti-IFN-omega / anti-IFN-alpha2 antibodies; AIRE genetic sequencing; calcium, phosphate, PTH, ACTH, 21-OH antibodies. APS-2: 21-OH antibodies, TSH, anti-TPO, islet antibodies. IPEX: FOXP3 sequencing, Treg flow cytometry.

atlas.title: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia and Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma in the Paediatric Population
atlas.summary: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes menin, a nuclear scaffold protein regulating gene transcription, cell cycle progression, and genome integrity. Following Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele leads to tumor development in classic endocrine target organs ('the 3 Ps'): parathyroid glands (>95% penetrance), enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tissues (pNETs; 30-70%), and the anterior pituitary gland (30-40%).
atlas.etiology: MEN1: Inactivating MEN1 tumor suppressor mutations (11q13); 3 Ps (parathyroid, pNET, pituitary). MEN2A: Activating RET mutations (codon 634; MTC, pheo, hyperparathyroid). MEN2B: RET M918T (infant MTC, pheo, mucosal neuromas, ganglioneuromatosis). FIPA: Inactivating AIP mutations (11q13.3). X-LAG: Xq26.3 GPR101 microduplication.
atlas.epidemiology: MEN1 prevalence is 1:30,000. MEN2 prevalence is 1:35,000 (MEN2A 95%, MEN2B 5%). AIP mutations found in 15-20% of FIPA.
atlas.diagnostics: MEN1: Calcium, PTH, gastrin, chromogranin A, prolactin, IGF-1, abdominal and pituitary MRI. MEN2: Calcitonin, plasma free metanephrines, neck US, RET genetic testing. FIPA/X-LAG: GH, IGF-1, prolactin, pituitary MRI, AIP/GPR101 genetic testing.

atlas.title: McCune-Albright Syndrome
atlas.summary: The classic clinical triad of MAS comprises: (1) Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (FD) of bone; (2) Café-au-lait skin hyperpigmentation; and (3) Hyperfunctioning autonomous endocrinopathies. Because the mutation occurs postzygotically during embryogenesis, the clinical phenotype is remarkably heterogeneous, depending entirely on the timing of the mutation and the anatomical distribution and percentage of mutated cells within tissue mosaics. Diagnosis is established clinically by the presence of >=2 classic triad features (or 1 classic feature plus confirmed GNAS mutation in tissue).
atlas.etiology: Postzygotic somatic mosaic activating missense mutations in GNAS (20q13.3; R201H or R201C); constitutively active Gs-alpha and continuous adenylyl cyclase/cAMP activation. Non-inherited.
atlas.epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at 1:100,000 to 1:1,000,000; equal gender distribution, but peripheral precocious puberty is much more clinically apparent in females.
atlas.diagnostics: Skeletal plain radiographs (ground-glass lesions) and 99mTc bone scan; pelvic ultrasound (unilateral follicular cysts); serum estradiol, LH, FSH, TSH, free T4, IGF-1, GH, phosphate, FGF23; GNAS mutant-specific PCR on affected tissue.

atlas.title: Management of Acute and Late Endocrine Effects of Childhood Cancer Treatment
atlas.summary: The hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) axis is highly vulnerable to cranial radiation therapy (CRT) used for brain tumors, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and leukemia prophylaxis. Radiation damage progresses in a dose- and time-dependent hierarchical vulnerability: Growth Hormone (GH) deficiency is the earliest and most sensitive defect, occurring at low-to-moderate doses (>=18-24 Gy) in >80-90% of exposed children within 2-5 years. Gonadotropin (LH/FSH) deficiency occurs at >=30-40 Gy; notably, low-dose cranial radiation (18-24 Gy) can paradoxically trigger central precocious puberty by damaging inhibitory cortical pathways. TSH deficiency and ACTH deficiency occur at higher doses (>=40-50 Gy), often presenting insidiously 5 to 15+ years after completion of cancer therapy.
atlas.etiology: Radiotherapy late effects: Cranial (GH deficiency >=18 Gy, precocious puberty 18-24 Gy, LH/FSH >=30-40 Gy, TSH/ACTH >=40-50 Gy); Neck (hypothyroidism, thyroid cancer); Pelvic/gonadal (azoospermia >=0.1-1.2 Gy, POI >=10-15 Gy).
