Chemotherapy: Alkylators (cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, procarbazine; CED >=4000-8000 mg/m2 causes germ cell failure).
atlas.epidemiology: Over 80% of childhood cancer patients survive >=5 years; >50-70% of long-term survivors develop at least one chronic endocrine disorder.
atlas.diagnostics: Annual growth velocity, bone age; fasting IGF-1, TSH, free T4; LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone; 8 AM cortisol or cosyntropin test for cranial RT >=30 Gy; annual thyroid exam; semen analysis; DXA.

atlas.title: Care of Transgender and Gender Diverse Youth
atlas.summary: Medical care for transgender and gender diverse (TGD) youth is guided by evidence-based consensus guidelines from the Endocrine Society and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH Standards of Care, Version 8). TGD identities are recognized as healthy expressions of human diversity. For prepubertal children (Tanner stage 1), care is strictly non-medical, focusing on social transition (clothing, name, hair, pronouns) and family counseling; medical or endocrine interventions are strictly contraindicated prior to the biological onset of puberty.
atlas.etiology: Gender diversity is a normal aspect of human variation. Gender dysphoria involves clinically significant distress from incongruence between gender identity and assigned sex.
atlas.epidemiology: Approximately 1.4-2.0% of adolescents identify as transgender or gender diverse.
atlas.diagnostics: Multidisciplinary psychological assessment; Tanner staging (stage 2 required for medical pubertal suppression); baseline CBC, CMP, lipid profile, LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone; DXA bone density.

atlas.title: Management of Endocrine Emergencies
atlas.summary: Pediatric endocrine emergencies are acute, life-threatening derangements of hormone excess, hormone deficiency, or metabolic fuel dysregulation requiring rapid clinical recognition and physiological stabilization. The major entities encompass: (1) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); (2) Acute adrenal crisis; (3) Thyroid storm and severe thyrotoxicosis; (4) Severe acute hypocalcemia and hypercalcemic crisis; and (5) Severe symptomatic neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.
atlas.etiology: Adrenal crisis: CAH, Addison disease, pituitary hypopituitarism, steroid cessation. DKA/HHS: T1D/T2D insulin deficiency. Thyroid storm: Decompensated Graves' disease. Hypocalcemia crisis: DiGeorge, surgical hypoparathyroidism, APS-1. Hypercalcemic crisis: Malignancy, NSHPT, immobilization.
atlas.epidemiology: DKA occurs in 30-40% of newly diagnosed pediatric T1D. Adrenal crisis incidence is 5-8 events per 100 patient-years in primary AI.
atlas.diagnostics: Point-of-care glucose, venous blood gas, electrolytes, BOHB, ionized/total calcium, free T4, TSH, cortisol, ECG (QTc interval).

atlas.title: The Endocrine Response to Critical Illness
atlas.summary: The endocrine response to severe critical illness (septic shock, polytrauma, major burns, cardiopulmonary bypass) follows an evolutionary conserved biphasic pattern: (1) Acute phase (first hours to days): marked hyperactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system, driving massive cortisol and catecholamine surges to maintain blood pressure and substrate delivery, alongside selective central down-regulation of anabolic pathways (suppression of TSH, low T3/T4 [NTIS], and hypogonadotropism) to conserve energy; (2) Chronic phase (prolonged critical illness >1-2 weeks): characterized by central neuroendocrine exhaustion, persistent hypopituitarism (suppressed pulsatile secretion of ACTH, TSH, GH, and gonadotropins), profound lean tissue catabolism, and immune dysfunction.
atlas.etiology: Acute stress response to sepsis, trauma, burns, cardiopulmonary bypass. Driven by cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha), catecholamines, cortisol, and central hypothalamic reprogramming. Progresses from acute hyperactivation to chronic neuroendocrine exhaustion.
atlas.epidemiology: CIRCI occurs in 30-50% of pediatric septic shock. NTIS occurs in 40-70% of PICU patients. Stress hyperglycemia occurs in >50% of critically ill children.
atlas.diagnostics: Blood glucose; lactate, blood gas, electrolytes; baseline cortisol in shock; TSH, free T4, free T3, reverse T3; continuous hemodynamic monitoring.

therapies.text: Recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) is administered subcutaneously daily at bedtime at a dosage of 22–35 mcg/kg/day (0.16–0.24 mg/kg/week). Dosing is adjusted according to growth velocity, weight changes, and serum IGF-I concentrations maintained within the age- and sex-adjusted reference range.
therapies.title: Childhood Growth Hormone Deficiency and Hypopituitarism

therapies.text: Recombinant human IGF-I (mecasermin) is indicated for severe primary IGF-I deficiency at an initial dose of 40–80 mcg/kg subcutaneously twice daily, titrated up to a maximum of 120 mcg/kg twice daily. Injections must be administered with or immediately after a meal or snack.
therapies.title: Growth Hormone Insensitivity

therapies.text: For severe idiopathic short stature (height SDS <-2.25 with projected adult height <-2 SD), somatropin is FDA-approved at doses of 0.30–0.37 mg/kg/week (43–53 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. For adolescent males with CDGP and psychological distress, testosterone enanthate 50–100 mg IM monthly for 3–6 months can be considered.
therapies.title: Normal Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

therapies.text: Somatropin is FDA-approved for children born SGA with failure of catch-up growth by 2 years of age at a dosage of 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. Titration is based on annual height velocity and keeping serum IGF-I below +2.0 SDS.
therapies.section: Somatropin Regimen in Children Born SGA
therapies.title: Growth Hormone Treatment of the Short Child Born Small for Gestational Age

therapies.text: Recombinant human growth hormone is administered at an initial dose of 0.5 mg/m2/day, titrating to a target maintenance dose of 1.0 mg/m2/day (approx 0.035 mg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. Baseline and 6- to 12-week post-initiation polysomnography and ENT evaluations are mandatory.
therapies.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Prader–Willi Syndrome

therapies.text: Somatropin is FDA-approved for Turner syndrome at 0.35–0.375 mg/kg/week (approx 50 mcg/kg/day); for Noonan syndrome up to 0.46 mg/kg/week (66 mcg/kg/day); and for SHOX deficiency at 0.35 mg/kg/week (50 mcg/kg/day). In Turner syndrome girls ≥9–10 years, adjunctive oxandrolone at 0.03–0.05 mg/kg/day can be added.
therapies.section: Somatropin Regimens in TS, NS, and SHOX
therapies.title: Growth Hormone Therapy in Children with Turner Syndrome, Noonan Syndrome, and SHOX Gene Mutations

therapies.text: Adult somatropin dosing is non-weight-based, initiating at 0.2 to 0.5 mg/day in the transition period (0.1 to 0.2 mg/day in older adults) subcutaneously at bedtime, titrating by 0.1 to 0.2 mg/day every 4–8 weeks to achieve an IGF-I within the middle of the age-adjusted reference range (0 to +1.0 SDS).
therapies.title: Management of Adults with Childhood-Onset Growth Hormone Deficiency

therapies.text: Vosoritide (recombinant human C-type natriuretic peptide analog) is approved for children with achondroplasia aged 5 years and older (and down to younger ages where approved) with open epiphyses, administered at 15 mcg/kg subcutaneously once daily. Somatropin produces only modest transient gains and is not standard of care.
therapies.title: Skeletal Dysplasias

therapies.text: First-line therapy is transsphenoidal surgical resection. Medical therapy for persistent hypersecretion includes somatostatin analogs (octreotide LAR 10–30 mg IM monthly; lanreotide 60–120 mg SC monthly), dopamine agonists (cabergoline 0.25–2.0 mg/week), or the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (10–30 mg SC daily).
therapies.title: Growth Hormone Excess and Other Conditions of Overgrowth

therapies.text: Maintenance hydrocortisone is dosed at 8–10 mg/m2/day orally in 3 divided doses. Primary AI also requires fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg once daily. For acute adrenal crisis, immediate resuscitation requires IV normal saline bolus (20 mL/kg) with 5–10% dextrose and IV hydrocortisone 50–100 mg/m2 (or age-based: <3 yr: 25 mg, 3–12 yr: 50 mg, >12 yr: 100 mg).
therapies.title: Adrenal Insufficiency

therapies.text: Maintenance glucocorticoid is oral hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m2/day divided in 3 doses. Salt-wasting forms require fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg once daily, plus oral sodium chloride 1–2 g/day (approx 17–34 mEq/day) in infants. Intercurrent febrile stress requires 2–3x maintenance hydrocortisone.
therapies.section: Standard Medical Regimen in Classic CAH
therapies.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

therapies.text: Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy is the curative treatment of choice for Cushing disease. Postoperative adrenal insufficiency is managed with hydrocortisone (10–12 mg/m2/day in 2–3 divided doses) until the HPA axis recovers (typically 6–18 months). Medical inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) are used for pre-surgical control.
therapies.section: Curative and Perioperative Management in Cushing Syndrome
therapies.title: Cushing Syndrome in Childhood

therapies.text: Treatment is etiology-specific: GRA is treated with low-dose dexamethasone (0.125–0.25 mg daily) or eplerenone. AME responds to spironolactone (1–3 mg/kg/day) and potassium supplementation. Liddle syndrome requires amiloride (5–10 mg daily) or triamterene; spironolactone is ineffective.
therapies.section: Targeted Medical Therapy in Endocrine Hypertension
therapies.title: Mineralocorticoid Disorders and Endocrine Hypertension

therapies.text: Initiate oral levothyroxine tablets (crushed in 3-5 mL of breastmilk or water) at 10-15 mcg/kg/day (typically 37.5 to 50 mcg/day for term infants) within the first 14 days of life. Avoid soy formula, iron, or calcium co-administration. Monitor TSH and FT4 every 1-2 months during the first 6 months, aiming for FT4 in the upper half of normal range and TSH <5 mIU/L.
therapies.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism

therapies.text: Methimazole (MMI) 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day (up to 1.0 mg/kg/day; maximum 30-40 mg daily) orally in 1-2 divided doses. Add atenolol 1-2 mg/kg/day or propranolol 1-2 mg/kg/day for adrenergic symptoms. Propylthiouracil is strictly contraindicated in children. If neutropenia/agranulocytosis occurs, stop immediately.
therapies.title: Autoimmune Thyroid Disease

therapies.text: Levothyroxine (L-T4) orally once daily: 1-5 yr: 4-6 mcg/kg/day; 6-12 yr: 2.5-3.5 mcg/kg/day; >12 yr: 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day (75-125 mcg daily). Administer on an empty stomach.
therapies.title: Autoimmune Thyroid Disease

therapies.text: Routine thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine (T4) or liothyronine (T3) is NOT recommended in pediatric non-thyroidal illness syndrome. Clinical management focuses on aggressive treatment of the underlying systemic illness, hemodynamic support, and nutritional recovery. Repeat thyroid testing 4-6 weeks after resolution of acute illness.
therapies.title: Non-thyroidal Illness Syndrome

therapies.text: Asymptomatic patients require no treatment. If resting tachycardia or palpitations are problematic, selective beta-blockers (atenolol 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day) provide symptomatic relief. If massive goiter or elevated TSH persists, tiratricol (TRIAC, 1-3 mg/day in divided doses) can be considered to suppress pituitary TSH secretion.
therapies.title: Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH) and Resistance to TSH (RTSH)

therapies.text: Total or near-total thyroidectomy with central compartment (level VI) lymph node dissection by a high-volume surgeon. For intermediate/high-risk differentiated thyroid cancer, administer adjuvant radioactive iodine (131I, 1-2 mCi/kg or dosimetry-based 30-100 mCi). Postoperative levothyroxine suppression: maintain TSH <0.1 mIU/L for high-risk disease, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for intermediate-risk.
therapies.title: Thyroid Neoplasia

therapies.text: 10% Calcium gluconate IV at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg; maximum 1-2 g or 10-20 mL) infused slowly over 10-20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring. If hypomagnesemia is present, administer 50% magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg IV.
therapies.title: Abnormalities in Calcium Homeostasis
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day (0.25-1.0 mcg/day) orally divided BID plus oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day divided TID. Target low-normal serum calcium (8.5-9.0 mg/dL) and urine Ca/Cr <0.20 to prevent nephrocalcinosis.
therapies.title: Abnormalities in Calcium Homeostasis
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: Burosumab-twza subcutaneous injection: initiate at 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (rounded to nearest 10 mg; maximum 90 mg). Measure fasting serum phosphate every 4 weeks initially; titrate step-wise to 1.2 mg/kg, then up to 2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks to maintain serum phosphate in the lower normal range.
therapies.title: Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.section: Conventional Oral Phosphate and Calcitriol Therapy
therapies.text: Oral elemental phosphate (Joulie solution or tablets) 20-40 mg/kg/day divided 4-5 times daily plus calcitriol 20-30 ng/kg/day divided BID. Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and urine Ca/Cr every 3 months; monitor renal US annually for nephrocalcinosis.
therapies.title: Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: Cholecalciferol (D3) or ergocalciferol (D2) 2000-6000 IU/day orally for 8-12 weeks (or single stoss dose 100,000-300,000 IU) PLUS oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day (typically 500 mg daily) to prevent hungry bone syndrome. Transition to 400-600 IU/day maintenance once healed.
therapies.title: Rickets: The Skeletal Disorders of Impaired Calcium or Phosphate Availability
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D) 20-40 ng/kg/day orally divided BID. Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and urine Ca/Cr monthly until healed.
therapies.title: Rickets: The Skeletal Disorders of Impaired Calcium or Phosphate Availability
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.section: Management of PTH Resistance in PHP
therapies.text: Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day (0.25-1.0 mcg/day) orally divided BID combined with oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day divided TID. Titrate to maintain serum calcium in the normal range (8.8-9.5 mg/dL) and bring PTH toward the upper normal range to avoid hyperparathyroid osteopenia. Supplement with levothyroxine for TSH resistance and rhGH if GH deficient.
therapies.title: Pseudohypoparathyroidism
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: Zoledronic acid: 0.025-0.05 mg/kg/dose (max 4 mg) IV infused over 30-45 minutes once every 6 months. Alternatively, intravenous pamidronate: 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day over 3 consecutive days every 3-4 months (annual dose: 9 mg/kg/year in infants <2 yr; 6 mg/kg/year in older children). Pre-treat to ensure 25-OH-D >20-30 ng/mL, provide oral calcium and acetaminophen for acute phase reaction.
therapies.title: The Management of Osteoporosis in Children
therapies.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

therapies.text: For CDGP: Testosterone enanthate or cypionate 25-50 mg IM once monthly for 3-6 months. For permanent hypogonadism: escalate slowly: 50 mg/month for 6-12 months, then 100 mg/month, then 150 mg/month, up to adult replacement 200 mg IM every 2 weeks.
therapies.title: Delayed Puberty Onset and Hypogonadism
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: Transdermal 17-beta estradiol patch 6.25-12.5 mcg/day changed weekly, or oral micronized estradiol 0.25-0.5 mg/day. Escalate annually over 2-3 years. Delay progesterone for 18-24 months; then add oral micronized progesterone 100-200 mg daily for days 1-12 of each calendar month.
therapies.title: Delayed Puberty Onset and Hypogonadism
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: Depot leuprolide acetate: 7.5-15 mg IM every 4 weeks or 11.25-30 mg IM every 12 weeks. Alternatively, histrelin acetate 50 mg subcutaneous implant replaced annually. Monitor growth velocity, bone age, Tanner stage, and stimulated LH (<2-3 IU/L) every 3-6 months. Discontinue around age 11-12 years.
therapies.title: Precocious Puberty
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: For testotoxicosis: combination therapy with an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole 1 mg daily or letrozole 2.5 mg daily) plus an antiandrogen (spironolactone 50-100 mg BID or bicalutamide 12.5-25 mg daily). For McCune-Albright: letrozole 2.5 mg daily or fulvestrant/tamoxifen.
therapies.title: Precocious Puberty
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: Intravenous normal saline bolus (20 mL/kg) for salt-wasting crisis; IV hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m2 (or 25 mg for infants) bolus, followed by 50-100 mg/m2/day. Chronic maintenance: oral hydrocortisone 10-15 mg/m2/day divided TID, fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg/day, and sodium chloride supplements 1-2 g/day.
therapies.title: Management of Infants Born with Disorders/Differences of Sex Development
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: Combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol 20-30 mcg + non-androgenic progestin like drospirenone or desogestrel) once daily. If hirsutism persists after 6 months, add spironolactone 50-100 mg orally BID. For impaired glucose tolerance/insulin resistance, add metformin 500-1000 mg BID.
therapies.title: Menstrual Disorders and Hyperandrogenism in Adolescence
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: Cabergoline: initiate at 0.25 mg orally once or twice weekly; titrate every 4-8 weeks to 0.5-1.0 mg twice weekly (maximum 2-3 mg/week) until serum prolactin normalizes and tumor shrinkage is confirmed on MRI. Second-line: bromocriptine 1.25-2.5 mg daily with food.
therapies.title: Hyperprolactinemia
therapies.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

therapies.text: 10% Dextrose (D10W) IV bolus at 2 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) over 2-3 minutes. Follow immediately with continuous IV glucose infusion rate (GIR) at 6-8 mg/kg/min, titrating to maintain blood glucose >70 mg/dL.
therapies.title: Hypoglycemia

therapies.text: Diazoxide: 5-15 mg/kg/day orally divided TID. Co-administer chlorothiazide 7-10 mg/kg/day divided BID to prevent pulmonary hypertension and heart failure. Second-line: Octreotide 5-25 mcg/kg/day SC divided Q6-8H.
therapies.title: Hypoglycemia

therapies.text: Initial fluid: 0.9% normal saline 10-20 mL/kg over 1 hour. Continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour started 1-2 hours AFTER fluid initiation (NEVER give an IV insulin bolus). Replace remaining fluid deficit over 24-48 hours. Add 40 mEq/L potassium once urine output confirmed. Add 5-10% dextrose when glucose <250-300 mg/dL. Treat cerebral edema immediately with 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg) or 20% mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg).
therapies.title: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents

therapies.text: Total Daily Dose (TDD): 0.5-1.0 units/kg/day (prepabertal: 0.5-0.8 U/kg/day; pubertal: 1.0-1.5 U/kg/day). Basal analog (glargine, detemir, degludec) comprises 40-50% of TDD. Rapid-acting analog (aspart, lispro) comprises 50-60% of TDD, divided by meals using ICR (500/TDD) and correction ISF (1800/TDD). Target HbA1c <7.0%, TIR 70-180 mg/dL >70%.
therapies.title: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents

therapies.text: Metformin: initiate at 500 mg orally once daily with meals; titrate weekly by 500 mg up to 1000 mg BID (max 2000 mg/day). If HbA1c >=8.5% or glucose >=250 mg/dL, add basal insulin (glargine/degludec) 0.25-0.5 units/kg/day SC. Second-line: Liraglutide 0.6 mg SC daily titrated to 1.8 mg daily, or Dulaglutide 0.75-1.5 mg SC weekly for youth >=10 years.
therapies.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Youth

therapies.text: Atorvastatin: initiate at 10 mg orally once daily in children >=10 years; titrate up to 20-40 mg daily to achieve LDL-C <130 mg/dL (or <100 mg/dL in high-risk). Rosuvastatin: 5-20 mg daily. Pravastatin: 10-40 mg daily. If target not met, add Ezetimibe 10 mg daily.
therapies.title: Disorders of Lipid Metabolism

therapies.text: Extreme fat restriction: restrict total dietary fat to <10-15% of total caloric intake (typically <15-20 g/day of fat) to keep triglycerides <1000 mg/dL and prevent acute pancreatitis. Supplement with fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
therapies.title: Disorders of Lipid Metabolism

therapies.section: Bone Protection in Adolescent Anorexia Nervosa
therapies.text: Transdermal 17-beta estradiol 100 mcg patch applied twice weekly plus oral micronized progesterone 200 mg daily on days 1-12 of each calendar month for adolescents with amenorrhea >6 months and DXA Z-score <-2.0. Avoid oral contraceptive pills for bone health. Calcium 1000-1300 mg/day and vitamin D 600-1000 IU/day.
therapies.title: Endocrinologic Sequelae of Anorexia Nervosa and Obesity

therapies.text: Semaglutide: initiate at 0.25 mg SC once weekly for 4 weeks; escalate monthly (0.5 mg, 1.0 mg, 1.7 mg) to target maintenance dose of 2.4 mg SC once weekly for youth >=12 years with BMI >=95th percentile, combined with lifestyle intervention. Alternatively, Liraglutide 3.0 mg SC daily.
therapies.title: Endocrinologic Sequelae of Anorexia Nervosa and Obesity

therapies.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP): Oral melt 60-120 mcg TID, oral tablets 0.1-0.2 mg TID, or intranasal 2.5-10 mcg once or twice daily. Titrate to control polyuria and nocturia while strictly enforcing a breakthrough period of polyuria prior to redosing. In infants, avoid DDAVP; use low-solute formula and free water.
therapies.title: Diabetes Insipidus: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance

therapies.text: Hydrochlorothiazide 2-4 mg/kg/day orally divided BID combined with amiloride 0.3 mg/kg/day or indomethacin 1.5-3.0 mg/kg/day divided TID, plus low-sodium diet (<1-2 mEq/kg/day) and unrestricted free water access.
therapies.title: Diabetes Insipidus: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance

therapies.text: Hypoparathyroidism: Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day orally plus oral calcium carbonate 30-50 mg/kg/day. Addison disease: Hydrocortisone 8-10 mg/m2/day orally divided TID plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg once daily. Chronic candidiasis: Oral fluconazole 3-6 mg/kg/day. Crucial rule: Always start hydrocortisone before levothyroxine.
therapies.title: Autoimmune Endocrine Disorders

therapies.text: MEN2B (RET M918T): Prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life (first months of life). MEN2A (codon 634): Prophylactic total thyroidectomy at or before age 5 years. MANDATORY: Screen for and surgically resect pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) BEFORE performing neck surgery.
therapies.title: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia and Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma in the Paediatric Population

therapies.text: Subtotal parathyroidectomy (resecting 3.5 glands) or total parathyroidectomy with forearm autotransplantation for multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia. Pancreatic NETs: surgical enucleation or partial pancreatectomy for insulinomas and tumors >1-2 cm.
therapies.title: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia and Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma in the Paediatric Population

therapies.section: Endocrine and Skeletal Therapies for MAS
therapies.text: Precocious puberty in girls: Letrozole 2.5 mg orally once daily (or tamoxifen/fulvestrant). Fibrous dysplasia bone pain: Intravenous pamidronate 1 mg/kg/day for 3 days every 4-6 months or zoledronic acid 0.025-0.05 mg/kg every 6 months. FGF23 hypophosphatemia: Oral phosphate salts 20-40 mg/kg/day plus calcitriol 20-30 ng/kg/day. GH excess: Octreotide LAR or Pegvisomant.
therapies.title: McCune-Albright Syndrome

therapies.text: rhGH: 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week SC divided daily (initiate only after >=1 year disease-free remission). Central adrenal insufficiency: Hydrocortisone 8-10 mg/m2/day orally divided TID with mandatory stress dosing. Hypothyroidism: Levothyroxine 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day. Hypogonadism: Testosterone or Estradiol pubertal induction protocols.
therapies.title: Management of Acute and Late Endocrine Effects of Childhood Cancer Treatment

therapies.text: Depot leuprolide acetate 11.25 mg or 30 mg IM every 12 weeks, or histrelin acetate 50 mg subcutaneous implant annually. Reversible; suppresses LH/FSH to prepubertal levels.
therapies.title: Care of Transgender and Gender Diverse Youth

therapies.text: Transgender Males (AFAB): Testosterone cypionate or enanthate 25-50 mg IM/SC every 2 weeks, titrating every 6 months to adult dose of 50-100 mg weekly (or 100-200 mg every 2 weeks); target testosterone 300-1000 ng/dL. Transgender Females (AMAB): Oral micronized 17-beta estradiol 1-2 mg daily titrating to 4-8 mg daily (or transdermal patch 50-200 mcg/day) plus spironolactone 50-100 mg BID; target estradiol 100-200 pg/mL, testosterone <50 ng/dL.
therapies.title: Care of Transgender and Gender Diverse Youth

therapies.text: Adrenal Crisis: Normal saline 20 mL/kg IV bolus + D5W/D10W. Hydrocortisone IV bolus: <3 yr: 25 mg; 3-12 yr: 50 mg; >12 yr: 100 mg (or 50-100 mg/m2), then 50-100 mg/m2/day. Thyroid Storm: Propranolol 0.01-0.1 mg/kg IV slow, Methimazole 0.5-1.0 mg/kg PO/PR, then Lugol's iodine 5-10 drops TID >=1 hr later, Hydrocortisone 100 mg/m2/day IV. Hypocalcemia: 10% Calcium gluconate 1-2 mL/kg IV over 10-20 min.
therapies.title: Management of Endocrine Emergencies

therapies.text: Vasopressor-Refractory Septic Shock: Hydrocortisone 50 mg/m2 (or 2 mg/kg) IV bolus, followed by 50-100 mg/m2/day continuous infusion or divided Q6H. Wean rapidly once vasopressors are stopped. Stress Hyperglycemia: Regular insulin continuous infusion titrating to moderate target 140-180 mg/dL (avoid tight 80-110 mg/dL). Avoid routine thyroid hormone replacement for NTIS.
therapies.title: The Endocrine Response to Critical Illness

cards.q: What classic triad in a male neonate strongly suggests congenital anterior pituitary hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Hypoglycemia, prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and micropenis (with or without undescended testes).

cards.q: Why is sex-steroid priming utilized prior to provocative GH stimulation testing in peripubertal children?
cards.a: Peripubertal children with constitutional growth delay have transient physiological hyposecretion of GH; priming with estrogen or testosterone enhances pituitary somatotroph responsiveness and prevents false-positive failure on provocative tests.

cards.q: What triad of findings on pituitary MRI defines the Pituitary Stalk Interruption Syndrome (PSIS)?
cards.a: An interrupted or absent (thin) pituitary infundibular stalk, an ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot (typically at the median eminence), and severe anterior pituitary hypoplasia.

cards.q: Mutations in which pituitary-specific transcription factor produce combined deficiencies of GH, TSH, and Prolactin while initially sparing ACTH and gonadotropins?
cards.a: POU1F1 (also known as PIT1), whereas PROP1 mutations cause progressive deficiency of GH, TSH, PRL, LH/FSH, and eventually ACTH in adulthood.

cards.q: What is the recommended initial daily starting dose of somatropin for pediatric isolated or combined GHD?
cards.a: 22 to 35 mcg/kg/day (0.16 to 0.24 mg/kg/week) administered as a daily subcutaneous injection at bedtime.

cards.q: A 10-year-old child 2 months into somatropin therapy develops persistent morning headaches and diplopia. What complication must be evaluated by funduscopic examination?
cards.a: Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), characterized by papilledema and elevated cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure, requiring temporary cessation or dose reduction.

cards.q: What orthopedic condition should be suspected in a patient on somatropin who develops groin, hip, or referred knee pain with an antalgic limp?
cards.a: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), related to rapid chondrocyte proliferation and structural biomechanical stress at the proximal femoral growth plate.

cards.q: What discordant biochemical profile distinguishes classic growth hormone insensitivity from growth hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Elevated or normal circulating GH levels combined with profoundly depressed or undetectable serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3.

cards.q: Why is serum growth hormone-binding protein (GHBP) undetectable in classic Laron syndrome?
cards.a: GHBP is generated by proteolytic cleavage of the extracellular domain of the GHR; mutations affecting the extracellular domain prevent GHBP production and release into the circulation.

cards.q: What approved pharmacological agent is indicated for children with severe primary IGF-I deficiency due to GHR mutations?
cards.a: Recombinant human IGF-I (mecasermin), dosed at 40 to 120 mcg/kg subcutaneously twice daily with meals.

cards.q: What critical administration guideline must be followed with every mecasermin injection to prevent an acute medical emergency?
cards.a: Mecasermin must be injected immediately before or after a meal or carbohydrate snack to prevent severe, life-threatening hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Mutations in STAT5B cause severe growth failure combined with which distinct non-endocrine clinical feature?
cards.a: Severe immune deficiency with eczema, recurrent pulmonary infections, and autoimmune lymphoproliferation, due to impaired regulatory T-cell signaling.

cards.q: What molecular defect causes moderate short stature with markedly low IGF-I and IGFBP-3, but normal free IGF-I and no hypoglycemia?
cards.a: IGFALS (acid-labile subunit) gene mutations, which disrupt formation of the 150-kDa circulating ternary complex but leave binary complexes intact.

cards.q: What unexpected long-term metabolic finding has been documented in Ecuadorian cohorts with homozygous E180splice GHR mutations?
cards.a: Near-total protection from malignant neoplasms (cancer) and clinical type 2 diabetes mellitus despite marked lifelong obesity.

cards.q: How does bone age typically differ between Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP) and Familial Short Stature (FSS)?
cards.a: In CDGP, bone age is significantly delayed relative to chronological age; in FSS, bone age is consistent with chronological age.

cards.q: How is midparental target height calculated for a boy and a girl?
cards.a: Boy: [Father's height + (Mother's height + 13 cm)] / 2. Girl: [(Father's height - 13 cm) + Mother's height] / 2.

cards.q: What height threshold defines Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) for consideration of growth hormone therapy?
cards.a: Height more than 2.25 standard deviations below the mean (height SDS <-2.25 or approximately below the 1.2th percentile) with poor predicted adult height.

cards.q: What regimen of low-dose androgen is used to jumpstart growth in adolescent boys with constitutional delay and severe psychosocial distress?
cards.a: Testosterone enanthate or cypionate 50 to 100 mg intramuscularly once monthly for 3 to 6 months.

cards.q: What is the typical FDA-approved somatropin dose range for idiopathic short stature?
cards.a: 0.30 to 0.37 mg/kg/week (approximately 43 to 53 mcg/kg/day) given by daily subcutaneous injection.

cards.q: What class of medication is sometimes combined with GH in adolescent males with short stature to slow bone age maturation?
cards.a: Aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole), which block the conversion of androgens to estrogens in growth plate chondrocytes.

cards.q: Why is a karyotype or chromosomal microarray indicated in every girl presenting with unexplained short stature, even without dysmorphic features?
cards.a: To rule out Turner syndrome (such as mosaic 45,X/46,XX), where short stature may be the only presenting physical feature in up to 10% of cases.

cards.q: What statistical criteria define an infant as born Small for Gestational Age (SGA)?
cards.a: Birth weight and/or birth length at least 2 standard deviations below the mean (SDS ≤ -2.0, <2.3rd percentile) for gestational age and sex.

cards.q: What percentage of children born SGA experience spontaneous catch-up growth to normal height by 2 years of age?
cards.a: Approximately 85% to 90%; the remaining 10% to 15% fail to catch up and are candidates for evaluation.

cards.q: What age and height criteria are required by the US FDA for initiating somatropin in a child born SGA?
cards.a: Age ≥ 2 years with height SDS ≤ -2.0 and documented failure to manifest catch-up growth.

cards.q: What is the approved somatropin dosage range for children born SGA without catch-up growth?
cards.a: 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (approximately 35 to 70 mcg/kg/day) given by daily subcutaneous injection.

cards.q: Which specific genetic syndrome presents with severe intrauterine growth restriction, body asymmetry, triangular facies, and fifth finger clinodactyly?
cards.a: Silver-Russell syndrome, associated with loss of methylation at 11p15.5 or maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 7.

cards.q: What long-term adult metabolic risks are increased in individuals born SGA who experience rapid post-infancy weight catch-up?
cards.a: Metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, visceral obesity, and premature cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: What circulating biochemical marker is routinely monitored during somatropin therapy in SGA children to adjust dosage safely?
cards.a: Serum IGF-I concentration, maintaining levels within +1 to +2 SDS for age and pubertal stage.

cards.q: What is the primary genetic mechanism causing Prader-Willi Syndrome in 65% to 75% of cases?
cards.a: Paternal microdeletion of the 15q11.2-q13 chromosomal region; maternal uniparental disomy (UPD15) accounts for most remaining cases.

cards.q: What pathognomonic body composition abnormality is present in infants with PWS even prior to the development of obesity?
cards.a: Markedly increased percent body fat and severely reduced lean muscle mass, accompanied by decreased resting energy expenditure.

cards.q: What diagnostic evaluation is mandatory prior to initiating somatropin in a child with PWS to prevent fatal airway complications?
cards.a: Polysomnography (sleep study) and an upper airway ENT examination to evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea and adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

cards.q: Name three absolute contraindications to starting or continuing somatropin therapy in Prader-Willi Syndrome.
cards.a: Severe uncontrolled obesity, severe untreated obstructive sleep apnea, and active systemic respiratory tract infection.

cards.q: What is the standard recommended maintenance dose of somatropin for children with Prader-Willi Syndrome?
cards.a: 1.0 mg/m2/day (approximately 0.035 mg/kg/day), often initiated at 0.5 mg/m2/day and titrated upward.

cards.q: Beyond linear height, what major developmental benefits does early somatropin therapy confer on young children with PWS?
cards.a: Accelerated gross motor milestone achievement, increased physical stamina, and improved expressive language and cognitive developmental quotients.

cards.q: When should repeat polysomnography be performed after initiating somatropin in an infant or child with PWS?
cards.a: Within 6 to 12 weeks after treatment initiation, or promptly if new or worsening snoring or sleep apnea occurs.

cards.q: Contrast the classic congenital cardiovascular anomalies characteristic of Turner syndrome versus Noonan syndrome.
cards.a: Turner syndrome features left-sided lesions (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, aortic root dilation); Noonan syndrome features right-sided and myocardial lesions (pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

cards.q: What specific gene located in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1) of the X and Y chromosomes is responsible for the short stature in Turner syndrome and Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis?
cards.a: SHOX (Short Stature Homeobox gene), whose haploinsufficiency causes disproportionate short stature and mesomelia.

cards.q: Mutations in which pathway cause Noonan syndrome and explain the relative resistance to growth hormone?
cards.a: The RAS-MAPK signal transduction pathway (most commonly PTPN11 gain-of-function mutations encoding SHP2), which impairs post-receptor IGF-I generation.

cards.q: What non-aromatizable androgen can be co-administered with somatropin in Turner syndrome girls older than 9-10 years to augment final adult height?
cards.a: Oxandrolone, typically administered at a low dose of 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg/day to minimize virilizing side effects.

cards.q: What characteristic wrist abnormality is observed in adolescent females with SHOX mutations and Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis?
cards.a: Madelung deformity, featuring bowing of the distal radius, dorsal subluxation of the distal ulna, and triangular carpal wedging.

cards.q: Which autoimmune conditions occur with increased frequency in girls with Turner syndrome, requiring annual laboratory screening?
cards.a: Autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis (hypothyroidism) and celiac disease.

cards.q: What is the recommended somatropin dosage for girls with Turner syndrome to achieve optimal adult height catch-up?
cards.a: 0.35 to 0.375 mg/kg/week (approximately 50 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection.

cards.q: What biological processes define the 'transition period' in growth hormone management after linear growth ceases?
cards.a: The acquisition of peak bone mass, accrual of adult muscle mass, maturation of cardiac ventricular geometry, and stabilization of adult lipid and metabolic homeostasis.

cards.q: Which patients with childhood-onset GHD do NOT require provocative re-testing after epiphyseal closure before adult GH continuation?
cards.a: Patients with ≥3 other pituitary hormone deficiencies, severe proven genetic defects, or severe structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesions with serum IGF-I < -2.0 SDS.

cards.q: What peak growth hormone cutoff on the insulin tolerance test (ITT) confirms persistent severe GHD during the transition period versus older adulthood?
cards.a: Peak GH < 5.0 mcg/L in the transition period, compared to < 3.0 mcg/L in older adult life.

cards.q: How does adult growth hormone replacement dosing fundamentally differ from pediatric growth hormone replacement dosing?
cards.a: Adult dosing is non-weight-based, starting at low fixed doses (0.1-0.3 mg/day) and titrated individually based on serum IGF-I concentrations and tolerance.

cards.q: Why do adult females taking oral estrogen contraceptives or hormone replacement require higher growth hormone doses than males?
cards.a: Oral estrogens undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, inducing SOCS2 and suppressing hepatic GH-stimulated IGF-I production.

cards.q: What common adverse effects reflect excessive somatropin dosing in adults?
cards.a: Fluid retention, peripheral edema, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome, and worsening insulin resistance.

cards.q: What is the recommended target serum IGF-I concentration during long-term adult growth hormone replacement?
cards.a: Within the age- and sex-adjusted normal range, typically targeted between 0 and +1.0 SDS.

cards.q: What specific genetic mutation accounts for more than 98% of cases of achondroplasia?
cards.a: A heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, most commonly c.1138G>A (p.Gly380Arg), resulting in constitutive activation of the receptor tyrosine kinase.

cards.q: What pattern of limb shortening is characteristically observed in achondroplasia?
cards.a: Rhizomelic shortening, where proximal segments (femur and humerus) are disproportionately shorter than middle or distal segments.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of vosoritide, the FDA-approved medical therapy for achondroplasia?
cards.a: It is a recombinant C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog that binds NPR-B, stimulating cGMP to inhibit the hyperactive MAPK/ERK pathway downstream of mutated FGFR3.

cards.q: What anatomical narrowing in infants with achondroplasia carries a significant risk of cervicomedullary compression and sudden death?
cards.a: Foramen magnum stenosis, requiring baseline polysomnography and high-resolution neuroimaging (CT/MRI) of the craniocervical junction.

cards.q: What pathognomonic finding is seen on anteroposterior lumbar spine radiography in achondroplasia?
cards.a: Progressive caudal narrowing of the interpedicular distance from L1 to L5 (in contrast to normal widening).

cards.q: Mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2 cause what skeletal disorder characterized by bone fragility and blue sclerae?
cards.a: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), ranging from perinatal lethal type II to mild non-deforming type I.

cards.q: What distinct physical feature of the hands is typical in achondroplasia?
cards.a: A 'trident hand' configuration, characterized by short, broad digits with persistent divergence between the third and fourth fingers.

cards.q: What dynamic endocrine test confirms autonomous growth hormone hypersecretion in a child with tall stature?
cards.a: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT, 1.75 g/kg up to 75 g), demonstrating failure to suppress serum GH to < 1.0 mcg/L (or < 0.4 mcg/L on modern ultrasensitive assays).

cards.q: What infant-onset overgrowth syndrome features duplication of chromosome Xq26.3 involving the GPR101 gene, causing massive gigantism and hyperprolactinemia before age 5?
cards.a: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG), presenting with extreme early-onset linear acceleration and large pituitary adenomas or hyperplasia.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of pegvisomant in the medical management of refractory growth hormone excess?
cards.a: It is a genetically engineered growth hormone receptor antagonist that prevents GHR functional dimerization and blocks peripheral IGF-I generation.

cards.q: Which overgrowth syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of the NSD1 gene, characterized by macrocephaly, prominent forehead, pointed chin, and developmental delay?
cards.a: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism).

cards.q: What is the primary definitive first-line treatment for pediatric pituitary gigantism caused by a somatotroph adenoma?
cards.a: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary adenoma.

cards.q: What class of medications (e.g., octreotide, lanreotide) acts on somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) to inhibit pituitary GH secretion?
cards.a: Somatostatin receptor ligands (somatostatin analogs).

cards.q: What major cardiac pathology is the leading cause of premature mortality in patients with chronic, untreated growth hormone excess?
cards.a: Acromegalic cardiomyopathy, characterized by biventricular concentric hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and heart failure.

cards.q: What two biochemical parameters distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency from central/secondary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: Markedly elevated plasma ACTH and hyperkalemia (with elevated renin/low aldosterone) are present in primary AI, whereas central AI features low/inappropriately normal ACTH with preserved mineralocorticoid secretion and normal potassium.

cards.q: What peak serum cortisol threshold during a 250 mcg cosyntropin stimulation test is required to define normal adrenocortical reserve?
cards.a: A peak serum cortisol of ≥ 18 mcg/dL (approx 500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes.

cards.q: What is the initial intravenous hydrocortisone stress dose for an acute adrenal crisis in a school-aged child (ages 3–12 years)?
cards.a: 50 mg IV bolus (or 50 to 100 mg/m2 IV), accompanied by 20 mL/kg isotonic saline with 5–10% dextrose.

cards.q: What is the physiological daily maintenance hydrocortisone dose in pediatric adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: 8 to 10 mg/m2/day (divided into three doses, with the highest dose taken first thing in the morning).

cards.q: What oral medication and standard starting dose are utilized for mineralocorticoid replacement in primary adrenal failure?
cards.a: Fludrocortisone acetate at 0.05 to 0.2 mg orally once daily, adjusted by blood pressure and plasma renin activity.

cards.q: What X-linked peroxisomal disorder causes progressive primary adrenal insufficiency and neurocognitive regression in boys aged 4 to 10 years?
cards.a: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD), caused by ABCD1 mutations leading to accumulation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs).

cards.q: Why does cutaneous hyperpigmentation occur in primary adrenal failure but not in secondary adrenal failure?
cards.a: Lack of cortisol negative feedback drives massive pituitary POMC cleavage into ACTH and alpha-MSH, which bind melanocortin 1 receptors (MC1R) on dermal melanocytes.

cards.q: What enzyme deficiency accounts for more than 90% to 95% of all cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
cards.a: 21-Hydroxylase deficiency, caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the CYP21A2 gene on chromosome 6p21.3.

cards.q: At what age do male infants with undiagnosed classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically present with acute crisis?
cards.a: At 7 to 21 days (1 to 3 weeks) of life, presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock.

cards.q: What primary analyte is measured on newborn dried blood spots to screen for classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
cards.a: 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), with cutoffs adjusted for gestational age and birth weight to reduce false-positive rates in premature infants.

cards.q: Why is oral sodium chloride supplementation (1 to 2 g/day) specifically required in infants with classic salt-wasting CAH in addition to fludrocortisone?
cards.a: Immature neonatal renal tubules have reduced sensitivity to mineralocorticoids and high fractional sodium excretion, requiring exogenous sodium supplementation until dietary sodium intake increases.

cards.q: What benign tumor occurs in the testes of adolescent and adult males with classic CAH due to poor disease control?
cards.a: Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART), which can cause testicular pain, obstruction of seminiferous tubules, and irreversible azoospermia.

cards.q: Which rare form of CAH features severe virilization accompanied by low-renin hypertension and hypokalemia?
cards.a: 11-Beta-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP11B1), due to accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), a potent mineralocorticoid agonist.

cards.q: What newly characterized pathway accounts for persistent virilization in classic CAH despite suppression of conventional circulating androgens?
cards.a: The alternative 'backdoor pathway' (generating 11-oxygenated androgens like 11-ketotestosterone and 11-hydroxytestosterone from 17-OHP).

cards.q: What pathognomonic growth pattern distinguishes pediatric Cushing syndrome from simple nutritional/exogenous obesity?
cards.a: Excessive weight gain accompanied by severe linear growth deceleration or arrest (in contrast to simple obesity, where height velocity is accelerated and children are tall for age).

cards.q: What is the most frequent cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome in children under 5 years versus children older than 7 years?
cards.a: In children <5 years, primary adrenal tumors (adenomas and carcinomas) predominate; in children >7 years, ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas (Cushing disease) account for >75% to 85% of cases.

cards.q: Name the three approved first-line screening tests used to establish pathological hypercortisolemia in children.
cards.a: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC), late-night (23:00 h) salivary cortisol (on two separate nights), and the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test.

cards.q: What serum cortisol cutoff following an overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test excludes Cushing syndrome with high sensitivity?
cards.a: Serum cortisol < 1.8 mcg/dL (approx 50 nmol/L) measured at 08:00 h following dexamethasone administration.

cards.q: What invasive procedure is the diagnostic reference standard for distinguishing pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when pituitary MRI is equivocal?
cards.a: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation, demonstrating an IPS-to-peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2.0 at baseline or ≥3.0 post-CRH.

cards.q: What biochemical finding within 24 to 72 hours following transsphenoidal surgery indicates surgical cure of Cushing disease?
cards.a: Profound transient central adrenal insufficiency with morning serum cortisol < 1.0 to 2.0 mcg/dL.

cards.q: Which syndrome featuring primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), cardiac myxomas, and spotty skin pigmentation is caused by PRKAR1A mutations?
cards.a: Carney complex, an autosomal dominant disorder causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome with cyclical hypercortisolemia.

cards.q: What electrolyte and acid-base triad is classic for states of mineralocorticoid excess?
cards.a: Hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, usually accompanied by suppressed plasma renin activity.

cards.q: What paired screening test establishes the diagnosis of low-renin primary aldosteronism?
cards.a: The plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) to plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio, where PAC/PRA > 20 to 30 (with PAC > 15 ng/dL) is diagnostic.

cards.q: What unique genetic mechanism causes Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA / Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I)?
cards.a: An unequal crossing-over event creating a chimeric gene linking the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter to the aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) coding sequence.

cards.q: What enzyme protects the non-selective mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol activation by rapidly converting cortisol to cortisone?
cards.a: 11-Beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11beta-HSD2), encoded by the HSD11B2 gene.

cards.q: Why is Liddle syndrome completely unresponsive to spironolactone, and which drug class provides effective treatment?
cards.a: The mutation causes constitutive ENaC channel surface overexpression independent of the mineralocorticoid receptor; treatment requires direct ENaC channel blockers (amiloride or triamterene).

cards.q: What clinical differences distinguish autosomal dominant Renal PHA1 from autosomal recessive Systemic PHA1?
cards.a: Renal PHA1 (MR mutation) is restricted to the kidney and improves spontaneously with age; Systemic PHA1 (ENaC subunit mutations) affects sweat, salivary, and lung epithelia, causing severe lifelong salt wasting.

cards.q: What common pediatric clinical scenario produces transient secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA3) in young infants?
cards.a: Acute pyelonephritis (urinary tract infection) associated with underlying congenital obstructive uropathy (e.g., posterior urethral valves or hydronephrosis).

cards.q: What is the most frequent overall developmental cause of permanent congenital hypothyroidism, and what is its most common anatomical subtype?
cards.a: Thyroid dysgenesis accounts for 80-85% of permanent primary congenital hypothyroidism, with ectopic thyroid (sublingual/lingual gland located along the migratory path) being the most common subtype (responsible for ~60% of dysgenesis cases).

cards.q: What is the recommended initial daily starting dose of oral levothyroxine in neonates with confirmed congenital hypothyroidism?
cards.a: 10-15 mcg/kg/day (equivalent to 37.5 to 50 mcg/day for most term infants), aimed at rapidly restoring serum free T4 into the upper half of the normal reference range within 3-7 days.

cards.q: Why is routine neonatal blood-spot screening for congenital hypothyroidism ideally obtained between 24 and 48 hours of life rather than immediately at birth?
cards.a: A physiological surge in neonatal TSH occurs within 30 minutes of birth, peaking up to 60-80 mIU/L and declining over the subsequent 24-48 hours. Testing during this initial surge produces high rates of false-positive TSH elevations.

cards.q: Which infant dietary components and nutritional supplements significantly impair the gastrointestinal absorption of crushed oral levothyroxine?
cards.a: Soy-based infant formulas, oral iron supplements (ferrous sulfate), oral calcium carbonate/citrate, and aluminum-containing medications chelate levothyroxine in the gut and must not be administered concurrently.

cards.q: What diagnostic radiologic sign on a newborn knee film indicates significant intra-uterine prenatal thyroid hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Absence of the distal femoral epiphysis (which normally ossifies by 36-37 weeks of gestation) reflects severe, long-standing prenatal hypothyroidism in term neonates.

cards.q: What maternal autoimmune factor causes transient primary congenital hypothyroidism in offspring of mothers with autoimmune thyroid disease?
cards.a: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH receptor-blocking antibodies (TRBAb), which inhibit fetal TSH receptor activation and resolve spontaneously over 2-4 months as maternal IgG antibodies clear.

cards.q: At what age and under what conditions should a trial off levothyroxine be performed to establish whether congenital hypothyroidism is permanent?
cards.a: At age 3 years, provided thyroid tissue was identified in situ on neonatal imaging and dysgenesis/permanent genetic mutations have not been confirmed; levothyroxine is discontinued for 30 days to measure serum TSH and free T4.

cards.q: Why is propylthiouracil (PTU) strictly contraindicated as first-line medical therapy for hyperthyroidism in children?
cards.a: PTU carries a black-box FDA warning in pediatric patients due to high risks of idiosyncratic fulminant hepatic necrosis, liver failure, and death requiring emergent liver transplantation. Methimazole is the only recommended antithyroid drug.

cards.q: What life-threatening adverse reaction to methimazole requires immediate complete blood count monitoring and drug cessation if fever or severe pharyngitis develops?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count <500/mcL), which occurs in ~0.3-0.5% of treated patients and predisposes to rapid, fatal sepsis.

cards.q: What is Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome, and what is its pathophysiological mechanism?
cards.a: A syndrome of severe, long-standing primary juvenile hypothyroidism presenting paradoxically with precocious puberty (isosexual precocity in girls, macrorchidism without virilization in boys) caused by extreme TSH elevation cross-activating gonadal FSH receptors.

cards.q: What causes neonatal Graves' disease, and how long does the clinical condition typically persist in the infant?
cards.a: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-receptor-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI / TRAb); the hyperthyroidism persists for 2 to 4 months until circulating maternal IgG antibodies are cleared from neonatal circulation.

cards.q: How does childhood Graves' disease affect linear growth and skeletal maturation compared to childhood hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Graves' disease accelerates linear growth velocity and advances skeletal maturation (accelerated bone age), whereas hypothyroidism profoundly decelerates linear growth velocity and delays bone age.

cards.q: Which circulating autoantibodies are most sensitive for confirming the diagnosis of Hashimoto thyroiditis in a child with a goiter?
cards.a: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies (>90-95% sensitive) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-TG) antibodies.

cards.q: What is the typical maintenance dosage of levothyroxine in an adolescent with overt Hashimoto hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Approximately 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day (typically 75 to 125 mcg once daily orally on an empty stomach).

cards.q: What is the earliest and most common circulating thyroid hormone alteration in non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS)?
cards.a: Low total and free triiodothyronine (T3) accompanied by elevated reverse T3 (rT3) ('low T3 syndrome'), caused by impaired 5'-deiodination of T4 to T3 and increased clearance to rT3.

cards.q: Which deiodinase enzyme is pathologically upregulated in peripheral tissues during severe systemic illness, driving the conversion of T4 into inactive reverse T3?
cards.a: Type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO3), which mediates inner-ring deiodination of T4 to rT3 and degrades active T3 to inactive 3,3'-T2.

cards.q: How does serum reverse T3 (rT3) distinguish severe non-thyroidal illness syndrome from central (pituitary) hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Reverse T3 is typically elevated or high-normal in NTIS (due to increased DIO3 activity and reduced rT3 clearance), whereas rT3 is low in central hypothyroidism (due to low substrate T4 secretion without peripheral shunting).

cards.q: What transient biochemical phenomenon occurs in serum TSH during clinical recovery from critical non-thyroidal illness?
cards.a: A transient rebound elevation of serum TSH (frequently 5-15 mIU/L) occurs as hypothalamic-pituitary suppression resolves, which normalizes spontaneously and should not be misdiagnosed as permanent primary hypothyroidism.

cards.q: Is routine thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3) recommended for critically ill pediatric patients with low T3/T4 in NTIS?
cards.a: No. Randomized controlled trials show no clinical benefit in mortality or ICU length of stay, and guidelines recommend against routine replacement therapy; management focuses on treating the underlying illness.

cards.q: Which common intensive care medications directly suppress pituitary TSH secretion, exacerbating low TSH levels in critically ill children?
cards.a: Dopamine infusions and high-dose exogenous glucocorticoids directly inhibit pituitary thyrotrope TSH release.

cards.q: What is the clinical prognostic significance of a profoundly depressed free T4 level in a child with severe critical illness?
cards.a: Profound reduction in free T4 correlates directly with illness severity, multi-organ failure, and increased risk of intensive care mortality.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in the classic form of resistance to thyroid hormone (RTH-beta), and what is its mode of inheritance?
cards.a: THRB gene (encoding thyroid hormone receptor beta), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with a dominant-negative effect (or occurring as de novo mutations).

cards.q: What is the hallmark circulating thyroid hormone pattern in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta)?
cards.a: Elevated serum free T4 and free T3 accompanied by an inappropriately normal or mildly elevated serum TSH concentration.

cards.q: What neuroendocrine tumor must be differentiated from RTH-beta, and what biochemical ratio helps confirm the tumor?
cards.a: TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (TSHoma); an elevated glycoprotein alpha-subunit concentration and alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio (>1.0) strongly favor a TSHoma.

cards.q: Why do patients with RTH-beta frequently suffer from resting tachycardia despite generalized peripheral tissue hormone resistance?
cards.a: Cardiac myocytes predominantly express the TR-alpha isoform (encoded by THRA), which is normal in RTH-beta; high circulating thyroid hormones therefore over-stimulate cardiac TR-alpha, causing tachycardia and palpitations.

cards.q: What is the biochemical and clinical phenotype of Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (MCT8 transporter deficiency)?
cards.a: X-linked severe neurodevelopmental disability, central hypotonia, progressive spastic quadriplegia, and dystonia, with a biochemical profile of markedly elevated free T3, low free T4, and normal/slightly elevated TSH.

cards.q: How does the thyroid hormone profile in RTH-alpha (THRA mutation) differ from classic RTH-beta?
cards.a: RTH-alpha features normal or near-normal TSH, low or low-normal free T4, high or high-normal free T3 (markedly low FT4/FT3 ratio), and very low reverse T3, accompanied by severe skeletal dysplasia and constipation.

cards.q: What thyroid hormone analog with high affinity for TR-beta can be used in symptomatic RTH-beta to suppress elevated TSH and reduce goiter size?
cards.a: Tiratricol (TRIAC / 3,5,3'-triiodothyroacetic acid), which binds TR-beta with higher relative affinity than T3 to inhibit pituitary TSH secretion without aggravating peripheral hyperthyroidism.

cards.q: How does the malignancy risk of a discrete thyroid nodule in a pediatric patient compare with that in an adult?
cards.a: A discrete pediatric thyroid nodule carries a significantly higher malignancy rate: ~22-26% in children compared to only 5-10% in adults.

cards.q: Which ultrasound characteristics of a thyroid nodule are most strongly associated with malignancy?
cards.a: Marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular/infiltrative margins, taller-than-wide geometry, absence of a halo, extrathyroidal extension, and abnormal cervical lymph nodes.

cards.q: When is ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy indicated for a pediatric thyroid nodule?
cards.a: For any solid nodule >=1 cm with suspicious sonographic features, any nodule associated with suspicious cervical lymph nodes, or a growing nodule in high-risk patients (e.g., prior head/neck radiation).

cards.q: What is the most prevalent histological type of differentiated thyroid cancer in pediatric patients, and what is its typical pattern of metastatic spread?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC, 80-90% of cases); it characteristically spreads early to regional cervical lymph nodes (40-80%) and hematogenously to the lungs (10-20%).

cards.q: What germline mutation causes hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in MEN2A and MEN2B, and what is the timing for prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2B?
cards.a: Gain-of-function RET proto-oncogene mutations; in MEN2B (codon M918T), prophylactic total thyroidectomy is recommended during the first year of life (within the first months of life) due to virulent early metastatic spread.

cards.q: What is the recommended surgical extent for pediatric differentiated thyroid cancer to minimize recurrence and facilitate radioiodine ablation?
cards.a: Total or near-total thyroidectomy coupled with central neck (level VI) lymph node dissection performed by a high-volume pediatric thyroid surgeon.

cards.q: What serum protein serves as the primary tumor marker for surveillance following total thyroidectomy and 131I ablation in differentiated thyroid cancer?
cards.a: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg), monitored alongside anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies (which can falsely suppress immunoassay measurements of Tg).

cards.q: What is the recommended dose and administration protocol for intravenous calcium gluconate in acute symptomatic hypocalcemia with tetany or seizures?
cards.a: Intravenous 10% calcium gluconate at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg; maximum 1-2 g or 10-20 mL) infused slowly over 10 to 20 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring to avoid bradycardia or cardiac arrest.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the targeted serum calcium level in children with chronic hypoparathyroidism on calcitriol and oral calcium therapy?
cards.a: Low-normal serum calcium (8.5-9.0 mg/dL), keeping the 24-hour urine calcium excretion <4 mg/kg/day (urine Ca/Cr ratio <0.2) to prevent nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What biochemical index distinguishes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) from primary hyperparathyroidism, and what is its cutoff value?
cards.a: The urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR); a ratio <0.01 strongly indicates FHH, whereas primary hyperparathyroidism typically displays CCCR >0.02.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What receptor mutation is responsible for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) and neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT)?
cards.a: Heterozygous loss-of-function/inactivating mutations in the CaSR gene cause FHH; homozygous or compound heterozygous inactivating mutations cause life-threatening NSHPT.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What characteristic electrocardiographic intervals reflect acute hypocalcemia and severe acute hypercalcemia, respectively?
cards.a: Acute hypocalcemia produces prolonged QTc interval (prolonged ST segment), whereas hypercalcemia produces shortened QTc interval.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the mechanism of hypercalcemia associated with subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn?
cards.a: Unregulated extra-renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) by activated macrophages within the inflammatory subcutaneous granulomas.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Which classes of medications are utilized in the acute inpatient treatment of severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (calcium >14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Vigorous IV 0.9% normal saline hyperhydration, loop diuretics (furosemide, only after volume restoration), IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate), and calcitonin.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What gene is mutated in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH), and what is its mode of inheritance?
cards.a: PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase homolog, X-linked) on chromosome Xp22.1; inherited in an X-linked dominant manner.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: How does elevated FGF23 affect renal tubular phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D metabolism?
cards.a: FGF23 downregulates NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters, causing renal phosphate wasting, and simultaneously inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) while inducing 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1), lowering 1,25-(OH)2D.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is burosumab, and what is its dosing schedule in pediatric patients with XLH?
cards.a: A fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting intact FGF23; administered subcutaneously at 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (titrated up to 2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks based on serum phosphate).
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Why is calcitriol contraindicated in hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH; SLC34A3 mutation)?
cards.a: In HHRH, FGF23 is suppressed, causing endogenous 1,25-(OH)2D to be markedly elevated; exogenous calcitriol would cause severe hypercalcemia, torrential hypercalciuria, and nephrolithiasis.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What distinctive dental pathology frequently leads to the initial diagnosis of XLH in early childhood?
cards.a: Spontaneous non-traumatic periapical dental abscesses occurring in caries-free primary teeth, caused by defective dentin mineralization with enlarged pulp chambers allowing bacterial tracking.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What diagnostic calculation establishes renal phosphate wasting in a hypophosphatemic child?
cards.a: Reduced tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per unit GFR (TmP/GFR), calculated from fasting simultaneous serum and urine phosphate and creatinine concentrations.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What molecular defects cause Hyperphosphatemic Familial Tumoral Calcinosis (HFTC)?
cards.a: Inactivating biallelic mutations in FGF23, GALNT3 (polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 3), or KL (Klotho), resulting in FGF23 deficiency/resistance, severe hyperphosphatemia, and ectopic periarticular calcifications.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Why is serum calcium characteristically normal in Stage 2 calcipenic nutritional rickets?
cards.a: Secondary hyperparathyroidism mobilizes calcium from bone and increases renal tubular reabsorption to normalize serum calcium, at the expense of PTH-induced renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphatemia.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What are the cardinal radiographic signs of active rickets seen at the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses?
cards.a: Widening of the physis, fraying (ragged margins), cupping (concave metaphyseal contour), and splaying (transverse expansion) of the metaphysis, with loss of the provisional zone of calcification.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the recommended daily dosage and duration of oral vitamin D for treating nutritional rickets in children over 12 months of age?
cards.a: 3000 to 6000 IU daily of oral cholecalciferol (D3) or ergocalciferol (D2) for 8 to 12 weeks, combined with 500 mg daily of elemental calcium, followed by 400-600 IU daily maintenance.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Why must oral elemental calcium supplementation always accompany vitamin D therapy when initiating treatment for nutritional rickets?
cards.a: Rapid skeletal remineralization ('hungry bone syndrome') drives circulating calcium into healing osteoid, which can precipitate severe, symptomatic hypocalcemia and tetany if calcium is not co-administered.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What enzymatic defect causes Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets Type 1A (VDDR1A), and what is its specific pharmacotherapy?
cards.a: Inactivating biallelic mutations in CYP27B1 (renal 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase); treated with physiological doses of active calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D, 20-40 ng/kg/day).
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is craniotabes, and in what pediatric age group is it the earliest physical manifestation of rickets?
cards.a: Softening and ping-pong ball-like indentability of the cranial vault bones (parietal/occipital); it is the earliest clinical sign in young infants under 3-6 months of age.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the earliest radiographic indicator of therapeutic response during medical treatment of rickets?
cards.a: Appearance of a dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphyseal growth plate margin, typically visible within 2 to 4 weeks.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Why does maternal transmission of a GNAS mutation produce multihormone resistance in PHP-1A, whereas paternal transmission produces PPHP without hormone resistance?
cards.a: GNAS undergoes tissue-specific maternal expression in the renal proximal tubule, thyroid, and pituitary; maternal mutations ablate Gs-alpha in these tissues, whereas paternal mutations leave the active maternal allele intact.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What physical features define the Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) phenotype?
cards.a: Short adult stature, rounded facies, early-onset centripetal obesity, brachydactyly (shortening of 4th and 5th metacarpals/metatarsals, dimple sign), subcutaneous heterotopic ossifications, and variable cognitive impairment.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What circulating biochemical profile defines untreated pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and markedly elevated intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, reflecting end-organ renal proximal tubular resistance to PTH.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What clinical feature distinguishes Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) from the subcutaneous ossifications seen in classic PHP-1A?
cards.a: POH features aggressive, progressive heterotopic ossification that penetrates deeply through the dermis into subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle, tendons, and deep fascia, severely restricting joint mobility.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Which endocrine hormone axes besides PTH frequently exhibit hormone resistance in children with PHP-1A?
cards.a: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (elevated TSH), growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH resistance with GH deficiency), and gonadotropins (LH/FSH resistance with delayed puberty/amenorrhea).
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What active vitamin D medication is essential to treat PTH resistance in PHP-1A and PHP-1B, and what is its starting dosage?
cards.a: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) at 20-40 ng/kg/day (typically 0.25 to 1.0 mcg daily in divided doses) combined with oral elemental calcium.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What consensus classification term established in 2016 unifies PHP, PPHP, POH, and acrodysostosis into a single diagnostic continuum?
cards.a: Inactivating PTH/PTHrP signaling disorders (iPPSD).
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What two clinical scenarios satisfy the ISCD pediatric diagnostic definition of osteoporosis?
cards.a: (1) One or more low-trauma vertebral compression fractures alone; OR (2) A clinically significant fracture history (>=2 long-bone fractures by 10 yr, or >=3 by 19 yr) PLUS a DXA Z-score <= -2.0 adjusted for size.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Can a low DXA bone mineral density Z-score (<= -2.0) alone be used to diagnose osteoporosis in a child?
cards.a: No. The diagnosis requires a documented low-trauma fracture history alongside the low DXA score (or a vertebral fracture regardless of DXA); a low Z-score alone represents 'low bone mineral mass for chronological age'.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the typical dose and administration schedule for intravenous zoledronic acid in pediatric osteoporosis?
cards.a: 0.025 to 0.05 mg/kg per dose (maximum 4 mg) administered as an intravenous infusion over 30-45 minutes once every 6 months.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What is the acute phase reaction associated with the first dose of intravenous bisphosphonates in children?
cards.a: Transient high fever, influenza-like myalgias, nausea, and mild hypocalcemia within 24-48 hours of infusion, mediated by inflammatory cytokine release from gamma-delta T cells.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What collagen genes are mutated in over 85-90% of individuals with classic osteogenesis imperfecta?
cards.a: COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode the pro-alpha1(I) and pro-alpha2(I) chains of type I collagen, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: Why do growing children with vertebral compression fractures respond more favorably to bisphosphonate therapy than adults?
cards.a: Growing vertebrae undergo endochondral ossification at the superior and inferior growth plates; bisphosphonate-stabilized trabeculae allow newly formed bone to reshape and rebuild vertebral height.
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What grading system is standardly used on lateral spine imaging to evaluate pediatric vertebral compression fractures?
cards.a: The modified Genant semi-quantitative visual scale, assessing anterior, middle, and posterior vertebral height reductions (grade 1: 20-25%; grade 2: 25-40%; grade 3: >40%).
cards.group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

cards.q: What chronological age cutoffs define delayed puberty in girls and boys, respectively?
cards.a: Lack of breast development (Tanner 2 thelarche) by age 13.0 years in girls; lack of testicular enlargement (volume <4 mL) by age 14.0 years in boys.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What clinical and radiographic findings characterize constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)?
cards.a: Family history of delayed puberty, delayed bone age matching height age, prepubertal growth velocity appropriate for bone age, normal predicted adult height, and eventual spontaneous pubertal completion.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What clinical feature uniquely differentiates Kallmann syndrome from normosmic congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?
cards.a: Anosmia or hyposmia (loss of smell), caused by embryonic failure of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons to migrate together from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What are the classic karyotypes and gonadal features of Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome?
cards.a: Turner syndrome is 45,X with streak gonads and ovarian failure; Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY with small, firm testes (<4 mL) and hypergonadotropic azoospermia.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: Why must progesterone therapy be delayed for at least 18-24 months when inducing puberty with estrogen in girls with primary hypogonadism?
cards.a: Premature progesterone exposure antagonizes estrogen-stimulated ductile branching, resulting in abnormal, tubular breast morphology, and interrupts maximal uterine growth.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the initial low-dose depot testosterone regimen used to promote pubertal onset in adolescent boys with constitutional delay?
cards.a: Intramuscular testosterone enanthate or cypionate 25 to 50 mg once monthly for 3 to 6 months, which accelerates linear growth and secondary sex characteristics without premature epiphyseal fusion.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: How does serum gonadotropin (LH/FSH) measurement differentiate primary from secondary hypogonadism?
cards.a: Elevated LH and FSH indicate primary (hypergonadotropic) gonadal failure, whereas low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH indicate central (hypogonadotropic) failure.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What chronological age cutoffs define precocious puberty in girls and boys, respectively?
cards.a: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.0 years in girls (thelarche or pubarche) or before age 9.0 years in boys (testicular volume >=4 mL).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: How does the likelihood of an identifiable central nervous system etiology in central precocious puberty differ between boys and girls?
cards.a: In girls, >85-90% of CPP is idiopathic; in boys, 40-75% of CPP is secondary to an identifiable intracranial lesion, mandating routine brain MRI in all affected males.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What biochemical result on a GnRH stimulation test confirms the diagnosis of central precocious puberty?
cards.a: A post-stimulation peak LH concentration >5.0 IU/L (or an ultrasensitive basal morning LH >0.2-0.3 IU/L), demonstrating activation of the pituitary gonadotropes.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What classic neurological seizure type is uniquely associated with hypothalamic hamartomas in young children with central precocious puberty?
cards.a: Gelastic seizures, characterized by involuntary, paroxysmal, unprovoked bouts of hollow laughter or smirking, often emerging in infancy.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What gene mutation is the most frequent cause of familial central precocious puberty, and what is its mode of transmission?
cards.a: Loss-of-function mutations in MKRN3 (makorin ring finger protein 3), a maternally imprinted gene that causes CPP only when inherited from the father (paternal transmission).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders
