cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide, histrelin) in treating central precocious puberty?
cards.a: Continuous, non-pulsatile stimulation of pituitary GnRH receptors, causing receptor downregulation, uncoupling, and profound suppression of LH and FSH secretion.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What triad of clinical features defines McCune-Albright syndrome presenting with peripheral precocious puberty?
cards.a: Autonomous recurrent estrogen-secreting ovarian follicular cysts, large café-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia of bone.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the most urgent medical emergency to exclude in a newborn infant presenting with atypical genitalia and bilateral non-palpable gonads?
cards.a: Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) in a virilized 46,XX infant, which can precipitate fatal salt-wasting shock within 1-2 weeks of life.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: Which testicular hormone is responsible for the regression of Müllerian ducts (uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina) in male fetal development?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH / Müllerian-inhibiting substance), synthesized and secreted by fetal Sertoli cells.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What biochemical test and ratio confirm the diagnosis of 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency in an infant with 46,XY DSD?
cards.a: An hCG stimulation test demonstrating an abnormally elevated plasma testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (T:DHT) ratio (>20-30:1).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What internal and external anatomical findings characterize an adolescent with Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)?
cards.a: Phenotypic female external genitalia with a blind-ending vagina, absent uterus and fallopian tubes, absent pubic/axillary hair, normal female breast development, and testes located in the abdomen or labia.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: Why is prophylactic gonadectomy recommended in individuals with 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis who have intra-abdominal dysgenetic gonads?
cards.a: Dysgenetic gonadal tissue containing Y-chromosomal material (TSPY) carries a 15-40% lifetime risk of developing malignant germ cell tumors (gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What clinical staging scale is standardly utilized to quantify the degree of genital virilization in female infants with CAH?
cards.a: The Prader staging scale (Prader stages 1 to 5, ranging from mild clitoromegaly [stage 1] to a completely virilized penile urethra with fused scrotum and absent palpable gonads [stage 5]).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What enzyme mediates the peripheral conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) required for external male genital virilization?
cards.a: Type 2 5-alpha-reductase, encoded by the SRD5A2 gene.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What two mandatory criteria are required to establish the diagnosis of PCOS in an adolescent?
cards.a: Both (1) Ovulatory dysfunction / menstrual irregularity abnormal for gynecological age AND (2) Clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism; ultrasound morphology is excluded.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: Why is polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound excluded from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS in adolescents?
cards.a: Multifollicular ovarian morphology is a normal, physiological finding in up to 30-40% of healthy, ovulating post-menarchal teenagers and has high false-positive rates.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the first-line medical therapy for menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in adolescent PCOS?
cards.a: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) containing low-dose ethinyl estradiol and a non-androgenic progestin, which restore regular bleeding, raise SHBG, and lower free testosterone.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What baseline test is used to rule out non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (NCAH) in an adolescent with hyperandrogenism?
cards.a: Early morning (8 AM) follicular-phase serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP); a value <200 ng/dL reliably excludes 21-hydroxylase deficiency NCAH.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What antiandrogenic medication is added to COCs if moderate-to-severe hirsutism does not improve after 6 months, and what is its dosage?
cards.a: Spironolactone at 50 to 100 mg orally twice daily (must be paired with contraception due to the risk of feminization of a male fetus).
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What are the acceptable lower and upper limits of menstrual cycle length in adolescents during the first 3 years after menarche?
cards.a: 21 to 45 days; any cycle shorter than 21 days or longer than 45 days (or an interval >90 days) is clinically abnormal.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What clinical and biochemical 'red flags' suggest an androgen-secreting neoplasm rather than adolescent PCOS?
cards.a: Rapid virilization (clitoromegaly, voice deepening, temporal balding) accompanied by serum total testosterone >150-200 ng/dL or DHEAS >700-800 mcg/dL.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for pediatric macroprolactinomas, and what is its dosing schedule?
cards.a: Cabergoline, a selective D2 dopamine receptor agonist, administered orally at 0.25 to 0.5 mg once or twice weekly.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the 'hook effect' in prolactin immunoassays, and how is it resolved in patients with large pituitary macroadenomas?
cards.a: Extremely high prolactin levels (>10,000 mcg/L) saturate assay antibodies, causing falsely low measured prolactin; it is resolved by performing assay testing on a 1:100 diluted serum sample.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is the typical upper limit of serum prolactin elevation caused by the 'stalk effect' (pituitary stalk compression by non-prolactinoma tumors)?
cards.a: Serum prolactin is almost universally less than 100 to 150 mcg/L (ng/mL); prolactin concentrations >200-250 mcg/L indicate a true prolactinoma.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What is macroprolactinemia, and what chemical laboratory method is used to diagnose it?
cards.a: Circulating biologically inactive prolactin-IgG autoantibody complexes; diagnosed by polyethylene glycol (PEG) serum precipitation to measure free monomeric prolactin.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: Why does severe untreated primary hypothyroidism frequently cause hyperprolactinemia?
cards.a: Elevated hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) acts as a prolactin-releasing factor, directly stimulating pituitary lactotropes to synthesize and release prolactin.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What are the most frequent presenting manifestations of macroprolactinomas in adolescent males?
cards.a: Headaches, bitemporal visual field loss, delayed puberty, arrested linear growth, and hypogonadism; galactorrhea is uncommon in males.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: When is transsphenoidal neurosurgery indicated in pediatric prolactinomas instead of dopamine agonist therapy?
cards.a: When tumors are completely refractory or intolerant to maximal dopamine agonist therapy, or in cases of acute pituitary apoplexy with sudden severe visual failure.
cards.group: V: Pediatric Pubertal and Reproductive Disorders

cards.q: What diagnostic critical blood analytes must be drawn at the moment of documented hypoglycemia (glucose <50 mg/dL) before giving dextrose?
cards.a: Plasma glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB), free fatty acids (FFA), lactate, cortisol, growth hormone, acylcarnitine profile, and carnitine, plus urine for organic acids and ketones.

cards.q: What glycemic response during a glucagon stimulation test at the time of hypoglycemia confirms hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: An increase in plasma glucose >30 mg/dL within 40 minutes of glucagon administration (1 mg IV/IM), reflecting inappropriate hepatic glycogen retention mediated by insulin.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of diazoxide in congenital hyperinsulinism, and what diuretic must be co-prescribed?
cards.a: Diazoxide opens beta-cell K-ATP channels to hyperpolarize the membrane and inhibit insulin exocytosis; chlorothiazide must be co-administered to prevent fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: What genes encode the beta-cell K-ATP channel implicated in the most common forms of congenital hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: ABCC8 (encoding the SUR1 regulatory subunit) and KCNJ11 (encoding the Kir6.2 pore-forming subunit) on chromosome 11p15.1.

cards.q: What imaging modality specifically localizes a resectable focal pancreatic lesion in congenital hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA positron emission tomography / computed tomography (18F-DOPA PET/CT).

cards.q: How does fatty acid oxidation disorder (e.g., MCAD deficiency) present during fasting compared to ketotic hypoglycemia?
cards.a: FAOD presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia (low ketones despite fasting) with elevated free fatty acids and dicarboxylic aciduria, whereas ketotic hypoglycemia displays high ketones (BOHB >2.5-3.0 mmol/L).

cards.q: What is the initial intravenous dextrose bolus dose and fluid choice for acute pediatric hypoglycemia?
cards.a: Intravenous 10% dextrose (D10W) at 2 mL/kg (equivalent to 200 mg/kg elemental dextrose) infused over 2-3 minutes.

cards.q: What three biochemical criteria define diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (venous pH <7.30 or bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L), and ketosis (blood BOHB >=3.0 mmol/L or moderate/large ketonuria).

cards.q: Why is an intravenous bolus of regular insulin strictly contraindicated when initiating DKA therapy?
cards.a: An IV insulin bolus precipitates rapid osmotic fluid shifts and acute hypokalemia, significantly increasing the risk of fatal cerebral edema; continuous infusion without a bolus is mandatory.

cards.q: What is the emergency medical therapy for acute cerebral edema complicating pediatric DKA?
cards.a: Intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3 to 5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or intravenous 20% mannitol (0.5 to 1.0 g/kg over 20 minutes), administered immediately without awaiting head CT.

cards.q: Which islet autoantibodies are standardly evaluated to confirm the autoimmune etiology of type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: GAD65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase-65), IA-2 (insulinoma-associated protein-2), IAA (insulin autoantibodies), and ZnT8 (zinc transporter 8).

cards.q: At what circulating blood glucose threshold should dextrose (5-10%) be added to intravenous fluids during DKA management?
cards.a: When blood glucose decreases to 250 to 300 mg/dL, in order to maintain glucose between 150-200 mg/dL while continuing insulin to clear acidosis and ketosis.

cards.q: What are the internationally recommended Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) targets for youth with type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL) >70%, Time Below Range (<70 mg/dL) <4%, and Time Below 54 mg/dL <1%.

cards.q: Which two autoimmune conditions require regular routine screening in all children with type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis, screening with TSH and anti-TPO) and Celiac disease (screening with tissue transglutaminase IgA [tTG-IgA] and total IgA).

cards.q: How does the annual rate of pancreatic beta-cell decline in youth-onset type 2 diabetes compare to adult-onset type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: Youth-onset T2D exhibits a 20-35% annual loss of beta-cell function (~4 times faster than adults), leading to rapid treatment failure and early insulin dependence.

cards.q: What laboratory findings define Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: Severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, and absence of significant ketoacidosis (venous pH >7.25-7.30, bicarbonate >15 mmol/L).

cards.q: What is the initial medical therapy for an asymptomatic adolescent diagnosed with T2D, HbA1c 7.6%, and no ketosis?
cards.a: Oral metformin (initiated at 500 mg daily, titrated to 2000 mg/day divided twice daily) combined with diet and lifestyle modifications.

cards.q: When is initial basal insulin therapy mandated at the time of diagnosis in pediatric type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: When blood glucose is >=250 mg/dL or HbA1c is >=8.5% at presentation, or whenever ketosis or acidosis is present.

cards.q: Which GLP-1 receptor agonists are FDA-approved for glycemic control and weight reduction in youth aged >=10 years with T2D?
cards.a: Liraglutide (once daily SC), dulaglutide (once weekly SC), and exenatide extended-release (once weekly SC).

cards.q: Why must pancreatic islet autoantibodies be checked in all overweight youth presenting with clinical features of T2D?
cards.a: To exclude autoimmune type 1 diabetes (or latent autoimmune diabetes), which occurs in ~10-15% of obese youth and requires lifelong intensive insulin therapy.

cards.q: At what point should screening for diabetic nephropathy and retinopathy begin in youth with type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: At the time of initial diagnosis (and annually thereafter), because microvascular complications frequently develop prior to clinical detection in youth.

cards.q: At what two specific pediatric age intervals is universal lipid screening officially recommended by the AAP and NHLBI?
cards.a: Once between ages 9 and 11 years, and once between ages 17 and 21 years.

cards.q: What is the defined threshold for an 'elevated' LDL cholesterol level in children and adolescents?
cards.a: LDL-C >=130 mg/dL (>=3.4 mmol/L); acceptable is <110 mg/dL, and borderline is 110-129 mg/dL.

cards.q: At what persistent LDL-C level is statin pharmacotherapy indicated in a 12-year-old child without other cardiovascular risk factors?
cards.a: LDL-C persistently >=190 mg/dL despite a 6-month trial of dietary and lifestyle modification.

cards.q: What circulating triglyceride threshold indicates high risk for acute pancreatitis requiring immediate medical and dietary intervention?
cards.a: Serum triglycerides >=1000 mg/dL (and especially >2000 mg/dL), representing massive chylomicronemia.

cards.q: What is the most common gene mutated in autosomal dominant heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH)?
cards.a: The LDLR gene (encoding the low-density lipoprotein receptor), accounting for >85-90% of identified mutations.

cards.q: What physical examination finding is pathognomonic for severe heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in older children?
cards.a: Tendon xanthomas, particularly nodular thickening of the Achilles tendons and extensor tendons of the hands.

cards.q: What is the foundational dietary therapy for children with familial chylomicronemia syndrome (LPL deficiency)?
cards.a: Extreme restriction of dietary fat to less than 10-15% of total daily caloric intake (typically <15-20 grams of fat per day).

cards.q: What characteristic discordance occurs in the growth hormone axis in patients with anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Elevated circulating growth hormone (GH) levels paired with low serum IGF-1 concentrations, reflecting starvation-induced hepatic growth hormone resistance.

cards.q: What thyroid hormone pattern defines the non-thyroidal illness syndrome seen in anorexia nervosa, and should it be treated?
cards.a: Low total and free T3, elevated reverse T3, and normal/low-normal T4 and TSH ('low T3 syndrome'); it is an adaptive conservation state and thyroid hormone replacement is contraindicated.

cards.q: Why is transdermal 17-beta estradiol superior to combined oral contraceptive pills for restoring bone density in adolescents with anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Transdermal estradiol bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, preserving liver IGF-1 synthesis, whereas oral ethinyl estradiol suppresses hepatic IGF-1, preventing bone accretion.

cards.q: How does 'pseudo-GH deficiency' in childhood obesity differ biochemically from true organic growth hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Obese children show blunted GH peaks on provocative stimulation testing, but have normal serum IGF-1 levels and normal or accelerated linear growth velocity.

cards.q: What circulating alterations in leptin and adiponectin characterize obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction?
cards.a: Elevated serum leptin (reflecting adipocyte expansion and central leptin resistance) and decreased serum adiponectin.

cards.q: How does the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis respond to chronic starvation in anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Hypercortisolemia develops with elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol and loss of diurnal rhythm, driven by increased hypothalamic CRH drive and impaired hepatic cortisol breakdown.

cards.q: Which GLP-1 receptor agonist is FDA-approved for chronic weight management in pediatric patients aged >=12 years with obesity?
cards.a: Semaglutide 2.4 mg administered subcutaneously once weekly (and liraglutide 3.0 mg daily).

cards.q: What are the updated international consensus terms for central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D) for central DI, and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R) for nephrogenic DI.

cards.q: What are the three distinct chronological phases of the triphasic response following pituitary neurosurgery?
cards.a: Phase 1 (days 1-2): acute polyuria (axonal shock); Phase 2 (days 3-7): transient SIADH with hyponatremia (uncontrolled AVP leak from dying axons); Phase 3 (day 8+): permanent AVP-D.

cards.q: What is the most frequent genetic defect in congenital AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI), and what is its inheritance?
cards.a: Inactivating mutations in the AVPR2 gene (encoding the V2 vasopressin receptor), inherited in an X-linked recessive manner (>90% of congenital cases).

cards.q: What circulating peptide biomarker has emerged as the gold standard to differentiate AVP deficiency from AVP resistance without prolonged water deprivation?
cards.a: Plasma copeptin (the C-terminal fragment of the AVP precursor); basal levels >21.4 pmol/L diagnose AVP-R, while stimulated levels <4.9 pmol/L confirm AVP-D.

cards.q: What critical administration rule must be observed when dosing desmopressin (DDAVP) to avoid severe water intoxication?
cards.a: Each dose must be withheld until a distinct breakthrough period of polyuria occurs, verifying water excretion and preventing life-threatening hyponatremia.

cards.q: What characteristic finding on T1-weighted cranial MRI is typically absent in patients with AVP deficiency?
cards.a: The hyperintense 'posterior pituitary bright spot' (which represents stored phospholipid-vesicle bound vasopressin) is absent in AVP-D.

cards.q: What pharmacological combination is used to treat congenital AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)?
cards.a: A low-sodium diet combined with a thiazide diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide) and either amiloride or indomethacin.

cards.q: What three cardinal clinical features comprise the diagnostic triad of Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1 / APECED)?
cards.a: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), chronic hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease); diagnosis requires >=2 of 3 (or 1 in a sibling).

cards.q: What gene is mutated in APS-1, and what is its physiological role in the immune system?
cards.a: The AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3; it mediates ectopic expression of peripheral self-antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells for negative selection of autoreactive T cells.

cards.q: What neutralizing circulating autoantibodies are present in >95-100% of APS-1 patients from early childhood, serving as a first-line diagnostic biomarker?
cards.a: Autoantibodies against type I interferons, specifically anti-interferon-omega (IFN-omega) and anti-interferon-alpha2 (IFN-alpha2).

cards.q: What endocrine components distinguish APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome) from APS-1?
cards.a: APS-2 requires primary adrenal insufficiency plus autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes, but characteristically lacks chronic candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy.

cards.q: What classic triad of symptoms characterizes IPEX syndrome in male infants, and what gene is mutated?
cards.a: Intractable secretory enteropathy (diarrhea), neonatal type 1 diabetes, and severe eczematous dermatitis, caused by hemizygous mutations in the FOXP3 gene.

cards.q: What dental enamel abnormality is present in over 80% of children with APS-1?
cards.a: Enamel hypoplasia, characterized by horizontal pitting, grooving, and thinning of the enamel of the permanent dentition.

cards.q: When a patient presents with concurrent untreated primary adrenal insufficiency and severe hypothyroidism, which hormone must be replaced first?
cards.a: Hydrocortisone MUST be initiated before or concurrently with levothyroxine; starting levothyroxine alone accelerates hepatic cortisol metabolism and precipitates fatal adrenal crisis.

cards.q: What three major endocrine organ systems are characteristically affected in Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)?
cards.a: Parathyroid glands (multigland hyperplasia), Pancreatic enteroneuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma), and Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma, somatotropinoma).

cards.q: What genes are mutated in MEN1 and MEN2, and what are their respective molecular mechanisms?
cards.a: MEN1 is caused by inactivating mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (encoding menin); MEN2 is caused by activating gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.

cards.q: Why must screening for pheochromocytoma always precede thyroid surgery in patients with MEN2A or MEN2B?
cards.a: Induction of general anesthesia or neck surgery in a patient with an unmanaged pheochromocytoma triggers massive catecholamine release, precipitating lethal hypertensive crisis and cardiac arrest.

cards.q: When should prophylactic total thyroidectomy be performed in an infant diagnosed with MEN2B carrying the RET M918T mutation?
cards.a: Within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life) due to the virulent, early metastatic spread of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) presenting in pediatric patients under 20 years with MEN1?
cards.a: Insulinoma, presenting with neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia, fasting hyperinsulinism, and positive critical blood sample.

cards.q: What tumor suppressor gene is mutated in 15-20% of Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) cases, predisposing to aggressive pediatric gigantism?
cards.a: AIP (aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein) on chromosome 11q13.3.

cards.q: What genetic duplication causes X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG syndrome) presenting with extreme linear overgrowth in infants <2 years?
cards.a: Microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 encompassing the GPR101 gene.

cards.q: Why is McCune-Albright syndrome never inherited or transmitted vertically from parent to child?
cards.a: It is caused by postzygotic somatic mosaic mutations in GNAS; a germline activating GNAS mutation would cause generalized adenylyl cyclase activation that is embryonic lethal.

cards.q: What specific biochemical defect results from the GNAS R201 codon mutation in McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: Loss of intrinsic GTPase activity in Gs-alpha, trapping the protein in an active GTP-bound conformation that constitutively drives adenylyl cyclase and cAMP production.

cards.q: How do the café-au-lait macules of McCune-Albright syndrome differ morphologically from those of Neurofibromatosis type 1?
cards.a: MAS macules are large, unilateral, respect the midline, and feature jagged, irregular 'coast of Maine' borders, unlike the smooth 'coast of California' borders of NF1.

cards.q: Why are standard GnRH agonists ineffective as initial therapy for precocious puberty in young girls with McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: The precocious puberty is peripheral (gonadotropin-independent), driven by autonomous ovarian follicular cysts secreting estrogen independent of pituitary LH and FSH.

cards.q: What metabolic electrolyte complication can severe, extensive polyostotic fibrous dysplasia cause via paracrine tumor secretion?
cards.a: Renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia, caused by excessive secretion of intact FGF23 by dysplastic bone stromal cells.

cards.q: What pathognomonic femoral deformity frequently develops in children with severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia?
cards.a: 'Shepherd's crook' deformity (severe coxa vara with bowing of the proximal femoral shaft under weight-bearing stress).

cards.q: What pharmacological class is the first-line medical treatment for peripheral precocious puberty in girls with McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: Aromatase inhibitors, such as oral letrozole (2.5 mg daily), which block estrogen biosynthesis by autonomous ovarian cysts.

cards.q: What is the most radio-sensitive anterior pituitary hormone axis, exhibiting deficiency at the lowest cranial radiation doses (>=18-24 Gy)?
cards.a: Growth hormone (GH) axis, resulting in radiation-induced GH deficiency in >80-90% of exposed children within 2-5 years.

cards.q: What pubertal disorder can paradoxically occur in young girls following low-to-moderate doses (18-24 Gy) of cranial irradiation?
cards.a: Central precocious puberty, caused by radiation-induced disruption of cortical and hypothalamic inhibitory pathways that normally suppress the GnRH pulse generator.

cards.q: What metric is used to calculate cumulative alkylating chemotherapy exposure, and what threshold confers high risk of permanent azoospermia?
cards.a: Cyclophosphamide Equivalent Dose (CED); a cumulative CED >=4000 to 8000 mg/m2 is associated with high risk of permanent germ cell failure and azoospermia.

cards.q: What is the most common secondary solid endocrine malignancy occurring in survivors of childhood cancer exposed to neck radiation?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), which has an increased incidence beginning 5-10 years post-radiation and peaking 15-25 years later.

cards.q: Does recombinant human growth hormone replacement increase the risk of primary disease recurrence in childhood cancer survivors in remission?
cards.a: No. Large-scale international cohort studies show no increased risk of primary cancer recurrence or leukemia relapse in survivors treated with rhGH.

cards.q: How does radiation sensitivity differ between testicular germ cells (spermatogenesis) and Leydig cells (testosterone production)?
cards.a: Germ cells are extraordinarily sensitive (damaged by >=0.1-1.2 Gy), whereas Leydig cells are much more radioresistant (tolerating up to 20-24 Gy before primary hypogonadism develops).

cards.q: Why is lifelong surveillance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis required in survivors exposed to high-dose cranial radiation (>=40-50 Gy)?
cards.a: Central ACTH deficiency can develop insidiously 10 to 15+ years after radiotherapy, predisposing survivors to fatal adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness.

cards.q: At what pubertal stage is pubertal suppression with GnRH agonists officially recommended in transgender youth?
cards.a: At the confirmed onset of biological puberty, defined as Tanner stage 2 (breast budding in AFAB; testicular volume >=4 mL in AMAB); it is not initiated in prepubertal children (Tanner 1).

cards.q: How does the reversibility of GnRH agonist pubertal suppression compare with gender-affirming sex steroid therapy?
cards.a: GnRH agonist pubertal suppression is fully reversible (endogenous puberty resumes if stopped), whereas gender-affirming sex steroid therapy induces partially irreversible changes (e.g., voice deepening, breast tissue).

cards.q: What hematologic parameter must be monitored regularly in transgender males receiving testosterone therapy to prevent polycythemia?
cards.a: Hemoglobin and hematocrit; testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis, and doses should be reduced if hematocrit exceeds 50-52%.

cards.q: What are the therapeutic serum hormone targets for transgender females undergoing feminizing hormone therapy?
cards.a: Serum 17-beta estradiol maintained between 100 and 200 pg/mL, with serum total testosterone suppressed to <50 ng/dL.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality requires routine monitoring in transgender females taking spironolactone as an antiandrogen?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), due to spironolactone's aldosterone-antagonist effect on the distal renal tubule.

cards.q: When must counseling regarding fertility preservation options be conducted with transgender youth and their families?
cards.a: Prior to initiating pubertal suppression (GnRHa) or gender-affirming hormone therapy (estrogen/testosterone), while gametogenesis is still intact.

cards.q: Why is DXA bone mineral density monitoring indicated during prolonged GnRH agonist pubertal suppression?
cards.a: Sex steroids are required for normal pubertal bone mineral accretion; prolonged gonadotropin suppression can delay peak bone mass acquisition, requiring calcium/vitamin D optimization.

cards.q: What is the emergency intravenous hydrocortisone bolus dose for an acute adrenal crisis in children based on age?
cards.a: <3 years: 25 mg; 3 to 12 years: 50 mg; >12 years: 100 mg IV bolus (or 50-100 mg/m2 IV), administered immediately alongside normal saline and dextrose.

cards.q: Why must Lugol's iodine solution be given at least 1 hour AFTER methimazole when treating thyroid storm?
cards.a: To ensure that methimazole has blocked thyroid peroxidase first; administering iodine before organification is blocked provides substrate that synthesizes more thyroid hormone (Jod-Basedow effect).

cards.q: Why is aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) strictly contraindicated in the management of hyperpyrexia during thyroid storm?
cards.a: Aspirin displaces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) from thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), sharply increasing free active thyroid hormone concentrations and worsening thyrotoxic storm.

cards.q: Why is 10% calcium gluconate preferred over 10% calcium chloride for peripheral intravenous treatment of acute hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Calcium chloride is highly irritating to veins and causes severe full-thickness tissue necrosis and sloughing if extravasation occurs; calcium gluconate carries a much lower tissue toxicity profile.

cards.q: What is the immediate bedside pharmacological treatment for cerebral edema complicating pediatric DKA?
cards.a: Intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg over 20 minutes) given immediately without awaiting imaging.

cards.q: What is the emergency rescue dose of glucagon for severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious child with type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: 0.5 mg SC/IM for children <25 kg (or <6 years) and 1.0 mg SC/IM for children >=25 kg (or >=6 years); alternatively, 3 mg nasal glucagon for age >=4 years.

cards.q: What is the first and most critical resuscitation step in the management of acute hypercalcemic crisis (calcium >14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Vigorous volume expansion with intravenous 0.9% normal saline at 2 to 3 times maintenance to restore renal perfusion and induce calciuresis.

cards.q: What neuroendocrine distinction differentiates the acute phase of critical illness from the chronic phase in pediatric intensive care?
cards.a: The acute phase features hypercortisolemia and sympathetic overdrive with adaptive downregulation of anabolic axes; the chronic phase features neuroendocrine exhaustion and persistent central anterior pituitary hypopituitarism.

cards.q: What is the primary clinical presentation that prompts initiation of stress-dose hydrocortisone for suspected CIRCI in pediatric intensive care?
cards.a: Vasopressor-refractory septic shock (persistent hypotension and poor perfusion requiring escalating doses of norepinephrine or epinephrine despite adequate fluid resuscitation).

cards.q: What is the recommended empiric stress dosage of intravenous hydrocortisone for vasopressor-refractory pediatric septic shock?
cards.a: 50 mg/m2 (or 2 mg/kg) IV bolus, followed by 50 to 100 mg/m2/day as a continuous infusion or divided every 6 hours, tapered as vasopressors are weaned.

cards.q: What blood glucose target range is internationally recommended for critically ill children in the PICU receiving insulin for stress hyperglycemia?
cards.a: Moderate glycemic control targeting blood glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10.0 mmol/L), avoiding strict normoglycemia (80-110 mg/dL) due to high hypoglycemia risk.

cards.q: What adverse complication was demonstrated in pediatric clinical trials (e.g., CHiP trial) evaluating tight glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL)?
cards.a: A high incidence of severe iatrogenic hypoglycemia (<40 mg/dL), which caused secondary brain injury and increased adverse outcomes.

cards.q: Is routine thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3) recommended for low T3/T4 levels in critically ill children?
cards.a: No. Randomized trials show no clinical benefit in mortality or ICU length of stay, and guidelines recommend against routine replacement therapy.

cards.q: What pattern of circulating growth hormone and IGF-1 characterizes the acute phase of critical illness?
cards.a: Elevated circulating growth hormone accompanied by markedly depressed serum IGF-1 concentrations, reflecting acute peripheral hepatic growth hormone resistance.

quizzes.q: A 2-week-old male infant born at term presents with lethargy, a blood glucose of 28 mg/dL, and a total bilirubin of 9.2 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 4.1 mg/dL. Physical examination reveals a stretched penile length of 1.6 cm (reference >2.5 cm) and bilateral descended testes. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is 1.8 mIU/L with free T4 0.6 ng/dL (reference 0.9-2.0 ng/dL). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate critical blood draw for cortisol, GH, and insulin, administration of IV dextrose and hydrocortisone, followed by pituitary MRI
High-dose oral diazoxide therapy for presumed primary congenital hyperinsulinism
Recombinant human growth hormone monotherapy at 50 mcg/kg/day
Observation with frequent feeding intervals and repeat bilirubin in 4 weeks
quizzes.explanation: The infant exhibits the classic presentation of congenital hypopituitarism: neonatal hypoglycemia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, micropenis, and central hypothyroidism. Prompt evaluation of adrenal status and hydrocortisone replacement are lifesaving before initiating other hormone therapies.

option_notes.option: Immediate critical blood draw for cortisol, GH, and insulin, administration of IV dextrose and hydrocortisone, followed by pituitary MRI
option_notes.text: Critical blood draw during hypoglycemia and immediate hydrocortisone replacement prevent fatal adrenal crisis in congenital hypopituitarism.

option_notes.option: High-dose oral diazoxide therapy for presumed primary congenital hyperinsulinism
option_notes.text: Diazoxide treats hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia but does not address central adrenal insufficiency or multiple pituitary deficiencies.

option_notes.option: Recombinant human growth hormone monotherapy at 50 mcg/kg/day
option_notes.text: Administering GH before establishing adequate cortisol replacement can precipitate acute adrenal collapse due to increased glucocorticoid clearance.

option_notes.option: Observation with frequent feeding intervals and repeat bilirubin in 4 weeks
option_notes.text: Observation is contraindicated because untreated neonatal hypoglycemia and central adrenal crisis carry severe mortality and neurodevelopmental morbidity.

quizzes.q: An 11-year-old boy with severe short stature (height SDS -3.2) and growth velocity of 3.2 cm/year undergoes evaluation. Baseline IGF-I is below the 5th percentile. His bone age is 8.5 years and testicular volume is 2 mL bilaterally. Before performing provocative testing with arginine and clonidine, what step should be taken to optimize diagnostic accuracy?
options: Priming with intramuscular testosterone enanthate or oral estrogen 2-3 days prior to testing
Performing an oral glucose tolerance test to rule out reactive hypoglycemia
Withholding evaluation until chronological age 14 years regardless of growth velocity
Administering a trial of oral levothyroxine for 6 months before biochemical testing
quizzes.explanation: In prepubertal boys older than 11 years with bone age delay, sex-steroid priming primes the somatotroph axis, preventing false-positive subnormal GH peaks that occur because of constitutional delay of puberty.

option_notes.option: Priming with intramuscular testosterone enanthate or oral estrogen 2-3 days prior to testing
option_notes.text: Sex-steroid priming enhances endogenous somatotroph responsiveness in peripubertal children with delayed maturation, avoiding misdiagnosis of true GHD.

option_notes.option: Performing an oral glucose tolerance test to rule out reactive hypoglycemia
option_notes.text: Oral glucose tolerance testing is used to evaluate GH excess/acromegaly through GH suppression, not somatotroph reserve deficiency.

option_notes.option: Withholding evaluation until chronological age 14 years regardless of growth velocity
option_notes.text: Delaying evaluation until age 14 causes permanent loss of linear height potential during critical prepubertal growing years.

option_notes.option: Administering a trial of oral levothyroxine for 6 months before biochemical testing
option_notes.text: Empiric levothyroxine in a euthyroid child does not correct somatotroph hyposecretion and may cause thyrotoxicosis.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old girl with confirmed isolated somatotroph deficiency begins subcutaneous somatropin at 30 mcg/kg/day. At her 3-month follow-up, she has grown 3.0 cm, but routine lab testing reveals a drop in free T4 from 1.2 ng/dL to 0.7 ng/dL (reference 0.8-1.8 ng/dL) with an unchanged normal TSH of 2.1 mIU/L. What is the physiological mechanism explaining this finding?
options: Enhanced peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and unmasking of incipient central hypothyroidism
Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells induced by recombinant protein antibodies
Competitive inhibition of thyroid iodine uptake by circulating somatropin molecules
False laboratory assay interference between growth hormone and thyroglobulin
quizzes.explanation: Growth hormone replacement stimulates hepatic and peripheral 5'-deiodinase activity, accelerating conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3). In patients with underlying pituitary pathology, this can unmask central hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine supplementation.

option_notes.option: Enhanced peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and unmasking of incipient central hypothyroidism
option_notes.text: Growth hormone therapy accelerates peripheral T4-to-T3 deiodination, reducing serum free T4 and revealing central hypothyroidism in patients with subclinical TSH deficiency.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells induced by recombinant protein antibodies
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not elicit autoimmune thyroiditis or anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody formation.

option_notes.option: Competitive inhibition of thyroid iodine uptake by circulating somatropin molecules
option_notes.text: Somatropin has no structural or pharmacological mechanism to inhibit the sodium-iodide symporter.

option_notes.option: False laboratory assay interference between growth hormone and thyroglobulin
option_notes.text: Modern automated chemiluminescent free T4 assays have zero cross-reactivity with somatropin.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old boy who received 24 Gy of prophylactic cranial irradiation for acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 5 is evaluated for linear growth failure. His height velocity is 2.8 cm/year. What is the pathophysiology of his radiation-induced somatotroph impairment?
options: Hypothalamic radiation injury with loss of pulsatile GHRH secretion and decreased somatotroph reserve
Direct total destruction of pituitary thyrotrophs with sparing of somatotrophs
Primary gonadal failure causing premature epiphyseal closure without pituitary involvement
Peripheral end-organ resistance due to radiation-induced growth hormone receptor mutations
quizzes.explanation: Cranial irradiation at doses ≥18-24 Gy preferentially damages hypothalamic regulatory neurons, causing blunted GHRH secretion and diminished somatotroph pulse amplitude (neurosecretory dysfunction), making somatotroph deficiency the earliest and most frequent post-radiation endocrinopathy.

option_notes.option: Hypothalamic radiation injury with loss of pulsatile GHRH secretion and decreased somatotroph reserve
option_notes.text: Radiation doses ≥18 Gy preferentially damage hypothalamic GHRH-secreting neurons; GHD is the most sensitive and earliest endocrinopathy after cranial irradiation.

option_notes.option: Direct total destruction of pituitary thyrotrophs with sparing of somatotrophs
option_notes.text: Somatotrophs and hypothalamic GHRH neurons are far more radiosensitive than thyrotrophs or corticotrophs.

option_notes.option: Primary gonadal failure causing premature epiphyseal closure without pituitary involvement
option_notes.text: Prophylactic cranial irradiation does not cause direct gonadal destruction; precocious puberty may occur from hypothalamic disinhibition, but the primary growth failure is somatotroph loss.

option_notes.option: Peripheral end-organ resistance due to radiation-induced growth hormone receptor mutations
option_notes.text: Radiation damages CNS neuroendocrine architecture, not the genetic coding sequence of somatic GH receptors.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old boy with isolated short stature and delayed bone age undergoes genetic evaluation. Sequencing demonstrates a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the POU1F1 (PIT1) gene. Which constellation of anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies is characteristically produced by this defect?
options: Deficiencies of Growth Hormone, Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone, and Prolactin, with normal ACTH and LH/FSH
Panhypopituitarism involving all anterior hormones plus central diabetes insipidus
Isolated adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency with preserved somatotroph function
Combined LH and FSH deficiency with intact GH, TSH, and ACTH
quizzes.explanation: POU1F1 (PIT1) is a POU-domain homeobox transcription factor required for the differentiation and maintenance of somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, and lactotrophs. Mutations cause combined GH, TSH, and PRL deficiency, while corticotrophs and gonadotrophs remain intact.

option_notes.option: Deficiencies of Growth Hormone, Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone, and Prolactin, with normal ACTH and LH/FSH
option_notes.text: POU1F1/PIT1 specifically directs the lineage differentiation of somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, and lactotrophs, leaving corticotrophs and gonadotrophs unaffected.

option_notes.option: Panhypopituitarism involving all anterior hormones plus central diabetes insipidus
option_notes.text: Central diabetes insipidus arises from neurohypophyseal or vasopressinergic hypothalamic defects, not POU1F1, which is anterior pituitary-specific.

option_notes.option: Isolated adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency with preserved somatotroph function
option_notes.text: Isolated ACTH deficiency is caused by TPIT mutations, not POU1F1.

option_notes.option: Combined LH and FSH deficiency with intact GH, TSH, and ACTH
option_notes.text: Isolated gonadotropin deficiency is caused by GnRHR, KISS1R, or TACR3 mutations, leaving GH and TSH unaffected.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe proportional short stature (height SDS -5.4), frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, small hands and feet, and high-pitched voice. Laboratory investigation shows basal serum GH 38 ng/mL (reference <5 ng/mL) and peak stimulated GH 64 ng/mL. Serum IGF-I is <15 ng/mL (reference 50-250 ng/mL) and IGFBP-3 is undetectable. A 4-day IGF-I generation test with high-dose rhGH yields no increase in serum IGF-I. What is the most likely molecular diagnosis?
options: Homozygous inactivating mutation in the Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) gene
Pituitary adenoma secreting bioinactive growth hormone
Homozygous mutation in the GHRH receptor gene
Isolated neurosecretory growth hormone deficiency
quizzes.explanation: High circulating GH with undetectable IGF-I, unresponsiveness to exogenous rhGH in an IGF-I generation test, and classic craniofacial dysmorphism are diagnostic of severe growth hormone insensitivity (Laron syndrome) due to GHR mutations.

option_notes.option: Homozygous inactivating mutation in the Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) gene
option_notes.text: Inactivating GHR mutations prevent downstream intracellular signaling and IGF-I synthesis despite massive endogenous or exogenous GH.

option_notes.option: Pituitary adenoma secreting bioinactive growth hormone
option_notes.text: A bioinactive GH would respond to exogenous wild-type rhGH with a prompt rise in serum IGF-I on the generation test.

option_notes.option: Homozygous mutation in the GHRH receptor gene
option_notes.text: GHRH receptor mutations cause profound GH deficiency with low, not elevated, serum GH levels.

option_notes.option: Isolated neurosecretory growth hormone deficiency
option_notes.text: Neurosecretory dysfunction exhibits low 24-hour integrated GH secretion and normal responsiveness to rhGH replacement.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old girl with confirmed severe primary IGF-I deficiency due to GHR exon deletion is prescribed mecasermin. Which instruction is mandatory for her parents to minimize the most frequent serious adverse effect of this therapy?
options: Administer each subcutaneous injection within 20 minutes before or after a meal or carbohydrate snack
Administer the injection strictly while fasting first thing in the morning
Co-administer a sodium polystyrene sulfonate resin to bind potassium
Limit fluid intake to less than 500 mL per day to prevent acute hypernatremia
quizzes.explanation: Because IGF-I possesses approximately 10% of the insulin receptor-activating potency of insulin, rhIGF-I induces rapid hypoglycemia. Injections must be paired with carbohydrate-containing food.

option_notes.option: Administer each subcutaneous injection within 20 minutes before or after a meal or carbohydrate snack
option_notes.text: Co-ingestion of carbohydrates with rhIGF-I prevents severe acute neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Administer the injection strictly while fasting first thing in the morning
option_notes.text: Fasting administration of rhIGF-I triggers severe hypoglycemic seizures.

option_notes.option: Co-administer a sodium polystyrene sulfonate resin to bind potassium
option_notes.text: rhIGF-I does not cause hyperkalemia; ion-exchange resins are irrelevant.

option_notes.option: Limit fluid intake to less than 500 mL per day to prevent acute hypernatremia
option_notes.text: Fluid restriction is contraindicated and has no role in mecasermin management.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with severe short stature (height SDS -4.8), severe generalized eczema, autoimmune thyroiditis, and recurrent bacterial pneumonia. Endocrine labs show peak GH 42 ng/mL and undetectable IGF-I. Genetic testing is most likely to identify a mutation in which gene?
options: STAT5B
GH1
POU1F1
GHRHR
quizzes.explanation: STAT5B is essential both for growth hormone receptor signal transduction in hepatocytes and for IL-2 receptor signaling in regulatory T cells. Inactivating STAT5B mutations uniquely combine severe growth failure with profound immune dysregulation.

option_notes.option: STAT5B
option_notes.text: STAT5B mutations cause a distinct clinical syndrome combining growth hormone insensitivity with severe immunodeficiency and autoimmunity.

option_notes.option: GH1
option_notes.text: GH1 mutations cause isolated growth hormone deficiency without immunological compromise.

option_notes.option: POU1F1
option_notes.text: POU1F1 mutations cause combined GH, TSH, and Prolactin deficiency without primary immunodeficiency.

option_notes.option: GHRHR
option_notes.text: GHRHR mutations cause isolated GHD without autoimmune lung disease or eczema.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old boy with mild short stature (height SDS -2.3) is evaluated. Laboratory testing reveals serum IGF-I SDS -3.4 and IGFBP-3 SDS -3.8. Surprisingly, his serum free IGF-I concentration is within normal limits, and he has never experienced hypoglycemia. What molecular defect accounts for this dissociation?
options: Inactivating mutation in the IGFALS gene encoding the acid-labile subunit
Complete deletion of the extracellular domain of the growth hormone receptor
Homozygous missense mutation in the insulin receptor gene (INSR)
Severe pituitary stalk transection with panhypopituitarism
quizzes.explanation: Acid-labile subunit (ALS) deficiency prevents formation of the 150-kDa ternary complex (IGF-I, IGFBP-3, ALS), accelerating clearance of bound IGF-I and leading to markedly reduced total IGF-I and IGFBP-3. However, free active IGF-I is preserved, resulting in only mild height reduction without hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Inactivating mutation in the IGFALS gene encoding the acid-labile subunit
option_notes.text: ALS deficiency impairs ternary complex assembly, severely lowering circulating total IGF-I and IGFBP-3 while free IGF-I remains relatively preserved.

option_notes.option: Complete deletion of the extracellular domain of the growth hormone receptor
option_notes.text: Complete GHR deletion produces extreme short stature (SDS -5 to -10) and very low free IGF-I with fasting hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Homozygous missense mutation in the insulin receptor gene (INSR)
option_notes.text: INSR mutations cause Donohue or Rabson-Mendenhall syndromes with extreme hyperinsulinemia and acanthosis nigricans.

option_notes.option: Severe pituitary stalk transection with panhypopituitarism
option_notes.text: Pituitary stalk transection produces multiple anterior hormone deficiencies and low free IGF-I.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy with severe Laron syndrome has been treated with mecasermin (120 mcg/kg twice daily) for 2 years. His parents note new-onset loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. Examination demonstrates marked enlargement of the palatine tonsils and adenoidal facies. What is the underlying cause of this finding?
options: IGF-I-mediated stimulation of lymphoid tissue proliferation in Waldeyer's ring
Recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis secondary to acquired agammaglobulinemia
Skeletal compression of the nasopharynx by acromegalic bone overgrowth
Allergic reaction to the preservative in the mecasermin formulation
quizzes.explanation: Mecasermin therapy commonly stimulates the growth of lymphoid tissues, particularly the tonsils and adenoids, which express high densities of IGF-I receptors. This can lead to upper airway obstruction and obstructive sleep apnea requiring surgical adenotonsillectomy.

option_notes.option: IGF-I-mediated stimulation of lymphoid tissue proliferation in Waldeyer's ring
option_notes.text: Tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy is a recognized adverse effect of rhIGF-I therapy due to strong mitogenic stimulation of lymphoid tissue.

option_notes.option: Recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis secondary to acquired agammaglobulinemia
option_notes.text: rhIGF-I does not cause agammaglobulinemia or selective humoral immunodeficiency.

option_notes.option: Skeletal compression of the nasopharynx by acromegalic bone overgrowth
option_notes.text: Patients with GHI do not develop acromegalic bony overgrowth; their cranial growth remains delayed.

option_notes.option: Allergic reaction to the preservative in the mecasermin formulation
option_notes.text: Lymphoid hypertrophy is a direct pharmacodynamic effect of IGF-I, not an allergic contact reaction.

quizzes.q: A 14.5-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of short stature and lack of pubertal development. His height is at the 1st percentile (height SDS -2.3). His father had a pubertal growth spurt at age 17 and his mother entered menarche at 14. Physical exam shows prepubertal Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and testicular volume of 3 mL bilaterally. Radiograph of the left hand and wrist reveals a bone age of 11.5 years. Provocative GH testing with clonidine yields a peak GH of 14 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP)
Familial Short Stature (FSS)
Classical Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency
Primary Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism with Kallmann Syndrome
quizzes.explanation: A family history of late maturation, delayed bone age (>2 years behind chronological age), prepubertal status at age 14.5, and normal peak GH (>10 ng/mL) characterize constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

option_notes.option: Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP)
option_notes.text: Delayed bone age, paternal history of delayed growth spurt, and intact GH reserve are diagnostic of CDGP.

option_notes.option: Familial Short Stature (FSS)
option_notes.text: In familial short stature, bone age is consistent with chronological age and adult height remains short.

option_notes.option: Classical Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency
option_notes.text: The peak GH of 14 ng/mL (>10 ng/mL) excludes classical growth hormone deficiency.

option_notes.option: Primary Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism with Kallmann Syndrome
option_notes.text: Permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is rare and typically accompanied by microphallus or anosmia; bone age delay and family history point to CDGP.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. Her height is at the 0.5th percentile (height SDS -2.6). Her midparental target height is at the 25th percentile. Past medical history and systemic review are negative. Laboratory workup reveals normal CBC, ESR, tissue transglutaminase IgA, thyroid panel, and electrolyte panel. Bone age is 8.0 years. What diagnostic step must be completed before categorizing her condition as idiopathic short stature?
options: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to exclude Turner syndrome
Immediate 24-hour urinary free cortisol measurement
Skeletal survey to look for osteogenesis imperfecta type IV
Diagnostic renal biopsy to evaluate for occult nephritis
quizzes.explanation: Guidelines recommend karyotype or chromosomal microarray in all girls presenting with unexplained short stature, as mosaic Turner syndrome frequently presents without overt classical physical stigmas.

option_notes.option: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to exclude Turner syndrome
option_notes.text: Chromosomal analysis is mandatory in any short female lacking an overt cause to detect non-dysmorphic Turner syndrome.

option_notes.option: Immediate 24-hour urinary free cortisol measurement
option_notes.text: Cushing syndrome presents with weight gain crossing percentiles upwards alongside growth cessation, not isolated short stature.

option_notes.option: Skeletal survey to look for osteogenesis imperfecta type IV
option_notes.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta features recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and skeletal deformity.

option_notes.option: Diagnostic renal biopsy to evaluate for occult nephritis
option_notes.text: Renal biopsy is invasive and unwarranted in a child with normal urinalysis, BUN, creatinine, and electrolytes.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old boy with constitutional delay of growth and puberty is experiencing severe depression and bullying due to short stature (height SDS -2.4, bone age 11.5 years). He has prepubertal genitalia. Which management strategy provides safe, targeted acceleration of linear growth without causing premature epiphyseal fusion?
options: Short-course intramuscular testosterone enanthate 50 mg monthly for 3 to 6 months
Oral ethinyl estradiol 50 mcg daily for 1 year
High-dose recombinant human growth hormone at 0.48 mg/kg/week until adult height
Continuous GnRH agonist therapy for 2 years
quizzes.explanation: Low-dose testosterone (50-100 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) is a safe, established intervention in adolescent boys ≥14 years with constitutional delay to promote linear growth and virilization without prematurely advancing epiphyseal fusion.

option_notes.option: Short-course intramuscular testosterone enanthate 50 mg monthly for 3 to 6 months
option_notes.text: Low-dose androgen therapy promotes growth velocity and virilization while preserving adult height potential in adolescent constitutional delay.

option_notes.option: Oral ethinyl estradiol 50 mcg daily for 1 year
option_notes.text: Estrogen therapy in males causes feminization and accelerates epiphyseal fusion.

option_notes.option: High-dose recombinant human growth hormone at 0.48 mg/kg/week until adult height
option_notes.text: Somatropin is not indicated for simple constitutional delay of growth and puberty in a child with normal adult height prediction.

option_notes.option: Continuous GnRH agonist therapy for 2 years
option_notes.text: GnRH agonists suppress pubertal development and worsen growth deceleration in delayed puberty.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy has non-familial idiopathic short stature with height SDS -2.7 and a Bayley-Pinneau predicted adult height of 156 cm (SDS -2.8). The family elects to initiate FDA-approved somatropin therapy. Based on clinical trial evidence, what is the expected average adult height gain associated with somatropin therapy in this setting?
options: Approximately 3.5 to 7.5 cm (1.4 to 3 inches) above untreated predicted height
Approximately 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches) above untreated predicted height
Zero change in adult height compared to untreated controls
A net decrease in adult height due to accelerated skeletal maturation
quizzes.explanation: Meta-analyses and randomized trials of somatropin in idiopathic short stature demonstrate an average adult height gain of 3.5 to 7.5 cm, with significant individual variation depending on starting age, dose, and adherence.

option_notes.option: Approximately 3.5 to 7.5 cm (1.4 to 3 inches) above untreated predicted height
option_notes.text: Published trials demonstrate an average height benefit of 3.5 to 7.5 cm in children with idiopathic short stature treated with somatropin.

option_notes.option: Approximately 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches) above untreated predicted height
option_notes.text: Gains of 15 to 20 cm are unrealistic and not supported by pediatric clinical trial data.

option_notes.option: Zero change in adult height compared to untreated controls
option_notes.text: Controlled studies demonstrate statistically significant height gains over untreated controls.

option_notes.option: A net decrease in adult height due to accelerated skeletal maturation
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not disproportionately advance bone age in ISS; it does not reduce adult height.

quizzes.q: An 11-year-old boy presents for short stature evaluation. His height is at the 3rd percentile, his father is 162 cm (5th percentile), and his mother is 148 cm (3rd percentile). His bone age is 11.0 years, matching his chronological age. His height velocity has been 5.2 cm/year over the past 2 years. Which diagnostic entity best accounts for these findings?
options: Familial Short Stature
Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
Primary Growth Hormone Insensitivity
quizzes.explanation: Familial short stature is characterized by short parents, child's height tracking near midparental target, normal annual height velocity (5 cm/year), and a bone age that matches chronological age.

option_notes.option: Familial Short Stature
option_notes.text: Familial short stature features normal growth velocity, concordant bone age, and height tracking within target midparental expectations.

option_notes.option: Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty
option_notes.text: Constitutional delay is distinguished by delayed bone age (>1.5-2 years behind) and delayed pubertal timing.

option_notes.option: Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
option_notes.text: Craniopharyngioma typically presents with severe growth deceleration (<4 cm/yr), headaches, or visual field deficits.

option_notes.option: Primary Growth Hormone Insensitivity
option_notes.text: Growth hormone insensitivity produces severe growth failure (SDS <-4) and markedly delayed bone age.

quizzes.q: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. She was born at 39 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2100 g (SDS -2.4) and length of 44 cm (SDS -2.5). Her current height is at the 0.2nd percentile (height SDS -2.8). Extensive evaluation reveals normal systemic, renal, and thyroid function. Which statement regarding her management is correct according to clinical guidelines?
options: She meets FDA criteria for recombinant human growth hormone therapy because she is older than 2 years with persistent height SDS <-2.0
Growth hormone therapy is contraindicated until bone age reaches chronological age 10 years
She should be managed with high-calorie nutritional supplementation alone until pubertal onset
Growth hormone therapy should be withheld until provocative GH stimulation testing confirms peak GH <5 ng/mL
quizzes.explanation: Children born SGA who fail to manifest catch-up growth by age 2 years with persistent height SDS <-2.0 are eligible for FDA-approved somatropin therapy regardless of GH stimulation test results.

option_notes.option: She meets FDA criteria for recombinant human growth hormone therapy because she is older than 2 years with persistent height SDS <-2.0
option_notes.text: FDA approval specifies age ≥2 years and persistent height SDS <-2.0 without spontaneous catch-up; GH stimulation testing is not required.

option_notes.option: Growth hormone therapy is contraindicated until bone age reaches chronological age 10 years
option_notes.text: Delaying treatment until age 10 misses the critical prepubertal window for optimal catch-up growth.

option_notes.option: She should be managed with high-calorie nutritional supplementation alone until pubertal onset
option_notes.text: Excessive high-calorie supplementation in SGA without catch-up induces rapid adiposity and worsens metabolic risk without improving linear height.

option_notes.option: Growth hormone therapy should be withheld until provocative GH stimulation testing confirms peak GH <5 ng/mL
option_notes.text: SGA children have relative GH resistance and normal or elevated stimulated GH; testing is not required for the SGA indication.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old boy born SGA at 38 weeks with birth weight 1950 g presents with height SDS -3.2. Physical exam reveals a prominent forehead, triangular facies, down-turned mouth, and significant hemihypotrophy of the left lower extremity. What is the most appropriate molecular testing to establish the diagnosis?
options: Methylation-specific multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MS-MLPA) for chromosome 11p15.5 and maternal UPD7
Sequencing of the GHR gene for Laron syndrome
Karyotype to evaluate for Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) for 22q11.2 deletion
quizzes.explanation: Triangular facies, relative macrocephaly, body asymmetry/hemihypotrophy, and severe intrauterine growth failure are the classic features of Silver-Russell syndrome, caused by loss of methylation at 11p15.5 (50%) or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (10%).

option_notes.option: Methylation-specific multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MS-MLPA) for chromosome 11p15.5 and maternal UPD7
option_notes.text: MS-MLPA detects 11p15.5 epimutations and maternal UPD7, the primary molecular etiologies of Silver-Russell syndrome.

option_notes.option: Sequencing of the GHR gene for Laron syndrome
option_notes.text: GHR mutations cause Laron syndrome, which presents with symmetrical growth failure, not hemihypotrophy.

option_notes.option: Karyotype to evaluate for Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
option_notes.text: Klinefelter syndrome presents with tall stature, eunuchoid proportions, and gynecomastia.

option_notes.option: Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) for 22q11.2 deletion
option_notes.text: 22q11.2 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome, featuring conotruncal cardiac defects, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old boy born SGA without catch-up growth begins somatropin at 45 mcg/kg/day. At baseline, his fasting blood glucose is 88 mg/dL and fasting insulin is 8 mcIU/mL. After 12 months, his growth velocity has accelerated from 4.0 to 9.2 cm/year. Repeat fasting labs show glucose 92 mg/dL and fasting insulin 16 mcIU/mL. What is the correct interpretation of these metabolic changes?
options: Physiological compensatory hyperinsulinemia secondary to the known anti-insulin actions of somatropin
Development of overt autoimmune type 1 diabetes requiring insulin initiation
Acute drug-induced ketoacidosis requiring immediate emergency hospitalization
Primary adrenal failure causing secondary reactive insulin hypersecretion
quizzes.explanation: Growth hormone possesses physiological anti-insulin (lipolytic and glycogenolytic) actions that mildly decrease peripheral insulin sensitivity, which is compensated for by an appropriate increase in fasting insulin without overt hyperglycemia.

option_notes.option: Physiological compensatory hyperinsulinemia secondary to the known anti-insulin actions of somatropin
option_notes.text: Somatropin induces mild peripheral insulin resistance that is normally compensated for by increased pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion.

option_notes.option: Development of overt autoimmune type 1 diabetes requiring insulin initiation
option_notes.text: Type 1 diabetes presents with absolute insulin deficiency, polyuria, weight loss, and marked hyperglycemia.

option_notes.option: Acute drug-induced ketoacidosis requiring immediate emergency hospitalization
option_notes.text: The patient has a normal glucose of 92 mg/dL with no acidosis or ketonemia.

option_notes.option: Primary adrenal failure causing secondary reactive insulin hypersecretion
option_notes.text: Adrenal failure causes hypoglycemia and decreased insulin secretion, not compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

quizzes.q: A pediatric endocrinologist plans somatropin therapy for a 3-year-old child born SGA (height SDS -2.8). Which dosing strategy is supported by international consensus guidelines for optimizing adult height outcomes?
options: 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day), titrating according to growth response and serum IGF-I
Low-dose pulse therapy at 5 mcg/kg/day administered once weekly
A fixed adult dose of 4.0 mg per day regardless of patient weight
High-dose intramuscular injections of 200 mcg/kg administered every 3 months
quizzes.explanation: Standard consensus guidelines recommend somatropin at 35 to 70 mcg/kg/day (0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week) as daily subcutaneous injections, adjusting the dose to maintain serum IGF-I in the upper normal range (+1 to +2 SDS).

option_notes.option: 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day), titrating according to growth response and serum IGF-I
option_notes.text: Standard approved dosing is 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week given daily subcutaneously.

option_notes.option: Low-dose pulse therapy at 5 mcg/kg/day administered once weekly
option_notes.text: Weekly low-dose pulsing is ineffective for overcoming the relative GH resistance characteristic of SGA.

option_notes.option: A fixed adult dose of 4.0 mg per day regardless of patient weight
option_notes.text: Fixed adult dosing in a 3-year-old child causes massive drug overdose and severe toxicity.

option_notes.option: High-dose intramuscular injections of 200 mcg/kg administered every 3 months
option_notes.text: Infrequent depot bolus dosing is unphysiological and does not stimulate sustained chondrocyte linear proliferation.

quizzes.q: During routine follow-up of a 7-year-old girl born SGA receiving somatropin (40 mcg/kg/day), her serum IGF-I is measured at +3.2 SDS for age and sex. Her linear growth rate is excellent at 8.5 cm/year. What is the most appropriate management decision?
options: Reduce the somatropin dosage by 15-25% and recheck serum IGF-I in 3 to 6 months
Double the dose of somatropin to maximize peak pubertal height velocity
Discontinue therapy permanently and tell the parents no further growth is possible
Initiate high-dose hydrocortisone to suppress circulating IGF-I concentrations
quizzes.explanation: When serum IGF-I exceeds +2.0 to +2.5 SDS during somatropin therapy, consensus guidelines recommend dose reduction (typically 15-25%) to maintain IGF-I within safe physiological bounds while monitoring growth velocity.

option_notes.option: Reduce the somatropin dosage by 15-25% and recheck serum IGF-I in 3 to 6 months
option_notes.text: Reducing the dose brings IGF-I back into the target reference range (+1 to +2 SDS) while avoiding supranormal mitogenic exposure.

option_notes.option: Double the dose of somatropin to maximize peak pubertal height velocity
option_notes.text: Doubling the dose is dangerous and will further elevate supranormal IGF-I levels.

option_notes.option: Discontinue therapy permanently and tell the parents no further growth is possible
option_notes.text: Permanent discontinuation is unwarranted when a simple downward titration safely resolves elevated IGF-I.

option_notes.option: Initiate high-dose hydrocortisone to suppress circulating IGF-I concentrations
option_notes.text: Glucocorticoids suppress growth plate chondrogenesis and are never used to manage elevated IGF-I levels.

quizzes.q: A 9-month-old infant with genetically confirmed Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal 15q11-q13 deletion) is evaluated for somatropin therapy. He has marked hypotonia, poor head control, and short stature (length SDS -2.3). Before prescribing somatropin, which diagnostic investigation is mandatory to establish treatment safety?
options: Overnight polysomnography and ENT evaluation for adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to assess total body calcium
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
Lumbar puncture to rule out elevated intracranial pressure
quizzes.explanation: Because somatropin can stimulate lymphoid tissue proliferation and potentially exacerbate preexisting upper airway obstruction in hypotonic infants with PWS, baseline polysomnography and ENT assessment are mandatory before initiation.

option_notes.option: Overnight polysomnography and ENT evaluation for adenotonsillar hypertrophy
option_notes.text: Polysomnography identifies occult obstructive sleep apnea, which must be addressed before safe somatropin initiation in PWS.

option_notes.option: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to assess total body calcium
option_notes.text: DXA scans are informative for body composition research but are not safety prerequisites for starting therapy.

option_notes.option: 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
option_notes.text: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is not a standard screening requirement in hypotonic infants with PWS.

option_notes.option: Lumbar puncture to rule out elevated intracranial pressure
option_notes.text: Lumbar puncture is an invasive test with no clinical indication prior to somatropin initiation in PWS.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome has been treated with somatropin (1.0 mg/m2/day) for 2 years. His parents ask what measurable changes in body composition have been established by long-term clinical trials. What is the most accurate response?
options: Statistically significant increase in lean muscle mass and sustained reduction in body fat percentage
Total cure of hyperphagia with normalization of satiety signaling
Complete conversion of white adipose tissue to functional brown adipose tissue
No measurable change in body composition despite acceleration of linear height
quizzes.explanation: Extensive randomized and longitudinal trials demonstrate that somatropin therapy significantly improves body composition in PWS by increasing lean muscle mass, decreasing fat mass, and boosting resting energy expenditure, though it does not abolish underlying hypothalamic hyperphagia.

option_notes.option: Statistically significant increase in lean muscle mass and sustained reduction in body fat percentage
option_notes.text: Clinical trials demonstrate consistent increases in lean body mass and decreases in fat mass with somatropin in PWS.

option_notes.option: Total cure of hyperphagia with normalization of satiety signaling
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not cure underlying hypothalamic hyperphagia; dietary environmental restriction remains essential.

option_notes.option: Complete conversion of white adipose tissue to functional brown adipose tissue
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not convert white fat to brown fat; its lipolytic effect operates through hormone-sensitive lipase.

option_notes.option: No measurable change in body composition despite acceleration of linear height
option_notes.text: Body composition benefits are well-established and represent one of the primary indications for GH in PWS.

quizzes.q: A 2-year-old girl with Prader-Willi syndrome is undergoing consideration for somatropin therapy. Pre-treatment polysomnography reveals severe obstructive sleep apnea with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 22 events/hour and oxygen desaturations to 74%. Examination reveals 4+ kissing tonsils. What is the correct clinical management?
options: Defer somatropin, refer for adenotonsillectomy, and re-evaluate with repeat polysomnography postoperatively
Start somatropin immediately at double dose to strengthen pharyngeal musculature
Initiate continuous mecasermin therapy as an alternative to somatropin
Administer high-dose dexamethasone for 2 weeks followed by immediate somatropin
quizzes.explanation: Severe obstructive sleep apnea is a contraindication to starting somatropin. Airway obstruction must be resolved surgically (adenotonsillectomy) or with positive airway pressure, with post-intervention polysomnography confirming resolution before somatropin can be safely initiated.

option_notes.option: Defer somatropin, refer for adenotonsillectomy, and re-evaluate with repeat polysomnography postoperatively
option_notes.text: Treating airway obstruction prior to somatropin prevents fatal respiratory compromise in patients with PWS.

option_notes.option: Start somatropin immediately at double dose to strengthen pharyngeal musculature
option_notes.text: Starting somatropin in the presence of severe OSA risks rapid worsening of lymphoid hypertrophy and fatal asphyxia.

option_notes.option: Initiate continuous mecasermin therapy as an alternative to somatropin
option_notes.text: Mecasermin has no indication in PWS and carries the same or greater risk of lymphoid proliferation.

option_notes.option: Administer high-dose dexamethasone for 2 weeks followed by immediate somatropin
option_notes.text: High-dose dexamethasone is catabolic to muscle, causes severe metabolic disturbance, and is contraindicated.

quizzes.q: A 14-month-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome initiates somatropin at 0.5 mg/m2/day. Six weeks into therapy, his mother reports that he has developed new-onset loud snoring and mouth breathing during sleep. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Suspend somatropin therapy and perform urgent ENT examination and polysomnography
Reassure the mother that snoring indicates expanding respiratory vital capacity
Increase the somatropin dose to 1.5 mg/m2/day to accelerate laryngeal maturation
Prescribe over-the-counter diphenhydramine at bedtime
quizzes.explanation: New-onset or worsening sleep-disordered breathing in a child with PWS following somatropin initiation warrants temporary suspension of therapy, clinical ENT evaluation for adenoid/tonsillar enlargement, and repeat polysomnography.

option_notes.option: Suspend somatropin therapy and perform urgent ENT examination and polysomnography
option_notes.text: New snoring suggests treatment-induced lymphoid hypertrophy or worsened OSA; safety requires immediate evaluation.

option_notes.option: Reassure the mother that snoring indicates expanding respiratory vital capacity
option_notes.text: Snoring is a symptom of upper airway obstruction, not healthy lung expansion.

option_notes.option: Increase the somatropin dose to 1.5 mg/m2/day to accelerate laryngeal maturation
option_notes.text: Increasing the dose increases the risk of acute respiratory obstruction.

option_notes.option: Prescribe over-the-counter diphenhydramine at bedtime
option_notes.text: Sedating antihistamines can relax pharyngeal muscle tone, worsening upper airway collapse.

quizzes.q: Which genetic mechanism underlying Prader-Willi syndrome carries a higher documented risk of maternal age-related meiotic non-disjunction and a lower risk of hypopigmentation compared to paternal deletions?
options: Maternal uniparental disomy 15 (UPD15)
Paternal 15q11.2-q13 microdeletion
Imprinting center microdeletion
Balanced paternal translocation involving 15q
quizzes.explanation: Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD15) accounts for ~25% of PWS cases and is associated with advanced maternal age. Because both OCA2 genes are retained, these children do not exhibit the marked hypopigmentation seen in large paternal 15q deletions.

option_notes.option: Maternal uniparental disomy 15 (UPD15)
option_notes.text: Maternal UPD15 is associated with older maternal age and preserves both maternal copies of OCA2, avoiding hypopigmentation.

option_notes.option: Paternal 15q11.2-q13 microdeletion
option_notes.text: Paternal deletions involve hemizygous loss of the OCA2 gene, leading to fair skin and light hair.

option_notes.option: Imprinting center microdeletion
option_notes.text: Imprinting center mutations are typically familial and not correlated with maternal age.

option_notes.option: Balanced paternal translocation involving 15q
option_notes.text: Paternal translocations are rare structural rearrangements not dependent on maternal age.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive growth deceleration. Her height is at the 1st percentile (height SDS -2.4). Examination reveals a low posterior hairline, high-arched palate, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and mild cubitus valgus. Cardiovascular exam reveals a grade 2/6 systolic murmur. Echocardiogram demonstrates a bicuspid aortic valve with normal ventricular function. What is the most definitive test to confirm her diagnosis?
options: 30-cell peripheral blood karyotype or chromosomal microarray
Provocative growth hormone stimulation testing with clonidine and arginine
Targeted sequencing of the PTPN11 gene
24-hour ambulatory urinary growth hormone excretion
