quizzes.explanation: A karyotype or chromosomal microarray is the gold standard to establish Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism), which accounts for her short stature, somatic stigmas, and bicuspid aortic valve.

option_notes.option: 30-cell peripheral blood karyotype or chromosomal microarray
option_notes.text: Karyotyping detects complete or mosaic absence of the second sex chromosome, confirming Turner syndrome.

option_notes.option: Provocative growth hormone stimulation testing with clonidine and arginine
option_notes.text: Girls with Turner syndrome are generally growth hormone sufficient; provocative testing is not the diagnostic test of choice.

option_notes.option: Targeted sequencing of the PTPN11 gene
option_notes.text: PTPN11 testing evaluates Noonan syndrome, which typically features right-sided heart defects, not bicuspid aortic valve.

option_notes.option: 24-hour ambulatory urinary growth hormone excretion
option_notes.text: Urinary GH excretion is unreliable and has no clinical utility in the diagnosis of Turner syndrome.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl with confirmed 45,X Turner syndrome has received somatropin (0.375 mg/kg/week) for 3 years, but her height SDS remains -2.7 despite good adherence. Her bone age is 8.5 years. To augment her final adult height, which adjunctive medication is supported by clinical consensus guidelines?
options: Low-dose oral oxandrolone at 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg/day
High-dose transdermal estradiol at adult feminizing doses
Continuous subcutaneous GnRH antagonist therapy
Daily oral fludrocortisone acetate
quizzes.explanation: In girls with Turner syndrome aged ≥9-10 years with significant height deficits, adding low-dose oxandrolone (0.03-0.05 mg/kg/day) to somatropin synergistically enhances linear height velocity and adult height without causing unacceptable virilization.

option_notes.option: Low-dose oral oxandrolone at 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg/day
option_notes.text: Low-dose oxandrolone acts as a non-aromatizable anabolic steroid that augments final height when combined with somatropin.

option_notes.option: High-dose transdermal estradiol at adult feminizing doses
option_notes.text: High-dose estrogen therapy prematurely fuses epiphyseal plates and drastically truncates final adult height.

option_notes.option: Continuous subcutaneous GnRH antagonist therapy
option_notes.text: GnRH antagonists are not indicated in prepubertal girls who already have primary hypogonadism.

option_notes.option: Daily oral fludrocortisone acetate
option_notes.text: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid for adrenal insufficiency and has no growth-promoting efficacy.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with short stature (height SDS -2.6), hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, a webbed neck, and pectus excavatum. Echocardiogram reveals dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis with mild right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal a pathogenic gain-of-function mutation in which gene?
options: PTPN11
GHR
FGFR3
GH1
quizzes.explanation: Noonan syndrome is most commonly (approx. 50%) caused by gain-of-function mutations in PTPN11, encoding the SHP2 protein tyrosine phosphatase in the RAS-MAPK pathway, classically presenting with pulmonary valve stenosis and dysmorphism.

option_notes.option: PTPN11
option_notes.text: PTPN11 mutations account for ~50% of Noonan syndrome cases, classically associated with pulmonary valve stenosis.

option_notes.option: GHR
option_notes.text: GHR mutations cause Laron syndrome without facial dysmorphism or pulmonary valve stenosis.

option_notes.option: FGFR3
option_notes.text: FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia or hypochondroplasia with marked rhizomelia and macrocephaly.

option_notes.option: GH1
option_notes.text: GH1 mutations cause isolated growth hormone deficiency without congenital heart defects or RASopathy facies.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and bilateral wrist pain. Physical exam reveals forearm shortening (mesomelia), prominent ulnar styloids, and limited wrist extension and supination. Wrist radiographs show bilateral curvature of the distal radius with triangular carpal bones and dorsal dislocation of the distal ulna (Madelung deformity). What is the underlying molecular defect?
options: Haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene on the pseudoautosomal region of chromosome Xp22.3/Yp11.3
Activating mutation in the PTH1R gene encoding the parathyroid hormone receptor
Inactivating mutation in the CASR gene encoding the calcium-sensing receptor
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the SOX9 gene
quizzes.explanation: Madelung deformity in association with mesomelic short stature is the hallmark of Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, caused by heterozygous deletion or point mutation of the SHOX gene in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1).

option_notes.option: Haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene on the pseudoautosomal region of chromosome Xp22.3/Yp11.3
option_notes.text: SHOX haploinsufficiency causes defective chondrocyte hypertrophy and premature growth plate fusion in the distal radius, producing Madelung deformity.

option_notes.option: Activating mutation in the PTH1R gene encoding the parathyroid hormone receptor
option_notes.text: PTH1R activating mutations cause Jansen-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with severe hypercalcemia.

option_notes.option: Inactivating mutation in the CASR gene encoding the calcium-sensing receptor
option_notes.text: CASR inactivating mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia without skeletal dysostosis.

option_notes.option: Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the SOX9 gene
option_notes.text: SOX9 mutations cause campomelic dysplasia with bowed long bones, sex reversal, and neonatal respiratory distress.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old female with Turner syndrome who is completing somatropin therapy presents for transition planning. Her blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates an aortic root diameter index of 2.6 cm/m2 (normal <2.0 cm/m2). What is the primary clinical significance of this finding?
options: High lifetime risk of catastrophic aortic dissection requiring aggressive blood pressure control and cardiac MRI monitoring
Normal physiological adaptation to growth hormone therapy requiring no intervention
Transient post-pubertal remodeling that will spontaneously regress by age 21
Indication for immediate cardiac transplantation within 30 days
quizzes.explanation: Aortic dilation in Turner syndrome carries a catastrophic risk of fatal aortic dissection and rupture. Aortic diameter index ≥2.5 cm/m2 requires tight blood pressure control (typically beta-blockers/ARBs), restriction of competitive isometric exertion, and serial surveillance by cardiac MRI.

option_notes.option: High lifetime risk of catastrophic aortic dissection requiring aggressive blood pressure control and cardiac MRI monitoring
option_notes.text: Aortic root enlargement in Turner syndrome is a major cause of premature mortality; surveillance and hemodynamic control are mandatory.

option_notes.option: Normal physiological adaptation to growth hormone therapy requiring no intervention
option_notes.text: Aortic dilation is not a normal physiological response to somatropin; it represents intrinsic medial vascular degeneration.

option_notes.option: Transient post-pubertal remodeling that will spontaneously regress by age 21
option_notes.text: Aortic dilation does not resolve spontaneously; it tends to expand progressively over time.

option_notes.option: Indication for immediate cardiac transplantation within 30 days
option_notes.text: Elective prophylactic surgical aortic root replacement is considered at critical dimensions, not immediate cardiac transplantation.

quizzes.q: An 18-year-old male with childhood-onset panhypopituitarism secondary to a large craniopharyngioma resected at age 8 has reached epiphyseal fusion (height velocity <1.5 cm/year). He is on stable replacement with levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, desmopressin, and testosterone. Somatropin is withheld for 6 weeks; his repeat serum IGF-I is 45 ng/mL (SDS -3.6). What is the appropriate next step regarding growth hormone management?
options: Resume somatropin at an adult transition starting dose without requiring provocative stimulation testing
Perform an insulin tolerance test to confirm severe growth hormone deficiency
Discontinue growth hormone permanently because linear growth is completed
Perform an oral glucose tolerance test to evaluate for residual somatotroph hypersecretion
quizzes.explanation: Patients with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (≥3) secondary to structural lesions with a low IGF-I (SDS <-2.0) have an extremely high probability of permanent severe GHD; consensus guidelines state they do not require provocative testing.

option_notes.option: Resume somatropin at an adult transition starting dose without requiring provocative stimulation testing
option_notes.text: Patients with panhypopituitarism and low IGF-I have documented permanent GHD; adult GH therapy should resume without re-testing.

option_notes.option: Perform an insulin tolerance test to confirm severe growth hormone deficiency
option_notes.text: Provocative testing with ITT is redundant and carries unnecessary hypoglycemic risks in patients with multiple documented central deficiencies.

option_notes.option: Discontinue growth hormone permanently because linear growth is completed
option_notes.text: Discontinuing GH leads to loss of bone mineral density, increased visceral adiposity, and unfavorable cardiovascular lipid profiles.

option_notes.option: Perform an oral glucose tolerance test to evaluate for residual somatotroph hypersecretion
option_notes.text: An oral glucose tolerance test evaluates GH excess, which is impossible in complete panhypopituitarism.

quizzes.q: A 19-year-old female with childhood isolated idiopathic growth hormone deficiency reaches final height. She stops somatropin for 2 months. She is healthy, takes an oral combined ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel contraceptive, and has a normal BMI. Her IGF-I is at -1.4 SDS. What is the most appropriate next step to evaluate whether she requires adult GH continuation?
options: Perform a validated provocative growth hormone stimulation test such as the insulin tolerance test or glucagon test
Resume pediatric-dose somatropin (30 mcg/kg/day) immediately based on the borderline IGF-I
Switch to oral mecasermin monotherapy for lifelong metabolic support
Perform a cranial MRI scan and prescribe growth hormone only if a microadenoma is seen
quizzes.explanation: In childhood isolated idiopathic GHD, up to 70-80% of patients demonstrate normal somatotroph reserve when re-tested after puberty. A provocative test (ITT or glucagon) is mandatory before diagnosing permanent adult GHD.

option_notes.option: Perform a validated provocative growth hormone stimulation test such as the insulin tolerance test or glucagon test
option_notes.text: Provocative re-testing is mandatory for isolated idiopathic childhood GHD because most patients test normal in adulthood.

option_notes.option: Resume pediatric-dose somatropin (30 mcg/kg/day) immediately based on the borderline IGF-I
option_notes.text: Resuming pediatric weight-based dosing in adults causes severe edema, arthralgias, and carpal tunnel syndrome.

option_notes.option: Switch to oral mecasermin monotherapy for lifelong metabolic support
option_notes.text: Mecasermin is indicated only for severe primary IGF-I deficiency, not secondary GHD.

option_notes.option: Perform a cranial MRI scan and prescribe growth hormone only if a microadenoma is seen
option_notes.text: Pituitary MRI does not evaluate dynamic somatotroph secretory capacity in idiopathic GHD.

quizzes.q: A 22-year-old female with confirmed persistent adult growth hormone deficiency is on stable somatropin replacement (0.3 mg daily) with an IGF-I of 0.0 SDS. She begins taking an oral combined estrogen-progestin contraceptive. Three months later, she reports fatigue, and her repeat serum IGF-I has dropped to -2.1 SDS despite strict adherence. What is the mechanism explaining this decline?
options: First-pass hepatic metabolism of oral estrogen induces SOCS2, inhibiting hepatic GH-mediated IGF-I generation
Estrogen binds directly to circulating somatropin, causing rapid renal clearance
Oral progestins directly destroy pituitary somatotroph secretory granules
Estrogen alters laboratory antibody recognition in automated IGF-I immunoassays
quizzes.explanation: Oral estrogens pass directly through the liver via the portal vein, upregulating suppressor of cytokine signaling 2 (SOCS2) and inhibiting Jak2/STAT5 signaling downstream of the hepatic GH receptor, attenuating IGF-I generation. Switching to transdermal estrogen or increasing the somatropin dose overcomes this effect.

option_notes.option: First-pass hepatic metabolism of oral estrogen induces SOCS2, inhibiting hepatic GH-mediated IGF-I generation
option_notes.text: First-pass hepatic exposure to oral estrogen suppresses GHR signaling, requiring higher somatropin doses or transdermal estrogen.

option_notes.option: Estrogen binds directly to circulating somatropin, causing rapid renal clearance
option_notes.text: Estrogen does not bind somatropin in circulation.

option_notes.option: Oral progestins directly destroy pituitary somatotroph secretory granules
option_notes.text: Progestins do not destroy somatotroph granules; the patient has persistent GHD with exogenous replacement.

option_notes.option: Estrogen alters laboratory antibody recognition in automated IGF-I immunoassays
option_notes.text: Estrogen does not interfere with modern automated IGF-I immunoassay antibodies.

quizzes.q: A 24-year-old male with persistent severe adult GHD starts somatropin at 0.8 mg daily (an inappropriately high starting dose). Within 3 weeks, he develops bilateral wrist paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, finger stiffness, and pitting pedal edema. What is the pathophysiological cause of these symptoms?
options: Growth hormone-induced sodium and water retention causing elevated tissue interstitial turgor and carpal tunnel compression
Autoimmune demyelinating peripheral polyneuropathy triggered by recombinant protein
Acute skeletal overgrowth of the carpal bones causing bony canal stenosis
Development of acute hypokalemic periodic paralysis
quizzes.explanation: Growth hormone stimulates renal tubular sodium reabsorption and extracellular fluid expansion. In adults, excessive starting doses commonly trigger fluid retention, soft tissue swelling, arthralgias, and compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

option_notes.option: Growth hormone-induced sodium and water retention causing elevated tissue interstitial turgor and carpal tunnel compression
option_notes.text: GH-mediated renal sodium retention and extracellular fluid expansion cause soft tissue edema and median nerve compression.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune demyelinating peripheral polyneuropathy triggered by recombinant protein
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not cause autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy.

option_notes.option: Acute skeletal overgrowth of the carpal bones causing bony canal stenosis
option_notes.text: Bony carpal remodeling takes years in acromegaly and does not occur in 3 weeks of replacement.

option_notes.option: Development of acute hypokalemic periodic paralysis
option_notes.text: Somatropin does not cause acute hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

quizzes.q: Which metabolic parameter has been demonstrated to improve consistently when growth hormone replacement is maintained during adulthood in patients with documented severe persistent GHD?
options: Increase in lean body mass, reduction in visceral fat, and improvement in lumbar spine bone mineral density
Complete reversal of central diabetes insipidus allowing cessation of desmopressin
Permanent cure of primary panhypopituitarism with spontaneous recovery of other axes
Reduction in total blood volume and reduction in left ventricular posterior wall thickness
quizzes.explanation: Adult GH replacement consistently produces favorable somatic and metabolic changes: increased lean body mass, decreased visceral and total body fat, improved bone mineral density accrual, and enhanced quality-of-life scores.

option_notes.option: Increase in lean body mass, reduction in visceral fat, and improvement in lumbar spine bone mineral density
option_notes.text: Prospective trials demonstrate gains in lean mass, reductions in trunk fat, and preservation of bone mineral density.

option_notes.option: Complete reversal of central diabetes insipidus allowing cessation of desmopressin
option_notes.text: GH replacement does not restore vasopressin secretion; diabetes insipidus requires lifelong desmopressin.

option_notes.option: Permanent cure of primary panhypopituitarism with spontaneous recovery of other axes
option_notes.text: Underlying pituitary damage is irreversible; other hormone deficiencies persist.

option_notes.option: Reduction in total blood volume and reduction in left ventricular posterior wall thickness
option_notes.text: GH normalizes, rather than decreases, left ventricular mass and cardiac output.

quizzes.q: A newborn infant is noted to have short limbs, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and a depressed nasal bridge. Radiographs demonstrate shortened long bones with flared metaphyses, square iliac wings with horizontal acetabular roofs, and narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances caudally. What is the fundamental cellular mechanism causing this skeletal dysplasia?
options: Constitutive activation of FGFR3 signaling that hyperactivates MAPK/ERK, inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
Defective synthesis of type II collagen alpha-1 chains impairing articular cartilage tensile strength
Overexpression of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) leading to chondrocyte hyperproliferation
Failure of osteoclast proton pump vacuolar ATPase causing generalized dense bone accumulation
quizzes.explanation: Achondroplasia is caused by a heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, which constitutively activates MAPK/ERK signaling and suppresses endochondral growth plate chondrogenesis.

option_notes.option: Constitutive activation of FGFR3 signaling that hyperactivates MAPK/ERK, inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
option_notes.text: FGFR3 gain-of-function constitutively signals through MAPK/ERK, inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.

option_notes.option: Defective synthesis of type II collagen alpha-1 chains impairing articular cartilage tensile strength
option_notes.text: Type II collagen defects cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, not achondroplasia.

option_notes.option: Overexpression of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) leading to chondrocyte hyperproliferation
option_notes.text: PTHrP does not cause achondroplasia; Jansen metaphyseal dysplasia involves the PTH1R receptor.

option_notes.option: Failure of osteoclast proton pump vacuolar ATPase causing generalized dense bone accumulation
option_notes.text: Osteoclast proton pump failure causes osteopetrosis with dense, marble-like bones, not achondroplasia.

quizzes.q: A 2-month-old infant with achondroplasia undergoes routine health supervision. The infant has hypotonia and head lag. Polysomnography demonstrates recurrent central apneas with desaturations to 82%. What urgent diagnostic test is indicated to guide clinical management?
options: MRI or thin-slice CT scan of the craniocervical junction to evaluate for foramen magnum stenosis
Continuous 24-hour video EEG to rule out infantile epileptic spasms
Echocardiogram to rule out coarctation of the aorta
Barium swallow study to assess for tracheoesophageal fistula
quizzes.explanation: In achondroplasia, endochondral ossification failure severely restricts the growth of the cranial base, causing foramen magnum stenosis. In infants, this can compress the brainstem and cervical spinal cord, causing central apneas and sudden death requiring suboccipital surgical decompression.

option_notes.option: MRI or thin-slice CT scan of the craniocervical junction to evaluate for foramen magnum stenosis
option_notes.text: Craniocervical neuroimaging identifies life-threatening foramen magnum stenosis and cervicomedullary compression in achondroplasia.

option_notes.option: Continuous 24-hour video EEG to rule out infantile epileptic spasms
option_notes.text: EEG does not identify the structural brainstem compression that causes central sleep apnea in achondroplasia.

option_notes.option: Echocardiogram to rule out coarctation of the aorta
option_notes.text: Coarctation of the aorta is a feature of Turner syndrome, not achondroplasia.

option_notes.option: Barium swallow study to assess for tracheoesophageal fistula
option_notes.text: Barium swallow is unrelated to the central neurogenic apnea of craniocervical compression.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old boy with genetically confirmed achondroplasia is started on vosoritide (15 mcg/kg subcutaneously daily). By what mechanism does this therapeutic agent counteract his underlying molecular disease process?
options: Binds to the natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B), increasing intracellular cGMP and inhibiting the hyperactive MAPK/ERK cascade
Directly cleaves circulating FGFR3 molecules via monoclonal antibody-mediated proteolysis
Stimulates hepatic growth hormone receptors to produce supranormal levels of IGF-I
Selectively binds bone hydroxyapatite crystals to prevent osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
quizzes.explanation: Vosoritide is a recombinant modified C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog that binds the NPR-B receptor, triggering intracellular cGMP generation. cGMP-dependent signals antagonize the overactive MAPK/ERK pathway downstream of mutant FGFR3, restoring growth plate chondrogenesis.

option_notes.option: Binds to the natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B), increasing intracellular cGMP and inhibiting the hyperactive MAPK/ERK cascade
option_notes.text: Vosoritide binds NPR-B to stimulate cGMP, which downregulates hyperactive MAPK/ERK signaling and promotes endochondral bone formation.

option_notes.option: Directly cleaves circulating FGFR3 molecules via monoclonal antibody-mediated proteolysis
option_notes.text: Vosoritide is a peptide analog, not a proteolytic antibody.

option_notes.option: Stimulates hepatic growth hormone receptors to produce supranormal levels of IGF-I
option_notes.text: Vosoritide works locally in cartilage growth plates, independent of hepatic GH/IGF-I axis stimulation.

option_notes.option: Selectively binds bone hydroxyapatite crystals to prevent osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
option_notes.text: Inhibiting osteoclast bone resorption describes bisphosphonates, not vosoritide.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old child presents with mild disproportionate short stature (height SDS -2.8). She does not have the classic macrocephaly, frontal bossing, or trident hand configuration seen in achondroplasia, but radiographs demonstrate mild rhizomelic shortening of the long bones and minimal lumbar interpedicular narrowing. Genetic testing reveals a heterozygous p.Asn540Lys mutation in FGFR3. What is the diagnosis?
options: Hypochondroplasia
Thanatophoric dysplasia type I
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita
Campomelic dysplasia
quizzes.explanation: Hypochondroplasia is a milder skeletal dysplasia caused by heterozygous FGFR3 mutations (most commonly p.Asn540Lys). Children have rhizomelic short stature but typically lack severe craniofacial dysmorphism.

option_notes.option: Hypochondroplasia
option_notes.text: Hypochondroplasia is classically caused by FGFR3 p.Asn540Lys, presenting with milder rhizomelia and subtle spine changes.

option_notes.option: Thanatophoric dysplasia type I
option_notes.text: Thanatophoric dysplasia is perinatal lethal with cloverleaf skull and extreme micromelia.

option_notes.option: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita
option_notes.text: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia is caused by COL2A1 mutations and features severe spinal shortening and epiphyseal dysplasia.

option_notes.option: Campomelic dysplasia
option_notes.text: Campomelic dysplasia is caused by SOX9 mutations with bowed tibia, sex reversal, and hypoplastic scapulae.

quizzes.q: A 3-year-old girl with recurrent fractures following minor trauma is evaluated. Physical examination reveals blue sclerae, joint hypermobility, and normal teeth (no dentinogenesis imperfecta). Radiographs demonstrate osteopenia, gracile long bones, and healed fractures without wormian bones or metaphyseal flaring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I
Achondroplasia
Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis
Hypochondroplasia
quizzes.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I (mild non-deforming) is caused by heterozygous null mutations in COL1A1 leading to quantitative reduction of normal type I collagen, presenting with recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and normal teeth.

option_notes.option: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I
option_notes.text: OI type I presents with skeletal fragility, blue sclerae, and normal dentition due to quantitative reduction in type I collagen.

option_notes.option: Achondroplasia
option_notes.text: Achondroplasia does not cause bone fragility, recurrent fractures, or blue sclerae.

option_notes.option: Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis
option_notes.text: Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis causes mesomelia and Madelung deformity, not recurrent fractures.

option_notes.option: Hypochondroplasia
option_notes.text: Hypochondroplasia is an FGFR3 chondrodysplasia with short limbs, not a collagen fragility syndrome.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of rapid linear growth. Over the past 18 months, his height has jumped from the 75th percentile to well above the 99th percentile (height SDS +3.4), with a height velocity of 12.5 cm/year. Physical exam reveals coarse facial features, mandibular prognathism, large fleshy hands and feet, and hyperhidrosis. Serum IGF-I is markedly elevated at +4.8 SDS. What test is required to confirm autonomous growth hormone hypersecretion?
options: Standard oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) evaluating for failure of serum growth hormone suppression
Arginine plus growth hormone-releasing hormone stimulation test
Random morning serum growth hormone measurement following an overnight fast
24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion
quizzes.explanation: In normal individuals, an oral glucose load suppresses serum GH to <1.0 mcg/L (or <0.4 mcg/L on sensitive assays). Failure to suppress GH during an OGTT confirms autonomous GH hypersecretion (pituitary gigantism/acromegaly).

option_notes.option: Standard oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) evaluating for failure of serum growth hormone suppression
option_notes.text: Failure to suppress GH to <1.0 mcg/L during an oral glucose challenge is the gold standard diagnostic confirmation of gigantism.

option_notes.option: Arginine plus growth hormone-releasing hormone stimulation test
option_notes.text: Arginine-GHRH is a provocative stimulation test used to diagnose GH deficiency, not hypersecretion.

option_notes.option: Random morning serum growth hormone measurement following an overnight fast
option_notes.text: Random GH is pulsatile and can be normally elevated in growing adolescents, leading to false-positive or false-negative results.

option_notes.option: 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion
option_notes.text: Urinary cortisol evaluates Cushing syndrome, which causes growth deceleration, not accelerated gigantism.

quizzes.q: A 2-year-old female presents with massive accelerated linear growth (height SDS +4.2), generalized soft tissue overgrowth, voracious appetite, and acromegalic facial features that began at 8 months of age. Laboratory workup reveals GH 68 ng/mL, IGF-I SDS +5.1, and prolactin 88 ng/mL (reference <20 ng/mL). Brain MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension. Microarray analysis is most likely to identify which molecular etiology?
options: Microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 involving the GPR101 gene (X-linked acrogigantism / X-LAG)
Inactivating mutation in the NSD1 gene causing Sotos syndrome
Heterozygous fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation causing Marfan syndrome
Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing Prader-Willi syndrome
quizzes.explanation: X-LAG (X-linked acrogigantism) is caused by microduplication of Xq26.3 encompassing GPR101. It is the classic cause of infancy-onset gigantism (onset <5 years, often <12 months) characterized by extreme growth velocity, high GH and prolactin, and massive pituitary adenomas or hyperplasia.

option_notes.option: Microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 involving the GPR101 gene (X-linked acrogigantism / X-LAG)
option_notes.text: Xq26.3 microduplication (GPR101) causes X-LAG, presenting with early infant-onset gigantism and hyperprolactinemia.

option_notes.option: Inactivating mutation in the NSD1 gene causing Sotos syndrome
option_notes.text: NSD1 mutations cause Sotos syndrome, which features overgrowth with macrocephaly, not pituitary macroadenomas.

option_notes.option: Heterozygous fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation causing Marfan syndrome
option_notes.text: FBN1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, presenting with tall stature and arachnodactyly without GH hypersecretion.

option_notes.option: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing Prader-Willi syndrome
option_notes.text: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, which features short stature and GHD.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old male undergoes transsphenoidal surgical debulking for an invasive pituitary somatotroph macroadenoma. Postoperatively, his serum IGF-I remains elevated at +3.2 SDS, and MRI demonstrates residual cavernous sinus invasion. He is initiated on long-acting octreotide, but his IGF-I remains elevated after 6 months. What pharmacological agent with a distinct mechanism of action can be added to block peripheral IGF-I generation?
options: Pegvisomant
Mecasermin
Somatropin
Fludrocortisone
quizzes.explanation: Pegvisomant is a genetically engineered growth hormone receptor antagonist that binds to the GHR and prevents functional receptor dimerization, blocking peripheral IGF-I production without requiring pituitary tumor shrinkage.

option_notes.option: Pegvisomant
option_notes.text: Pegvisomant acts as a GHR competitive antagonist, directly reducing serum IGF-I in patients refractory to somatostatin analogs.

option_notes.option: Mecasermin
option_notes.text: Mecasermin is recombinant IGF-I and would dangerously exacerbate hyper-IGF-I toxicity.

option_notes.option: Somatropin
option_notes.text: Somatropin is recombinant growth hormone and is absolutely contraindicated in gigantism.

option_notes.option: Fludrocortisone
option_notes.text: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid with no effect on the growth hormone receptor.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with accelerated growth (height SDS +3.1), macrocephaly (head circumference >98th percentile), prominent high forehead with frontoparietal balding, down-slanting palpebral fissures, a long narrow face, and a pointed chin. He has mild intellectual disability. Endocrine testing demonstrates a normal basal IGF-I and normal suppression of GH on oral glucose testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism)
Pituitary gigantism secondary to somatotroph adenoma
Precocious puberty secondary to a hypothalamic hamartoma
McCune-Albright syndrome with autonomous somatotroph hyperplasia
quizzes.explanation: Sotos syndrome (caused by NSD1 haploinsufficiency) is a classic genetic overgrowth disorder presenting with macrocephaly, characteristic facial gestalt (high forehead, pointed chin), intellectual disability, and normal growth hormone regulation.

option_notes.option: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism)
option_notes.text: Sotos syndrome presents with non-endocrine genetic overgrowth, macrocephaly, pointed chin, and learning difficulties.

option_notes.option: Pituitary gigantism secondary to somatotroph adenoma
option_notes.text: Pituitary gigantism exhibits autonomous failure of GH suppression on OGTT and elevated IGF-I.

option_notes.option: Precocious puberty secondary to a hypothalamic hamartoma
option_notes.text: Precocious puberty presents with secondary sexual characteristics, testicular enlargement, and advanced bone age.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome with autonomous somatotroph hyperplasia
option_notes.text: McCune-Albright syndrome features fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait macules, and elevated GH/IGF-I.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old girl with Marfan syndrome is evaluated for severe tall stature (height SDS +3.2, current height 184 cm) with projected adult height of 195 cm. She has severe pectus excavatum, arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, and aortic root dilation (Z-score +2.8). Which management strategy is contraindicated for reducing her linear growth potential?
options: High-dose estrogen therapy, due to the unacceptable risk of accelerating aortic root dilation and thromboembolism
Percutaneous bilateral epiphysiodesis of the distal femur and proximal tibia
Tight blood pressure control with an angiotensin receptor blocker or beta-blocker
Annual surveillance with transthoracic echocardiogram
quizzes.explanation: Historically, high-dose supraphysiological estrogen was used to accelerate epiphyseal fusion in tall girls; however, in Marfan syndrome, high-dose estrogens are contraindicated because they can increase cardiovascular risk, accelerate aortic root enlargement, and increase thromboembolic complications. Percutaneous epiphysiodesis is preferred if height reduction is indicated.

option_notes.option: High-dose estrogen therapy, due to the unacceptable risk of accelerating aortic root dilation and thromboembolism
option_notes.text: High-dose estrogen therapy carries significant vascular risks and may worsen connective tissue laxity and aortic dilation in Marfan syndrome.

option_notes.option: Percutaneous bilateral epiphysiodesis of the distal femur and proximal tibia
option_notes.text: Percutaneous epiphysiodesis is a safe, targeted orthopedic procedure to arrest long-bone growth without systemic hormonal adverse effects.

option_notes.option: Tight blood pressure control with an angiotensin receptor blocker or beta-blocker
option_notes.text: Hemodynamic control with ARBs or beta-blockers is the standard of care to retard aortic root enlargement in Marfan syndrome.

option_notes.option: Annual surveillance with transthoracic echocardiogram
option_notes.text: Serial echocardiography is mandatory in all Marfan patients to monitor aortic root dimensions.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe vomiting, lethargy, and dehydration. Blood pressure is 74/42 mmHg and heart rate is 144 bpm. Physical exam reveals marked hyperpigmentation of the gingival mucosa and knuckles. Laboratory analysis shows sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.8 mEq/L, and blood glucose 42 mg/dL. What is the immediate life-saving treatment?
options: Intravenous bolus of 0.9% normal saline (20 mL/kg) with 5% dextrose and immediate IV hydrocortisone 50 mg
Continuous intravenous insulin infusion with 50% dextrose to treat hyperkalemia
Immediate oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg and oral rehydration solution
Intravenous hypertonic 3% sodium chloride bolus without glucocorticoids
quizzes.explanation: This patient is in acute primary adrenal crisis with hypotensive shock, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Immediate resuscitation with isotonic saline/dextrose boluses and parenteral hydrocortisone is vital.

option_notes.option: Intravenous bolus of 0.9% normal saline (20 mL/kg) with 5% dextrose and immediate IV hydrocortisone 50 mg
option_notes.text: Isotonic fluid resuscitation and parenteral hydrocortisone rapidly correct intravascular volume depletion and adrenal collapse.

option_notes.option: Continuous intravenous insulin infusion with 50% dextrose to treat hyperkalemia
option_notes.text: Insulin will exacerbate the life-threatening hypoglycemia (glucose 42 mg/dL); hydrocortisone and IV fluids correct the hyperkalemia.

option_notes.option: Immediate oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg and oral rehydration solution
option_notes.text: Oral administration is contraindicated in an emetic, obtunded child in hypovolemic shock.

option_notes.option: Intravenous hypertonic 3% sodium chloride bolus without glucocorticoids
option_notes.text: Administering hypertonic saline without hydrocortisone fails to treat the underlying vascular collapse and risks pontine myelinolysis.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old previously healthy boy develops progressive fatigue, declining school performance, and skin bronzing over 6 months. Neurological exam reveals hyperreflexia and mild visual tracking impairment. Plasma ACTH is 840 pg/mL with morning cortisol 2.1 mcg/dL. Plasma renin activity is elevated. What diagnostic test should be prioritized to identify the underlying etiology?
options: Plasma very long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) analysis and brain MRI
Sweat chloride test to rule out cystic fibrosis
Serum anti-streptolysin O titer and complement levels
Gastric emptying scintigraphy and upper endoscopy
quizzes.explanation: In young boys presenting with primary adrenal insufficiency (elevated ACTH, low cortisol) and subtle neurocognitive changes, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1 mutation) must be excluded by measuring plasma very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) and brain MRI to detect cerebral demyelination.

option_notes.option: Plasma very long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) analysis and brain MRI
option_notes.text: Elevated hexacosanoic acid (C26:0) and VLCFA ratios confirm X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, a leading cause of primary AI in young males.

option_notes.option: Sweat chloride test to rule out cystic fibrosis
option_notes.text: Cystic fibrosis does not cause primary adrenal failure or cutaneous hyperpigmentation.

option_notes.option: Serum anti-streptolysin O titer and complement levels
option_notes.text: Post-streptococcal disease causes glomerulonephritis, not primary adrenal failure.

option_notes.option: Gastric emptying scintigraphy and upper endoscopy
option_notes.text: Gastric scintigraphy does not diagnose adrenal failure or white matter neurodegenerative disease.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl with autoimmune Addison disease (primary adrenocortical failure) on maintenance hydrocortisone (9 mg/m2/day) and fludrocortisone (0.1 mg daily) develops acute streptococcal pharyngitis with fever of 39.4°C (103°F). What instruction must be given to her parents regarding steroid dosing?
options: Triple her oral hydrocortisone dose (25–30 mg/m2/day) divided every 8 hours until fever resolves, keeping fludrocortisone unchanged
Discontinue hydrocortisone completely to allow the immune system to fight the bacterial infection
Increase fludrocortisone to 1.0 mg daily and reduce hydrocortisone to half dose
Administer oral dexamethasone 4 mg once daily without taking any fluids
quizzes.explanation: During febrile illness (>38.5°C), endogenous cortisol secretion in healthy individuals triples. Patients with adrenal insufficiency require 'stress dosing' (doubling or tripling the maintenance oral hydrocortisone dose) to prevent adrenal crisis. Fludrocortisone dosing remains unchanged.

option_notes.option: Triple her oral hydrocortisone dose (25–30 mg/m2/day) divided every 8 hours until fever resolves, keeping fludrocortisone unchanged
option_notes.text: Stress dosing (2-3x maintenance hydrocortisone) replicates normal physiological stress responses during fever and prevents adrenal crisis.

option_notes.option: Discontinue hydrocortisone completely to allow the immune system to fight the bacterial infection
option_notes.text: Discontinuing hydrocortisone during febrile illness precipitates fatal adrenal crisis within hours.

option_notes.option: Increase fludrocortisone to 1.0 mg daily and reduce hydrocortisone to half dose
option_notes.text: Fludrocortisone dose is not increased during routine fever; hydrocortisone at high doses provides cross-reactive mineralocorticoid activity.

option_notes.option: Administer oral dexamethasone 4 mg once daily without taking any fluids
option_notes.text: High-dose dexamethasone is unmonitored, causes prolonged suppression, and omitting fluids leads to hypovolemia.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old boy with severe Crohn disease has been treated with oral prednisone (40 mg daily) for 6 months. His gastroenterologist abruptly stops the prednisone after achieving mucosal healing. Five days later, the boy presents with severe fatigue, dizziness, nausea, and a blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. Laboratory testing shows sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, and glucose 64 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis?
options: Tertiary (iatrogenic) adrenal insufficiency due to prolonged hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression
Acute primary autoimmune adrenalitis with destruction of all three adrenocortical zones
Acute primary mineralocorticoid deficiency secondary to renal tubular injury
Cushing disease relapse secondary to an ACTH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
quizzes.explanation: Prolonged exogenous supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH secretion, resulting in adrenocortical atrophy. Abrupt cessation unmasks central/tertiary adrenal insufficiency, characterized by normal potassium (intact mineralocorticoid axis) but symptomatic glucocorticoid deficiency.

option_notes.option: Tertiary (iatrogenic) adrenal insufficiency due to prolonged hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression
option_notes.text: Abrupt withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids is the most common cause of tertiary adrenal insufficiency, requiring gradual tapering.

option_notes.option: Acute primary autoimmune adrenalitis with destruction of all three adrenocortical zones
option_notes.text: Primary autoimmune destruction presents with hyperkalemia, elevated ACTH, and skin hyperpigmentation, which are absent here.

option_notes.option: Acute primary mineralocorticoid deficiency secondary to renal tubular injury
option_notes.text: Mineralocorticoid secretion (aldosterone) is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, not ACTH, and remains preserved.

option_notes.option: Cushing disease relapse secondary to an ACTH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
option_notes.text: Cushing disease features hypercortisolemia and hypertension, the opposite of this presentation.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, fatigue, and alacrima (inability to produce tears). Physical examination also reveals mild difficulty swallowing (achalasia). Laboratory testing confirms primary adrenocortical failure with ACTH 650 pg/mL and cortisol 1.8 mcg/dL. What rare autosomal recessive syndrome is defined by this constellation of findings?
options: Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome, caused by AAAS mutations)
Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1, caused by AIRE mutations)
Werdnig-Hoffmann spinal muscular atrophy
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
quizzes.explanation: Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the AAAS gene (encoding the nuclear pore protein aladin), characterized by the triad of Adrenal insufficiency, Achalasia, and Alacrima.

option_notes.option: Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome, caused by AAAS mutations)
option_notes.text: AAAS mutations cause Triple A syndrome with ACTH-resistant adrenal failure, achalasia, and alacrima.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1, caused by AIRE mutations)
option_notes.text: APS-1 presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease, without achalasia.

option_notes.option: Werdnig-Hoffmann spinal muscular atrophy
option_notes.text: Spinal muscular atrophy affects anterior horn cells and does not cause primary adrenal failure.

option_notes.option: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
option_notes.text: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency features virilization and hypertension due to DOC accumulation, without alacrima.

quizzes.q: A 12-day-old male infant born at term presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and a 15% weight loss from birth. He has normal male external genitalia with bilateral descended testes and hyperpigmentation of the scrotum. Serum electrolytes demonstrate sodium 116 mEq/L and potassium 8.2 mEq/L. Blood glucose is 48 mg/dL. What diagnostic finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
options: Markedly elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (>10,000 ng/dL) and high plasma renin activity
Elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin activity
Low ACTH with elevated serum cortisol (>35 mcg/dL)
Elevated 11-deoxycorticosterone with metabolic alkalosis
quizzes.explanation: The male infant exhibits acute salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presenting in the second week of life with hyperkalemia, severe hyponatremia, and scrotal hyperpigmentation. Massive elevation of 17-OHP and elevated plasma renin confirm classic salt-wasting CAH.

option_notes.option: Markedly elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (>10,000 ng/dL) and high plasma renin activity
option_notes.text: Massive 17-OHP accumulation due to 21-hydroxylase block coupled with aldosterone deficiency drives high renin and severe salt loss.

option_notes.option: Elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin activity
option_notes.text: Aldosterone is deficient in salt-wasting CAH; high aldosterone with low renin defines primary aldosteronism.

option_notes.option: Low ACTH with elevated serum cortisol (>35 mcg/dL)
option_notes.text: Cortisol is deficient and ACTH is elevated due to loss of negative feedback.

option_notes.option: Elevated 11-deoxycorticosterone with metabolic alkalosis
option_notes.text: Accumulation of DOC occurs in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, causing hypertension and hypokalemia, not salt wasting.

quizzes.q: A full-term newborn is noted to have ambiguous genitalia: marked clitoromegaly with a glanular groove, complete labial fusion, and a single perineal urogenital orifice (Prader stage IV). Neither gonad is palpable in the labioscrotal folds. Peripheral blood karyotype reveals 46,XX. What is the underlying hormonal mechanism producing this phenotype?
options: Inability to 21-hydroxylate progesterone precursors, resulting in massive ACTH stimulation and shunting into adrenal androgen biosynthesis in utero
Complete peripheral end-organ resistance to dihydrotestosterone due to an androgen receptor mutation
Autonomous secretion of testosterone from an undifferentiated dysgenetic intra-abdominal ovary
Placental aromatase hyperactivation converting fetal estrogens into testosterone
quizzes.explanation: In 46,XX classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, impaired cortisol synthesis removes negative feedback on the pituitary, causing massive ACTH secretion. Accumulated precursors are shunted into androstenedione and testosterone, virilizing the bipotential external genitalia in utero.

option_notes.option: Inability to 21-hydroxylate progesterone precursors, resulting in massive ACTH stimulation and shunting into adrenal androgen biosynthesis in utero
option_notes.text: Prenatal excess adrenal androgens virilize 46,XX external genitalia while internal Müllerian ducts remain intact.

option_notes.option: Complete peripheral end-organ resistance to dihydrotestosterone due to an androgen receptor mutation
option_notes.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs in 46,XY individuals and presents with female or ambiguous external genitalia, not virilized 46,XX.

option_notes.option: Autonomous secretion of testosterone from an undifferentiated dysgenetic intra-abdominal ovary
option_notes.text: Dysgenetic ovaries do not produce massive androgens in utero.

option_notes.option: Placental aromatase hyperactivation converting fetal estrogens into testosterone
option_notes.text: Placental aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; deficiency (not hyperactivation) causes virilization.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old male with classic salt-wasting CAH maintained on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone undergoes routine evaluation. Testicular examination reveals firm, painless, multinodular lobulated masses bilaterally in the medial aspect of the testes adjacent to the mediastinum testis. Serum 17-OHP is 4,200 ng/dL (reference <200 ng/dL) and androstenedione is elevated. Testicular ultrasound confirms bilateral hypoechoic lobulated lesions. What is the diagnosis and correct clinical management?
options: Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART); optimize compliance and intensify glucocorticoid suppression to regress the lesions
Bilateral malignant testicular seminomas; proceed with immediate bilateral radical orchiectomy
Bilateral epididymal cysts; observe with annual scrotal palpation alone
Leydig cell adenomas; initiate high-dose mitotane chemotherapy
quizzes.explanation: Testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) are benign ACTH-responsive lesions arising from aberrant adrenal cortical cells in the testes of males with CAH. Poor endocrine control (elevated ACTH/17-OHP) stimulates tumor hypertrophy. Increasing glucocorticoid therapy to suppress ACTH leads to tumor regression and preserves fertility.

option_notes.option: Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART); optimize compliance and intensify glucocorticoid suppression to regress the lesions
option_notes.text: TARTs are benign, ACTH-dependent tumors that regress with intensified glucocorticoid replacement; biopsy or orchiectomy is contraindicated.

option_notes.option: Bilateral malignant testicular seminomas; proceed with immediate bilateral radical orchiectomy
option_notes.text: TARTs are completely benign and must not be misdiagnosed as malignant seminomas, avoiding tragic unnecessary bilateral orchiectomy.

option_notes.option: Bilateral epididymal cysts; observe with annual scrotal palpation alone
option_notes.text: The lesions reside within the testicular parenchyma at the rete testis, not the epididymis.

option_notes.option: Leydig cell adenomas; initiate high-dose mitotane chemotherapy
option_notes.text: Mitotane is adrenolytic chemotherapy for adrenocortical carcinoma and has no role in benign TART management.

quizzes.q: A 17-year-old female presents with severe facial acne, male-pattern terminal hair growth on the chin and lower abdomen (Ferriman-Gallwey score 12), and oligomenorrhea (3 periods per year). Baseline morning 17-OHP is 380 ng/dL (reference <100 ng/dL). An intravenous cosyntropin stimulation test (250 mcg) produces a 60-minute 17-OHP of 2,400 ng/dL. What is the definitive diagnosis?
options: Non-classic (late-onset) Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome with normal adrenal steroidogenesis
Cushing disease secondary to pituitary ACTH macroadenoma
Primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure)
quizzes.explanation: A cosyntropin-stimulated 17-OHP level >1,500 ng/dL (and typically >1,000-2,000 ng/dL) is diagnostic of non-classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which commonly masquerades as PCOS in adolescent and young adult females.

option_notes.option: Non-classic (late-onset) Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
option_notes.text: Post-ACTH 17-OHP >1,500 ng/dL confirms non-classic CAH, distinguishing it from idiopathic polycystic ovary syndrome.

option_notes.option: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome with normal adrenal steroidogenesis
option_notes.text: In classic PCOS without CAH, stimulated 17-OHP remains well below 1,000 ng/dL.

option_notes.option: Cushing disease secondary to pituitary ACTH macroadenoma
option_notes.text: Cushing disease presents with central obesity, moon facies, striae, and elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol.

option_notes.option: Primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure)
option_notes.text: Premature ovarian failure presents with elevated gonadotropins (FSH >40 IU/L) and hypoestrogenism without 17-OHP hypersecretion.

quizzes.q: A 3-week-old female infant with confirmed classic simple-virilizing CAH (46,XX, Prader III) is prescribed maintenance therapy. Her serum electrolytes and blood pressure are normal. Which medication regimen should be prescribed for ongoing maintenance?
options: Oral hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m2/day divided in three daily doses, with fludrocortisone monitoring
High-dose oral dexamethasone 2 mg daily given as a single nighttime dose
Spironolactone monotherapy at 5 mg/kg/day without glucocorticoid replacement
Continuous subcutaneous infusion of octreotide at 20 mcg/kg/day
quizzes.explanation: In growing infants and children with classic CAH, short-acting hydrocortisone (10-15 mg/m2/day divided three times daily) is the preferred glucocorticoid because longer-acting agents (dexamethasone, prednisone) cause severe linear growth suppression and metabolic toxicity.

option_notes.option: Oral hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m2/day divided in three daily doses, with fludrocortisone monitoring
option_notes.text: Short-acting oral hydrocortisone suppresses adrenal androgens while minimizing growth plate suppression in young pediatric patients.

option_notes.option: High-dose oral dexamethasone 2 mg daily given as a single nighttime dose
option_notes.text: Dexamethasone is 30-40 times more potent than hydrocortisone, lacks mineralocorticoid activity, and severely suppresses growth in infants.

option_notes.option: Spironolactone monotherapy at 5 mg/kg/day without glucocorticoid replacement
option_notes.text: Spironolactone does not replace deficient cortisol and will precipitate fatal adrenal crisis.

option_notes.option: Continuous subcutaneous infusion of octreotide at 20 mcg/kg/day
option_notes.text: Octreotide has no role in CAH and inhibits growth hormone secretion.

quizzes.q: An 11-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of rapid weight gain. Over the past 2 years, her BMI percentile increased from the 60th to the 98th percentile, while her linear height velocity plummeted from 5.5 cm/year to 1.8 cm/year (height dropping from the 50th to the 10th percentile). She has plethoric moon facies, dark purplish abdominal striae measuring 1.5 cm in width, and a blood pressure of 136/88 mmHg. What is the most critical feature differentiating her condition from simple exogenous obesity?
options: Severe deceleration of linear growth velocity in the presence of advancing weight gain
Elevated fasting serum insulin concentrations
Development of mild acanthosis nigricans in skin folds
Presence of increased subcutaneous adipose tissue over the triceps
quizzes.explanation: Simple nutritional obesity stimulates linear growth and bone age maturation, so children are tall for their age. Conversely, Cushing syndrome uniquely combines rapid weight gain with dramatic growth deceleration and bone age delay due to the catabolic effects of glucocorticoids on the growth plate.

option_notes.option: Severe deceleration of linear growth velocity in the presence of advancing weight gain
option_notes.text: Linear growth arrest paired with weight gain is the hallmark clinical feature that distinguishes Cushing syndrome from simple obesity.

option_notes.option: Elevated fasting serum insulin concentrations
option_notes.text: Hyperinsulinemia is universal in simple obesity and does not distinguish Cushing syndrome.

option_notes.option: Development of mild acanthosis nigricans in skin folds
option_notes.text: Acanthosis nigricans occurs in both conditions due to hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance.

option_notes.option: Presence of increased subcutaneous adipose tissue over the triceps
option_notes.text: Subcutaneous fat accumulation occurs in all forms of generalized obesity.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old boy has confirmed pathological hypercortisolemia based on elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol (4-fold above normal) and elevated late-night salivary cortisol. His 08:00 h plasma ACTH is measured at 2.4 pg/mL (reference 10–60 pg/mL, with undetectable repeated value <5 pg/mL). What is the appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: High-resolution dedicated contrast-enhanced adrenal CT or MRI scan
Pituitary MRI with dynamic gadolinium enhancement
Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation
High-resolution chest CT scan to evaluate for bronchial carcinoid tumor
quizzes.explanation: A suppressed plasma ACTH (<5 pg/mL) indicates ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, pointing directly to primary autonomous adrenal pathology (adenoma, carcinoma, PPNAD). Imaging of the adrenal glands is the mandatory next step.

option_notes.option: High-resolution dedicated contrast-enhanced adrenal CT or MRI scan
option_notes.text: Suppressed plasma ACTH confirms ACTH-independent hypercortisolemia; adrenal imaging is mandatory to locate the primary adrenal lesion.

option_notes.option: Pituitary MRI with dynamic gadolinium enhancement
option_notes.text: Pituitary MRI is indicated for ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, not when ACTH is suppressed.

option_notes.option: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation
option_notes.text: BIPSS differentiates pituitary from ectopic sources when ACTH is elevated, and is contraindicated in ACTH-independent disease.

option_notes.option: High-resolution chest CT scan to evaluate for bronchial carcinoid tumor
option_notes.text: Bronchial carcinoids secrete ectopic ACTH, which causes elevated, not suppressed, ACTH.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old boy with severe Cushing syndrome has elevated 24-hour UFC and a plasma ACTH of 65 pg/mL. Pituitary MRI demonstrates no visible focal adenoma. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test produces a 75% reduction in morning cortisol, and peripheral CRH administration elicits a 95% rise in ACTH. What diagnostic test should be performed before proceeding with neurosurgical exploration?
options: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation to confirm central ACTH gradient and lateralization
Total bilateral adrenalectomy as first-line definitive management
Lifelong high-dose metyrapone monotherapy without further testing
Abdominal ultrasound to look for ovarian rest tumors
quizzes.explanation: When ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is diagnosed but pituitary MRI is normal or equivocal (<6 mm lesion), BIPSS with CRH stimulation is the gold standard to prove a pituitary source (central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2 baseline or ≥3 post-CRH) and aid inter-sinus lateralization.

option_notes.option: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation to confirm central ACTH gradient and lateralization
option_notes.text: BIPSS confirms a pituitary origin over occult ectopic ACTH and guides the neurosurgeon when MRI fails to identify a clear microadenoma.

option_notes.option: Total bilateral adrenalectomy as first-line definitive management
option_notes.text: Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last-resort therapy that causes Nelson syndrome (invasive corticotroph tumor growth) and permanent adrenal insufficiency.

option_notes.option: Lifelong high-dose metyrapone monotherapy without further testing
option_notes.text: Metyrapone is a temporary medical inhibitor, not definitive diagnostic or curative management.

option_notes.option: Abdominal ultrasound to look for ovarian rest tumors
option_notes.text: Ovarian rest tumors occur in CAH, not Cushing disease, and the patient is a male.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl undergoes successful transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy for a 4 mm corticotroph microadenoma. On postoperative day 2, she feels weak and nauseated. Laboratory testing reveals morning serum cortisol 0.6 mcg/dL (reference 5–20 mcg/dL) and ACTH 4.2 pg/mL. What is the clinical significance of this finding?
options: Indicates complete surgical resection and cure, requiring temporary hydrocortisone replacement therapy
Represents acute surgical failure and indicates immediate re-exploration of the sella
Reflects permanent panhypopituitarism requiring permanent desmopressin and levothyroxine
Indicates transformation of the corticotroph tumor into an aggressive silent carcinoma
quizzes.explanation: Profound transient hypocortisolemia (morning cortisol <1-2 mcg/dL) following transsphenoidal adenomectomy is the hallmark of surgical cure. It reflects suppression of the normal surrounding hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis by prolonged prior hypercortisolemia. Temporary hydrocortisone replacement is required until the HPA axis recovers.

option_notes.option: Indicates complete surgical resection and cure, requiring temporary hydrocortisone replacement therapy
option_notes.text: Postoperative morning cortisol <1-2 mcg/dL demonstrates complete resection of the autonomous adenoma and confirms surgical cure.

option_notes.option: Represents acute surgical failure and indicates immediate re-exploration of the sella
option_notes.text: Surgical failure would manifest as persistently elevated or normal unsuppressed cortisol (>5 mcg/dL).

option_notes.option: Reflects permanent panhypopituitarism requiring permanent desmopressin and levothyroxine
option_notes.text: Selective adenomectomy preserves other pituitary cell lines; hypocortisolemia is temporary and usually recovers over 6-18 months.

option_notes.option: Indicates transformation of the corticotroph tumor into an aggressive silent carcinoma
option_notes.text: Low cortisol indicates absence of functional corticotroph tissue, the opposite of carcinoma progression.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for Cushing syndrome. Physical examination reveals pigmented lentigines on her eyelids, lips, and oral mucosa. Echocardiogram demonstrates a benign right atrial myxoma. Endocrine testing reveals ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. What gene defect is responsible for this condition?
options: Inactivating mutation in PRKAR1A encoding the protein kinase A regulatory subunit type 1A
Activating mutation in the GNAS gene encoding G-alpha-s
Loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 gene encoding menin
Germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene
quizzes.explanation: Carney complex is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A, leading to constitutive PKA activation, cardiac myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation (lentigines), and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD).

option_notes.option: Inactivating mutation in PRKAR1A encoding the protein kinase A regulatory subunit type 1A
option_notes.text: PRKAR1A mutations cause Carney complex with PPNAD, cardiac myxomas, and spotty pigmentation.

option_notes.option: Activating mutation in the GNAS gene encoding G-alpha-s
option_notes.text: GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome featuring fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty, and cafe-au-lait macules.

option_notes.option: Loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 gene encoding menin
option_notes.text: MEN1 causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors, not cardiac myxomas or PPNAD.

option_notes.option: Germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene
option_notes.text: RET mutations cause MEN2 with medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for severe hypertension (blood pressure 152/96 mmHg). Laboratory testing reveals sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and serum bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is profoundly suppressed (<0.1 ng/mL/h), and plasma aldosterone concentration is also undetectable (<1.0 ng/dL). Urinary free cortisol-to-cortisone ratio is normal. Treatment with high-dose spironolactone produces no reduction in blood pressure. However, initiating oral amiloride normalizes her blood pressure and potassium within 72 hours. What is the molecular diagnosis?
options: Liddle syndrome, caused by a gain-of-function mutation in an epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) subunit
Primary aldosteronism secondary to a solitary unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma
Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA) secondary to a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene
Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) secondary to an HSD11B2 gene mutation
quizzes.explanation: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant channelopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCNN1B or SCNN1G that disrupt the PY motif, preventing ENaC degradation. The constitutive channel activation reabsorbs sodium independently of aldosterone, suppressing both renin and aldosterone. Because the mineralocorticoid receptor is bypassed, spironolactone fails, while direct ENaC blockers (amiloride) are curative.

option_notes.option: Liddle syndrome, caused by a gain-of-function mutation in an epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) subunit
option_notes.text: Liddle syndrome uniquely combines low renin, low aldosterone, hypokalemia, and selective responsiveness to amiloride over spironolactone.

option_notes.option: Primary aldosteronism secondary to a solitary unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma
option_notes.text: Primary aldosteronism features markedly elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC >15 ng/dL).

option_notes.option: Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA) secondary to a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene
option_notes.text: GRA features elevated aldosterone (driven by ACTH) that suppresses with dexamethasone.

option_notes.option: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) secondary to an HSD11B2 gene mutation
option_notes.text: AME exhibits a markedly elevated urinary free cortisol-to-cortisone ratio (>10:1) and responds to spironolactone.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with severe hypertension (148/92 mmHg) and mild hypokalemia (potassium 3.1 mEq/L). His father and paternal grandfather had early-onset hypertension and suffered fatal hemorrhagic strokes in their early 30s. Lab evaluation shows suppressed plasma renin activity (<0.2 ng/mL/h) and elevated plasma aldosterone (38 ng/dL). Administering oral dexamethasone 0.5 mg daily for 4 days results in complete normalization of blood pressure and normalization of plasma aldosterone to <2 ng/dL. What is the genetic basis of this disorder?
options: Unequal crossover fusing the promoter region of 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) with the coding region of aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (HSD11B2) gene
Activating somatic mutation in the KCNJ5 potassium channel gene in the adrenal cortex
Germline loss-of-function mutation in the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2) gene
quizzes.explanation: Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA / Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 fusion gene. Aldosterone is ectopically synthesized in the zona fasciculata under the regulation of ACTH rather than angiotensin II. Low-dose dexamethasone suppresses ACTH, completely shutting down aldosterone production and curing the hypertension.

option_notes.option: Unequal crossover fusing the promoter region of 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) with the coding region of aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)
option_notes.text: The chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene places aldosterone synthase under ACTH regulation; suppression with dexamethasone is pathognomonic.

option_notes.option: Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (HSD11B2) gene
option_notes.text: HSD11B2 mutations cause AME, which features low, not elevated, aldosterone levels.

option_notes.option: Activating somatic mutation in the KCNJ5 potassium channel gene in the adrenal cortex
option_notes.text: KCNJ5 somatic mutations cause sporadic aldosterone-producing adenomas, which do not suppress with dexamethasone.

option_notes.option: Germline loss-of-function mutation in the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2) gene
option_notes.text: NR3C2 loss-of-function causes pseudohypoaldosteronism with hypotension and hyperkalemia.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe hypertension (142/90 mmHg), growth failure, and recurrent hypokalemic weakness (serum potassium 2.4 mEq/L). Plasma renin activity is <0.1 ng/mL/h and plasma aldosterone is undetectable (<1.0 ng/dL). 24-hour urine steroid metabolite profiling by GC-MS demonstrates a urinary ratio of (tetrahydrocortisol + 5alpha-tetrahydrocortisol) to tetrahydrocortisone of 18:1 (normal reference <1.0). What is the diagnosis?
options: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME)
Liddle syndrome
Primary aldosteronism
Renal artery stenosis
quizzes.explanation: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in HSD11B2. Cortisol is not inactivated to cortisone in renal tubular cells, flooding the mineralocorticoid receptor (which has equal affinity for cortisol and aldosterone) and producing low-renin, low-aldosterone hypertension with a massively elevated urinary cortisol-to-cortisone metabolite ratio.

option_notes.option: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME)
option_notes.text: Inactivating HSD11B2 mutations allow cortisol to hyperactivate the MR, marked by low renin, low aldosterone, and a massive urinary cortisol/cortisone ratio.

option_notes.option: Liddle syndrome
option_notes.text: Liddle syndrome is an ENaC channelopathy with normal urinary cortisol-to-cortisone ratios.

option_notes.option: Primary aldosteronism
option_notes.text: Primary aldosteronism presents with high plasma aldosterone concentrations, not undetectable levels.

option_notes.option: Renal artery stenosis
option_notes.text: Renal artery stenosis causes high-renin, high-aldosterone secondary hypertension.

quizzes.q: A 3-week-old male infant presents with failure to thrive, vomiting, and profound dehydration. Lab testing shows sodium 121 mEq/L, potassium 7.6 mEq/L, and BUN 38 mg/dL. He has normal male genitalia. Urinalysis reveals pyuria, and renal ultrasound shows severe bilateral hydronephrosis with a dilated posterior urethra. Plasma aldosterone is markedly elevated at 280 ng/dL, and plasma renin activity is high. What is the diagnosis?
options: Secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA3) triggered by urinary tract obstruction and infection
Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Congenital aldosterone synthase deficiency (CYP11B2)
Liddle syndrome
quizzes.explanation: Secondary (type 3) pseudohypoaldosteronism is a transient resistance of the renal tubules to aldosterone, classically triggered in infants by acute urinary tract infection in the setting of congenital obstructive uropathy (posterior urethral valves). High aldosterone and renin in the presence of severe salt wasting and hyperkalemia confirm mineralocorticoid resistance.

option_notes.option: Secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA3) triggered by urinary tract obstruction and infection
option_notes.text: Pyelonephritis with obstructive uropathy impairs tubular responsiveness to aldosterone, causing transient severe salt loss and hyperkalemia.

option_notes.option: Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
option_notes.text: Classic salt-wasting CAH features aldosterone deficiency, not massive elevation of circulating aldosterone.

option_notes.option: Congenital aldosterone synthase deficiency (CYP11B2)
option_notes.text: Aldosterone synthase deficiency features undetectable or low aldosterone with elevated precursors.

option_notes.option: Liddle syndrome
option_notes.text: Liddle syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalemia, the exact opposite of salt-wasting hyperkalemia.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with hypertension (150/94 mmHg) and hypokalemia (potassium 2.8 mEq/L). Laboratory testing shows suppressed plasma renin and suppressed aldosterone. On detailed dietary history, he admits to eating large quantities (200 g daily) of traditional black licorice imported from Europe over the past 3 months. What active substance in the licorice is responsible for his presentation?
options: Glycyrrhetinic acid, which reversibly inhibits the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 enzyme
Ephedrine alkaloids that directly stimulate alpha-1 adrenergic vascular receptors
Sodium chloride crystals that saturate the proximal tubule sodium-glucose cotransporter
Cyanogenic glycosides that block mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase
quizzes.explanation: Black licorice contains glycyrrhizin, which is metabolized to glycyrrhetinic acid. Glycyrrhetinic acid is a potent competitive inhibitor of 11beta-HSD2 in the renal collecting duct, preventing the normal enzymatic conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone and producing an acquired form of Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess.

option_notes.option: Glycyrrhetinic acid, which reversibly inhibits the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 enzyme
option_notes.text: Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11beta-HSD2, enabling endogenous cortisol to flood and hyperactivate renal mineralocorticoid receptors.

option_notes.option: Ephedrine alkaloids that directly stimulate alpha-1 adrenergic vascular receptors
option_notes.text: Ephedrine causes tachycardia and vasoconstriction but does not cause profound hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with suppressed aldosterone.

option_notes.option: Sodium chloride crystals that saturate the proximal tubule sodium-glucose cotransporter
option_notes.text: Sodium loading suppresses renin and aldosterone but does not cause hypokalemia with 11beta-HSD2 inhibition.

option_notes.option: Cyanogenic glycosides that block mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase
option_notes.text: Cyanide toxicity causes cellular hypoxia and lactic acidosis, not mineralocorticoid excess.

quizzes.q: A 9-day-old male infant born at 39 weeks of gestation is recalled after newborn screening reveals an elevated TSH of 74 mIU/L. Confirmatory serum testing demonstrates venous TSH >100 mIU/L and free T4 0.3 ng/dL (reference: 1.1-2.2 ng/dL). Examination shows an infant with a 1.5-cm posterior fontanel, mild macroglossia, and an umbilical hernia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?
options: Levothyroxine oral suspension at 2-5 mcg/kg/day administered with soy formula
Oral levothyroxine tablets crushed in breastmilk at 10-15 mcg/kg/day on an empty stomach
Intravenous liothyronine (triiodothyronine) bolus followed by maintenance L-T3
Observation for 4 weeks with repeat serum TSH before initiating therapy
quizzes.explanation: Guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology (ESPE) mandate immediate treatment of confirmed primary congenital hypothyroidism with oral levothyroxine at 10-15 mcg/kg/day (typically 37.5-50 mcg/day). The tablet should be crushed in a few milliliters of water or breastmilk. Soy formula impairs absorption and should be avoided. Liothyronine is not standard initial therapy and causes erratic peaks.

option_notes.option: Levothyroxine oral suspension at 2-5 mcg/kg/day administered with soy formula
option_notes.text: Incorrect. 2-5 mcg/kg/day is inadequate for a neonate (neonatal clearance is high), and soy formula binds levothyroxine, preventing absorption.

option_notes.option: Oral levothyroxine tablets crushed in breastmilk at 10-15 mcg/kg/day on an empty stomach
option_notes.text: Correct. 10-15 mcg/kg/day using crushed commercial tablets rapidly normalizes free T4 within 3-7 days, which is vital for cerebral neurodevelopment.

option_notes.option: Intravenous liothyronine (triiodothyronine) bolus followed by maintenance L-T3
option_notes.text: Incorrect. T3 (liothyronine) is unnecessary, causes abrupt unphysiological fluctuations, and does not provide stable cerebral intracrine T3 generation.

option_notes.option: Observation for 4 weeks with repeat serum TSH before initiating therapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Delaying treatment past 2-3 weeks of life is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive intelligence quotients.

quizzes.q: A 2-week-old female diagnosed with severe primary neonatal hypothyroidism undergoes diagnostic thyroid imaging. Radionuclide scintigraphy using technetium-99m pertechnetate demonstrates intense focal radioisotope uptake at the base of the tongue with complete absence of uptake in the lower anterior neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Athyreosis (complete thyroid agenesis)
Lingual thyroid (ectopic thyroid dysgenesis)
Thyroid dyshormonogenesis due to TPO gene mutation
Maternal antithyroid drug-induced goitrous hypothyroidism
quizzes.explanation: Ectopic thyroid occurs when embryonic thyroid tissue fails to migrate normally along the thyroglossal duct tract from the foramen cecum to the normal pretracheal cervical position. Scintigraphy demonstrating focal tracer accumulation at the base of the tongue with no tracer in the lower neck is diagnostic of a lingual or sublingual ectopic thyroid, which represents ~60% of thyroid dysgenesis cases.

option_notes.option: Athyreosis (complete thyroid agenesis)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Athyreosis shows complete absence of tracer accumulation in both the tongue base and the neck.

option_notes.option: Lingual thyroid (ectopic thyroid dysgenesis)
option_notes.text: Correct. Focal radiotracer uptake at the tongue base along the midline thyroglossal tract is pathognomonic for ectopic lingual thyroid tissue.

option_notes.option: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis due to TPO gene mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Dyshormonogenesis features an in situ cervical gland, frequently enlarged (goiter), with variable tracer trapping depending on the defect.

option_notes.option: Maternal antithyroid drug-induced goitrous hypothyroidism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Maternal drug transfer causes an enlarged, normally positioned (cervical) in situ goiter.

quizzes.q: A full-term infant with severe neonatal hypothyroidism is started on levothyroxine 12 mcg/kg/day at day 10 of life. Which of the following monitoring targets reflects optimal early therapy during the first 6 months of life?
options: Serum TSH maintained between 5 and 10 mIU/L with free T4 in the lower quartile of reference range
Serum free T4 rapidly normalized into the upper half of the normal reference range with TSH suppressed <0.01 mIU/L
Serum free T4 in the upper half of the reference range and serum TSH normalized <5 mIU/L within 2-4 weeks
Discontinuation of levothyroxine every 2 months to assess spontaneous endogenous thyroid recovery
quizzes.explanation: Treatment goals in congenital hypothyroidism emphasize restoring serum free T4 into the upper half of the normal age-specific reference interval (e.g., 1.4-2.3 ng/dL) within 1-2 weeks and lowering TSH to <5 mIU/L within 2-4 weeks. Over-suppression (TSH <0.01 mIU/L) carries risks of craniosynostosis and behavior disturbance, while under-treatment compromises brain development.

option_notes.option: Serum TSH maintained between 5 and 10 mIU/L with free T4 in the lower quartile of reference range
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Free T4 in the lower quartile with TSH 5-10 mIU/L represents under-treatment, which degrades cognitive outcomes.

option_notes.option: Serum free T4 rapidly normalized into the upper half of the normal reference range with TSH suppressed <0.01 mIU/L
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Completely suppressing TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) risks iatrogenic hyperthyroidism, craniosynostosis, and cardiac overdrive.

option_notes.option: Serum free T4 in the upper half of the reference range and serum TSH normalized <5 mIU/L within 2-4 weeks
option_notes.text: Correct. Maintaining free T4 in the upper half of the normal range while achieving normal TSH (<5 mIU/L) ensures adequate brain myelination without toxicity.
