option_notes.option: Discontinuation of levothyroxine every 2 months to assess spontaneous endogenous thyroid recovery
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Intermittent withdrawal during the critical first 3 years of brain development is contraindicated and causes neurocognitive damage.

quizzes.q: An infant with sensorineural deafness and primary neonatal hypothyroidism is found to have an enlarged in situ goitrous thyroid on ultrasound. Scintigraphy demonstrates normal pertechnetate trapping, but rapid discharge of iodide occurs upon administration of sodium perchlorate (positive perchlorate discharge test >30%). What gene mutation is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: SLC26A4 (Pendrin)
PAX8 (Paired box gene 8)
TSHR (Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor)
NKX2-1 (Thyroid transcription factor 1)
quizzes.explanation: Pendred syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in SLC26A4, which encodes pendrin, an anion exchanger involved in iodide transport at the apical follicular membrane. It is characterized by sensorineural hearing loss (associated with enlarged vestibular aqueducts on temporal bone CT), goitrous dyshormonogenesis, and an abnormal perchlorate discharge test reflecting impaired iodide organification.

option_notes.option: SLC26A4 (Pendrin)
option_notes.text: Correct. SLC26A4 mutations cause Pendred syndrome, combining goitrous dyshormonogenesis, organification defect, and sensorineural deafness.

option_notes.option: PAX8 (Paired box gene 8)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PAX8 mutations cause thyroid dysgenesis (hypoplasia/ectopia) without sensorineural hearing loss.

option_notes.option: TSHR (Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause resistance to TSH or thyroid hypoplasia with blunted cAMP signaling, not an organification defect with deafness.

option_notes.option: NKX2-1 (Thyroid transcription factor 1)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NKX2-1 mutations cause brain-lung-thyroid syndrome (choreoathetosis, infant respiratory distress, and CH).

quizzes.q: A female infant born at 39 weeks has an initial newborn screen revealing low total T4 with a normal TSH of 4.2 mIU/L. Repeat venous testing confirms low free T4 (0.6 ng/dL) with persistently normal TSH (3.1 mIU/L). Which of the following evaluations is most urgently indicated?
options: Diagnostic radioiodine uptake and perchlorate discharge test
Evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis for central hypopituitarism and cortisol deficiency
Measurement of maternal antithyroglobulin and anti-TPO antibodies
Observation without treatment until 6 months of age
quizzes.explanation: Low free T4 in the presence of an inappropriately normal or low TSH indicates central (hypothalamic-pituitary) hypothyroidism. Central hypothyroidism is rarely isolated and is frequently associated with congenital hypopituitarism (multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies), including potentially fatal central adrenal insufficiency (ACTH deficiency) and growth hormone deficiency. An urgent pituitary axis evaluation and pituitary MRI are required. If hydrocortisone deficiency is present, glucocorticoid replacement must precede or accompany levothyroxine to prevent acute adrenal crisis.

option_notes.option: Diagnostic radioiodine uptake and perchlorate discharge test
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Scintigraphy and perchlorate discharge are used for primary goitrous dyshormonogenesis, not central hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis for central hypopituitarism and cortisol deficiency
option_notes.text: Correct. Central hypothyroidism demands urgent screening for ACTH/cortisol deficiency and GH deficiency, alongside neuroimaging of the pituitary gland.

option_notes.option: Measurement of maternal antithyroglobulin and anti-TPO antibodies
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Maternal thyroid autoantibodies produce primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, not central low-TSH hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Observation without treatment until 6 months of age
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Ignoring low FT4 in an infant risks profound developmental disability and unaddressed adrenal crisis.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old girl is evaluated for declining academic grades, emotional lability, heat intolerance, and resting palpitations. On examination, pulse is 118 bpm, blood pressure is 128/62 mmHg, and she has a smooth, non-tender, diffusely enlarged thyroid gland with an audible continuous bruit. Laboratory testing reveals TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3.8 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and highly elevated thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI). What is the most appropriate initial medical therapy?
options: Propylthiouracil 5 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours
Methimazole 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day once daily plus atenolol for symptom control
Immediate radioactive iodine (131I) ablation at 15 mCi
Lugol's strong iodine solution monotherapy
quizzes.explanation: Methimazole (MMI, 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day, up to 1.0 mg/kg/day) is the only antithyroid drug recommended for pediatric Graves' disease. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is black-box contraindicated due to fulminant hepatic necrosis. Beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol 1-2 mg/kg/day) are added to control adrenergic hyperactivation (tachycardia, tremor). 131I is a definitive modality usually considered if medical therapy fails or causes toxic reactions.

option_notes.option: Propylthiouracil 5 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PTU has an FDA black-box warning prohibiting its use in pediatric patients due to fatal hepatic failure.

option_notes.option: Methimazole 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day once daily plus atenolol for symptom control
option_notes.text: Correct. Methimazole at 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day combined with a beta-blocker is the first-line medical therapy for pediatric Graves' disease.

option_notes.option: Immediate radioactive iodine (131I) ablation at 15 mCi
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Radioactive iodine is a definitive second-line option, not standard immediate emergency therapy before medical stabilization.

option_notes.option: Lugol's strong iodine solution monotherapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Lugol's iodine alone results in transient Wolff-Chaikoff effect followed by escape and exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old male with Graves' disease has been taking methimazole 20 mg daily for 4 weeks. He presents to the urgent care clinic with a 2-day history of high fever (39.2°C), severe sore throat, and dysphagia. Examination shows an erythematous pharynx with tonsillar exudate. What is the most critical immediate clinical action?
options: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and continue methimazole unchanged
Immediately discontinue methimazole and obtain an emergent complete blood count with differential
Increase methimazole to 30 mg daily to treat an acute thyrotoxic storm
Switch methimazole immediately to oral propylthiouracil
quizzes.explanation: Agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count <500/mcL) is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic complication of methimazole occurring in 0.3-0.5% of patients. Any child on antithyroid medication who develops acute fever or severe sore throat must stop the drug immediately and have an urgent CBC with differential to rule out neutropenia. If agranulocytosis is confirmed, the drug is permanently discontinued and broad-spectrum antibiotics/G-CSF are initiated.

option_notes.option: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and continue methimazole unchanged
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Continuing methimazole without checking the neutrophil count risks fatal septic shock from drug-induced agranulocytosis.

option_notes.option: Immediately discontinue methimazole and obtain an emergent complete blood count with differential
option_notes.text: Correct. Immediate drug cessation and emergent CBC evaluation are mandatory to diagnose or exclude drug-induced agranulocytosis.

option_notes.option: Increase methimazole to 30 mg daily to treat an acute thyrotoxic storm
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Fever and pharyngitis suggest agranulocytosis or severe infection; increasing the drug dose could prove lethal.

option_notes.option: Switch methimazole immediately to oral propylthiouracil
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PTU shares cross-reactivity for agranulocytosis and is contraindicated in children due to fulminant hepatotoxicity.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of declining height velocity. Over the past 2 years, her height percentile has dropped from the 50th to the 10th percentile, while her weight percentile has increased from the 45th to the 75th percentile. On physical exam, she has dry skin, sluggish deep tendon reflexes, and a firm, non-tender, lobulated goiter. Bone age is delayed by 3.5 years. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Cushing syndrome due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
Chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis
Isolated growth hormone neurosecretory dysfunction
Graves' disease with autonomous toxic nodule
quizzes.explanation: The classic growth pattern of juvenile acquired hypothyroidism (most commonly Hashimoto thyroiditis) is marked linear growth deceleration with preserved or increasing weight-for-height (crossing height percentiles downward while BMI increases), accompanied by severe bone age retardation and a firm, lobulated goiter. Cushing syndrome also causes growth failure with obesity, but is not accompanied by a lobulated goiter or marked bone age delay of this degree.

option_notes.option: Cushing syndrome due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cushing syndrome presents with hypercortisolemia, central obesity, striae, and hypertension, not a firm lobulated goiter.

option_notes.option: Chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis
option_notes.text: Correct. Hashimoto thyroiditis classically produces growth arrest with reciprocal weight gain, delayed bone age, and a lobulated goiter.

option_notes.option: Isolated growth hormone neurosecretory dysfunction
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Isolated GH deficiency does not cause goiter, dry skin, or sluggish relaxation of deep tendon reflexes.

option_notes.option: Graves' disease with autonomous toxic nodule
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Graves' disease accelerates linear growth velocity and advances bone age rather than delaying it.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old girl presents with significant bilateral breast enlargement (Tanner stage 3) and an episode of vaginal bleeding. Her height is at the 15th percentile (down from the 50th percentile 2 years ago), and bone age is delayed by 2 years. Pelvic ultrasound reveals enlarged multicystic ovaries. Thyroid panel reveals TSH 480 mIU/L and free T4 0.1 ng/dL. What is the term and physiological mechanism for this clinical condition?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome due to TSH cross-reactivity at the ovarian FSH receptor
Central precocious puberty due to hypothalamic hamartoma
Autonomous granulosa cell tumor secreting estradiol
quizzes.explanation: Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome is a rare manifestation of long-standing, severe, untreated primary juvenile hypothyroidism characterized by isosexual pseudoprecocious puberty (breast development, vaginal bleeding, multicystic ovaries) occurring paradoxically with delayed linear growth and delayed bone age. The extreme elevation of circulating TSH exhibits weak cross-reactivity and agonism at the G-protein-coupled FSH receptor in the ovaries. Prompt treatment with levothyroxine completely reverses the ovarian cysts, pubertal signs, and elevated TSH.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. McCune-Albright features café-au-lait macules, fibrous dysplasia, and advanced bone age, whereas bone age is delayed here.

option_notes.option: Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome due to TSH cross-reactivity at the ovarian FSH receptor
option_notes.text: Correct. Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome results from massive TSH elevations cross-stimulating ovarian FSH receptors, resolving completely with L-T4.

option_notes.option: Central precocious puberty due to hypothalamic hamartoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Central precocious puberty features accelerated growth velocity and advanced bone age, not severe growth arrest and delayed bone age.

option_notes.option: Autonomous granulosa cell tumor secreting estradiol
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumor does not cause massive TSH elevations or delayed bone age.

quizzes.q: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with Graves' disease treated with methimazole delivers a male infant. At day 4 of life, the infant becomes irritable, with a resting heart rate of 190 bpm, poor feeding, diaphoresis, and a small palpable goiter. Serum free T4 is markedly elevated at 4.6 ng/dL with TSH <0.02 mIU/L. What is the primary etiology of this infant's thyrotoxicosis?
options: Autonomous activating mutation in the neonatal TSH receptor gene
Transplacental transfer of maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI / TRAb)
Neonatal thyroid adenoma
Neonatal iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow)
quizzes.explanation: Neonatal Graves' disease is caused by the passive transplacental passage of maternal IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI/TRAb) during pregnancy. Clinical onset is often delayed until day 2-7 of life as transplacentally transferred maternal antithyroid drug (methimazole) clears from the infant's circulation. It is self-limited, typically resolving in 2 to 4 months as maternal IgG antibodies are degraded.

option_notes.option: Autonomous activating mutation in the neonatal TSH receptor gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSHR germline activating mutations cause persistent familial non-autoimmune hyperthyroidism, not transient neonatal disease.

option_notes.option: Transplacental transfer of maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI / TRAb)
option_notes.text: Correct. Transplacental transfer of maternal TSI causes transient neonatal Graves' disease that resolves as maternal IgG antibodies clear.

option_notes.option: Neonatal thyroid adenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Toxic adenomas are exceptionally rare in neonates and do not resolve spontaneously.

option_notes.option: Neonatal iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Iodine overload in neonates typically causes transient hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), not neonatal Graves'.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old boy in the pediatric intensive care unit with severe septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and dopamine infusion undergoes routine thyroid testing. Results show TSH 0.12 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L), total T3 22 ng/dL (reference: 85-170 ng/dL), and free T4 0.6 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL). Serum reverse T3 (rT3) is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding his thyroid status?
options: Initiate intravenous levothyroxine 2 mcg/kg/day to restore normal cellular metabolism
Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) replacement to normalize circulating T3 levels
Do not administer thyroid hormones; continue intensive management of septic shock and monitor
Perform urgent emergent total thyroidectomy
quizzes.explanation: This patient exhibits classic severe non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS, low T4/low T3 with suppressed TSH and elevated rT3) compounded by dopamine infusion, which suppresses TSH secretion. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that treating NTIS with either T4 or T3 does not improve clinical outcomes or survival and may be harmful. Current guidelines advise against thyroid hormone replacement and mandate focus on treating the primary systemic pathology.

option_notes.option: Initiate intravenous levothyroxine 2 mcg/kg/day to restore normal cellular metabolism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. IV levothyroxine has been shown in clinical trials not to improve survival, extubation rates, or hemodynamics in pediatric critical illness.

option_notes.option: Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) replacement to normalize circulating T3 levels
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Liothyronine therapy does not reduce mortality and may exacerbate tissue catabolism during acute critical illness.

option_notes.option: Do not administer thyroid hormones; continue intensive management of septic shock and monitor
option_notes.text: Correct. Guidelines recommend against routine thyroid hormone replacement in NTIS; therapy centers on treating the underlying sepsis.

option_notes.option: Perform urgent emergent total thyroidectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thyroidectomy has no therapeutic role in NTIS and would be catastrophic in septic shock.

quizzes.q: Which enzymatic alteration is primarily responsible for the rapid reduction of active triiodothyronine (T3) and simultaneous rise of reverse T3 (rT3) in acute non-thyroidal illness?
options: Upregulation of hepatic type 1 deiodinase (DIO1)
Upregulation of type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) with downregulation of type 1 (DIO1) and type 2 (DIO2) deiodinases
Inactivation of thyroid peroxidase (TPO) by circulating endotoxins
Increased activity of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) degrading proteases
quizzes.explanation: In NTIS, inflammatory cytokines downregulate type 1 (DIO1) and type 2 (DIO2) iodothyronine deiodinases, impairing 5'-deiodination of T4 to T3. Concurrently, type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) is induced in peripheral tissues, which actively deiodinates T4 into reverse T3 and degrades T3 into T2, causing the hallmark low T3 and high rT3 pattern.

option_notes.option: Upregulation of hepatic type 1 deiodinase (DIO1)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hepatic DIO1 is downregulated, not upregulated, during acute critical illness.

option_notes.option: Upregulation of type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) with downregulation of type 1 (DIO1) and type 2 (DIO2) deiodinases
option_notes.text: Correct. Induction of DIO3 coupled with downregulation of DIO1 and DIO2 shunts thyroid hormone metabolism toward inactive rT3 and degrades active T3.

option_notes.option: Inactivation of thyroid peroxidase (TPO) by circulating endotoxins
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TPO is an intrathyroidal enzyme involved in hormone synthesis, not the primary driver of peripheral T3/rT3 shunting.

option_notes.option: Increased activity of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) degrading proteases
option_notes.text: Incorrect. While TBG levels can drop, alterations in TBG do not explain the selective reciprocal changes in free T3 and rT3.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl is recovering from severe bacterial pneumonia in the pediatric ward. Three weeks ago in the ICU, her TSH was 0.2 mIU/L with a low free T3. Today, repeat morning labs show TSH 8.4 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L) with normal free T4 1.2 ng/dL and normal free T3. She is clinically asymptomatic and eating well. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Diagnose permanent primary Hashimoto thyroiditis and initiate levothyroxine 50 mcg daily
Recognize this as a transient TSH rebound surge during recovery from non-thyroidal illness and recheck in 4-6 weeks without starting medication
Order emergent radioiodine thyroid scintigraphy and thyroid ultrasound
Obtain pituitary MRI to evaluate for a TSH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
quizzes.explanation: During recovery from severe non-thyroidal illness, hypothalamic-pituitary suppression resolves, frequently producing a transient rebound elevation of serum TSH (typically 5-15 mIU/L) with normal or recovering peripheral thyroid hormone levels. This transient physiological surge stimulates the thyroid gland to replenish hormone stores and normalizes spontaneously within 4 to 8 weeks. Levothyroxine is not indicated.

option_notes.option: Diagnose permanent primary Hashimoto thyroiditis and initiate levothyroxine 50 mcg daily
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Initiating levothyroxine is inappropriate for a benign, self-limited post-illness physiological rebound.

option_notes.option: Recognize this as a transient TSH rebound surge during recovery from non-thyroidal illness and recheck in 4-6 weeks without starting medication
option_notes.text: Correct. The transient TSH elevation represents expected neuroendocrine recovery from NTIS; re-evaluation in 4-6 weeks will confirm resolution.

option_notes.option: Order emergent radioiodine thyroid scintigraphy and thyroid ultrasound
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Scintigraphy and ultrasound are not indicated for an expected transient biochemical surge post-illness.

option_notes.option: Obtain pituitary MRI to evaluate for a TSH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSHoma is an exceedingly rare condition that presents with elevated FT4 and unsuppressed TSH, not post-pneumonia recovery.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old child with severe septic shock is receiving continuous infusions of dopamine, epinephrine, and high-dose hydrocortisone. Thyroid function testing reveals TSH <0.05 mIU/L and free T4 0.5 ng/dL. Which factor is most directly contributing to the profound suppression of TSH in this patient?
options: Direct central inhibition of pituitary thyrotropes by dopamine and pharmacological glucocorticoids
Severe metabolic acidosis accelerating renal excretion of TSH
Activation of pituitary TSH receptor antibodies
Elevated circulating free fatty acids competing for TSH binding sites
quizzes.explanation: Both dopamine and pharmacological doses of glucocorticoids are potent central inhibitors of pituitary thyrotropes, directly suppressing pulsatile and basal TSH secretion. In critically ill children receiving dopamine and hydrocortisone, TSH is almost universally suppressed to undetectable or near-undetectable levels, simulating severe central hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Direct central inhibition of pituitary thyrotropes by dopamine and pharmacological glucocorticoids
option_notes.text: Correct. Dopamine and glucocorticoids directly suppress pituitary thyrotrope secretion of TSH.

option_notes.option: Severe metabolic acidosis accelerating renal excretion of TSH
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Acidosis does not accelerate renal clearance of glycoprotein hormones like TSH.

option_notes.option: Activation of pituitary TSH receptor antibodies
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSH receptor antibodies do not suppress pituitary TSH directly; they stimulate the thyroid gland.

option_notes.option: Elevated circulating free fatty acids competing for TSH binding sites
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Free fatty acids interfere with protein binding of T4/T3 in vitro, but do not directly suppress pituitary thyrotrope gene expression.

quizzes.q: When evaluating a critically ill pediatric patient with low free T4 and low-normal TSH, which biochemical test is most useful to help differentiate euthyroid sick syndrome from central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism?
options: Serum reverse T3 (rT3)
Serum thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies
Serum thyroglobulin concentration
Urinary iodine concentration
quizzes.explanation: Serum reverse T3 (rT3) is the most valuable differentiator: in non-thyroidal illness syndrome, rT3 is characteristically elevated or high-normal due to DIO3 activation and reduced peripheral clearance. In contrast, in central hypothyroidism, pituitary failure causes a global deficiency of substrate T4 secretion without peripheral shunting, resulting in a low or undetectable serum rT3.

option_notes.option: Serum reverse T3 (rT3)
option_notes.text: Correct. Serum rT3 is elevated in NTIS due to enhanced DIO3 clearance of T4, whereas rT3 is low in central hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Serum thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TPO antibodies identify autoimmune thyroiditis (primary hypothyroidism), but do not distinguish NTIS from central hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Serum thyroglobulin concentration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thyroglobulin is a non-specific marker of thyroid tissue integrity and does not reliably distinguish central AI/hypothyroidism from NTIS.

option_notes.option: Urinary iodine concentration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Urinary iodine assesses nutritional iodine sufficiency, which is not the distinguishing feature between NTIS and hypopituitarism.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for learning difficulties and hyperactivity. Routine screening reveals free T4 2.8 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), free T3 6.4 pg/mL (reference: 2.3-4.2 pg/mL), and TSH 3.8 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Examination reveals a resting heart rate of 105 bpm and a mild, diffuse, non-tender goiter without orbitopathy. His mother and maternal uncle are reported to have similar laboratory findings and were erroneously treated with radioactive iodine in the past. What is the most likely molecular defect?
options: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TSHR gene
Heterozygous dominant-negative mutation in the THRB gene
Hemizygous inactivating mutation in the SLC16A2 (MCT8) gene
Activating mutation in the GNAS gene
quizzes.explanation: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the THRB gene. It is characterized by elevated free T4 and free T3 with an unsuppressed (normal or slightly elevated) TSH. Due to differential receptor expression, TR-alpha in the heart is stimulated by elevated hormones, causing resting sinus tachycardia, while goiter arises from unsuppressed TSH. Autosomal dominant transmission in the mother and uncle confirms RTH-beta.

option_notes.option: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TSHR gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause resistance to TSH (elevated TSH with low or normal FT4), not elevated FT4/FT3.

option_notes.option: Heterozygous dominant-negative mutation in the THRB gene
option_notes.text: Correct. Heterozygous mutations in THRB cause RTH-beta, displaying elevated FT4/FT3 with unsuppressed TSH and familial autosomal dominant transmission.

option_notes.option: Hemizygous inactivating mutation in the SLC16A2 (MCT8) gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. SLC16A2 mutations cause Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome with high T3, low T4, and severe neurological spastic quadriplegia.

option_notes.option: Activating mutation in the GNAS gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Activating GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome with fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules, and precocious puberty.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old girl is found to have elevated free T4 (2.6 ng/dL) and free T3 (5.8 pg/mL) with a serum TSH of 4.5 mIU/L. To differentiate between resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta) and a TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (TSHoma), which diagnostic finding would most strongly support a TSHoma?
options: A markedly elevated glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit concentration and alpha-subunit/TSH ratio >1.0
A 3-fold rise in serum TSH in response to an intravenous TRH stimulation test
Presence of a heterozygous mutation in the THRB gene
Complete absence of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis
quizzes.explanation: Both RTH-beta and TSHomas present with high free T4/T3 and unsuppressed TSH. A TSHoma is distinguished by an elevated circulating pituitary glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit level and an alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio >1.0 (present in >80% of TSHomas), blunted TSH response to TRH stimulation, and a visible pituitary lesion on contrast MRI. In contrast, RTH-beta typically shows a normal alpha-subunit ratio and a brisk, normal TSH rise to TRH.

option_notes.option: A markedly elevated glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit concentration and alpha-subunit/TSH ratio >1.0
option_notes.text: Correct. Elevated free alpha-subunit and an alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio >1.0 strongly indicate an autonomous TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor.

option_notes.option: A 3-fold rise in serum TSH in response to an intravenous TRH stimulation test
option_notes.text: Incorrect. A brisk 3-fold TSH rise after TRH stimulation is characteristic of RTH-beta, whereas TSHomas show a blunted or flat response.

option_notes.option: Presence of a heterozygous mutation in the THRB gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. A THRB mutation confirms RTH-beta, refuting the diagnosis of TSHoma.

option_notes.option: Complete absence of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Both conditions can present with minimal or mixed thyrotoxic symptoms.

quizzes.q: A 7-month-old infant boy is evaluated for profound hypotonia, failure to achieve head control, and severe developmental delay. Examination reveals generalized weakness, spasticity in lower extremities, dystonic posturing, and poor weight gain. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum total T3 380 ng/dL (reference: 105-245 ng/dL), free T4 0.5 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and TSH 3.2 mIU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta)
Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (MCT8 deficiency)
Congenital hypopituitarism with isolated TSH deficiency
Thyroid dysgenesis with lingual thyroid
quizzes.explanation: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is an X-linked inherited neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC16A2 (encoding MCT8), which mediates thyroid hormone transport into neurons. Affected males exhibit severe cognitive disability, central hypotonia, progressive spasticity, dystonia, and a pathognomonic serum thyroid panel: high total and free T3, low free T4, and normal or slightly elevated TSH.

option_notes.option: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. RTH-beta presents with high free T4 and high free T3, not low free T4.

option_notes.option: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (MCT8 deficiency)
option_notes.text: Correct. Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome features severe spastic quadriplegia, profound cognitive impairment, high T3, low T4, and normal TSH.

option_notes.option: Congenital hypopituitarism with isolated TSH deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Isolated TSH deficiency produces low T4 and low TSH without markedly elevated T3.

option_notes.option: Thyroid dysgenesis with lingual thyroid
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thyroid dysgenesis causes primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low T4/T3.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old child presents with severe skeletal dysplasia, delayed fontanel closure, delayed tooth eruption, marked constipation, and bradycardia. Biochemical evaluation reveals normal TSH (2.1 mIU/L), low-normal free T4 (0.8 ng/dL), high-normal free T3 (4.4 pg/mL), a markedly reduced free T4 to free T3 ratio, and very low reverse T3. What receptor is defective in this child?
options: Thyroid hormone receptor beta (TR-beta)
Thyroid hormone receptor alpha (TR-alpha1)
TSH receptor (TSHR)
Glucocorticoid receptor (GR)
quizzes.explanation: Resistance to thyroid hormone alpha (RTH-alpha) is caused by heterozygous mutations in THRA. Because TR-alpha1 is heavily expressed in bone, brain, and intestine, while TR-beta regulates pituitary feedback, patients exhibit tissue-specific hypothyroid symptoms (skeletal dysplasia, delayed tooth eruption, macrocephaly, constipation, bradycardia) with a distinctive hormonal signature: near-normal TSH, low-normal FT4, high FT3, low FT4/FT3 ratio, and extremely low rT3.

option_notes.option: Thyroid hormone receptor beta (TR-beta)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TR-beta defects cause RTH-beta with high FT4, high FT3, unsuppressed TSH, and cardiac tachycardia.

option_notes.option: Thyroid hormone receptor alpha (TR-alpha1)
option_notes.text: Correct. Mutations in THRA (TR-alpha1) cause severe skeletal dysplasia, delayed bone age, constipation, bradycardia, low FT4/FT3 ratio, and very low rT3.

option_notes.option: TSH receptor (TSHR)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause elevated TSH with normal/low thyroid hormones (resistance to TSH).

option_notes.option: Glucocorticoid receptor (GR)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Glucocorticoid receptor defects cause Chrousos syndrome (adrenal hyperandrogenism, hypertension, fatigue).

quizzes.q: An 11-year-old asymptomatic boy is diagnosed with RTH-beta after genetic testing confirms a heterozygous pathogenic mutation in THRB. His free T4 is 2.5 ng/dL, free T3 is 5.2 pg/mL, and TSH is 3.1 mIU/L. His resting pulse is 80 bpm and height is tracking along the 50th percentile. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate radioactive iodine ablation to normalize circulating thyroid hormones
Observation and clinical monitoring without antithyroid medications or levothyroxine
High-dose methimazole to normalize free T4 and free T3
Subtotal thyroidectomy to treat subclinical thyrotoxicosis
quizzes.explanation: In asymptomatic patients with RTH-beta who have normal growth and no cardiovascular compromise, no pharmacological treatment is required. Elevated circulating thyroid hormone levels are necessary to overcome the end-organ receptor resistance. Attempting to lower thyroid hormone levels with antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or surgery causes pituitary TSH overdrive, massive goiter expansion, and severe tissue hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Immediate radioactive iodine ablation to normalize circulating thyroid hormones
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Radioiodine ablation or surgery leads to massive TSH elevation, pituitary thyrotrope hyperplasia, and severe tissue hypothyroid symptoms.

option_notes.option: Observation and clinical monitoring without antithyroid medications or levothyroxine
option_notes.text: Correct. Asymptomatic patients with RTH-beta compensate well with elevated endogenous hormones; conservative observation without treatment is standard of care.

option_notes.option: High-dose methimazole to normalize free T4 and free T3
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Methimazole reduces thyroid hormone levels, which triggers massive TSH surge, rapid goiter growth, and clinical hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Subtotal thyroidectomy to treat subclinical thyrotoxicosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thyroidectomy is contraindicated and induces severe pituitary hypertrophy.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl is found to have an asymptomatic 1.4-cm solitary firm nodule in the right thyroid lobe on routine physical examination. Serum TSH is 1.8 mIU/L (normal: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Thyroid ultrasound reveals a solid, hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.4 x 1.1 x 1.3 cm with multiple punctate microcalcifications and irregular margins; two ipsilateral jugular lymph nodes show rounded morphology and loss of fatty hila. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Radioiodine (123I) uptake and scan to evaluate nodule functionality
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the nodule and suspicious lymph nodes
Empirical levothyroxine therapy to suppress TSH and reassess nodule size in 6 months
Immediate core needle biopsy of the right lobe under general anesthesia
quizzes.explanation: In a euthyroid child with a solitary solid thyroid nodule >=1 cm displaying high-risk sonographic features (hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular borders) and suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of both the primary nodule and the suspicious lymph nodes is the gold-standard diagnostic step. 123I scan is indicated only if TSH is suppressed. Levothyroxine suppression is ineffective and delays diagnosis. FNA is preferred over core needle biopsy.

option_notes.option: Radioiodine (123I) uptake and scan to evaluate nodule functionality
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Scintigraphy is indicated only if TSH is subnormal/suppressed to look for a toxic adenoma.

option_notes.option: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the nodule and suspicious lymph nodes
option_notes.text: Correct. Ultrasound-guided FNA of the nodule and suspicious lymph nodes is the primary diagnostic procedure of choice.

option_notes.option: Empirical levothyroxine therapy to suppress TSH and reassess nodule size in 6 months
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Levothyroxine suppression therapy has no role in modern management and dangerously delays oncologic diagnosis.

option_notes.option: Immediate core needle biopsy of the right lobe under general anesthesia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Core needle biopsy carries higher complication risks in children and is not the standard first-line diagnostic modality.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old male undergoes total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for a 2.5-cm papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Final pathology reveals multifocal PTC with extrathyroidal extension and 6 of 11 central lymph nodes positive for metastatic carcinoma. Staging chest CT reveals multiple 2-3 mm bilateral pulmonary nodules with radioiodine avidity. Which postoperative adjuvant therapy is indicated?
options: External beam radiotherapy to the neck and thorax
Radioactive iodine (131I) therapy following recombinant human TSH (rhTSH) or thyroid hormone withdrawal
Systemic multi-agent cytotoxic chemotherapy (doxorubicin and cisplatin)
Observation without levothyroxine suppression
quizzes.explanation: In pediatric differentiated thyroid carcinoma with high-risk features (extrathyroidal extension, multiple lymph node metastases, distant pulmonary metastases), radioactive iodine (131I) ablation and treatment is the established standard adjuvant therapy. Pediatric pulmonary metastases from PTC are overwhelmingly radioiodine-avid and respond favorably to 131I. Chemotherapy and external beam radiation are ineffective and contraindicated.

option_notes.option: External beam radiotherapy to the neck and thorax
option_notes.text: Incorrect. External beam radiotherapy is reserved for rare refractory, non-iodine avid, locally aggressive adult anaplastic tumors.

option_notes.option: Radioactive iodine (131I) therapy following recombinant human TSH (rhTSH) or thyroid hormone withdrawal
option_notes.text: Correct. Radioactive iodine (131I) is the definitive adjuvant systemic therapy for radioiodine-avid nodal and pulmonary metastatic PTC.

option_notes.option: Systemic multi-agent cytotoxic chemotherapy (doxorubicin and cisplatin)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy is ineffective against differentiated papillary thyroid carcinoma.

option_notes.option: Observation without levothyroxine suppression
option_notes.text: Incorrect. High-risk PTC requires both radioiodine therapy and aggressive TSH suppression (<0.1 mIU/L) with levothyroxine.

quizzes.q: A newborn infant is found on genetic testing to carry a de novo heterozygous RET proto-oncogene germline mutation (M918T in exon 16), diagnostic of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B). When is prophylactic total thyroidectomy recommended to prevent metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)?
options: Within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life)
At age 5 to 6 years before entering elementary school
At the onset of spontaneous puberty (Tanner stage 2)
Only after serum calcitonin rises above 100 pg/mL
quizzes.explanation: MEN2B caused by the RET M918T mutation confers the highest risk category ('highest risk / ATA-HST') for medullary thyroid carcinoma. MTC in MEN2B develops within the first year of life and exhibits extremely virulent, early metastatic spread to lymph nodes and liver. American Thyroid Association guidelines recommend prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life, preferably in the first months of life.

option_notes.option: Within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life)
option_notes.text: Correct. In MEN2B (RET M918T), prophylactic total thyroidectomy is performed in the first year (first months) of life due to aggressive infancy metastasis.

option_notes.option: At age 5 to 6 years before entering elementary school
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Age 5 years is the recommended cutoff for MEN2A (e.g., codon 634), which has a less virulent course than MEN2B.

option_notes.option: At the onset of spontaneous puberty (Tanner stage 2)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Waiting until puberty in MEN2B guarantees incurable widely disseminated metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma.

option_notes.option: Only after serum calcitonin rises above 100 pg/mL
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Prophylactic thyroidectomy must precede calcitonin elevation or clinical tumor detection to ensure curative resection.

quizzes.q: What is the targeted postoperative serum TSH suppression level for a 13-year-old child who has undergone total thyroidectomy for high-risk papillary thyroid carcinoma with gross extrathyroidal extension and lung metastases?
options: TSH maintained in the upper normal range (2.5-4.5 mIU/L)
TSH suppressed to <0.1 mIU/L
TSH maintained at 1.0-2.0 mIU/L
TSH elevated above 30 mIU/L to stimulate residual tissue differentiation
quizzes.explanation: In high-risk pediatric differentiated thyroid carcinoma (persistent metastatic disease, extensive nodal involvement, gross extrathyroidal invasion), TSH acts as a trophic growth factor for follicular cells. Guidelines recommend aggressive TSH suppression to <0.1 mIU/L using supra-physiological levothyroxine dosing, while monitoring for iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis and maintaining bone density.

option_notes.option: TSH maintained in the upper normal range (2.5-4.5 mIU/L)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Upper normal TSH provides trophic stimulus for tumor cell growth and recurrence.

option_notes.option: TSH suppressed to <0.1 mIU/L
option_notes.text: Correct. TSH suppression to <0.1 mIU/L is recommended for high-risk pediatric thyroid cancer to inhibit residual tumor proliferation.

option_notes.option: TSH maintained at 1.0-2.0 mIU/L
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSH 1.0-2.0 mIU/L is targeted in low-risk patients who have achieved complete clinical and biochemical remission.

option_notes.option: TSH elevated above 30 mIU/L to stimulate residual tissue differentiation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TSH >30 mIU/L is used only transiently immediately prior to diagnostic or therapeutic 131I administration.

quizzes.q: During surveillance of a pediatric patient 1 year after total thyroidectomy and 131I ablation for papillary thyroid cancer, serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is reported as undetectable (<0.1 ng/mL). However, anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) are markedly elevated at 450 IU/mL (reference: <20 IU/mL). How should the clinician interpret these laboratory results?
options: The undetectable Tg proves complete cure and absence of any residual thyroid tissue
The undetectable Tg result may be falsely low due to antibody interference in immunometric assays
High TgAb levels prove that the original tumor was an anaplastic carcinoma
Elevated TgAb levels indicate concurrent Graves' disease of the remnant
quizzes.explanation: In immunometric assays (sandwich ICMA), endogenous anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) bind to serum thyroglobulin and sterically hinder assay antibody binding, producing falsely low or undetectable measured Tg values. Whenever TgAb is positive, a low/undetectable Tg cannot be relied upon as evidence of tumor absence; trending serial TgAb titers (rising titers indicate recurrence) and radioiodine/ultrasound surveillance are required.

option_notes.option: The undetectable Tg proves complete cure and absence of any residual thyroid tissue
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Undetectable Tg is unreliable in the presence of high TgAb because antibodies cause false-negative immunoassay results.

option_notes.option: The undetectable Tg result may be falsely low due to antibody interference in immunometric assays
option_notes.text: Correct. Anti-Tg antibodies cause steric hindrance in immunometric assays, causing falsely low or undetectable measured thyroglobulin levels.

option_notes.option: High TgAb levels prove that the original tumor was an anaplastic carcinoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. TgAb elevation reflects thyroid autoimmunity or tumor-associated immune response, not anaplastic transformation.

option_notes.option: Elevated TgAb levels indicate concurrent Graves' disease of the remnant
option_notes.text: Incorrect. After total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation, Graves' disease does not occur; rising TgAb suggests residual antigen/tumor.

quizzes.q: A 10-day-old male infant presents with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum total calcium 5.8 mg/dL (reference: 8.8-10.5 mg/dL), ionized calcium 0.70 mmol/L (reference: 1.15-1.32 mmol/L), serum phosphate 9.8 mg/dL (reference: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, and intact PTH 4 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). Cardiac evaluation reveals a conotruncal cardiac defect (truncus arteriosus). What is the underlying genetic diagnosis?
options: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome)
Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (GNAS mutation)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (CaSR mutation)
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX mutation)
quizzes.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) results from defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to congenital hypoparathyroidism (absent or hypoplastic parathyroid glands presenting with profound hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and inappropriately low PTH), conotruncal cardiac anomalies (truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch, tetralogy of Fallot), thymic hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), and facial dysmorphisms.

option_notes.option: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome)
option_notes.text: Correct. 22q11.2 deletion causes parathyroid hypoplasia, congenital hypocalcemia, truncus arteriosus, and immune defect.

option_notes.option: Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (GNAS mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GNAS mutations cause pseudohypoparathyroidism with elevated PTH, not low/absent PTH.

option_notes.option: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (CaSR mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CaSR loss-of-function causes hypercalcemia (FHH), not severe hypocalcemia.

option_notes.option: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PHEX mutations cause hypophosphatemia and rickets, not hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia and low PTH.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old asymptomatic boy is referred for incidental hypercalcemia found on a sports physical. Serum total calcium is 11.2 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.42 mmol/L, serum phosphate 3.2 mg/dL, and intact PTH 52 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). A 24-hour urine collection reveals low urinary calcium with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) of 0.005. His father and paternal grandfather also have mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent four-gland surgical parathyroid exploration and subtotal parathyroidectomy
Reassurance and observation without surgical intervention
Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
High-dose oral furosemide and sodium chloride tablets daily
quizzes.explanation: This patient has classic familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), an autosomal dominant condition caused by a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the CaSR gene. Diagnostic hallmarks are lifelong mild-to-moderate hypercalcemia, inappropriately normal intact PTH, and marked hypocalciuria with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) <0.01. FHH is entirely benign, does not cause end-organ injury (no nephrolithiasis or bone loss), and parathyroidectomy does not cure the condition. Surgical intervention is contraindicated.

option_notes.option: Urgent four-gland surgical parathyroid exploration and subtotal parathyroidectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Parathyroidectomy does not correct the altered CaSR set-point throughout tissues and is completely ineffective and contraindicated.

option_notes.option: Reassurance and observation without surgical intervention
option_notes.text: Correct. FHH is a benign familial trait requiring no medical or surgical intervention; observation and reassurance are indicated.

option_notes.option: Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates are unnecessary and ineffective for the reset homeostatic set-point in FHH.

option_notes.option: High-dose oral furosemide and sodium chloride tablets daily
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diuretics and sodium loading are indicated for acute hypercalcemic crisis, not benign asymptomatic FHH.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old girl with postsurgical hypoparathyroidism following total thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer is treated with calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and oral calcium carbonate 500 mg elemental calcium twice daily. On follow-up, serum total calcium is 8.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 5.2 mg/dL, and a spot urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio is 0.38 mg/mg (normal <0.20). Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. What adjustment in medical therapy is indicated?
options: Increase calcitriol to 1.0 mcg daily to bring serum calcium into the high-normal range
Decrease calcitriol and oral calcium to lower urine calcium excretion, targeting serum calcium of 8.0-8.5 mg/dL, and consider adding a thiazide diuretic
Discontinue calcitriol and start daily recombinant human parathyroid hormone injections
Add oral sodium phosphate supplements
quizzes.explanation: In hypoparathyroidism, the absence of PTH removes the primary stimulus for renal tubular calcium reabsorption. Exogenous calcium and calcitriol easily precipitate hypercalciuria (urine Ca/Cr >0.2 mg/mg) and nephrocalcinosis. Management requires reducing calcitriol/calcium to keep serum calcium in the low-normal range (8.0-8.5 mg/dL) and adding a thiazide diuretic (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide), which promotes proximal and distal tubular calcium reabsorption to reduce urinary calcium excretion.

option_notes.option: Increase calcitriol to 1.0 mcg daily to bring serum calcium into the high-normal range
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Increasing calcitriol will exacerbate hypercalciuria and worsen nephrocalcinosis.

option_notes.option: Decrease calcitriol and oral calcium to lower urine calcium excretion, targeting serum calcium of 8.0-8.5 mg/dL, and consider adding a thiazide diuretic
option_notes.text: Correct. Reducing calcitriol/calcium to maintain low-normal serum calcium and initiating a thiazide diuretic reduces hypercalciuria.

option_notes.option: Discontinue calcitriol and start daily recombinant human parathyroid hormone injections
option_notes.text: Incorrect. While rhPTH is an emerging therapy, standard established pediatric management begins with dosing adjustment and thiazide diuretics.

option_notes.option: Add oral sodium phosphate supplements
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Oral phosphate will cause severe hyperphosphatemia and metastatic tissue calcification.

quizzes.q: A newborn infant presents at 4 days of life with severe hypotonia, failure to thrive, rib fractures, and respiratory distress. Serum calcium is markedly elevated at 17.5 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.8 mg/dL, and intact PTH is 650 pg/mL. Skeletal radiographs show diffuse demineralization and subperiosteal resorption. Genetic testing confirms a homozygous inactivating mutation in the CaSR gene. What is the definitive life-saving therapy?
options: Emergent total parathyroidectomy
Lifelong high-dose intravenous calcium infusions
Oral calcitriol and dietary phosphate restriction
Bilateral adrenalectomy
quizzes.explanation: Neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in CaSR. Without functioning calcium sensors, parathyroid cells do not recognize extreme hypercalcemia, producing massive PTH secretion and torrential skeletal resorption with fractures and respiratory failure. Emergent total parathyroidectomy (with autotransplantation of parathyroid tissue or lifelong hypoparathyroidism management) is life-saving; medical therapy alone is rarely sufficient.

option_notes.option: Emergent total parathyroidectomy
option_notes.text: Correct. Total parathyroidectomy is the definitive life-saving intervention for neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism.

option_notes.option: Lifelong high-dose intravenous calcium infusions
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Administering calcium would be fatal in a neonate with calcium of 17.5 mg/dL.

option_notes.option: Oral calcitriol and dietary phosphate restriction
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Calcitriol would further elevate serum calcium and worsen hypercalcemic crisis.

option_notes.option: Bilateral adrenalectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adrenalectomy has no role in parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor disorders.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with carpopedal spasm and facial twitching upon tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear. What are the clinical names of these two physical signs, and what electrolyte disturbance do they indicate?
options: Trousseau sign and Chvostek sign; acute hypocalcemia
Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign; hypomagnesemia
Gowers sign and Trendelenburg sign; hypercalcemia
Tinels sign and Phalens sign; hyperphosphatemia
quizzes.explanation: Carpopedal spasm induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes is Trousseau sign. Twitching of facial muscles elicited by tapping the facial nerve trunk anterior to the external auditory meatus is Chvostek sign. Both are classical clinical signs of latent neuromuscular excitability (tetany) secondary to acute hypocalcemia (or profound hypomagnesemia).

option_notes.option: Trousseau sign and Chvostek sign; acute hypocalcemia
option_notes.text: Correct. Trousseau (carpopedal spasm) and Chvostek (facial twitch) signs are pathognomonic physical markers of hypocalcemia.

option_notes.option: Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign; hypomagnesemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Kernig and Brudzinski signs indicate meningeal irritation in meningitis.

option_notes.option: Gowers sign and Trendelenburg sign; hypercalcemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Gowers and Trendelenburg signs indicate proximal muscle weakness and hip abductor insufficiency.

option_notes.option: Tinels sign and Phalens sign; hyperphosphatemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Tinel and Phalen signs detect median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome.

quizzes.q: An 18-month-old toddler boy presents with marked progressive bowing of both legs (genu varum) and waddling gait since starting to walk at 14 months. Serum testing reveals: calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 2.1 mg/dL (normal: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 950 U/L (normal: 150-400 U/L), intact PTH 55 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 ng/mL, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 28 pg/mL (inappropriately normal), and TmP/GFR 1.8 mg/dL (severely reduced). His mother has short stature and bowlegs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH)
Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (CYP27B1 mutation)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A
quizzes.explanation: This toddler exhibits classic X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH), an X-linked dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in PHEX. Hallmarks are normal serum calcium, severe hypophosphatemia due to renal phosphate wasting (reduced TmP/GFR), elevated alkaline phosphatase, normal PTH, and inappropriately normal (rather than elevated) 1,25-(OH)2D driven by elevated intact FGF23. The maternal family history of short stature and bowed legs supports X-linked dominant inheritance.

option_notes.option: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Nutritional rickets presents with low 25-OH-D, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), and low/normal calcium.

option_notes.option: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH)
option_notes.text: Correct. Normal calcium, low phosphate, reduced TmP/GFR, inappropriately normal 1,25-(OH)2D, and maternal history define XLH.

option_notes.option: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (CYP27B1 mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. VDDR1A presents with severe hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D.

option_notes.option: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PHP1A features hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and markedly elevated PTH, the exact opposite of this patient's profile.

quizzes.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of burosumab in the treatment of pediatric X-linked hypophosphatemia?
quizzes.a: Direct inhibition of intact FGF23 signaling by binding circulating FGF23, thereby restoring renal tubular NaPi-IIa/c expression and normalizing 1,25-(OH)2D synthesis
options: Direct inhibition of intact FGF23 signaling by binding circulating FGF23, thereby restoring renal tubular NaPi-IIa/c expression and normalizing 1,25-(OH)2D synthesis
Allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in parathyroid tissue
Competitive antagonism of parathyroid hormone at the PTH-1 receptor in the proximal tubule
Stimulation of renal 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) to promote phosphate reabsorption
quizzes.explanation: Burosumab is a recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds to and neutralizes circulating intact FGF23. By blocking excess FGF23 action at the FGFR1/Klotho complex in the renal proximal tubule, burosumab increases tubular expression of NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters, enhancing renal phosphate reabsorption, and relieves suppression of CYP27B1, boosting endogenous 1,25-(OH)2D production.

option_notes.option: Direct inhibition of intact FGF23 signaling by binding circulating FGF23, thereby restoring renal tubular NaPi-IIa/c expression and normalizing 1,25-(OH)2D synthesis
option_notes.text: Correct. Burosumab binds circulating intact FGF23, normalizing renal phosphate reabsorption and 1,25-(OH)2D generation.

option_notes.option: Allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in parathyroid tissue
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CaSR activation is the mechanism of calcimimetics like cinacalcet, not burosumab.

option_notes.option: Competitive antagonism of parathyroid hormone at the PTH-1 receptor in the proximal tubule
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Burosumab does not antagonize the PTH receptor; PTH remains in the normal range during treatment.

option_notes.option: Stimulation of renal 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) to promote phosphate reabsorption
option_notes.text: Incorrect. FGF23 induces CYP24A1; burosumab suppresses CYP24A1 while restoring CYP27B1 activity.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with rickets, genu valgum, and severe recurrent kidney stones. Serum phosphate is low at 2.2 mg/dL with low TmP/GFR. Serum calcium is normal (9.8 mg/dL), but 24-hour urine calcium is markedly elevated at 7.5 mg/kg/day (hypercalciuria). Intact FGF23 is suppressed (<10 pg/mL) and serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is markedly elevated at 145 pg/mL. What is the diagnosis and appropriate therapy?
options: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets; treat with burosumab
Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH); treat with oral phosphate salts alone
Vitamin D deficiency rickets; treat with high-dose ergocalciferol
Primary hyperparathyroidism; perform parathyroidectomy
quizzes.explanation: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in SLC34A3 (encoding NaPi-IIc). Defective renal phosphate reabsorption leads to hypophosphatemia, which appropriately suppresses FGF23. Low FGF23 disinhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase, causing massive 1,25-(OH)2D production, hyperabsorption of intestinal calcium, and severe hypercalciuria with nephrolithiasis. Treatment is oral phosphate salts alone to replenish phosphate, which suppresses 1,25-(OH)2D and cures hypercalciuria. Exogenous calcitriol is strictly contraindicated.

option_notes.option: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets; treat with burosumab
option_notes.text: Incorrect. XLH features high/normal FGF23, low/normal 1,25-(OH)2D, and hypocalciuria, the opposite of this profile.

option_notes.option: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH); treat with oral phosphate salts alone
option_notes.text: Correct. HHRH exhibits low phosphate, suppressed FGF23, high 1,25-(OH)2D, and hypercalciuria; oral phosphate alone is the curative therapy.

option_notes.option: Vitamin D deficiency rickets; treat with high-dose ergocalciferol
option_notes.text: Incorrect. High-dose vitamin D would aggravate the already dangerous hypercalciuria and nephrolithiasis.

option_notes.option: Primary hyperparathyroidism; perform parathyroidectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PTH is normal or suppressed in HHRH; parathyroidectomy is not indicated.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old child with XLH has been treated for 5 years with conventional therapy consisting of high-dose oral phosphate supplements and calcitriol. Routine surveillance reveals serum calcium 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 3.0 mg/dL, but intact PTH has risen progressively to 450 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). Renal ultrasound demonstrates bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. What complication of conventional therapy has developed?
options: Tertiary (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism secondary to chronic phosphate administration
Transformation of XLH into osteogenesis imperfecta
Development of a parathyroid carcinoma
Acute renal cortical necrosis
quizzes.explanation: Conventional therapy for XLH with oral phosphate salts causes repeated transient spikes in serum phosphate, which bind ionized calcium and stimulate parathyroid gland hyperplasia. Over years, this chronic stimulation can induce secondary and ultimately tertiary (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism with profound PTH elevation, compounded by calcitriol-induced hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. This severe complication is a primary reason why burosumab has superseded conventional therapy.

option_notes.option: Tertiary (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism secondary to chronic phosphate administration
option_notes.text: Correct. Chronic oral phosphate loading triggers parathyroid hyperplasia, driving secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

option_notes.option: Transformation of XLH into osteogenesis imperfecta
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Genetic disorders of mineralization do not transform into collagen mutations like osteogenesis imperfecta.

option_notes.option: Development of a parathyroid carcinoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Parathyroid carcinoma is extraordinarily rare in children and not the typical consequence of XLH therapy.

option_notes.option: Acute renal cortical necrosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. The findings reflect chronic medullary nephrocalcinosis and parathyroid hyperplasia, not acute cortical necrosis.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and multiple metatarsal insufficiency fractures. Labs show serum phosphate 1.6 mg/dL, normal calcium, normal PTH, normal 25-OH-D, low 1,25-(OH)2D, and marked renal phosphate wasting (TmP/GFR 1.2 mg/dL). Serum intact FGF23 is markedly elevated. There is no family history of bone disease. Full-body 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT reveals an intensely avid 1.2-cm soft-tissue lesion in the distal femur. What is the diagnosis?
options: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) caused by a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
Osteosarcoma with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia
Fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome
Ewing sarcoma with ectopic ACTH production
quizzes.explanation: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a paraneoplastic syndrome caused by benign, slow-growing phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) that oversecrete FGF23. This results in severe hypophosphatemia, renal phosphate wasting, inappropriately low 1,25-(OH)2D, and severe osteomalacia/fractures. PMTs overexpress somatostatin receptors (SSTR2), making 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT the most sensitive localization modality. Complete surgical resection of the tumor cures the condition.

option_notes.option: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) caused by a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
option_notes.text: Correct. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors secrete excess FGF23 causing TIO, localized by 68Ga-DOTATATE and cured by surgical excision.

option_notes.option: Osteosarcoma with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma produces osteolytic or blastic lesions, not isolated hypophosphatemic TIO with high FGF23.

option_notes.option: Fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. McCune-Albright fibrous dysplasia can occasionally secrete FGF23, but DOTATATE uptake in an isolated soft tissue tumor indicates PMT.

option_notes.option: Ewing sarcoma with ectopic ACTH production
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Ewing sarcoma does not present with isolated high-FGF23 hypophosphatemic rickets.

quizzes.q: A 14-month-old dark-skinned boy who has been exclusively breastfed without vitamin D supplementation presents with delayed walking, frontal bossing, prominent costochondral enlargement ('rachitic rosary'), and marked widening of both wrists. Serum labs show: calcium 8.9 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 2.8 mg/dL (normal: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 1250 U/L (normal: 150-400 U/L), intact PTH 185 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 7 ng/mL (deficiency <12 ng/mL). What biochemical stage of calcipenic nutritional rickets is present?
options: Stage 1 (early rickets with transient hypocalcemia)
Stage 2 (secondary hyperparathyroidism with normal calcium and hypophosphatemia)
Stage 3 (severe decompensated rickets with hypocalcemia and bone buffering failure)
Adynamic bone disease
quizzes.explanation: This child is in Stage 2 calcipenic rickets. In Stage 2, secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH 185 pg/mL) successfully normalizes serum calcium (8.9 mg/dL) by mobilizing bone mineral and increasing renal calcium reabsorption. However, excess PTH causes renal phosphate wasting, leading to hypophosphatemia (2.8 mg/dL) and marked alkaline phosphatase elevation with classic rachitic skeletal lesions.

option_notes.option: Stage 1 (early rickets with transient hypocalcemia)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Stage 1 presents with hypocalcemia before significant PTH-induced renal phosphaturia develops.

option_notes.option: Stage 2 (secondary hyperparathyroidism with normal calcium and hypophosphatemia)
option_notes.text: Correct. Stage 2 features robust secondary hyperparathyroidism that normalizes calcium while causing hypophosphatemia and high ALP.

option_notes.option: Stage 3 (severe decompensated rickets with hypocalcemia and bone buffering failure)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Stage 3 presents with severe, decompensated hypocalcemia alongside profound hypophosphatemia.

option_notes.option: Adynamic bone disease
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adynamic bone disease is a low-turnover state with suppressed PTH and normal/low ALP.

quizzes.q: A 2-year-old child with severe nutritional rickets is prescribed high-dose ergocalciferol 50,000 IU weekly. The physician also prescribes oral elemental calcium 500 mg daily. What adverse complication does concurrent calcium supplementation specifically prevent during the initial weeks of therapy?
options: Hungry bone syndrome with precipitous hypocalcemia and tetany
Acute renal tubular acidosis
Hypercalcemic crisis and nephrocalcinosis
Hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis
quizzes.explanation: When active mineralization is restored by vitamin D administration, large amounts of extracellular calcium and phosphate are rapidly incorporated into the unmineralized osteoid ('hungry bone syndrome'). Without adequate oral calcium supplementation, circulating serum calcium drops precipitously, triggering acute hypocalcemic tetany, seizures, or laryngospasm.

option_notes.option: Hungry bone syndrome with precipitous hypocalcemia and tetany
option_notes.text: Correct. Co-administering elemental calcium prevents hungry bone syndrome-induced hypocalcemia during rapid remineralization.

option_notes.option: Acute renal tubular acidosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Calcium supplementation does not prevent proximal or distal renal tubular acidosis.

option_notes.option: Hypercalcemic crisis and nephrocalcinosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. At recommended doses with rickets, calcium prevents hypocalcemia; hypercalcemic crisis does not occur unless gross overdose occurs.

option_notes.option: Hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Tumoral calcinosis is caused by FGF23 deficiency, not nutritional rickets treatment.

quizzes.q: An 8-month-old infant presents with severe rickets, hypocalcemia (6.8 mg/dL), elevated PTH (320 pg/mL), and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal (45 ng/mL), but serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is undetectable (<5 pg/mL). High-dose parent vitamin D3 produces no clinical or biochemical improvement. What gene mutation is responsible for this autosomal recessive disorder?
options: CYP27B1 (encoding 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase)
CYP2R1 (encoding hepatic 25-hydroxylase)
VDR (encoding vitamin D receptor)
PHEX (encoding phosphate-regulating endopeptidase)
quizzes.explanation: Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets type 1A (VDDR1A) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in CYP27B1, which encodes renal 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase. Patients cannot convert 25-OH-D into active 1,25-(OH)2D, resulting in early severe rickets with normal 25-OH-D and undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D. The condition responds completely to physiological doses of calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D).

option_notes.option: CYP27B1 (encoding 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase)
option_notes.text: Correct. CYP27B1 mutations cause VDDR1A with undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D despite normal 25-OH-D, treated with calcitriol.

option_notes.option: CYP2R1 (encoding hepatic 25-hydroxylase)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CYP2R1 mutations cause VDDR1B, which features low 25-OH-D.

option_notes.option: VDR (encoding vitamin D receptor)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. VDR mutations cause VDDR2A, which features markedly elevated 1,25-(OH)2D levels (hormone resistance) and total alopecia.

option_notes.option: PHEX (encoding phosphate-regulating endopeptidase)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PHEX mutations cause X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, with normal calcium and normal 25-OH-D.

quizzes.q: A 10-month-old infant with severe rickets is found to have total alopecia (complete absence of scalp hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes). Laboratory testing shows severe hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and strikingly elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (>250 pg/mL). What is the underlying disease mechanism?
options: Inactivating mutation in the vitamin D receptor (VDR) causing end-organ hormone resistance (VDDR2A)
CYP27B1 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Subcutaneous fat necrosis with hypercalcemia
Nutritional zinc deficiency
quizzes.explanation: Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets type 2A (VDDR2A) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Because target tissues cannot respond to 1,25-(OH)2D, serum 1,25-(OH)2D levels rise massively due to loss of negative feedback. Alopecia totalis is a unique phenotypic marker of severe VDR disruption because VDR is essential for hair follicle cycling.

option_notes.option: Inactivating mutation in the vitamin D receptor (VDR) causing end-organ hormone resistance (VDDR2A)
option_notes.text: Correct. VDR mutations cause end-organ 1,25-(OH)2D resistance, marked 1,25-(OH)2D elevation, and pathognomonic total alopecia.

option_notes.option: CYP27B1 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CYP27B1 deficiency (VDDR1A) has undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D and normal hair development.

option_notes.option: Subcutaneous fat necrosis with hypercalcemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Fat necrosis causes hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemic rickets with alopecia.

option_notes.option: Nutritional zinc deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Zinc deficiency causes periorificial dermatitis, not rickets with massive calcitriol elevation and total alopecia.

quizzes.q: What classic radiographic finding on wrist radiographs confirms healing of rickets following 3 weeks of vitamin D and calcium therapy?
quizzes.a: Appearance of a well-defined, dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis
options: Appearance of a well-defined, dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis
Complete disappearance of the distal radial epiphysis
Development of diffuse subperiosteal cortical thinning
Formation of Looser zones along the ulnar diaphysis
quizzes.explanation: The earliest objective radiographic evidence of rachitic healing is the deposition of calcium in the newly mineralizing hypertrophic zone, forming a crisp, linear radiodense band—the line of provisional calcification—across the metaphyseal margin, typically visible within 2 to 4 weeks of starting therapy.

option_notes.option: Appearance of a well-defined, dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis
option_notes.text: Correct. A dense line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis confirms active mineral deposition and rachitic healing.

option_notes.option: Complete disappearance of the distal radial epiphysis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Epiphyses become more visible and dense during healing, not disappear.

option_notes.option: Development of diffuse subperiosteal cortical thinning
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Subperiosteal cortical thinning reflects hyperparathyroidism or demineralization, not healing.

option_notes.option: Formation of Looser zones along the ulnar diaphysis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Looser zones are pseudofractures reflecting active osteomalacia, not healing.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature, rounded facies, and obesity. Physical exam reveals shortening of the 4th and 5th digits of both hands; when she makes a fist, dimples appear in place of the 4th and 5th knuckles (Archibald sign). Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum calcium 7.2 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 6.8 mg/dL (normal: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), intact PTH 380 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), TSH 9.2 mIU/L (normal: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L), and normal free T4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
Primary hypoparathyroidism
Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
quizzes.explanation: This patient exhibits the classic triad of Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A): Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy physical phenotype (short stature, obesity, round facies, brachydactyly with Archibald sign), renal PTH resistance (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, markedly elevated PTH), and subclinical TSH resistance (elevated TSH). PHP-1A is caused by maternal inheritance of an inactivating GNAS mutation.

option_notes.option: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
option_notes.text: Correct. AHO features combined with hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH, and high TSH define PHP-1A.

option_notes.option: Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PPHP exhibits the identical physical AHO phenotype but has completely normal calcium, phosphate, PTH, and TSH.

option_notes.option: Primary hypoparathyroidism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Primary hypoparathyroidism features low or undetectable PTH and lacks AHO skeletal features.

option_notes.option: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Nutritional rickets presents with hypophosphatemia, not hyperphosphatemia, and lacks AHO brachydactyly.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with short stature, round face, and shortened 4th and 5th metacarpals identical to his sister who has PHP-1A. However, his laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 4.2 mg/dL (normal: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), intact PTH 32 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), and TSH 2.1 mIU/L. From whom did this boy inherit the GNAS mutation?
options: From his father (paternal inheritance)
From his mother (maternal inheritance)
A de novo somatic postzygotic mutation in bone progenitor cells
Mitochondrial maternal transmission
quizzes.explanation: Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP) is caused by paternal inheritance of an inactivating GNAS mutation. Because Gs-alpha expression in the renal proximal tubule and thyroid thyrotrope is derived almost exclusively from the maternal allele, paternal mutations leave the functioning maternal allele intact, preserving normal renal and thyroid hormone signaling (normal calcium, phosphate, PTH, TSH). However, because growth plates express Gs-alpha biallelically, Gs-alpha haploinsufficiency causes AHO physical features.

option_notes.option: From his father (paternal inheritance)
option_notes.text: Correct. Paternal inheritance of a GNAS mutation causes PPHP (AHO phenotype with normal serum biochemistry).

option_notes.option: From his mother (maternal inheritance)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Maternal inheritance causes PHP-1A (AHO phenotype WITH severe PTH and TSH resistance).

option_notes.option: A de novo somatic postzygotic mutation in bone progenitor cells
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Postzygotic activating GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome, not PPHP.

option_notes.option: Mitochondrial maternal transmission
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GNAS is an imprinted nuclear gene on chromosome 20q13.3, not a mitochondrial gene.

quizzes.q: What active metabolite must be prescribed to correct hypocalcemia and lower parathyroid hormone levels in a child with PHP type 1A (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy with hormone resistance)?
options: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2)
Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3)
Recombinant human PTH (teriparatide)
quizzes.explanation: In PHP-1A, proximal tubular resistance to PTH impairs PTH-stimulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) activity, resulting in deficient synthesis of active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Unhydroxylated native vitamin D (D2 or D3) is ineffective. Calcitriol bypasses the enzymatic block, directly restoring intestinal calcium absorption, normalizing serum calcium, and suppressing parathyroid PTH overdrive.

option_notes.option: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
option_notes.text: Correct. Calcitriol is required because renal PTH resistance impairs endogenous 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-OH-D.

option_notes.option: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Native ergocalciferol requires intact renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, which is impaired due to PTH resistance.

option_notes.option: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Native cholecalciferol cannot bypass the proximal tubular PTH signaling defect.

option_notes.option: Recombinant human PTH (teriparatide)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Teriparatide (PTH 1-34) is ineffective because the end-organ PTH-1 receptor signaling pathway is defective.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old girl with PHP-1A has well-controlled calcium and phosphate on calcitriol and calcium carbonate. However, her height has plateaued at the 1st percentile with growth velocity <2 cm/year. Detailed endocrine testing demonstrates impaired GH peak on clonidine/arginine stimulation tests with low IGF-1. What is the mechanism of growth hormone deficiency in PHP-1A?
options: Pituitary somatotrope resistance to growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) due to maternal Gs-alpha deficiency
