Structural destruction of the anterior pituitary gland by ectopic ossifications
Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis
Accelerated hepatic clearance of circulating growth hormone
quizzes.explanation: Pituitary somatotropes express Gs-alpha predominantly from the maternal allele. In PHP-1A, maternally inherited GNAS mutations cause end-organ resistance to GHRH, which signals through Gs-alpha to stimulate GH synthesis and secretion. GHRH resistance causes secondary growth hormone deficiency, contributing significantly to short stature. Recombinant human GH therapy improves linear growth in these patients.

option_notes.option: Pituitary somatotrope resistance to growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) due to maternal Gs-alpha deficiency
option_notes.text: Correct. Maternal Gs-alpha deficiency in somatotropes causes resistance to GHRH, leading to growth hormone deficiency.

option_notes.option: Structural destruction of the anterior pituitary gland by ectopic ossifications
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Pituitary tissue is not destroyed by heterotopic ossifications; the pituitary gland is structurally intact.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hypophysitis is an autoimmune disorder unrelated to GNAS mutations.

option_notes.option: Accelerated hepatic clearance of circulating growth hormone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GH clearance is normal; the primary defect is impaired GHRH-stimulated GH synthesis.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with hypocalcemia (7.4 mg/dL), hyperphosphatemia (6.2 mg/dL), and markedly elevated PTH (290 pg/mL). Thyroid function tests show mildly elevated TSH (6.5 mIU/L). On physical examination, he has normal height (50th percentile), normal body weight, no brachydactyly, and no subcutaneous ossifications. Genetic analysis reveals loss of methylation at the GNAS exon A/B differentially methylated region on the maternal allele. What is the diagnosis?
options: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP-1B)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
Progressive osseous heteroplasia (POH)
quizzes.explanation: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP-1B) is characterized by isolated renal PTH resistance (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH) and mild TSH resistance, without the physical features of Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (normal stature, no brachydactyly or subcutaneous ossifications). It is caused by epigenetic loss of methylation at maternal GNAS DMRs (specifically exon A/B), leading to tissue-specific suppression of Gs-alpha in renal proximal tubules.

option_notes.option: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP-1B)
option_notes.text: Correct. Epigenetic GNAS methylation defect causing PTH/TSH resistance without AHO physical features defines PHP-1B.

option_notes.option: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PHP-1A is caused by GNAS coding mutations and characteristically features the full AHO physical phenotype.

option_notes.option: Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PPHP exhibits AHO physical features with completely normal serum biochemistry.

option_notes.option: Progressive osseous heteroplasia (POH)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. POH features deep, invasive heterotopic ossification without endocrine resistance.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old boy with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome who has received oral prednisone (1-2 mg/kg/day) for 14 months complains of mild mid-back ache. Lateral thoracolumbar spine radiograph demonstrates a 30% anterior height loss (wedge deformity) of the L1 vertebral body after jumping from a curb. Lumbar spine DXA reveals a bone mineral density Z-score of -1.4. Which statement is correct regarding his bone status?
options: He meets criteria for pediatric osteoporosis based on the presence of a low-trauma vertebral fracture, regardless of the DXA Z-score
He cannot be diagnosed with osteoporosis because his DXA Z-score is greater than -2.0
He has osteopenia, but osteoporosis cannot be diagnosed until he sustains three additional peripheral fractures
His vertebral collapse represents Scheuermann disease rather than osteoporosis
quizzes.explanation: According to the official pediatric positions of the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), the finding of one or more low-trauma vertebral compression fractures is sufficient on its own to establish the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents, regardless of the measured bone mineral density Z-score. A DXA Z-score <= -2.0 is not required when a fragility vertebral fracture is documented.

option_notes.option: He meets criteria for pediatric osteoporosis based on the presence of a low-trauma vertebral fracture, regardless of the DXA Z-score
option_notes.text: Correct. A fragility vertebral fracture alone establishes the diagnosis of pediatric osteoporosis regardless of DXA Z-score.

option_notes.option: He cannot be diagnosed with osteoporosis because his DXA Z-score is greater than -2.0
option_notes.text: Incorrect. A DXA Z-score <= -2.0 is only required when the fracture history consists exclusively of long-bone fractures, not vertebral fractures.

option_notes.option: He has osteopenia, but osteoporosis cannot be diagnosed until he sustains three additional peripheral fractures
option_notes.text: Incorrect. The term 'osteopenia' is officially obsolete in pediatric densitometry, and additional fractures are not required.

option_notes.option: His vertebral collapse represents Scheuermann disease rather than osteoporosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Acute post-steroid height loss following minimal trauma is a steroid-induced vertebral compression fracture, not Scheuermann disease.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old girl with severe osteogenesis imperfecta type III is admitted to receive her first planned intravenous infusion of pamidronate (1 mg/kg/dose). Which of the following prophylactic clinical measures is most essential prior to initiating the infusion?
options: Verification and repletion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to >20-30 ng/mL and provision of oral calcium and antipyretics
Administration of high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg/m2
Placement of a permanent tunneled central venous line
Restriction of oral fluids to prevent hypervolemia
quizzes.explanation: The first intravenous bisphosphonate infusion universally triggers an acute phase reaction (fever, flu-like symptoms, myalgias) and rapid influx of extracellular calcium into skeleton. If a patient is vitamin D deficient or hypocalcemic prior to infusion, severe life-threatening hypocalcemia and tetany can occur. Pre-infusion repletion of 25-OH-D (>20-30 ng/mL), normal ionized calcium, oral calcium supplementation, and antipyretic prophylaxis (acetaminophen/ibuprofen) are mandatory standard of care.

option_notes.option: Verification and repletion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to >20-30 ng/mL and provision of oral calcium and antipyretics
option_notes.text: Correct. Ensuring vitamin D sufficiency (>20-30 ng/mL), adequate oral calcium, and antipyretic preparation prevents acute hypocalcemic crisis.

option_notes.option: Administration of high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg/m2
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Glucocorticoids further impair bone metabolism and are not standard prophylaxis for bisphosphonate infusions.

option_notes.option: Placement of a permanent tunneled central venous line
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates can be infused safely through a peripheral IV catheter; central venous lines are not required.

option_notes.option: Restriction of oral fluids to prevent hypervolemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Patients should be well hydrated, not fluid restricted, to facilitate renal excretion.

quizzes.q: What is the primary cellular and molecular mechanism by which intravenous bisphosphonates (such as pamidronate and zoledronic acid) increase bone mass and vertebral height in children with osteoporosis?
options: Inhibition of osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, inducing osteoclast apoptosis and suppressing bone resorption while growing physis adds new bone
Direct stimulation of osteoblast proliferation and collagen synthesis through the parathyroid hormone receptor
Activation of osteocytic sclerostin secretion to promote Wnt signaling
Inhibition of renal tubular calcium and phosphate excretion
quizzes.explanation: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) are taken up selectively by active osteoclasts during bone resorption and inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases essential for osteoclast cytoskeletal function and survival, inducing osteoclast apoptosis. By arresting resorption, ongoing endochondral bone formation at growing physeal growth plates continuously deposits new bone, progressively thickening cortical and trabecular architecture and reshaping collapsed vertebral bodies.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, inducing osteoclast apoptosis and suppressing bone resorption while growing physis adds new bone
option_notes.text: Correct. Nitrogenous bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast FPP synthase, suppressing resorption while growing physis reshapes bone.

option_notes.option: Direct stimulation of osteoblast proliferation and collagen synthesis through the parathyroid hormone receptor
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates do not bind the PTH receptor; they are antiresorptive agents, not direct osteoblast stimulants.

option_notes.option: Activation of osteocytic sclerostin secretion to promote Wnt signaling
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling; bisphosphonates do not activate sclerostin.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of renal tubular calcium and phosphate excretion
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates act directly on skeleton, not primarily on renal tubular mineral transport.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old non-ambulatory adolescent male with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on deflazacort therapy sustains his third low-trauma femur fracture. His lumbar spine DXA Z-score adjusted for height is -3.2. He is initiated on intravenous zoledronic acid 0.05 mg/kg every 6 months. What is the expected physiological impact of bisphosphonate therapy on his vertebral and long-bone health?
options: Reduction in bone pain, prevention of future vertebral compression fractures, and partial or complete vertebral body remodeling
Accelerated progression of scoliosis requiring immediate spinal fusion
Permanent arrest of longitudinal growth at epiphyseal growth plates
Spontaneous cure of Duchenne muscular dystrophy muscle weakness
quizzes.explanation: In glucocorticoid-treated children with secondary osteoporosis (such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy), intravenous zoledronic acid markedly reduces bone pain, prevents new vertebral and long-bone fractures, increases areal and volumetric bone density, and allows growing vertebral bodies to remodel and restore height. It does not arrest growth plate growth and has no curative effect on underlying dystrophin deficiency.

option_notes.option: Reduction in bone pain, prevention of future vertebral compression fractures, and partial or complete vertebral body remodeling
option_notes.text: Correct. IV bisphosphonates relieve bone pain, prevent fractures, and permit robust vertebral reshaping in growing children.

option_notes.option: Accelerated progression of scoliosis requiring immediate spinal fusion
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates stabilize vertebral architecture, which helps protect against progressive kyphoscoliotic deformity.

option_notes.option: Permanent arrest of longitudinal growth at epiphyseal growth plates
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Standard doses of bisphosphonates do not impair linear growth plate elongation or cause premature epiphyseal fusion.

option_notes.option: Spontaneous cure of Duchenne muscular dystrophy muscle weakness
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates treat bone fragility, not the primary muscle dystrophin deficiency.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple recurrent fractures following minimal falls, blue-tinted sclerae, triangular facies, and opalescent amber-brown teeth that chip easily (dentinogenesis imperfecta). Hearing screening shows conductive hearing loss. What is the most likely mode of inheritance and underlying molecular defect?
options: Autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 (Osteogenesis Imperfecta)
Autosomal recessive mutations in the VDR gene
X-linked recessive mutation in the DMD gene
Autosomal dominant activating mutation in the FGFR3 gene
quizzes.explanation: The clinical constellation of recurrent fragility fractures, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and hearing impairment is pathognomonic for Osteogenesis Imperfecta (types I-IV), caused in over 85-90% of cases by heterozygous autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, which encode the alpha chains of type I collagen.

option_notes.option: Autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 (Osteogenesis Imperfecta)
option_notes.text: Correct. Classic OI with blue sclerae and dentinogenesis imperfecta is caused by autosomal dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations.

option_notes.option: Autosomal recessive mutations in the VDR gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. VDR mutations cause vitamin D-dependent rickets with alopecia, not blue sclerae and dentinogenesis imperfecta.

option_notes.option: X-linked recessive mutation in the DMD gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. DMD mutations cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which presents with proximal weakness and pseudohypertrophy.

option_notes.option: Autosomal dominant activating mutation in the FGFR3 gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia with rhizomelic dwarfism, not fragile bones with dentinogenesis imperfecta.

quizzes.q: A 14.5-year-old boy is brought to the endocrine clinic by his parents because he has not shown any signs of puberty. On examination, he is prepubertal (Tanner stage 1: no pubic hair, bilateral testicular volume 2.5 mL). His height is at the 5th percentile, but his calculated midparental target height is at the 50th percentile. His father underwent a late growth spurt at age 16. Left hand radiograph reveals a bone age of 11.5 years (delayed by 3 years). Serum LH is 0.4 IU/L, FSH is 0.8 IU/L, and morning total testosterone is 15 ng/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
quizzes.explanation: This boy exhibits the classic hallmark profile of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP): male sex, lack of pubertal onset by age 14 (testicular volume <4 mL), positive paternal history of delayed pubertal timing ('late bloomer'), delayed bone age (11.5 years) that matches his height age, and normal prepubertal gonadotropins and testosterone. When his bone age advances to 12-13 years, spontaneous puberty will occur.

option_notes.option: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)
option_notes.text: Correct. CDGP is characterized by delayed bone age matching height age, familial late pubertal timing, and low prepubertal gonadotropins.

option_notes.option: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome presents with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) in mid-puberty, tall stature, and small firm testes.

option_notes.option: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Complete androgen insensitivity occurs in 46,XY phenotypic females with female external genitalia, not boys presenting with delayed male puberty.

option_notes.option: Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma causes severe growth arrest, headaches, visual field defects, and multiple anterior pituitary deficiencies.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and lack of pubertal development. Physical examination reveals Tanner stage 1 breasts, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, a high-arched palate, low posterior hairline, and wide-spaced nipples. Her height is well below the 3rd percentile. Serum FSH is markedly elevated at 88 IU/L and LH is 34 IU/L. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a small prepubertal uterus and bilateral streak ovaries. What diagnostic test should be ordered next?
options: Peripheral blood karyotype analysis
Intravenous GnRH stimulation test
Head MRI with dedicated pituitary cuts
24-hour urinary free cortisol
quizzes.explanation: The clinical constellation of short stature, primary amenorrhea, absent breast development, webbed neck/low hairline, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (elevated FSH/LH with streak ovaries) is pathognomonic for Turner syndrome. A peripheral blood karyotype analysis (with count of at least 30-50 metaphase cells to rule out mosaicism and Y-chromosome material) is the mandatory next diagnostic test.

option_notes.option: Peripheral blood karyotype analysis
option_notes.text: Correct. Blood karyotype confirms Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism) in a girl with short stature and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

option_notes.option: Intravenous GnRH stimulation test
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GnRH stimulation is redundant because baseline gonadotropins are already strikingly elevated due to absence of ovarian feedback.

option_notes.option: Head MRI with dedicated pituitary cuts
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Pituitary MRI is indicated for hypogonadotropic (central) hypogonadism, not primary ovarian dysgenesis.

option_notes.option: 24-hour urinary free cortisol
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Urinary free cortisol evaluates Cushing syndrome, which does not cause streak ovaries with elevated FSH.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with complete absence of pubertal development (testicular volume 2 mL bilaterally). On detailed review of systems, he reports that he has never been able to smell coffee, smoke, or perfume. Serum LH and FSH are low-normal, and morning testosterone is <10 ng/dL. Cranial MRI reveals aplasia of the olfactory bulbs and absent olfactory sulci. What is the diagnosis?
options: Kallmann syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Vanishing testes syndrome
quizzes.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism paired with anosmia or hyposmia. It is caused by mutations in genes such as ANOS1 (KAL1), FGFR1, or PROKR2 that disrupt the embryonic co-migration of GnRH neuroendocrine cells and olfactory axons from the olfactory placode into the forebrain. Absent olfactory bulbs/sulci on MRI confirms the diagnosis.

option_notes.option: Kallmann syndrome
option_notes.text: Correct. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and absent olfactory bulbs on MRI defines Kallmann syndrome.

option_notes.option: Klinefelter syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome presents with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic), normal olfaction, and small firm testes.

option_notes.option: Prader-Willi syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Prader-Willi presents with infantile hypotonia, childhood hyperphagia, morbid obesity, and normal olfaction.

option_notes.option: Vanishing testes syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Vanishing testes syndrome produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (elevated LH/FSH) with impalpable gonads and normal olfaction.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old girl with confirmed Turner syndrome (45,X) and complete ovarian failure is ready to begin pubertal induction. What is the recommended strategy for introducing estrogen and progesterone?
options: Initiate very low-dose transdermal 17-beta estradiol monotherapy, gradually escalating over 2-3 years, and delay adding cyclic progesterone for at least 18-24 months
Initiate combination oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate immediately
Administer high-dose oral conjugated estrogens with daily medroxyprogesterone from day 1
Withhold estrogen therapy until chronological age 18 years to maximize final adult height
quizzes.explanation: Consensus guidelines for Turner syndrome recommend initiating pubertal induction at age 11-12 years with very low-dose 17-beta estradiol (preferably transdermal patches at 6.25-12.5 mcg/day) to mimic normal physiological puberty. Estrogen is escalated gradually over 2 to 3 years to optimize breast contour, alveolar development, and uterine dimensions. Cyclic progesterone is delayed for 18-24 months (or until breakthrough bleeding occurs) to avoid tubular breast deformity and premature cessation of ductal proliferation.

option_notes.option: Initiate very low-dose transdermal 17-beta estradiol monotherapy, gradually escalating over 2-3 years, and delay adding cyclic progesterone for at least 18-24 months
option_notes.text: Correct. Gradual low-dose transdermal estradiol monotherapy with progesterone delayed for 18-24 months optimizes breast and uterine maturation.

option_notes.option: Initiate combination oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate immediately
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adult combination birth control pills provide supraphysiological ethinyl estradiol that causes premature epiphyseal closure and abnormal tubular breasts.

option_notes.option: Administer high-dose oral conjugated estrogens with daily medroxyprogesterone from day 1
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Conjugated estrogens are non-physiological mixtures, and adding progesterone from day 1 halts normal ductile breast budding.

option_notes.option: Withhold estrogen therapy until chronological age 18 years to maximize final adult height
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Delaying estrogen to age 18 causes severe osteoporosis, psychological distress, and uterine hypoplasia.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old male with constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is experiencing severe anxiety, social withdrawal, and school bullying due to his short stature and lack of sexual development. His bone age is 12 years and testicular volume is 3 mL bilaterally. What is the most appropriate medical management?
options: Reassurance alone with strict refusal of any pharmacological intervention
A short 3- to 6-month course of low-dose depot testosterone enanthate (25-50 mg IM once monthly)
Full adult replacement testosterone enanthate (200 mg IM every 2 weeks)
Subcutaneous recombinant growth hormone therapy at supraphysiological doses
quizzes.explanation: In adolescent boys with CDGP >=14 years of age with significant psychological distress, a short course of low-dose depot testosterone (25-50 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) is the standard of care. This regimen accelerates linear growth, induces virilization (pubic hair, phallic enlargement), and promotes psychological well-being without causing excessive bone age advancement or compromising adult height. It frequently stimulates the endogenous hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator.

option_notes.option: Reassurance alone with strict refusal of any pharmacological intervention
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Dismissing significant psychological distress when a safe, proven, low-dose regimen exists is suboptimal medical care.

option_notes.option: A short 3- to 6-month course of low-dose depot testosterone enanthate (25-50 mg IM once monthly)
option_notes.text: Correct. A 3-6 month course of low-dose depot testosterone (25-50 mg IM monthly) safely promotes growth and virilization without compromising height.

option_notes.option: Full adult replacement testosterone enanthate (200 mg IM every 2 weeks)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Full adult replacement (200 mg every 2 weeks) causes rapid skeletal maturation and premature epiphyseal closure, compromising adult height.

option_notes.option: Subcutaneous recombinant growth hormone therapy at supraphysiological doses
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Growth hormone is not indicated for CDGP in the absence of documented GH deficiency.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for bilateral breast development (Tanner stage 3) and a growth spurt over the past 8 months. Height is at the 97th percentile (previously 50th percentile). Left hand radiograph reveals a bone age of 8.5 years. A GnRH stimulation test is performed: baseline LH is 0.8 IU/L, and peak stimulated LH at 30 minutes is 9.4 IU/L with peak FSH 7.2 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate long-acting GnRH agonist therapy (e.g., depot leuprolide or histrelin implant)
Perform bilateral laparoscopic oophorectomy
Prescribe oral spironolactone and anastrozole
Observation without treatment until menarche occurs
quizzes.explanation: This patient has idiopathic central precocious puberty (CPP), documented by early thelarche (<8 years), accelerated growth velocity, advanced bone age, and a robust pubertal peak LH >5.0 IU/L on GnRH stimulation test with a normal brain MRI. In girls under 7-8 years with rapidly progressive CPP and compromised predicted adult height, long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., depot leuprolide 11.25 mg every 3 months or histrelin implant) are the first-line treatment to preserve final adult height and arrest sexual maturation.

option_notes.option: Initiate long-acting GnRH agonist therapy (e.g., depot leuprolide or histrelin implant)
option_notes.text: Correct. GnRH agonist therapy is the established standard of care for progressive central precocious puberty.

option_notes.option: Perform bilateral laparoscopic oophorectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Oophorectomy is mutilating and contraindicated; ovarian activity in CPP is secondary to pituitary drive.

option_notes.option: Prescribe oral spironolactone and anastrozole
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Spironolactone and anastrozole are used in peripheral precocious puberty (e.g., testotoxicosis or McCune-Albright), not CPP.

option_notes.option: Observation without treatment until menarche occurs
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Withholding treatment will lead to premature epiphyseal fusion, severe compromise of adult height, and early menarche.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with pubic hair development, penile enlargement, and linear growth acceleration. On physical examination, his phallus is 8.5 cm in length, pubic hair is Tanner stage 3, and his testes are symmetric with a volume of 2.0 mL bilaterally (prepubertal). Morning laboratory evaluation reveals serum total testosterone 180 ng/dL (elevated for age), and basal and GnRH-stimulated LH levels are <0.1 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Non-salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
Idiopathic central precocious puberty
Hypothalamic hamartoma
Leydig cell testicular adenoma
quizzes.explanation: This boy exhibits peripheral precocious puberty (isosexual pseudoprecocity), characterized by marked virilization (phallic growth, pubic hair, high testosterone) with completely prepubertal testes (<4 mL bilaterally) and suppressed gonadotropins (LH <0.1 IU/L). In boys, the most common cause of peripheral precocity with small prepubertal testes is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency), where adrenal androgens virilize the external genitalia while suppressing the pituitary HPG axis.

option_notes.option: Non-salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
option_notes.text: Correct. CAH produces adrenal hyperandrogenism, virilizing the phallus while keeping the testes prepubertal (<4 mL) and LH suppressed.

option_notes.option: Idiopathic central precocious puberty
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Central precocious puberty features testicular enlargement (>=4 mL) and a robust LH response on GnRH testing.

option_notes.option: Hypothalamic hamartoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hypothalamic hamartomas cause central precocious puberty with enlarged testes and pubertal LH secretion.

option_notes.option: Leydig cell testicular adenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Leydig cell tumors produce asymmetric testicular enlargement, with one testis palpably enlarged and firm.

quizzes.q: A 3-year-old male presents with aggressive behavior, accelerated linear growth, phallic enlargement, and bilateral symmetric testicular enlargement (testicular volume 6-8 mL bilaterally). Total testosterone is 350 ng/dL. A GnRH stimulation test shows baseline and peak LH <0.1 IU/L. Cranial MRI is completely normal. Genetic testing reveals an activating heterozygous missense mutation in the LHCGR gene. What is the diagnosis?
options: Testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty)
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
McCune-Albright syndrome
Hypothalamic hamartoma
quizzes.explanation: Testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by activating mutations in LHCGR (luteinizing hormone / choriogonadotropin receptor). The constitutively active LH receptor autonomously stimulates Leydig cell cAMP production, causing bilateral testicular enlargement (6-8 mL) and adult-level testosterone secretion in early childhood despite prepubertal/suppressed pituitary LH. Females carrying the mutation are unaffected because ovarian steroidogenesis requires both LH and FSH.

option_notes.option: Testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty)
option_notes.text: Correct. Activating LHCGR mutations cause testotoxicosis, with bilateral testicular enlargement, high testosterone, and suppressed LH.

option_notes.option: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Complete AIS involves loss of androgen receptor function in 46,XY females, causing lack of virilization.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by GNAS somatic mutations and classically causes precocity in girls, not testotoxicosis in boys.

option_notes.option: Hypothalamic hamartoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hypothalamic hamartoma causes GnRH-dependent central precocious puberty with elevated LH levels.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of vaginal bleeding without breast enlargement or pubic hair. Physical examination reveals two large light-brown macules on her lower back and buttocks with jagged, irregular borders that do not cross the midline. Skeletal radiographs demonstrate expansile radiolucent lesions with ground-glass appearance in the left femur and pelvis. What is the diagnosis and molecular etiology?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome due to postzygotic activating somatic mutation in GNAS
Neurofibromatosis type 1 due to NF1 germline mutation
Central precocious puberty due to MKRN3 mutation
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome due to STK11 mutation
quizzes.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS) is defined by the classical triad of: (1) peripheral precocious puberty with recurrent large autonomous ovarian cysts and vaginal bleeding; (2) large café-au-lait pigmentation with jagged, irregular 'coast of Maine' borders that typically respect the midline; and (3) polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (ground-glass bone lesions). MAS is caused by a postzygotic mosaic activating somatic mutation in GNAS (encoding Gs-alpha, typically at Arg201), constitutively activating adenylyl cyclase.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome due to postzygotic activating somatic mutation in GNAS
option_notes.text: Correct. Postzygotic GNAS activating mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome with fibrous dysplasia, jagged café-au-lait macules, and autonomous cysts.

option_notes.option: Neurofibromatosis type 1 due to NF1 germline mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NF1 features smooth-bordered 'coast of California' café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and optic gliomas, not fibrous dysplasia with MAS cysts.

option_notes.option: Central precocious puberty due to MKRN3 mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MKRN3 mutations cause central precocious puberty with pubertal LH levels and no fibrous dysplasia or jagged macules.

option_notes.option: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome due to STK11 mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers presents with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation of lips and hamartomatous intestinal polyps.

quizzes.q: A 15-month-old healthy, thriving girl is noted to have bilateral palpable breast tissue (Tanner stage 2) on routine examination. There is no pubic or axillary hair. Her growth velocity is tracking steadily along the 50th percentile, and left hand radiograph confirms that her bone age is identical to chronological age (15 months). Pelvic ultrasound shows prepubertal uterine length (2.2 cm) without endometrial thickening and normal infantile ovaries. What is the recommended management?
options: Observation and reassurance without pharmacological intervention (benign premature thelarche)
Initiate depot leuprolide 7.5 mg IM monthly
Order emergent head MRI to rule out a hypothalamic tumor
Perform bilateral breast needle aspiration biopsy
quizzes.explanation: This infant has isolated premature thelarche, a common benign pubertal variant that occurs in girls under 2 years of age. It represents transient sensitivity of breast tissue to maternal/neonatal estrogens or transient incomplete activation of the HPG axis with isolated FSH secretion. It is characterized by normal growth velocity, normal bone age, prepubertal pelvic ultrasound, and spontaneous regression or stabilization over 1-2 years. No medical intervention or brain MRI is indicated.

option_notes.option: Observation and reassurance without pharmacological intervention (benign premature thelarche)
option_notes.text: Correct. Isolated premature thelarche in a child <2 years with normal growth and bone age is benign and requires only observation.

option_notes.option: Initiate depot leuprolide 7.5 mg IM monthly
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GnRH agonists are contraindicated in benign pubertal variants.

option_notes.option: Order emergent head MRI to rule out a hypothalamic tumor
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Brain MRI is unnecessary because there are no signs of progressive central precocious puberty.

option_notes.option: Perform bilateral breast needle aspiration biopsy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Breast biopsy in an infant will damage the developing breast bud and cause permanent amastia.

quizzes.q: A full-term newborn is found to have ambiguous external genitalia with a 2.5-cm phallus, severe chordee, a single perineal urogenital orifice, and completely fused labioscrotal folds with no palpable gonads in the folds or inguinal canals. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a distinct uterus and normal upper vaginal cavity. Blood pressure is 68/42 mmHg. Which laboratory test is most critical to obtain immediately?
options: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) and serum electrolytes
Serum dihydrotestosterone (DHT) concentration
Urinary gonadotropin peptides
Serum Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)
quizzes.explanation: A newborn presenting with atypical genitalia, bilateral impalpable gonads, and a documented uterus on ultrasound is a virilized 46,XX infant with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) until proven otherwise. Immediate measurement of 17-OHP and serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium) is mandatory because life-threatening adrenal salt-wasting crisis can develop rapidly.

option_notes.option: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) and serum electrolytes
option_notes.text: Correct. 17-OHP and electrolytes urgently diagnose or exclude salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH.

option_notes.option: Serum dihydrotestosterone (DHT) concentration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. DHT evaluates 5-alpha-reductase deficiency in 46,XY infants (who lack a uterus), not 46,XX infants with a uterus.

option_notes.option: Urinary gonadotropin peptides
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Urinary gonadotropins have no role in acute neonatal DSD crisis management.

option_notes.option: Serum Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. AMH is absent in 46,XX infants without testes; it does not replace urgent adrenal steroid evaluation.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. Physical examination shows excellent Tanner stage 5 breast development, but completely absent pubic and axillary hair (Tanner stage 1). Pelvic examination reveals a blind-ending vagina measuring 2.5 cm in depth. Pelvic ultrasound confirms the absence of a uterus and ovaries. Bilateral masses are palpated in the inguinal canals. Karyotype is 46,XY. Serum testosterone is in the normal adult male range. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)
Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)
5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency
Turner syndrome (45,X)
quizzes.explanation: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the androgen receptor (AR). In 46,XY individuals, testes produce AMH (causing complete Müllerian regression: absent uterus/upper vagina) and testosterone. Because all androgen receptors are completely non-functional, external genitalia develop as phenotypic female, and pubic/axillary hair does not develop. At puberty, high testosterone is peripherally aromatized to estrogen, inducing normal female breast development.

option_notes.option: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)
option_notes.text: Correct. 46,XY karyotype, absent uterus, normal breast development, absent pubic hair, and male testosterone levels define CAIS.

option_notes.option: Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MRKH syndrome occurs in 46,XX females with normal ovaries, normal pubic hair, and female testosterone levels.

option_notes.option: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency presents with significant virilization (phallic enlargement, hirsutism) at puberty, not breast development.

option_notes.option: Turner syndrome (45,X)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Turner syndrome is 45,X with a normal uterus, streak ovaries, short stature, and absent breast development.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old individual raised as a female in a rural community presents with rapid virilization at puberty: deepening of the voice, marked enlargement of the clitoral phallus into an 8-cm penis, development of facial and body hair, and progressive muscular development. There is no breast development. Karyotype is 46,XY. Physical exam reveals a bifid scrotum containing palpable 12-mL testes and a perineal hypospadias. Baseline testosterone is 650 ng/dL, but serum dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is 14 ng/dL (testosterone-to-DHT ratio >40). What enzyme is deficient?
options: Steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2)
Aromatase (CYP19A1)
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 (HSD17B3)
P450 oxidoreductase (POR)
quizzes.explanation: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in SRD5A2. Impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT in utero impairs external genital virilization, so 46,XY infants are often assigned female at birth. At puberty, massive LH-driven testosterone production virilizes tissues directly through the androgen receptor, causing penile growth, muscle development, and voice deepening without gynecomastia. A markedly elevated testosterone-to-DHT ratio (>20-30:1) is diagnostic.

option_notes.option: Steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2)
option_notes.text: Correct. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency characteristically causes marked pubertal virilization in 46,XY individuals with high T:DHT ratio.

option_notes.option: Aromatase (CYP19A1)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Aromatase deficiency causes virilization in 46,XX females at birth and prevents breast development, but does not occur in 46,XY males.

option_notes.option: 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 (HSD17B3)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. 17-beta-HSD-3 deficiency impairs conversion of androstenedione to testosterone, presenting with an elevated androstenedione-to-testosterone ratio.

option_notes.option: P450 oxidoreductase (POR)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. POR deficiency features skeletal malformations (Antley-Bixler phenotype) and combined steroid enzyme blocks.

quizzes.q: A newborn infant presents with asymmetric genitalia: a fully descended normal testis in the right hemiscrotum, and an empty left labioscrotal fold. Laparoscopy reveals a dysgenetic streak gonad and a rudimentary fallopian tube and hemi-uterus on the left side, and a normal testis and vas deferens on the right side. Karyotype is 45,X/46,XY. What is the diagnosis and the most critical oncological recommendation?
options: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis; surgical excision of the dysgenetic streak gonad due to high gonadoblastoma risk
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome; retain gonads indefinitely
Klinefelter syndrome; initiation of testosterone at birth
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia; high-dose hydrocortisone monotherapy
quizzes.explanation: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis (MGD) is typically associated with a 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype. It features asymmetric internal and external genitalia: a dysgenetic testis on one side with Wolffian structures, and a streak gonad on the contralateral side with persistent Müllerian structures (hemi-uterus). Intra-abdominal dysgenetic gonads containing Y-chromosomal material carry a 15-40% lifetime risk of malignant transformation into gonadoblastoma or dysgerminoma. Immediate surgical removal of the dysgenetic streak gonad is strongly recommended.

option_notes.option: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis; surgical excision of the dysgenetic streak gonad due to high gonadoblastoma risk
option_notes.text: Correct. 45,X/46,XY mosaicism with asymmetric streak/testis is mixed gonadal dysgenesis; the streak gonad must be removed due to high cancer risk.

option_notes.option: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome; retain gonads indefinitely
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CAIS has bilateral normal testes without streak gonads or Müllerian structures.

option_notes.option: Klinefelter syndrome; initiation of testosterone at birth
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Klinefelter is 47,XXY without asymmetric internal genitalia, and testosterone is not given at birth.

option_notes.option: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia; high-dose hydrocortisone monotherapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CAH does not present with a 45,X/46,XY karyotype or asymmetric streak gonads.

quizzes.q: What is the recommended modern management approach regarding immediate sex assignment and irreversible genitoplasty in a newborn with ambiguous genitalia?
options: Perform immediate emergency feminizing genitoplasty within the first 48 hours to relieve parental anxiety
Withhold definitive gender assignment until multidisciplinary diagnostic evaluation is complete, and defer non-emergency cosmetic genitoplasty until the child can participate in decision-making
Assign male sex automatically to all infants with a phallus >1.5 cm
Perform mandatory bilateral gonadectomy in all infants with 46,XX DSD
quizzes.explanation: Modern international consensus guidelines on DSD emphasize: (1) withholding definitive gender assignment until rapid comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation (karyotype, imaging, steroid profiles) is synthesized; (2) fully engaging parents with specialized psychological counseling; and (3) deferring non-urgent, irreversible cosmetic genitoplasty until the patient is old enough to provide informed assent or consent, except for surgeries required to establish unobstructed urinary drainage.

option_notes.option: Perform immediate emergency feminizing genitoplasty within the first 48 hours to relieve parental anxiety
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Immediate irreversible surgery without full evaluation violates modern clinical guidelines and human rights standards.

option_notes.option: Withhold definitive gender assignment until multidisciplinary diagnostic evaluation is complete, and defer non-emergency cosmetic genitoplasty until the child can participate in decision-making
option_notes.text: Correct. Multi-specialty diagnostic evaluation must precede assignment, and cosmetic surgery should be deferred when feasible.

option_notes.option: Assign male sex automatically to all infants with a phallus >1.5 cm
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sex assignment is never based purely on phallic length; underlying etiology, fertility potential, and brain exposure guide decisions.

option_notes.option: Perform mandatory bilateral gonadectomy in all infants with 46,XX DSD
option_notes.text: Incorrect. In 46,XX CAH, ovaries are completely normal and must be preserved for future endogenous fertility.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for irregular menses. Menarche occurred at age 12, but over the past 2 years she has had only 3 menstrual periods per year (cycle intervals 60-90 days). On examination, BMI is 28.5 kg/m2 (96th percentile), she has moderate inflammatory facial acne, and terminal hair growth on the upper lip, chin, and lower abdomen (modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 9). Serum total testosterone is elevated at 68 ng/dL (reference: 15-45 ng/dL). Pelvic ultrasound reveals multifollicular ovaries bilaterally. 17-OHP is 110 ng/dL, TSH is 2.1 mIU/L, and prolactin is normal. What is the diagnosis?
options: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Cushing syndrome
Normal physiological adolescent anovulation
quizzes.explanation: This adolescent meets consensus pediatric criteria for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): (1) ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhea with cycles >45 days >2 years post-menarche); and (2) both clinical hyperandrogenism (mFG score 9, severe acne) and biochemical hyperandrogenism (elevated testosterone), with exclusion of NCAH (17-OHP <200 ng/dL), thyroid disease, and hyperprolactinemia.

option_notes.option: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
option_notes.text: Correct. Documented ovulatory dysfunction plus clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism establishes adolescent PCOS.

option_notes.option: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NCAH is excluded by a normal morning baseline 17-OHP of 110 ng/dL (<200 ng/dL).

option_notes.option: Cushing syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cushing syndrome presents with rapid central weight gain, purple striae, muscle weakness, and hypertension.

option_notes.option: Normal physiological adolescent anovulation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cycle lengths >45 days and hirsutism with elevated testosterone >2 years post-menarche exceed normal anovulatory variation.

quizzes.q: Why do international pediatric endocrinology consensus guidelines specifically exclude polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS in adolescents?
options: Multifollicular ovarian morphology is a normal physiological finding in up to 30-40% of healthy ovulating teenagers
Pelvic ultrasound cannot visualize ovaries in adolescent females
Ovarian cysts in adolescents always represent malignant teratomas
Transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory and cannot be performed in adolescents
quizzes.explanation: During normal adolescent pubertal development, developing follicles frequently impart a multifollicular or polycystic appearance to ovaries in 30-40% of completely healthy, regularly cycling teenagers. Using ultrasound morphology as a diagnostic criterion in adolescents creates high rates of false-positive overdiagnosis. Thus, guidelines require both ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, omitting ultrasound morphology.

option_notes.option: Multifollicular ovarian morphology is a normal physiological finding in up to 30-40% of healthy ovulating teenagers
option_notes.text: Correct. High rates of physiological multifollicular ovaries in healthy teenagers invalidate ultrasound as a reliable diagnostic criterion.

option_notes.option: Pelvic ultrasound cannot visualize ovaries in adolescent females
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound readily visualizes ovaries in adolescents.

option_notes.option: Ovarian cysts in adolescents always represent malignant teratomas
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Simple functional follicular cysts in adolescents are benign, not malignant teratomas.

option_notes.option: Transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory and cannot be performed in adolescents
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Transabdominal ultrasound with a full bladder is the standard non-invasive modality.

quizzes.q: What is the primary mechanism by which combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) improve hirsutism and hyperandrogenemia in adolescents with PCOS?
options: Suppression of pituitary LH secretion and stimulation of hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) synthesis
Direct irreversible inhibition of ovarian 17-alpha-hydroxylase
Selective destruction of the adrenal zona reticularis
Degradation of circulating dihydrotestosterone by renal tubular filtration
quizzes.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives improve hyperandrogenism through a dual mechanism: (1) the progestin component suppresses pituitary LH pulse frequency, decreasing LH-stimulated ovarian theca cell androgen production; and (2) the estrogen component stimulates hepatic synthesis of SHBG, which binds circulating testosterone and sharply lowers the biologically active free testosterone fraction.

option_notes.option: Suppression of pituitary LH secretion and stimulation of hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) synthesis
option_notes.text: Correct. COCs suppress pituitary LH-driven theca androgen synthesis and elevate hepatic SHBG, lowering free testosterone.

option_notes.option: Direct irreversible inhibition of ovarian 17-alpha-hydroxylase
option_notes.text: Incorrect. COCs do not destroy or irreversibly inhibit steroidogenic enzymes.

option_notes.option: Selective destruction of the adrenal zona reticularis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. COCs do not destroy the adrenal zona reticularis.

option_notes.option: Degradation of circulating dihydrotestosterone by renal tubular filtration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. COCs do not enhance renal clearance of DHT.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with severe, rapidly progressive hirsutism, temporal hair thinning, and deepening of her voice over the past 4 months. Physical examination reveals a 2.5-cm clitoromegaly. Serum total testosterone is markedly elevated at 280 ng/dL (reference: 15-45 ng/dL). DHEAS is normal. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a 4.5-cm solid vascular mass within the right ovary. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Severe polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of the ovary
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Adrenal adenoma secreting DHEAS
quizzes.explanation: Rapid onset of virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, male-pattern alopecia), massive elevation of serum total testosterone (>150-200 ng/dL), and a solid unilateral ovarian mass is pathognomonic for an ovarian androgen-secreting neoplasm, most commonly a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. PCOS does not cause rapid virilization, clitoromegaly, or a solid unilateral ovarian mass.

option_notes.option: Severe polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PCOS causes gradual hirsutism, not rapid virilization, clitoromegaly, testosterone >200 ng/dL, or solid ovarian masses.

option_notes.option: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of the ovary
option_notes.text: Correct. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor presents with rapid virilization, extreme testosterone elevation, and a solid ovarian tumor.

option_notes.option: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NCAH does not cause an isolated solid ovarian tumor.

option_notes.option: Adrenal adenoma secreting DHEAS
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adrenal androgen tumors are characterized by massive elevations of DHEAS (>700-800 mcg/dL), which is normal here.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old female high school distance runner presents with secondary amenorrhea for 8 months. She runs 50 miles per week and has restricted her caloric intake. BMI is 17.2 kg/m2. Examination shows Tanner 5 breasts and pubic hair without hirsutism or acne. Pregnancy test is negative. Serum LH is 0.8 IU/L, FSH is 2.4 IU/L, estradiol is 18 pg/mL (low), and total testosterone is 12 ng/dL (low-normal). What is the underlying pathophysiology?
options: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) due to relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)
Polycystic ovary syndrome with atypical presentation
Premature ovarian insufficiency (POF)
Androgen insensitivity syndrome
quizzes.explanation: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) in athletes is caused by chronic low energy availability (energy expenditure exceeding dietary intake, known as Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport [RED-S]). This suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, leading to low/suppressed LH and FSH, hypoestrogenemia (estradiol <20-30 pg/mL), and secondary amenorrhea. In contrast to PCOS, patients with FHA are typically underweight/lean and have low (not high) androgens without hirsutism.

option_notes.option: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) due to relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)
option_notes.text: Correct. Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility, causing hypogonadotropic hypoestrogenemic amenorrhea (FHA).

option_notes.option: Polycystic ovary syndrome with atypical presentation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PCOS features hyperandrogenism, elevated LH/FSH ratio, and oligomenorrhea, not low androgens and low LH.

option_notes.option: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POF)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Premature ovarian insufficiency presents with elevated gonadotropins (high FSH >40 IU/L), not low LH/FSH.

option_notes.option: Androgen insensitivity syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Androgen insensitivity syndrome causes primary amenorrhea in 46,XY individuals, not secondary amenorrhea after normal menarche.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old male presents with persistent frontal headaches and bitemporal hemianopsia on visual field testing. Brain MRI reveals a 2.8-cm sellar and suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Initial serum prolactin is reported as 62 mcg/L (reference: <20 mcg/L). The neurosurgeon suspects a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma with stalk compression and schedules emergent surgical resection. However, the pediatric endocrinologist requests that the laboratory re-assay the sample with a 1:100 dilution, which returns a true prolactin concentration of 4800 mcg/L. What phenomenon explains the initial low reading, and what is the proper therapy?
options: Hook effect; initiate medical therapy with cabergoline immediately
Macroprolactinemia; proceed with transsphenoidal surgical resection
Assay cross-reactivity with GH; administer pegvisomant
Secondary adrenal insufficiency; give high-dose dexamethasone
quizzes.explanation: This patient has a giant macroprolactinoma displaying the 'hook effect' (high-dose hook effect). Immense antigen (prolactin) concentrations saturate both capture and signal antibodies in two-site immunometric assays, causing falsely low readings that mimic stalk compression. A 1:100 dilution reveals the true massive elevation (4800 mcg/L). Macroprolactinomas respond dramatically to medical therapy with dopamine agonists (cabergoline), which rapidly shrinks the tumor and decompresses the optic chiasm, making cabergoline the treatment of choice over immediate surgery.

option_notes.option: Hook effect; initiate medical therapy with cabergoline immediately
option_notes.text: Correct. The hook effect falsely lowers measured prolactin; true macroprolactinomas are treated primarily with cabergoline, not surgery.

option_notes.option: Macroprolactinemia; proceed with transsphenoidal surgical resection
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Macroprolactinemia is a benign artifact of inactive antibody complexes, not giant invasive macroadenomas.

option_notes.option: Assay cross-reactivity with GH; administer pegvisomant
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist for acromegaly, not the primary treatment for prolactinomas.

option_notes.option: Secondary adrenal insufficiency; give high-dose dexamethasone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Dexamethasone does not shrink prolactinomas or cure prolactin-mediated chiasmal compression.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old girl presents with secondary amenorrhea and spontaneous bilateral milky breast discharge (galactorrhea). Serum prolactin is 145 mcg/L. Sellar MRI reveals a 6-mm well-circumscribed microadenoma in the left pituitary wing. What is the most effective initial management?
options: Oral cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly
Immediate stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife)
Transsphenoidal microdissection of the left pituitary wing
High-dose combined oral contraceptives
quizzes.explanation: Cabergoline (0.25 to 0.5 mg once or twice weekly) is the established first-line therapy for microprolactinomas in adolescents. Cabergoline normalizes prolactin, resolves galactorrhea, restores regular ovulatory menses, and shrinks or stabilizes tumor size in >90% of patients with minimal adverse effects. Surgery and radiation are reserved for rare refractory cases.

option_notes.option: Oral cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly
option_notes.text: Correct. Cabergoline twice weekly is the first-line treatment of choice for microprolactinomas.

option_notes.option: Immediate stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Radiosurgery carries significant long-term risks of hypopituitarism and secondary neoplasms and is not first-line.

option_notes.option: Transsphenoidal microdissection of the left pituitary wing
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Surgery is second-line, reserved only for medical therapy failures or intolerance.

option_notes.option: High-dose combined oral contraceptives
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Combined oral contraceptives can provide estrogen but do not treat the underlying microprolactinoma and may stimulate tumor growth.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old adolescent with schizophrenia treated with risperidone 3 mg daily for 6 months presents with bilateral breast enlargement and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is 85 mcg/L. Pituitary MRI is completely normal. What is the pharmacological mechanism causing pathologically elevated prolactin levels in this patient?
options: Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotropes
Direct stimulation of hypothalamic TRH secretion
Inhibition of hepatic prolactin degradation
Downregulation of peripheral estrogen receptors
quizzes.explanation: Risperidone and other first- and second-generation antipsychotics are potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonists. By blocking D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotrope cell membranes, they relieve tonic hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition, resulting in autonomous prolactin synthesis and secretion with hyperprolactinemia (typically 40-150 mcg/L) and galactorrhea.

option_notes.option: Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotropes
option_notes.text: Correct. Risperidone blocks pituitary lactotrope D2 receptors, abolishing tonic dopamine inhibition.

option_notes.option: Direct stimulation of hypothalamic TRH secretion
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Risperidone acts via dopamine receptor antagonism, not by stimulating TRH.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of hepatic prolactin degradation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Prolactin clearance is renal and hepatic; antipsychotics do not block degradative enzymes.

option_notes.option: Downregulation of peripheral estrogen receptors
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Antipsychotics do not directly downregulate peripheral estrogen receptors.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with severe fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, growth arrest, and mild galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is 58 mcg/L. Pituitary MRI reveals diffuse, symmetric pituitary enlargement ('pituitary hyperplasia'). Thyroid function testing demonstrates TSH 420 mIU/L and free T4 0.1 ng/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Initiate oral levothyroxine replacement and repeat prolactin and MRI after achieving euthyroidism
Initiate high-dose cabergoline and schedule transsphenoidal pituitary resection
Perform urgent biopsy of the pituitary mass to rule out craniopharyngioma
Order whole-brain external beam radiation therapy
quizzes.explanation: Severe primary hypothyroidism causes extreme compensatory hypersecretion of hypothalamic TRH. TRH acts as a potent prolactin secretagogue, causing secondary hyperprolactinemia. Concurrently, chronic lack of thyroid hormone negative feedback causes profound hypertrophy and hyperplasia of pituitary thyrotropes and lactotropes, mimicking a pituitary macroadenoma on MRI. Treatment with levothyroxine restores euthyroidism, normalizes prolactin, and completely resolves pituitary enlargement, avoiding unnecessary pituitary surgery.

option_notes.option: Initiate oral levothyroxine replacement and repeat prolactin and MRI after achieving euthyroidism
option_notes.text: Correct. Levothyroxine replacement corrects the primary hypothyroidism, resolves hyperprolactinemia, and reverses pituitary hyperplasia.

option_notes.option: Initiate high-dose cabergoline and schedule transsphenoidal pituitary resection
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cabergoline and surgery are unnecessary and inappropriate for reactive pituitary thyrotrope hyperplasia secondary to hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Perform urgent biopsy of the pituitary mass to rule out craniopharyngioma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Biopsy is contraindicated and carries risks of hypopituitarism for a benign reversible hyperplasia.

option_notes.option: Order whole-brain external beam radiation therapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Radiation therapy has no role in benign thyrotrope hyperplasia.

quizzes.q: An asymptomatic 17-year-old girl has an incidental serum prolactin of 92 mcg/L measured during a dermatology workup for mild acne. She has completely regular monthly menses and no galactorrhea. Sellar MRI is normal. Serum treatment with polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation reveals that 88% of circulating prolactin precipitates as macroprolactin, with normal free monomeric prolactin. What is the appropriate clinical approach?
options: Reassurance and observation without dopamine agonist therapy
Initiate cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly to prevent future tumor development
Repeat pituitary MRI with dynamic contrast every 6 months
Perform bilateral prophylactic mastectomy
quizzes.explanation: Macroprolactinemia is a benign condition where circulating prolactin forms complexes with immunoglobulin G (IgG) autoantibodies. These high-molecular-weight complexes (>150 kDa) cannot cross capillary walls to bind target tissue prolactin receptors, rendering them biologically inactive (hence the patient has regular menses and no galactorrhea). However, standard immunoassays detect macroprolactin, causing elevated reported levels. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation precipitates the immune complexes, confirming normal monomeric prolactin. No treatment or imaging surveillance is required.

option_notes.option: Reassurance and observation without dopamine agonist therapy
option_notes.text: Correct. Macroprolactinemia is a benign laboratory artifact requiring reassurance and no dopamine agonist treatment.

option_notes.option: Initiate cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly to prevent future tumor development
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cabergoline is unnecessary and causes unnecessary side effects for biologically inactive macroprolactin.

option_notes.option: Repeat pituitary MRI with dynamic contrast every 6 months
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Surveillance MRIs are not indicated when sellar imaging is normal and free monomeric prolactin is normal.

option_notes.option: Perform bilateral prophylactic mastectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Mastectomy is completely inappropriate and mutilating.

quizzes.q: A 2-day-old macrosomic male infant (birth weight 4.4 kg) born to a non-diabetic mother presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and jitteriness. Point-of-care blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. A critical blood sample drawn prior to IV dextrose administration reveals: glucose 30 mg/dL, insulin 14 mcU/mL (inappropriately elevated), C-peptide 2.8 ng/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.2 mmol/L (suppressed), and free fatty acids 0.3 mmol/L (suppressed). Glucagon 1 mg IV is given, and blood glucose rises to 78 mg/dL at 30 minutes. What is the diagnosis?
options: Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI)
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
Growth hormone deficiency
Glycogen storage disease type I
quizzes.explanation: This neonate exhibits the classic biochemical signature of congenital hyperinsulinism: hypoglycemia (30 mg/dL) accompanied by detectable/elevated insulin (14 mcU/mL), elevated C-peptide, suppressed ketones (BOHB 0.2 mmol/L), suppressed free fatty acids, and a robust glycemic rise >30 mg/dL following glucagon challenge. Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis while locking glycogen in the liver.

option_notes.option: Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI)
option_notes.text: Correct. Measurable insulin/C-peptide with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and positive glucagon challenge is diagnostic of hyperinsulinism.

option_notes.option: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MCAD deficiency features suppressed insulin and elevated free fatty acids with abnormal acylcarnitine profile.

option_notes.option: Growth hormone deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GH deficiency causes ketotic hypoglycemia with elevated BOHB and low/undetectable insulin.

option_notes.option: Glycogen storage disease type I
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GSD type I features massive hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and poor response to glucagon.

quizzes.q: A 1-week-old full-term neonate is diagnosed with diffuse congenital hyperinsulinism due to a homozygous ABCC8 mutation. Diazoxide therapy is initiated at 10 mg/kg/day. Which additional medication must be routinely co-prescribed with diazoxide to prevent a well-documented, life-threatening adverse complication?
options: Chlorothiazide (thiazide diuretic) to prevent fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension
Levothyroxine to prevent acute hypothyroidism
Potassium chloride to prevent severe hypokalemia
Sodium bicarbonate to treat proximal renal tubular acidosis
quizzes.explanation: Diazoxide stimulates renal tubular sodium and water retention through antidiuretic mechanisms. In neonates and young infants, this can precipitate massive fluid overload, congestive heart failure, and life-threatening pulmonary hypertension. Co-administration of a thiazide diuretic (such as chlorothiazide 7-10 mg/kg/day) is mandatory to promote natriuresis, prevent edema, and exert a synergistic hyperglycemic effect.

option_notes.option: Chlorothiazide (thiazide diuretic) to prevent fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension
option_notes.text: Correct. Chlorothiazide is routinely co-prescribed to counteract diazoxide-induced fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension.

option_notes.option: Levothyroxine to prevent acute hypothyroidism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diazoxide does not cause acute hypothyroidism.

option_notes.option: Potassium chloride to prevent severe hypokalemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diazoxide does not typically cause severe hypokalemia requiring routine prophylactic KCl.

option_notes.option: Sodium bicarbonate to treat proximal renal tubular acidosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diazoxide does not cause proximal RTA requiring bicarbonate.

quizzes.q: A 14-month-old girl with a mild viral gastroenteritis and 14 hours of poor oral intake presents with lethargy, vomiting, and stupor. Serum glucose is 32 mg/dL. Critical labs show: beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L (suppressed), free fatty acids 3.2 mmol/L (markedly elevated), insulin <1.0 mcU/mL (undetectable), and serum ammonia 120 mcmol/L. Plasma acylcarnitine analysis reveals a marked elevation of octanoylcarnitine (C8). What is the underlying disorder?
options: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia
Insulinoma
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
quizzes.explanation: MCAD deficiency is the most common fatty acid oxidation defect. During prolonged fasting or catabolic stress, impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids prevents generation of acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies, resulting in hypoketotic hypoglycemia (low BOHB despite elevated FFA) and hyperammonemia. The diagnostic hallmark is marked accumulation of medium-chain acylcarnitines, specifically octanoylcarnitine (C8).

option_notes.option: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
option_notes.text: Correct. Hypoketotic hypoglycemia with elevated free fatty acids, hyperammonemia, and high C8 acylcarnitine confirms MCAD deficiency.

option_notes.option: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia features robust ketosis (BOHB >3.0 mmol/L), not hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Insulinoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Insulinomas produce elevated insulin and suppress both ketones and free fatty acids.

option_notes.option: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CAH produces salt-wasting, hyperkalemia, and elevated 17-OHP, not isolated C8 acylcarnitine elevation.

quizzes.q: A 3-year-old slender boy presents with morning drowsiness and difficulty waking after having an early dinner and missing breakfast. Point-of-care glucose is 42 mg/dL. Blood drawn at that time reveals: insulin <1 mcU/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.2 mmol/L, free fatty acids 2.8 mmol/L, cortisol 22 mcg/dL, and growth hormone 12 ng/mL. Following a glass of orange juice, he rapidly returns to his normal playful self. What is the diagnosis?
options: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia of childhood
Nesidioblastosis (congenital hyperinsulinism)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) deficiency
Primary adrenal insufficiency
quizzes.explanation: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia is the most common cause of hypoglycemia in children between 18 months and 5 years. It represents an exaggerated physiological response to fasting (accelerated starvation) in young, lean children who have limited hepatic glycogen stores and small muscle mass (limiting alanine for gluconeogenesis). The biochemical profile shows robust ketosis (BOHB >3-4 mmol/L), suppressed insulin (<1 mcU/mL), and appropriate counter-regulatory hormone surges (cortisol >18 mcg/dL, GH >10 ng/mL). It resolves spontaneously by age 6-8 years as muscle mass increases.

option_notes.option: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia of childhood
option_notes.text: Correct. Fasting hypoglycemia with brisk ketosis, suppressed insulin, and robust cortisol/GH response in a toddler is idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Nesidioblastosis (congenital hyperinsulinism)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hyperinsulinism is hypoketotic (BOHB <1.5-2.0 mmol/L) with measurable insulin.

option_notes.option: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CPT-1 deficiency is a fatty acid oxidation disorder causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

option_notes.option: Primary adrenal insufficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency is excluded by the robust cortisol peak of 22 mcg/dL.

quizzes.q: A newborn male with recurrent persistent neuroglycopenia and low plasma glucose unresponsive to diazoxide undergoes genetic sequencing revealing a single paternally inherited ABCC8 mutation. What diagnostic imaging modality should be performed next to guide surgical planning?
options: 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET/CT of the pancreas
Abdominal ultrasound with color Doppler
Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
quizzes.explanation: Paternal inheritance of a monoallelic K-ATP channel mutation (ABCC8 or KCNJ11) combined with somatic maternal loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at 11p15 causes focal congenital hyperinsulinism. Because beta cells take up L-DOPA and convert it to dopamine via DOPA decarboxylase, 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET/CT specifically visualizes and localizes the adenomatous focal lesion, allowing a curative, organ-sparing partial pancreatectomy rather than near-total pancreatectomy.

option_notes.option: 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET/CT of the pancreas
option_notes.text: Correct. 18F-DOPA PET/CT is the gold standard for localizing focal adenomatous lesions in congenital hyperinsulinism.

option_notes.option: Abdominal ultrasound with color Doppler
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound lacks the spatial and biochemical sensitivity to distinguish focal beta-cell hyperplasia.

option_notes.option: Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Contrast CT cannot distinguish microscopic adenomatous hyperplasia from surrounding normal parenchyma.

option_notes.option: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MRCP visualizes ductal anatomy, not functional neuroendocrine beta-cell hyperfunction.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of polydipsia, polyuria, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul respirations. Point-of-care glucose is 480 mg/dL. Venous blood gas reveals pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, and blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L. She is alert but tachypneic. After administering an initial 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% normal saline over 1 hour, what is the most appropriate next step in her medical management?
options: Administer an IV bolus of regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg followed by continuous infusion
Initiate continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour without an insulin bolus, and plan fluid replacement over 24-48 hours
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg to correct severe acidosis
Add 10% dextrose to IV fluids immediately
quizzes.explanation: International consensus guidelines (ISPAD/PEDS) dictate that in pediatric moderate-to-severe DKA: (1) Insulin should be administered as a continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour started 1-2 hours after beginning IV fluid resuscitation; (2) An IV insulin bolus is strictly contraindicated because it causes sudden osmotic shifts and triggers hypokalemia, increasing cerebral edema risk; (3) Fluid replacement must be distributed evenly over 24-48 hours; (4) Bicarbonate is contraindicated due to paradoxical CSF acidosis and hypokalemia.

option_notes.option: Administer an IV bolus of regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg followed by continuous infusion
option_notes.text: Incorrect. IV insulin boluses are strictly contraindicated in pediatric DKA due to increased risk of fatal cerebral edema.

option_notes.option: Initiate continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour without an insulin bolus, and plan fluid replacement over 24-48 hours
option_notes.text: Correct. Continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr without a bolus, coupled with 24-48 hour fluid deficit replacement, is standard.

option_notes.option: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg to correct severe acidosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated; it worsens cerebral acidosis and precipitates life-threatening hypokalemia.

option_notes.option: Add 10% dextrose to IV fluids immediately
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Dextrose is added only after blood glucose declines to 250-300 mg/dL, not at 480 mg/dL.

quizzes.q: During management of severe DKA in a 10-year-old boy, blood glucose drops from 480 mg/dL to 260 mg/dL after 4 hours of IV fluids and continuous regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour. Venous blood gas shows persistent acidosis: pH 7.18, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, and urine ketones remain large. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop the insulin infusion because the blood glucose is approaching normal
Reduce insulin infusion to 0.01 units/kg/hour and administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
Add 5% dextrose to the IV hydration fluids and continue the insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour to clear the ketoacidosis
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to accelerate acidosis resolution
quizzes.explanation: In DKA, insulin is required not merely to lower blood glucose, but fundamentally to suppress lipolysis, suppress ketogenesis, and stimulate peripheral ketone clearance. When blood glucose approaches 250-300 mg/dL, 5% dextrose (and later 10% dextrose if needed) must be added to the IV fluids while maintaining the insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr. This prevents hypoglycemia while allowing insulin to completely resolve the ketoacidosis.

option_notes.option: Stop the insulin infusion because the blood glucose is approaching normal
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Stopping insulin allows ketoacidosis to worsen, even if glucose is temporarily lower.

option_notes.option: Reduce insulin infusion to 0.01 units/kg/hour and administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Inadequately reducing insulin halts the suppression of ketogenesis and prolongs DKA.

option_notes.option: Add 5% dextrose to the IV hydration fluids and continue the insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour to clear the ketoacidosis
option_notes.text: Correct. Adding 5% dextrose while maintaining insulin infusion keeps glucose 150-200 mg/dL while clearing ketoacidosis.

option_notes.option: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to accelerate acidosis resolution
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is contraindicated in pediatric DKA.

quizzes.q: Six hours into treatment for severe DKA, an 11-year-old girl complains of a severe, worsening headache. On exam, her heart rate has dropped from 110 bpm to 58 bpm, blood pressure has risen from 104/65 to 138/88 mmHg, and she is difficult to arouse. What is the most critical immediate intervention?
options: Transport the patient immediately to the radiology suite for an emergent unenhanced head CT
Administer intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol immediately at the bedside
Increase the rate of 0.9% normal saline infusion to treat hypovolemia
Administer intravenous lorazepam for suspected subclinical status epilepticus
quizzes.explanation: The sudden onset of severe headache, bradycardia, and hypertension (Cushing triad) with neurological deterioration represents impending cerebral herniation from DKA-related cerebral edema. Cerebral edema is a medical emergency with high mortality. Treatment with hyperosmolar therapy (3% hypertonic saline 3-5 mL/kg or 20% mannitol 0.5-1.0 g/kg) must be administered immediately at the bedside; diagnostic imaging must NEVER delay treatment.

option_notes.option: Transport the patient immediately to the radiology suite for an emergent unenhanced head CT
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Delaying hyperosmolar therapy to obtain a CT scan can result in brainstem herniation and fatal arrest.

option_notes.option: Administer intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol immediately at the bedside
option_notes.text: Correct. Immediate bedside administration of 3% hypertonic saline or mannitol is life-saving and must precede neuroimaging.
