option_notes.option: Increase the rate of 0.9% normal saline infusion to treat hypovolemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Increasing fluid infusion rate will worsen cerebral edema and accelerate herniation.

option_notes.option: Administer intravenous lorazepam for suspected subclinical status epilepticus
option_notes.text: Incorrect. The findings reflect acute intracranial hypertension (Cushing triad), not primary status epilepticus.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old male with established type 1 diabetes weighs 50 kg and takes a total daily dose of 40 units of insulin. Using the 500 Rule and 1800 Rule, calculate his estimated Insulin-to-Carbohydrate Ratio (ICR) and Insulin Sensitivity Factor (ISF):
options: ICR: 1 unit per 12.5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 45 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 20 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 25 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 70 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 90 mg/dL
quizzes.explanation: The standard clinical formulas for estimating starting pump and MDI parameters based on Total Daily Dose (TDD = 40 units) are: (1) 500 Rule for ICR = 500 / TDD = 500 / 40 = 12.5 grams of carbohydrate per 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin; (2) 1800 Rule for ISF = 1800 / TDD = 1800 / 40 = 45 mg/dL reduction in blood glucose per 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin.

option_notes.option: ICR: 1 unit per 12.5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 45 mg/dL
option_notes.text: Correct. ICR = 500/40 = 12.5 g/unit; ISF = 1800/40 = 45 mg/dL/unit.

option_notes.option: ICR: 1 unit per 5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 20 mg/dL
option_notes.text: Incorrect. 1:5 and 20 mg/dL reflect a massively high TDD of ~90-100 units.

option_notes.option: ICR: 1 unit per 25 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 70 mg/dL
option_notes.text: Incorrect. 1:25 and 70 mg/dL reflect a low TDD of ~20-25 units.

option_notes.option: ICR: 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 90 mg/dL
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Mathematical calculation error.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago has an HbA1c of 6.2% on a total daily insulin dose of 0.25 units/kg/day. His parents ask if he has been cured of diabetes. What is the explanation for his current low insulin requirement?
options: He is experiencing the 'honeymoon' (partial remission) phase due to temporary recovery of surviving beta cells
He was misdiagnosed and actually has maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
He has developed complete insulin sensitivity due to low carbohydrate intake
His islet autoantibodies have permanently disappeared
quizzes.explanation: The 'honeymoon' or partial clinical remission phase occurs in up to 60-80% of children shortly after diagnosis and initial glycemic stabilization. Relief of glucotoxicity allows surviving beta cells to temporarily produce sufficient endogenous insulin to maintain near-normal glycemic control with very low exogenous insulin requirements (<0.5 units/kg/day). This phase typically lasts several months to a year before autoimmune destruction inevitably progresses to absolute insulin deficiency.

option_notes.option: He is experiencing the 'honeymoon' (partial remission) phase due to temporary recovery of surviving beta cells
option_notes.text: Correct. The honeymoon phase represents transient endogenous beta-cell recovery with low insulin requirements.

option_notes.option: He was misdiagnosed and actually has maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MODY is a monogenic defect; high initial presentation with subsequent partial remission is classic for T1D.

option_notes.option: He has developed complete insulin sensitivity due to low carbohydrate intake
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Insulin sensitivity does not account for low insulin requirements in the setting of beta-cell rest.

option_notes.option: His islet autoantibodies have permanently disappeared
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Autoantibodies persist throughout the disease course and do not permanently disappear during remission.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old Hispanic male with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 (98th percentile) presents for a routine sports physical. Examination reveals prominent velvety hyperpigmented plaques on the back of his neck and axillae (acanthosis nigricans). Random blood glucose is 215 mg/dL. Confirmatory testing demonstrates fasting blood glucose 152 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.8%. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without ketones. Islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) are negative. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
options: Oral metformin initiated at 500 mg once daily, titrated up to 2000 mg daily in divided doses, plus lifestyle intervention
Immediate initiation of basal-bolus insulin at 1.0 units/kg/day
Sulfonylurea monotherapy with glipizide 10 mg daily
Lifestyle modification alone with no medication for 12 months
quizzes.explanation: In youth diagnosed with antibody-negative type 2 diabetes who are metabolically stable (HbA1c <8.5%, blood glucose <250 mg/dL, no ketosis/acidosis), oral metformin monotherapy (titrated from 500 mg daily up to 1000 mg twice daily) combined with diabetes self-management education and lifestyle modification is the recommended first-line therapy according to ADA and ISPAD guidelines.

option_notes.option: Oral metformin initiated at 500 mg once daily, titrated up to 2000 mg daily in divided doses, plus lifestyle intervention
option_notes.text: Correct. Metformin 500-2000 mg/day plus lifestyle intervention is the established first-line regimen for stable youth-onset T2D.

option_notes.option: Immediate initiation of basal-bolus insulin at 1.0 units/kg/day
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Basal-bolus insulin is reserved for patients presenting with ketoacidosis or marked decompensation (HbA1c >=8.5%).

option_notes.option: Sulfonylurea monotherapy with glipizide 10 mg daily
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sulfonylureas are second-line and accelerate beta-cell exhaustion in youth-onset T2D.

option_notes.option: Lifestyle modification alone with no medication for 12 months
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Lifestyle therapy alone has a very high failure rate in youth; guidelines mandate starting metformin at diagnosis.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old obese female presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue. Serum glucose is 340 mg/dL and HbA1c is 10.4%. Serum electrolytes: sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and venous pH 7.36. Urinalysis shows 4+ glucose and trace ketones. What is the recommended initial medical management?
options: Initiation of once-daily subcutaneous basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) combined with oral metformin
Intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour according to DKA protocol
Metformin monotherapy 500 mg daily without insulin
Immediate bariatric Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery
quizzes.explanation: In youth with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes presenting with marked hyperglycemia (blood glucose >=250 mg/dL and/or HbA1c >=8.5%) WITHOUT ketoacidosis (normal pH and bicarbonate), the recommended management is initiation of once-daily subcutaneous basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) combined with oral metformin. Once glucotoxicity is relieved and glycemic stability is attained, insulin can frequently be tapered.

option_notes.option: Initiation of once-daily subcutaneous basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) combined with oral metformin
option_notes.text: Correct. Basal insulin combined with metformin is the guideline-directed therapy for marked hyperglycemia (HbA1c >=8.5%) without acidosis.

option_notes.option: Intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour according to DKA protocol
option_notes.text: Incorrect. IV insulin DKA protocol is indicated only when systemic ketoacidosis (pH <7.30, bicarb <15) is present.

option_notes.option: Metformin monotherapy 500 mg daily without insulin
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Metformin monotherapy is inadequate to rapidly relieve glucotoxicity in a patient with HbA1c of 10.4%.

option_notes.option: Immediate bariatric Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Metabolic bariatric surgery is an elective option for severe obesity after glycemic stabilization and multidisciplinary review.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old African American male with newly discovered T2D presents in a somnolent, severely dehydrated state. Laboratory findings demonstrate: serum glucose 1050 mg/dL, venous pH 7.32, serum bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, serum sodium 152 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 54 mg/dL. Effective serum osmolality is calculated at 345 mOsm/kg. Urine dipstick shows trace ketones. What is the diagnosis, and what is the primary initial resuscitation priority?
options: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); vigorous isotonic fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline
Severe diabetic ketoacidosis; immediate IV insulin bolus followed by high-dose infusion
Central diabetes insipidus; intravenous desmopressin administration
Lactic acidosis secondary to metformin toxicity; emergent hemodialysis
quizzes.explanation: This patient has Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS), characterized by extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), severe hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), and altered sensorium in the absence of significant ketoacidosis (pH >7.30, bicarb >15). HHS carries a 10-30% mortality in youth. The primary resuscitation priority is urgent, aggressive expansion of the intravascular volume using isotonic fluids (0.9% saline 20 mL/kg boluses) to restore tissue perfusion before starting low-dose insulin.

option_notes.option: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); vigorous isotonic fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline
option_notes.text: Correct. Extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality >320 mOsm/kg, and mild acidosis define HHS; isotonic fluid resuscitation is priority one.

option_notes.option: Severe diabetic ketoacidosis; immediate IV insulin bolus followed by high-dose infusion
option_notes.text: Incorrect. DKA features severe acidosis (pH <7.30, bicarb <15) with high ketones; IV insulin boluses are contraindicated.

option_notes.option: Central diabetes insipidus; intravenous desmopressin administration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diabetes insipidus features dilute polyuria with normal/high sodium, not glucose >1000 mg/dL.

option_notes.option: Lactic acidosis secondary to metformin toxicity; emergent hemodialysis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Lactic acidosis presents with a profound high anion gap metabolic acidosis with low pH, not isolated hyperosmolar hyperglycemia.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old female with youth-onset T2D on metformin 2000 mg daily has a repeat HbA1c of 8.2% after 6 months. She has a BMI of 35 kg/m2. She expresses desire to improve glycemic control and lose weight without daily fingerstick insulin adjustments. Which class of medication is FDA-approved for youth aged >=10 years and addresses both glycemic control and weight reduction?
options: GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., once-weekly subcutaneous dulaglutide or once-daily liraglutide)
Sulfonylurea (e.g., glimepiride)
Thiazolidinedione (e.g., pioglitazone)
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor (e.g., acarbose)
quizzes.explanation: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (e.g., once-daily liraglutide or once-weekly dulaglutide/exenatide) are FDA-approved as add-on therapy for youth aged >=10 years with type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 receptor agonists stimulate glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon release, delay gastric emptying, and promote central satiety, leading to significant HbA1c reductions and clinically meaningful weight loss.

option_notes.option: GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., once-weekly subcutaneous dulaglutide or once-daily liraglutide)
option_notes.text: Correct. GLP-1 receptor agonists are FDA-approved in youth >=10 years to improve glycemic control and promote weight loss.

option_notes.option: Sulfonylurea (e.g., glimepiride)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sulfonylureas cause significant weight gain and hypoglycemia and accelerate beta-cell exhaustion.

option_notes.option: Thiazolidinedione (e.g., pioglitazone)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thiazolidinediones are not approved in youth and cause fluid retention and weight gain.

option_notes.option: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor (e.g., acarbose)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Acarbose has poor efficacy, frequent gastrointestinal side effects, and does not promote weight loss.

quizzes.q: Unlike children with type 1 diabetes where microvascular screening begins after 2 to 5 years, why must screening for diabetic kidney disease (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and retinopathy begin at the time of initial diagnosis in youth with type 2 diabetes?
options: Youth with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical disease for months to years prior to diagnosis, and microvascular complications progress far more rapidly
Screening tests are only valid during the first month of diabetes diagnosis
Type 2 diabetes damages renal glomeruli through immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Retinal examination is required to rule out retinitis pigmentosa
quizzes.explanation: In youth-onset type 2 diabetes, the preceding asymptomatic period of insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance often persists for years before clinical diagnosis. Studies (such as the TODAY study) have shown that up to 10-20% of youth already have microalbuminuria or early diabetic retinopathy at the time of initial diagnosis, and microvascular complications progress at an accelerated rate compared to type 1 diabetes. Therefore, immediate baseline screening is mandatory.

option_notes.option: Youth with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical disease for months to years prior to diagnosis, and microvascular complications progress far more rapidly
option_notes.text: Correct. Pre-existing subclinical hyperglycemia and aggressive complication progression mandate immediate baseline screening.

option_notes.option: Screening tests are only valid during the first month of diabetes diagnosis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Screening tests remain valid throughout life; the timing reflects clinical disease risk.

option_notes.option: Type 2 diabetes damages renal glomeruli through immune-complex glomerulonephritis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Diabetic kidney disease results from hemodynamic and metabolic microvascular injury, not immune complexes.

option_notes.option: Retinal examination is required to rule out retinitis pigmentosa
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Screening detects diabetic microvascular retinopathy, not retinitis pigmentosa.

quizzes.q: An 11-year-old boy undergoes routine universal lipid screening. Fasting lipid profile reveals: total cholesterol 284 mg/dL, triglycerides 95 mg/dL, HDL-C 48 mg/dL, and LDL-C 217 mg/dL. His father suffered a fatal myocardial infarction at age 38. Physical examination reveals nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons. After 6 months of strict dietary modification (CHILD-2 diet), his repeat fasting LDL-C remains 208 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) therapy, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, targeting LDL-C <130 mg/dL
Continue dietary modification alone without medications until age 18
Initiate fibrate therapy with fenofibrate
Perform emergency coronary artery bypass grafting
quizzes.explanation: This patient has heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HeFH), documented by severe LDL elevation (>190 mg/dL), tendon xanthomas, and a strong family history of premature CAD. NHLBI and AAP guidelines recommend initiating statin pharmacotherapy (e.g., atorvastatin 10 mg or rosuvastatin 5-10 mg daily) in children >=10 years whose LDL-C remains persistently >=190 mg/dL (or >=160 mg/dL with premature CVD family history) after lifestyle intervention. The therapeutic target is LDL-C <130 mg/dL.

option_notes.option: Initiate HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) therapy, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, targeting LDL-C <130 mg/dL
option_notes.text: Correct. Statin therapy is the guideline-directed first-line therapy for children >=10 years with persistent LDL-C >=190 mg/dL.

option_notes.option: Continue dietary modification alone without medications until age 18
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Delaying pharmacotherapy until age 18 allows extensive coronary atheroma accumulation and early cardiovascular death.

option_notes.option: Initiate fibrate therapy with fenofibrate
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Fibrates are indicated for hypertriglyceridemia, not isolated familial hypercholesterolemia.

option_notes.option: Perform emergency coronary artery bypass grafting
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Coronary bypass is an operative intervention for active severe ischemic disease, not initial medical management.

quizzes.q: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for yellow-orange papules with erythematous bases on her buttocks, elbows, and knees (eruptive xanthomas). Her blood sample drawn in the laboratory separates into a supernatant that resembles heavy cream over clear infranatant. Fasting triglycerides are 2450 mg/dL, while total cholesterol is 210 mg/dL. Genetic testing confirms biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the LPL gene. What acute medical emergency is she at highest risk for developing?
options: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis
Acute myocardial infarction
Hepatic encephalopathy
Rhabdomyolysis
quizzes.explanation: Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome (FCS) caused by LPL deficiency results in massive accumulation of circulating chylomicrons, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and triglyceride concentrations exceeding 1000-2000 mg/dL. The most dangerous acute complication of severe hypertriglyceridemia is acute necrotizing pancreatitis, triggered when pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes massive chylomicron triglycerides, generating toxic free fatty acids that cause capillary thrombosis and acinar necrosis.

option_notes.option: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis
option_notes.text: Correct. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (>1000-2000 mg/dL) precipitates acute, life-threatening pancreatitis.

option_notes.option: Acute myocardial infarction
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Myocardial infarction is a long-term risk of hypercholesterolemia (high LDL), not acute chylomicronemia in a 4-year-old.

option_notes.option: Hepatic encephalopathy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. FCS does not primarily cause acute hepatic encephalopathy.

option_notes.option: Rhabdomyolysis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Rhabdomyolysis is an adverse drug reaction or metabolic myopathy, not the hallmark complication of FCS.

quizzes.q: What is the mechanism of action of ezetimibe, an adjunctive medication used in children with refractory familial hypercholesterolemia who do not meet LDL targets on statins alone?
options: Selective inhibition of the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter in the jejunal brush border, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption
Inhibition of hepatic HMG-CoA reductase
Binding and sequestration of intestinal bile acids
Monoclonal inhibition of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9)
quizzes.explanation: Ezetimibe localizes to the brush border of the small intestine and selectively inhibits the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) sterol transporter. This inhibits the absorption of biliary and dietary cholesterol into enterocytes, reducing intestinal cholesterol delivery to the liver, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors, and lowering circulating LDL-C by an additional 15-20% when added to a statin.

option_notes.option: Selective inhibition of the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter in the jejunal brush border, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption
option_notes.text: Correct. Ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1 in enterocytes, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of hepatic HMG-CoA reductase
option_notes.text: Incorrect. HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the mechanism of statins.

option_notes.option: Binding and sequestration of intestinal bile acids
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bile acid sequestration is the mechanism of colesevelam and cholestyramine.

option_notes.option: Monoclonal inhibition of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PCSK9 monoclonal antibody inhibition is the mechanism of evolocumab and alirocumab.

quizzes.q: An 18-month-old child presents with extensive planar xanthomas in the interdigital webs of the hands, popliteal fossae, and buttocks. Fasting lipid panel reveals total cholesterol 840 mg/dL, LDL-C 780 mg/dL, and normal triglycerides. Echocardiogram reveals supravalvular aortic stenosis and aortic root thickening. Both parents have mild hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ~175 mg/dL). What is the diagnosis?
options: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH)
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III hyperlipidemia)
Niemann-Pick disease type C
Familial combined hyperlipidemia
quizzes.explanation: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) is a rare, severe condition (1:300,000) caused by biallelic LDLR (or APOB/PCSK9) mutations inherited from both heterozygous parents. Hallmark features include extreme LDL-C elevations (>400-1000 mg/dL), early planar cutaneous xanthomas in infancy/toddlerhood, and rapid development of aortic root atheroma/supravalvular aortic stenosis and fatal myocardial infarction in early childhood without aggressive treatment (such as LDL apheresis and lomitapide/evinacumab).

option_notes.option: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH)
option_notes.text: Correct. LDL-C >700 mg/dL, planar xanthomas in infancy, and aortic root stenosis confirm Homozygous FH.

option_notes.option: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III hyperlipidemia)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Type III hyperlipidemia features equal elevation of cholesterol and triglycerides (remnant removal disease), presenting in adulthood.

option_notes.option: Niemann-Pick disease type C
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Niemann-Pick type C is a lysosomal storage disease presenting with neurodegeneration and hepatosplenomegaly.

option_notes.option: Familial combined hyperlipidemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Familial combined hyperlipidemia presents with moderate elevations of both LDL and triglycerides in adults.

quizzes.q: A 13-year-old obese male with BMI at the 98th percentile has a fasting lipid profile showing: total cholesterol 195 mg/dL, triglycerides 280 mg/dL, HDL-C 32 mg/dL, and calculated LDL-C 107 mg/dL. Fasting ALT is 55 U/L. What is the most likely etiology of this lipid abnormality?
options: Obesity-associated dyslipidemia secondary to insulin resistance and increased hepatic VLDL production
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
Abetalipoproteinemia
quizzes.explanation: The most common lipid abnormality in pediatric practice is secondary dyslipidemia related to obesity and insulin resistance. The characteristic atherogenic lipid triad consists of: (1) elevated fasting triglycerides (typically 150-400 mg/dL) driven by excessive hepatic VLDL synthesis and impaired LPL clearance; (2) low HDL cholesterol (<40 mg/dL); and (3) normal or borderline LDL-C with an increased proportion of atherogenic small dense LDL particles. It is frequently accompanied by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (elevated ALT).

option_notes.option: Obesity-associated dyslipidemia secondary to insulin resistance and increased hepatic VLDL production
option_notes.text: Correct. Obesity and insulin resistance characteristically cause high triglycerides, low HDL-C, and normal/borderline LDL-C.

option_notes.option: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. LPL deficiency causes extreme hypertriglyceridemia (>1000-2000 mg/dL) with chylomicronemia, not mild TG elevation of 280 mg/dL.

option_notes.option: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Heterozygous FH features marked isolated elevation of LDL-C with normal triglycerides.

option_notes.option: Abetalipoproteinemia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Abetalipoproteinemia causes complete absence of apoB-containing lipoproteins with undetectable LDL and triglycerides.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old girl with severe anorexia nervosa has lost 18 kg over the past 8 months. Her current BMI is 14.8 kg/m2. She has been amenorrheic for 7 months. Endocrine laboratory evaluation reveals: serum LH 0.4 IU/L, FSH 1.2 IU/L, estradiol <10 pg/mL, basal growth hormone 18 ng/mL (elevated), IGF-1 92 ng/mL (severely low), total T3 45 ng/dL (low), free T4 0.8 ng/dL (low-normal), and TSH 1.4 mIU/L. What is the physiological mechanism underlying her elevated growth hormone and low IGF-1?
options: Starvation-induced hepatic growth hormone resistance secondary to downregulation of cell-surface GH receptors
A growth hormone-secreting pituitary somatotrope adenoma
Ectopic production of GHRH by retroperitoneal adipose tissue
Excessive renal tubular reabsorption of pituitary growth hormone
quizzes.explanation: In anorexia nervosa and severe under-nutrition, starvation triggers acquired peripheral growth hormone resistance. Nutrient and insulin deprivation causes marked downregulation of hepatic growth hormone receptors and post-receptor signaling pathways (JAK2/STAT5b). Consequently, hepatic synthesis of IGF-1 falls precipitously. The absence of negative feedback inhibition by circulating IGF-1 on the pituitary somatotropes leads to compensatory hypersecretion of growth hormone.

option_notes.option: Starvation-induced hepatic growth hormone resistance secondary to downregulation of cell-surface GH receptors
option_notes.text: Correct. Starvation causes hepatic GH receptor downregulation, causing profound IGF-1 deficiency and high compensatory GH.

option_notes.option: A growth hormone-secreting pituitary somatotrope adenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. A GH-secreting somatotrope adenoma (acromegaly/gigantism) produces high IGF-1 and accelerated growth, not starvation with low IGF-1.

option_notes.option: Ectopic production of GHRH by retroperitoneal adipose tissue
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adipose tissue does not secrete ectopic GHRH in anorexia nervosa.

option_notes.option: Excessive renal tubular reabsorption of pituitary growth hormone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Elevated GH is due to increased pituitary pulsatile secretion, not altered renal handling.

quizzes.q: A 17-year-old female with anorexia nervosa who has been amenorrheic for 14 months undergoes dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Her lumbar spine bone mineral density Z-score is -2.8. In addition to nutritional rehabilitation and calcium/vitamin D repletion, what pharmacological intervention has been shown in randomized controlled trials to effectively increase bone mineral density in this setting?
options: Physiological replacement with transdermal 17-beta estradiol patches combined with cyclic oral micronized progesterone
Combined oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol
Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
Subcutaneous teriparatide (PTH 1-34) monotherapy
quizzes.explanation: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that physiological transdermal 17-beta estradiol (100 mcg patches applied twice weekly) combined with cyclic oral micronized progesterone (200 mg/day for 12 days/month) significantly increases lumbar spine and femoral bone mineral density in adolescents with anorexia nervosa. In contrast, standard oral contraceptive pills (ethinyl estradiol) do not improve bone density because hepatic first-pass metabolism suppresses hepatic IGF-1 synthesis.

option_notes.option: Physiological replacement with transdermal 17-beta estradiol patches combined with cyclic oral micronized progesterone
option_notes.text: Correct. Transdermal estradiol with cyclic progesterone bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism and increases bone density in AN.

option_notes.option: Combined oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Oral contraceptive pills suppress hepatic IGF-1 production through first-pass metabolism and fail to increase bone mass in AN.

option_notes.option: Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates are not first-line in adolescents with anorexia nervosa due to long-term skeletal retention and teratogenicity concerns.

option_notes.option: Subcutaneous teriparatide (PTH 1-34) monotherapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Teriparatide is an anabolic agent approved for postmenopausal osteoporosis, not standard for adolescent anorexia nervosa.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa is found on routine screening to have total T3 42 ng/dL (reference: 85-170 ng/dL), free T4 0.9 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and TSH 1.6 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Reverse T3 is elevated. She complains of cold intolerance and has bradycardia (pulse 48 bpm). What is the appropriate clinical approach to her thyroid status?
options: Withhold thyroid hormone replacement; this represents an adaptive non-thyroidal illness syndrome that will resolve with nutritional refeeding
Initiate oral levothyroxine 50 mcg daily to restore normal metabolic rate
Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) 25 mcg daily to normalize circulating T3
Perform radioiodine uptake scan to rule out toxic adenoma
quizzes.explanation: The thyroid hormone pattern in anorexia nervosa represents non-thyroidal illness syndrome ('low T3 syndrome'), an adaptive hypometabolic state mediated by down-regulation of 5'-deiodinase (reducing T4 to T3 conversion) and upregulation of DIO3 (increasing reverse T3). This adaptation minimizes energy expenditure and tissue catabolism during severe energy deficit. Administering exogenous thyroid hormone (T4 or T3) is strictly contraindicated because it accelerates protein breakdown, induces cardiac arrhythmias, and worsens cachexia.

option_notes.option: Withhold thyroid hormone replacement; this represents an adaptive non-thyroidal illness syndrome that will resolve with nutritional refeeding
option_notes.text: Correct. Low T3 in anorexia is an adaptive conservation mechanism; exogenous thyroid hormone is harmful and contraindicated.

option_notes.option: Initiate oral levothyroxine 50 mcg daily to restore normal metabolic rate
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Levothyroxine increases basal metabolic rate and tissue catabolism in a starving patient.

option_notes.option: Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) 25 mcg daily to normalize circulating T3
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Liothyronine administration worsens cardiac strain and accelerates wasting.

option_notes.option: Perform radioiodine uptake scan to rule out toxic adenoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Scintigraphy is not indicated for non-thyroidal illness syndrome without a nodule.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy with severe generalized obesity (BMI 29 kg/m2, >99th percentile) undergoes endocrine evaluation. His linear growth velocity is 7.2 cm/year (accelerated, 85th percentile for age), and his bone age is 10.5 years. Provocative growth hormone testing with clonidine reveals a peak GH of 4.2 ng/mL (subnormal; cut-off <7-10 ng/mL). Serum IGF-1 is normal (240 ng/mL). How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Pseudo-GH deficiency secondary to obesity-induced blunted somatotrope responsiveness, with normal tissue IGF-1 action and accelerated growth
Isolated organic pituitary growth hormone deficiency requiring daily rhGH therapy
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
Growth hormone receptor insensitivity (Laron syndrome)
quizzes.explanation: Children with simple obesity characteristically demonstrate blunted stimulated growth hormone secretion on provocative testing ('pseudo-GH deficiency'). Despite low GH peaks, these children maintain normal or elevated serum IGF-1 concentrations, accelerated prepubertal linear growth velocity, and normal or mildly advanced skeletal maturation. This is mediated by hyperinsulinemia and altered neuroendocrine feedback. Daily rhGH therapy is not indicated.

option_notes.option: Pseudo-GH deficiency secondary to obesity-induced blunted somatotrope responsiveness, with normal tissue IGF-1 action and accelerated growth
option_notes.text: Correct. Pseudo-GH deficiency in obesity features blunted GH peaks but normal IGF-1 and accelerated linear growth.

option_notes.option: Isolated organic pituitary growth hormone deficiency requiring daily rhGH therapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. True GH deficiency causes profound linear growth deceleration and delayed bone age, not accelerated growth.

option_notes.option: Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma causes severe growth failure, low IGF-1, and visual field deficits.

option_notes.option: Growth hormone receptor insensitivity (Laron syndrome)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Laron syndrome features extreme short stature, elevated GH, and undetectable/low IGF-1.

quizzes.q: What is the primary mechanism by which visceral obesity and hyperinsulinemia contribute to clinical hyperandrogenism and hirsutism in adolescent girls?
options: Hyperinsulinemia directly suppresses hepatic production of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), markedly elevating the circulating free, unbound testosterone fraction
Visceral adipocytes directly synthesize testosterone from cholesterol via CYP17A1
Insulin blocks adrenal 21-hydroxylase activity
Leptin stimulates pituitary LH secretion to adult male levels
quizzes.explanation: Hyperinsulinemia resulting from obesity-induced insulin resistance acts directly on hepatocytes to suppress the gene expression and synthesis of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). Reduced circulating SHBG lowers the binding capacity of serum, resulting in a marked increase in the biologically active free, unbound testosterone fraction. Concurrently, hyperinsulinemia synergizes with LH in ovarian theca cells to augment androgen production.

option_notes.option: Hyperinsulinemia directly suppresses hepatic production of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), markedly elevating the circulating free, unbound testosterone fraction
option_notes.text: Correct. Insulin suppresses hepatic SHBG synthesis, increasing the biologically active free testosterone fraction.

option_notes.option: Visceral adipocytes directly synthesize testosterone from cholesterol via CYP17A1
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adipocytes express aromatase (converting androgens to estrogens), but do not synthesize de novo testosterone from cholesterol.

option_notes.option: Insulin blocks adrenal 21-hydroxylase activity
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Insulin does not block 21-hydroxylase; 21-hydroxylase deficiency is a genetic enzyme defect (CAH).

option_notes.option: Leptin stimulates pituitary LH secretion to adult male levels
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Leptin does not drive LH to adult male levels.

quizzes.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with intense polydipsia, drinking 6 liters of ice water daily, and waking 4 to 5 times per night to urinate. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 304 mOsm/kg, and random urine osmolality is 95 mOsm/kg. Subcutaneous desmopressin (DDAVP 1 mcg) is administered. Two hours later, repeat urine osmolality rises to 680 mOsm/kg with a sharp decline in urine output. Sellar MRI demonstrates complete absence of the normal T1 posterior pituitary bright spot and thickening of the pituitary stalk. What is the diagnosis?
options: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D / central DI)
Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R / nephrogenic DI)
Primary psychogenic polydipsia
Solute diuresis secondary to type 1 diabetes
quizzes.explanation: This patient has classic Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D; central DI): hypertonic polyuria with low baseline urine osmolality (<100 mOsm/kg) in the presence of hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/kg), followed by a >100% surge in urine osmolality (>600 mOsm/kg) after desmopressin administration. Absence of the T1 posterior pituitary bright spot and stalk thickening on MRI confirm hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal pathology (such as germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis).

option_notes.option: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D / central DI)
option_notes.text: Correct. Hypertonic polyuria, dramatic >100% response to desmopressin, and absent MRI bright spot confirm AVP-D.

option_notes.option: Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R / nephrogenic DI)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. AVP-R is completely unresponsive to desmopressin, with urine osmolality remaining <300 mOsm/kg.

option_notes.option: Primary psychogenic polydipsia
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Primary polydipsia presents with hyponatremia/low serum osmolality and concentrates urine spontaneously with fluid restriction.

option_notes.option: Solute diuresis secondary to type 1 diabetes
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Solute diuresis in T1D features heavy glucosuria and high urine specific gravity/osmolality, not dilute urine.

quizzes.q: A 12-year-old girl undergoes gross total resection of a suprasellar craniopharyngioma. On postoperative day 1, her urine output surges to 6 mL/kg/hour, urine specific gravity is 1.002, and serum sodium is 149 mEq/L. She is started on IV desmopressin. On postoperative day 4, while still receiving desmopressin, her urine output abruptly plummets, and serum sodium drops sharply to 121 mEq/L. What physiological phase of the post-hypophysectomy triphasic response has occurred?
options: Phase 2: Transient SIADH secondary to uncontrolled AVP release from degenerating hypothalamic neurons
Phase 1: Acute vasopressin deficiency due to surgical axon shock
Phase 3: Permanent neurohypophyseal fibrosis and AVP deficiency
Acute postoperative adrenal crisis
quizzes.explanation: The triphasic response occurs following pituitary stalk or hypothalamic neurosurgery. Phase 1 (days 1-2) is acute DI due to mechanical axon shock. Phase 2 (days 3-7) is transient SIADH: dying, degenerating magnocellular axons unregulatedly release their entire remaining stores of AVP into the circulation, precipitous oliguria and severe dilutional hyponatremia if desmopressin or fluid intake is not halted. Phase 3 (day 8 onward) is permanent AVP-D after all stores are exhausted.

option_notes.option: Phase 2: Transient SIADH secondary to uncontrolled AVP release from degenerating hypothalamic neurons
option_notes.text: Correct. Phase 2 represents transient SIADH from dying axon AVP leakage, causing dilutional hyponatremia.

option_notes.option: Phase 1: Acute vasopressin deficiency due to surgical axon shock
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Phase 1 is the initial transient polyuric DI phase seen on days 1-2.

option_notes.option: Phase 3: Permanent neurohypophyseal fibrosis and AVP deficiency
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Phase 3 is the permanent AVP deficiency phase occurring after day 7-8.

option_notes.option: Acute postoperative adrenal crisis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Adrenal crisis causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia with hypotension, not the expected isolated AVP release surge.

quizzes.q: A 3-month-old infant boy presents with recurrent unexplained fevers, vomiting, severe dehydration, and failure to thrive. Laboratory evaluation shows serum sodium 168 mEq/L, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and simultaneous urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. Subcutaneous desmopressin 2 mcg is administered; two hours later, urine osmolality is unchanged at 115 mOsm/kg, and baseline plasma copeptin is markedly elevated at 48 pmol/L. What is the most likely genetic diagnosis?
options: X-linked Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVPR2 mutation)
Autosomal dominant AVP deficiency (AVP-neurophysin II mutation)
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2 mutation)
Bartter syndrome type 1 (SLC12A1 mutation)
quizzes.explanation: This infant has congenital Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R; nephrogenic DI), which is X-linked recessive in >90% of cases due to loss-of-function AVPR2 mutations. Hallmark features are extreme hypernatremic dehydration with dilute urine that fails to concentrate following desmopressin, accompanied by high baseline copeptin (>21.4 pmol/L) reflecting appropriate endogenous hypothalamic AVP hypersecretion acting on a completely resistant collecting duct.

option_notes.option: X-linked Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVPR2 mutation)
option_notes.text: Correct. Complete lack of response to desmopressin with high copeptin in an infant male confirms X-linked AVPR2 deficiency.

option_notes.option: Autosomal dominant AVP deficiency (AVP-neurophysin II mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Central AVP deficiency responds briskly to desmopressin and exhibits low copeptin.

option_notes.option: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2 mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CAH causes severe hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (salt-wasting shock), not extreme hypernatremic dehydration.

option_notes.option: Bartter syndrome type 1 (SLC12A1 mutation)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bartter syndrome features hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, not isolated AVP resistance with copeptin >40.

quizzes.q: What is the paradoxical mechanism by which thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) reduce urine volume in patients with AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)?
options: Inhibition of the distal tubule NaCl cotransporter induces mild volume contraction, triggering compensatory proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water
Direct binding and activation of renal collecting duct V2 receptors
Inhibition of renal medullary aquaporin-2 degradation
Direct stimulation of hypothalamic vasopressin synthesis
quizzes.explanation: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, producing mild natriuresis and extracellular volume depletion. In response to hypovolemia, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and glomerulotubular balance markedly increase sodium and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule. This reduces the total volume of fluid delivered to the collecting ducts, reducing 24-hour urine output by 30-50% in patients with nephrogenic DI.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of the distal tubule NaCl cotransporter induces mild volume contraction, triggering compensatory proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water
option_notes.text: Correct. Thiazides induce mild volume depletion, promoting proximal fluid reabsorption and reducing distal fluid delivery.

option_notes.option: Direct binding and activation of renal collecting duct V2 receptors
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thiazides do not bind or stimulate V2 vasopressin receptors.

option_notes.option: Inhibition of renal medullary aquaporin-2 degradation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thiazides do not inhibit aquaporin-2 degradation.

option_notes.option: Direct stimulation of hypothalamic vasopressin synthesis
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thiazides act on the kidney, not hypothalamic AVP synthesis.

quizzes.q: A 7-year-old child with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and confirmed AVP deficiency is maintained on oral desmopressin 0.1 mg twice daily. The mother is instructed to administer the evening dose only after observing an episode of breakthrough urination. Why is this breakthrough period mandatory?
options: To ensure that water intoxication and life-threatening dilutional hyponatremia do not occur from chronic antidiuresis
To prevent rapid development of tachyphylaxis and drug tolerance
To avoid medication accumulation in the biliary tract
To stimulate endogenous posterior pituitary vasopressin regeneration
quizzes.explanation: Desmopressin produces potent antidiuresis. If consecutive doses are given on a rigid schedule without allowing the drug to wear off, free water intake will exceed urinary excretion, leading to progressive water retention, expansion of intravascular volume, and severe dilutional hyponatremia with brain edema and fatal seizures. Allowing a period of breakthrough polyuria prior to redosing ensures that the patient clears excess free water.

option_notes.option: To ensure that water intoxication and life-threatening dilutional hyponatremia do not occur from chronic antidiuresis
option_notes.text: Correct. Allowing breakthrough urination prevents water retention and fatal dilutional hyponatremic seizures.

option_notes.option: To prevent rapid development of tachyphylaxis and drug tolerance
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Desmopressin does not undergo significant tachyphylaxis.

option_notes.option: To avoid medication accumulation in the biliary tract
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Desmopressin is excreted renally, not via biliary accumulation.

option_notes.option: To stimulate endogenous posterior pituitary vasopressin regeneration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Desmopressin is replacement therapy; breakthrough urination does not regenerate destroyed hypothalamic neurons.

quizzes.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with tetany and generalized seizures. Serum calcium is 6.1 mg/dL, phosphate is 8.4 mg/dL, and intact PTH is 4 pg/mL (inappropriately low). His medical history is notable for recurrent, treatment-resistant oral and esophageal thrush since age 18 months, as well as pitted transverse grooves across his permanent incisors. What is the underlying genetic defect?
options: Autosomal recessive mutation in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3
Hemizygous mutation in the FOXP3 gene on chromosome Xp11.23
Heterozygous activating mutation in the CaSR gene
Autosomal dominant mutation in the MEN1 gene
quizzes.explanation: This patient meets criteria for Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1 / APECED), having chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, and dental enamel hypoplasia. APS-1 is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which disrupts thymic negative selection of autoreactive T-cell clones.

option_notes.option: Autosomal recessive mutation in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3
option_notes.text: Correct. AIRE mutations cause APS-1, presenting with candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy.

option_notes.option: Hemizygous mutation in the FOXP3 gene on chromosome Xp11.23
option_notes.text: Incorrect. FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX syndrome with infantile diarrhea, neonatal diabetes, and eczema.

option_notes.option: Heterozygous activating mutation in the CaSR gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. CaSR activating mutations cause autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, not candidiasis or enamel hypoplasia.

option_notes.option: Autosomal dominant mutation in the MEN1 gene
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MEN1 causes primary hyperparathyroidism (hypercalcemia), not hypoparathyroidism.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old girl with established type 1 diabetes presents with progressive fatigue, postural dizziness, weight loss, and darkening of her skin across her palmar creases and gums. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, TSH 18.4 mIU/L, free T4 0.6 ng/dL, and morning baseline cortisol 2.2 mcg/dL with plasma ACTH 850 pg/mL. Thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO) and 21-hydroxylase antibodies are strongly positive. What autoimmune syndrome is present?
options: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2 / Schmidt syndrome)
Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APECED)
McCune-Albright syndrome
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1
quizzes.explanation: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2 / Schmidt syndrome) is characterized by the mandatory presence of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; elevated ACTH, low cortisol, hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation) in combination with autoimmune thyroid disease (elevated TSH, low FT4) and/or type 1 diabetes. Chronic candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism are absent, distinguishing it from APS-1.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2 / Schmidt syndrome)
option_notes.text: Correct. The triad of primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune thyroiditis, and type 1 diabetes defines APS-2.

option_notes.option: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APECED)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. APS-1 features chronic candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy in early childhood.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome
option_notes.text: Incorrect. McCune-Albright is a mosaic GNAS disorder with fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty.

option_notes.option: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MEN1 features parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

quizzes.q: A 3-week-old male infant presents with failure to thrive, severe exfoliative eczematous dermatitis, intractable voluminous watery diarrhea, and a random blood glucose of 480 mg/dL with glucosuria. Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells. What is the diagnosis and definitive curative treatment?
options: IPEX syndrome; allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
APS-1; high-dose oral fluconazole and calcium carbonate
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); enzyme replacement therapy with pegademase
Cystic fibrosis; pancreatic enzyme replacement
quizzes.explanation: IPEX (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked) syndrome is caused by mutations in FOXP3 on chromosome Xp11.23, leading to absence or functional failure of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells. Male infants present in the first weeks of life with the lethal triad of intractable autoimmune enteropathy (secretory diarrhea), neonatal type 1 diabetes, and severe dermatitis/eczema. Without allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), IPEX is fatal in early childhood.

option_notes.option: IPEX syndrome; allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
option_notes.text: Correct. FOXP3 deficiency causing neonatal diabetes, enteropathy, and eczema is IPEX syndrome, cured by HSCT.

option_notes.option: APS-1; high-dose oral fluconazole and calcium carbonate
option_notes.text: Incorrect. APS-1 presents later in childhood with candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism, not neonatal diabetes and secretory diarrhea.

option_notes.option: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); enzyme replacement therapy with pegademase
option_notes.text: Incorrect. SCID causes absent T/B cells with opportunistic infections, not the specific triad of neonatal T1D, enteropathy, and eczema.

option_notes.option: Cystic fibrosis; pancreatic enzyme replacement
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis causes malabsorption, not neonatal autoimmune diabetes with absent Tregs.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl with confirmed Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) has hypoparathyroidism controlled on calcitriol. She is being monitored for development of additional autoimmune endocrinopathies. What is the most common subsequent endocrine component that typically develops between ages 10 and 15 years?
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)
Central diabetes insipidus
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Medullary thyroid carcinoma
quizzes.explanation: In APS-1, primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) is the third cardinal component of the diagnostic triad, typically developing between 10 and 15 years of age (following candidiasis in infancy and hypoparathyroidism in early childhood). Annual surveillance with plasma renin activity, morning ACTH, and electrolytes, or testing for 21-hydroxylase antibodies, is mandatory to detect subclinical adrenal insufficiency before fatal crisis occurs.

option_notes.option: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)
option_notes.text: Correct. Addison disease is the third cardinal feature of APS-1, typically developing in late childhood/adolescence.

option_notes.option: Central diabetes insipidus
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Central DI is not a component of APS-1.

option_notes.option: Primary hyperparathyroidism
option_notes.text: Incorrect. APS-1 causes autoimmune hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia), not hyperparathyroidism.

option_notes.option: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is part of MEN2, not APS-1.

quizzes.q: Why must oral hydrocortisone always be initiated prior to or concurrently with levothyroxine in a patient diagnosed with concurrent Addison disease and autoimmune hypothyroidism?
options: Levothyroxine accelerates hepatic clearance and metabolic turnover of cortisol, which will precipitate acute adrenal crisis in a cortisol-deficient patient
Hydrocortisone prevents thyroid hormone binding to plasma albumin
Levothyroxine causes severe hyperkalemia if given alone
Hydrocortisone inhibits renal excretion of levothyroxine
quizzes.explanation: Thyroid hormone stimulates the hepatic expression of corticosteroid-metabolizing enzymes (such as 11-beta-HSD and 5-alpha/beta-reductases), markedly accelerating the clearance and degradation of endogenous cortisol. In a patient with underlying, untreated adrenal insufficiency, administering levothyroxine alone rapidly depletes residual circulating cortisol, precipitating an acute, life-threatening adrenal crisis with shock and vascular collapse.

option_notes.option: Levothyroxine accelerates hepatic clearance and metabolic turnover of cortisol, which will precipitate acute adrenal crisis in a cortisol-deficient patient
option_notes.text: Correct. Levothyroxine accelerates hepatic cortisol clearance, which triggers acute adrenal crisis if cortisol is not replaced first.

option_notes.option: Hydrocortisone prevents thyroid hormone binding to plasma albumin
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hydrocortisone does not alter thyroid hormone binding to albumin.

option_notes.option: Levothyroxine causes severe hyperkalemia if given alone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Levothyroxine does not directly cause hyperkalemia; adrenal insufficiency causes hyperkalemia.

option_notes.option: Hydrocortisone inhibits renal excretion of levothyroxine
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Hydrocortisone does not inhibit renal elimination of thyroid hormone.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old boy whose mother has MEN1 is brought for routine screening. Serum calcium is elevated at 10.8 mg/dL (reference: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), ionized calcium is 1.42 mmol/L, and intact PTH is 95 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). 24-hour urine calcium is 340 mg (elevated). Neck ultrasound reveals four enlarged, hypoechoic parathyroid glands. What is the most appropriate surgical management for primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN1?
options: Subtotal parathyroidectomy (resecting 3.5 glands) or total parathyroidectomy with heterotopic forearm autotransplantation
Resection of a single parathyroid adenoma alone
Conservative observation with oral cinacalcet until age 25
Total thyroidectomy without parathyroid exploration
quizzes.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN1 is characterized by asymmetric multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia involving all four glands, rather than a solitary adenoma. Resection of a single enlarged gland results in virtually 100% recurrence. Consensus guidelines recommend subtotal parathyroidectomy (resection of 3.5 glands with marking of the remnant) or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation of parathyroid tissue into the forearm musculature to treat hypercalcemia while minimizing permanent hypoparathyroidism.

option_notes.option: Subtotal parathyroidectomy (resecting 3.5 glands) or total parathyroidectomy with heterotopic forearm autotransplantation
option_notes.text: Correct. Subtotal parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation treats multiglandular MEN1 disease.

option_notes.option: Resection of a single parathyroid adenoma alone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Resecting a single gland leads to rapid recurrence because all remaining glands harbor the germline MEN1 mutation.

option_notes.option: Conservative observation with oral cinacalcet until age 25
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive therapy to prevent nephrolithiasis and bone mineral loss in young patients.

option_notes.option: Total thyroidectomy without parathyroid exploration
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Thyroidectomy has no therapeutic effect on parathyroid hyperplasia in MEN1.

quizzes.q: A 15-year-old girl with a documented germline RET codon 634 mutation (MEN2A) is scheduled to undergo total thyroidectomy for an elevated basal calcitonin. Before proceeding to the operating room, which diagnostic evaluation is mandatory to prevent an intraoperative mortality?
options: Measurement of plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines to rule out pheochromocytoma
Evaluation of serum gastrin and chromogranin A
Brain MRI to rule out a prolactinoma
Technetium-99m sestamibi parathyroid scan
quizzes.explanation: In patients with MEN2A or MEN2B, pheochromocytoma occurs in up to 50% of cases. It is a cardinal rule of endocrine surgery that pheochromocytoma must ALWAYS be excluded (using plasma or urinary free fractionated metanephrines) or surgically resected prior to any planned thyroid or neck surgery. Anesthesia or intraoperative manipulation in a patient with an occult pheochromocytoma can trigger a massive catecholamine surge, fatal hypertensive crisis, and malignant arrhythmia.

option_notes.option: Measurement of plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines to rule out pheochromocytoma
option_notes.text: Correct. Screening for pheochromocytoma with metanephrines is mandatory before thyroidectomy to prevent intraoperative death.

option_notes.option: Evaluation of serum gastrin and chromogranin A
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Gastrinomas are part of MEN1, not MEN2.

option_notes.option: Brain MRI to rule out a prolactinoma
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Pituitary adenomas occur in MEN1, not MEN2.

option_notes.option: Technetium-99m sestamibi parathyroid scan
option_notes.text: Incorrect. While hyperparathyroidism occurs in MEN2A, unrecognized pheochromocytoma poses the acute life-threatening operative risk.

quizzes.q: A 2-month-old infant is evaluated for chronic severe constipation, abdominal distension, and poor weight gain. Physical examination reveals prominent fleshy bumps along the mucosal margins of the tongue and inner lips, thickened eyelids with everted margins, and long, slender limbs. Genetic testing reveals a de novo heterozygous RET M918T mutation in exon 16. What is the diagnosis and the most urgent surgical recommendation?
options: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B); prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first months of life
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1); subtotal pancreatectomy
Neurofibromatosis Type 1; optic pathway glioma resection
Cowden syndrome; prophylactic bilateral mastectomy
quizzes.explanation: This infant has classic Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B), characterized by mucosal neuromas of the tongue/lips, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (causing chronic megacolon/constipation), marfanoid habitus, and the pathognomonic RET M918T mutation. Medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN2B develops in early infancy and metastasizes aggressively. ATA guidelines recommend prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life, preferably in the first months of life.

option_notes.option: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B); prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first months of life
option_notes.text: Correct. RET M918T confirms MEN2B; prophylactic total thyroidectomy in early infancy is life-saving.

option_notes.option: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1); subtotal pancreatectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Pancreatectomy is not indicated for MEN2B, which affects C-cells, adrenal medulla, and autonomic nerves.

option_notes.option: Neurofibromatosis Type 1; optic pathway glioma resection
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NF1 does not feature mucosal neuromas of the tongue or the RET M918T mutation.

option_notes.option: Cowden syndrome; prophylactic bilateral mastectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Cowden syndrome is caused by PTEN mutations and features hamartomas, not infant MTC in MEN2B.

quizzes.q: A 16-year-old male presents with extreme tall stature (height 204 cm, >99.9th percentile, +4.2 SD), coarse facial features, prognathism, and massive hands and feet. Sellar MRI reveals a 3.2-cm invasive pituitary macroadenoma invading both cavernous sinuses. Serum IGF-1 is markedly elevated. Genetic analysis reveals a heterozygous germline mutation in the AIP gene. Which family condition is this patient suffering from?
options: Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) with pituitary gigantism
Carney complex due to PRKAR1A mutation
McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A
quizzes.explanation: Inactivating germline mutations in AIP (aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein) account for ~15-20% of Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) kindreds. AIP-associated pituitary neuroendocrine tumors characteristically manifest in children and adolescents as aggressive, macroadenomatous GH-secreting tumors (somatotropinomas) that cause severe pituitary gigantism, invade parasellar structures, and respond poorly to somatostatin analog medical therapy.

option_notes.option: Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) with pituitary gigantism
option_notes.text: Correct. AIP mutation presenting with young-onset aggressive somatotropinoma and gigantism is classic FIPA.

option_notes.option: Carney complex due to PRKAR1A mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Carney complex is caused by PRKAR1A mutations and features spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, and PPNAD.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by somatic mosaic GNAS mutations, not germline AIP mutations.

option_notes.option: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MEN2A causes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism, not pituitary macroadenomas.

quizzes.q: A 14-month-old female infant is evaluated for rapid, dramatic linear overgrowth. Her height velocity has exceeded 20 cm/year, and her height is +5.5 SD above the mean. Laboratory testing demonstrates elevated serum growth hormone, unsuppressed GH on oral glucose testing, and high serum prolactin. Pituitary MRI demonstrates diffuse pituitary enlargement with macroadenoma. Chromosomal microarray reveals a microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3. What is the diagnosis?
options: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG syndrome) involving GPR101 duplication
Sotos syndrome due to NSD1 mutation
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to 11p15 imprinting defect
Marfan syndrome due to FBN1 mutation
quizzes.explanation: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG) syndrome is caused by germline or somatic mosaic microduplications on chromosome Xq26.3 encompassing the GPR101 gene. Affected children present in early infancy (<12-24 months of age) with the earliest onset and most severe form of pituitary gigantism known, characterized by marked hypersecretion of both growth hormone and prolactin due to diffuse pituitary hyperplasia or mixed somato-lactotrope macroadenomas.

option_notes.option: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG syndrome) involving GPR101 duplication
option_notes.text: Correct. Microduplication of Xq26.3 containing GPR101 causes X-LAG syndrome with severe infantile gigantism.

option_notes.option: Sotos syndrome due to NSD1 mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Sotos syndrome is an overgrowth disorder with macrocephaly and distinctive facies, without high GH/prolactin or sellar mass.

option_notes.option: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to 11p15 imprinting defect
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Beckwith-Wiedemann features macrosomia, omphalocele, and hemihypertrophy, not pituitary GH-secreting adenomas.

option_notes.option: Marfan syndrome due to FBN1 mutation
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature with arachnodactyly and aortic root dilation, with normal GH and normal sella.

quizzes.q: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for an acute episode of painless vaginal bleeding. Physical examination reveals unilateral Tanner stage 3 breast development, no pubic hair, and a large, jagged light-brown macule on the right buttock with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders that terminates abruptly at the sacral midline. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a solitary 4-cm cystic lesion in the right ovary with an endometrial stripe; the left ovary is normal. Serum estradiol is 165 pg/mL, and baseline and stimulated LH are <0.1 IU/L. What is the diagnosis?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Granulosa cell ovarian tumor
Idiopathic central precocious puberty
quizzes.explanation: This patient exhibits classic features of McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS): peripheral precocious puberty (recurrent autonomous estrogen-secreting ovarian cysts with vaginal bleeding, suppressed LH), paired with a pathognomonic large café-au-lait macule displaying jagged 'coast of Maine' borders that respects the midline. MAS is caused by a somatic activating GNAS mutation.

option_notes.option: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS)
option_notes.text: Correct. Autonomous unilateral ovarian cyst, suppressed LH, and jagged midline-respecting macule establish McCune-Albright syndrome.

option_notes.option: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
option_notes.text: Incorrect. NF1 features smooth-bordered 'coast of California' macules and axillary freckling, not autonomous ovarian cysts.

option_notes.option: Granulosa cell ovarian tumor
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumors present with precocious puberty but do not have jagged café-au-lait macules or mosaic GNAS mutations.

option_notes.option: Idiopathic central precocious puberty
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Central precocity features bilateral ovarian follicular activity and elevated, pubertal stimulated LH levels.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old girl with mosaic activating GNAS mutation and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia presents with chronic bone pain and lower-extremity fatigue. Plain radiographs reveal expansile ground-glass lesions involving the skull, pelvis, and both femurs. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 9.2 mg/dL, serum phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (low; reference: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 890 U/L, and TmP/GFR 1.6 mg/dL (severely reduced). Serum intact FGF23 is elevated at 95 pg/mL. What is the mechanism of her hypophosphatemia?
options: Direct oversecretion of intact FGF23 by dysplastic osteogenic cells within the fibrous dysplasia bone lesions
Parathyroid adenoma secreting excess parathyroid hormone
Proximal renal tubular necrosis caused by hypercalciuria
Defective intestinal phosphate absorption
quizzes.explanation: In patients with extensive polyostotic fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome, the dysplastic osteogenic stromal cells oversecrete intact fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Circulating FGF23 acts on the renal proximal tubule to downregulate sodium-phosphate cotransporters, producing profound renal phosphate wasting, severe hypophosphatemia, and secondary osteomalacia that exacerbates bone pain and fractures.

option_notes.option: Direct oversecretion of intact FGF23 by dysplastic osteogenic cells within the fibrous dysplasia bone lesions
option_notes.text: Correct. Dysplastic fibrous bone tissue oversecretes intact FGF23, driving renal phosphate wasting and osteomalacia.

option_notes.option: Parathyroid adenoma secreting excess parathyroid hormone
option_notes.text: Incorrect. PTH is typically normal; hypophosphatemia is driven by FGF23, not hyperparathyroidism.

option_notes.option: Proximal renal tubular necrosis caused by hypercalciuria
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Tubular necrosis is not the mechanism; the defect is specific hormonal down-regulation of NaPi cotransporters.

option_notes.option: Defective intestinal phosphate absorption
option_notes.text: Incorrect. FGF23 suppresses renal phosphate reabsorption, which is the primary driver of hypophosphatemia.

quizzes.q: A 5-year-old girl with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and coast-of-Maine café-au-lait pigmentation suffers from recurrent autonomous ovarian cysts and multiple episodes of vaginal bleeding. Treatment with depot leuprolide (GnRH agonist) for 6 months produced no reduction in bleeding or cyst frequency. What is the recommended pharmacological therapy to prevent recurrent estrogenic bleeding?
options: Oral letrozole (third-generation aromatase inhibitor) 2.5 mg daily
Doubling the dose of depot leuprolide
Intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
Bilateral total oophorectomy
quizzes.explanation: In young girls with McCune-Albright syndrome, precocious puberty is peripheral (gonadotropin-independent), driven by autonomous Gs-alpha activation in ovarian follicular cells. GnRH agonists are ineffective because pituitary gonadotropins are already suppressed. First-line medical therapy is oral letrozole (2.5 mg daily), a potent aromatase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of androgens to estrogens in the cysts, halting vaginal bleeding and slowing skeletal maturation.

option_notes.option: Oral letrozole (third-generation aromatase inhibitor) 2.5 mg daily
option_notes.text: Correct. Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) block autonomous ovarian estrogen synthesis and are first-line for MAS precocity.

option_notes.option: Doubling the dose of depot leuprolide
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Increasing GnRH agonists is completely futile because the ovaries are functioning independently of LH/FSH.

option_notes.option: Intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates treat fibrous dysplasia bone pain, but have no effect on ovarian steroidogenesis.

option_notes.option: Bilateral total oophorectomy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Oophorectomy is mutilating and destroys future fertility; cysts fluctuate and respond to medical aromatase inhibition.

quizzes.q: A 14-year-old male with mosaic GNAS activation and craniofacial fibrous dysplasia is noted to have accelerating head circumference, coarse facial features, and expanding jaw lesions. Laboratory testing reveals elevated IGF-1 and unsuppressed growth hormone on oral glucose loading. Why is growth hormone excess particularly dangerous in children with mosaic GNAS activation and fibrous dysplasia?
options: Excess GH and IGF-1 directly stimulate rapid expansion of craniofacial fibrous dysplasia lesions, causing visual loss and hearing impairment
GH excess leads to spontaneous malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia into osteosarcoma in >80% of patients
GH excess causes acute rupture of hepatic adenomas
GH excess triggers immediate renal failure
quizzes.explanation: Growth hormone excess occurs in 20-30% of MAS patients due to somatotrope hyperplasia. GH and IGF-1 are potent mitogenic and osteotropic factors that accelerate the rapid growth and expansion of fibrous dysplasia lesions, particularly in the craniofacial bones. This expansile growth can compress the optic canals and auditory canals, leading to permanent optic nerve compression, irreversible blindness, and severe deafness. Aggressive medical management of GH excess is imperative.

option_notes.option: Excess GH and IGF-1 directly stimulate rapid expansion of craniofacial fibrous dysplasia lesions, causing visual loss and hearing impairment
option_notes.text: Correct. GH/IGF-1 stimulates craniofacial FD expansion, causing optic nerve compression and blindness.

option_notes.option: GH excess leads to spontaneous malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia into osteosarcoma in >80% of patients
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Malignant transformation is rare (<1%) and not primarily driven by GH excess.

option_notes.option: GH excess causes acute rupture of hepatic adenomas
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MAS is not associated with hepatic adenoma rupture.

option_notes.option: GH excess triggers immediate renal failure
option_notes.text: Incorrect. GH excess does not cause immediate acute renal failure.

quizzes.q: A pregnant woman who was diagnosed in childhood with mosaic GNAS activating syndrome (MAS) asks her genetic counselor about the risk of transmitting the condition to her unborn child. What is the accurate recurrence risk?
options: Essentially 0% risk of transmission, because McCune-Albright syndrome is caused exclusively by somatic postzygotic mutations
50% risk, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
25% risk, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
100% risk if the fetus is female
quizzes.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused exclusively by postzygotic somatic mosaic mutations in GNAS that arise spontaneously during embryonic development. Because the mutation is postzygotic and somatic, it is not present in the germline of all cells, and germline transmission to offspring has never been documented. The recurrence risk for the offspring of an affected patient is virtually zero.

option_notes.option: Essentially 0% risk of transmission, because McCune-Albright syndrome is caused exclusively by somatic postzygotic mutations
option_notes.text: Correct. MAS is caused exclusively by somatic postzygotic mutations and cannot be transmitted to offspring (risk ~0%).

option_notes.option: 50% risk, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MAS is not inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

option_notes.option: 25% risk, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
option_notes.text: Incorrect. MAS is not an autosomal recessive disorder.

option_notes.option: 100% risk if the fetus is female
option_notes.text: Incorrect. There is no sex-linked transmission of postzygotic somatic mutations.

quizzes.q: A 10-year-old boy who completed treatment for a standard-risk medulloblastoma 3 years ago (including surgical resection and 23.4 Gy craniospinal irradiation with posterior fossa boost) is evaluated for severe growth deceleration. His height velocity has dropped from the 50th percentile to 1.8 cm/year (<3rd percentile). He is in complete oncologic remission. Bone age is delayed by 2.5 years. Two provocative growth hormone stimulation tests show peak GH levels of 2.1 ng/mL and 1.8 ng/mL, with low serum IGF-1. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy at 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week with regular clinical and oncologic monitoring
Withhold growth hormone therapy permanently due to an unacceptably high risk of medulloblastoma recurrence
Initiate high-dose depot testosterone enanthate 200 mg monthly to promote linear growth
Perform immediate emergent craniotomy and repeat posterior fossa resection
quizzes.explanation: Growth hormone deficiency is the most common and earliest endocrine complication of cranial irradiation (occurring at doses >=18 Gy). Landmark data from the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS) have conclusively proven that rhGH replacement does NOT increase the risk of primary central nervous system tumor recurrence or leukemia relapse in disease-free survivors. Because he has been in remission for >1 year, initiating rhGH therapy is standard care to restore linear growth.

option_notes.option: Initiate recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy at 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week with regular clinical and oncologic monitoring
option_notes.text: Correct. rhGH replacement is safe, does not increase medulloblastoma recurrence, and restores normal growth velocity.

option_notes.option: Withhold growth hormone therapy permanently due to an unacceptably high risk of medulloblastoma recurrence
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Permanently withholding rhGH based on unproven fears of tumor recurrence severely compromises adult height and metabolic health.

option_notes.option: Initiate high-dose depot testosterone enanthate 200 mg monthly to promote linear growth
option_notes.text: Incorrect. High-dose testosterone causes rapid epiphyseal fusion and arrests remaining growth potential.

option_notes.option: Perform immediate emergent craniotomy and repeat posterior fossa resection
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Neurosurgical re-exploration is completely inappropriate in an asymptomatic patient in complete remission.

quizzes.q: A 6-year-old girl who received 24 Gy cranial irradiation for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) 2 years ago presents with rapid linear growth acceleration and bilateral breast enlargement (Tanner stage 3). Bone age is advanced by 2 years. A GnRH stimulation test reveals a peak stimulated LH of 8.4 IU/L. Cranial MRI shows no leukemic relapse or mass. What is the mechanism of precocious puberty in this patient?
options: Radiation-induced damage to cortical and hypothalamic inhibitory pathways, disinhibiting the GnRH pulse generator
Ectopic LH secretion by residual leukemic blast cells
Primary ovarian granulosa cell tumor induced by chemotherapy
Peripheral aromatization of adrenal androgens
quizzes.explanation: Low-to-moderate dose cranial irradiation (18-24 Gy), particularly in girls treated at a young age (<8 years), frequently causes central precocious puberty. Radiation damages the higher cortical and hypothalamic neural pathways that normally exert tonic inhibitory restraint over the GnRH pulse generator, resulting in premature disinhibition of GnRH pulsatility, true central precocious puberty, accelerated bone age, and compromised adult height.

option_notes.option: Radiation-induced damage to cortical and hypothalamic inhibitory pathways, disinhibiting the GnRH pulse generator
option_notes.text: Correct. Low-dose cranial radiation disrupts inhibitory neural inputs, triggering early central GnRH release.

option_notes.option: Ectopic LH secretion by residual leukemic blast cells
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Leukemic blasts do not secrete bioactive LH.

option_notes.option: Primary ovarian granulosa cell tumor induced by chemotherapy
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumors cause peripheral precocity with suppressed (not pubertal) stimulated LH levels.

option_notes.option: Peripheral aromatization of adrenal androgens
option_notes.text: Incorrect. Elevated peak LH >5 IU/L on GnRH testing confirms central gonadotropin-dependent precocity, not peripheral aromatization.

quizzes.q: A 17-year-old male survivor of adolescent Hodgkin lymphoma who received cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and procarbazine (cumulative Cyclophosphamide Equivalent Dose [CED] 9500 mg/m2) presents for late-effects evaluation. Physical examination reveals normal virilization (Tanner stage 5 pubic hair, adult phallus), but bilateral soft, small testes measuring 6 mL each. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum testosterone 540 ng/dL (normal male), LH 4.8 IU/L (normal), and FSH 32 IU/L (markedly elevated). Semen analysis confirms azoospermia. How should these findings be explained?
options: Selective alkylator-induced germ cell destruction (azoospermia with high FSH) with spared, functioning Leydig cells (normal testosterone and LH)
Secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to hypothalamic radiation damage
Complete primary hypogonadism requiring immediate testosterone replacement therapy
Retrograde ejaculation caused by vincristine autonomic neuropathy
